# PREFACE.

Soon after I was appointed Professor of <term>Sanskrit</term> and <term>Comparative Philology<note>The study of how different languages evolved from common ancestors by comparing their structures and words.</note></term> at the Presidency College in Madras, and in that capacity took charge of the office of the Curator of the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library, the late Mr. G. H. Stuart, who was then the Director of Public Instruction, asked me to find out if in the Manuscripts Library in my charge there was any work of value capable of throwing new light on the history of Hindu mathematics, and to publish it, if found, with an English translation and with such notes as were necessary for the elucidation of its contents. 

Accordingly the mathematical manuscripts in the Library were examined with this object in view; and the examination revealed the existence of three incomplete manuscripts of <term>Mahāvīrācārya’s<note>A prominent 9th-century Jain mathematician who lived in what is now southern India.</note></term> *<term>Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha<note>original: "Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha," which translates to "The Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics."</note></term>*. A cursory perusal of these manuscripts made the value of this work evident in relation to the history of Hindu Mathematics. The late Mr. G. H. Stuart’s interest in working out this history was so great that, when the existence of the manuscripts and the historical value of the work were brought to his notice, he at once urged me to try to procure other manuscripts and to do all else that was necessary for its proper publication. He gave me much advice and encouragement in the early stages of my endeavour to publish it; and I can well guess how it would have gladdened his heart to see the work published in the form he <unclear>desired.</unclear> It has been to me a source of

<summary>The editor explains how he was commissioned by the Director of Public Instruction in Madras to find and translate important historical mathematical texts, leading to the discovery of Mahāvīrācārya’s 9th-century treatise.</summary>
<keywords>Presidency College Madras, Government Oriental Manuscripts Library, G. H. Stuart, Mahāvīrācārya, Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha, Hindu mathematics, Sanskrit philology</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor's preface from page vii. The author is reflecting on the death of Mr. G. H. Stuart, who originally commissioned the project, and is now beginning a detailed description of the various manuscripts (designated P, K, and M) used to reconstruct the text.</meta>

<page-num>viii</page-num>

### COMPENDIUM OF THE ESSENCE OF MATHEMATICS.
### (GAṆITASĀRASAṄGRAHA)

...very deep regret that it did not please Providence to allow him to live long enough to enable me to improve the quality of this publication through his ongoing guidance and advice; my only comfort now is that I have been able to complete the work which he, with the joy of a scholar, set before me as a duty.

Of the three manuscripts found in the library, one is written on paper in the <term>Grantha script<note>A South Indian script used historically to write Sanskrit, particularly in Tamil-speaking regions.</note></term>, and contains the first five chapters of the work along with a continuous commentary in <term>Sanskrit</term>; this has been labeled here with the letter **P**. The remaining two are palm-leaf manuscripts in <term>Kannada<note>Referred to in the text as "Kanarese," the language and script of the state of Karnataka.</note></term> characters. One of them, like **P**, contains the first five chapters, while the other contains the seventh chapter, which focuses on the geometrical measurement of areas. In both of these manuscripts, one finds—in addition to the original <term>Sanskrit</term> text—a brief explanation in the <term>Kannada</term> language of the numbers and figures used in the various example problems, as well as the answers to those problems. Because these two manuscripts share similar characteristics and their contents do not overlap, it was decided to treat them as a single source and label them with the letter **K**. 

Another manuscript, labeled **M**, belongs to the Government Oriental Library at Mysore and was borrowed from Mr. A. Mahadeva Sastri, the head of that institution. This manuscript is a paper transcription in <term>Kannada</term> script of an original palm-leaf manuscript that belonged to a <term>Jain<note>original: "Jaina." A follower of Jainism, an ancient Indian religion that emphasizes non-violence and has a rich history of mathematical scholarship.</note></term> scholar. It contains the entire work, including a short commentary in the <term>Kannada</term> language by a man named Vallabha, who claims to have also written a <term>Telugu<note>A Dravidian language spoken primarily in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.</note></term> commentary on the same work.

<summary>The editor describes the three primary manuscript sources (P, K, and M) used to compile the text, noting their physical materials, scripts, and geographical origins.</summary>
<keywords>manuscripts, Grantha script, Kannada script, Sanskrit, Jain mathematics, Vallabha, Mahadeva Sastri, geometry</keywords>

# PREFACE.

A Dravidian language spoken predominantly in the state of Karnataka, India.</note></term> commentary; and my thanks are specially due to Mr. A. Mahadeva Sastri for his leaving it sufficiently long at my disposal. A fifth manuscript, denoted by **B**, is a transcription on paper in <term>Kannada</term> characters of a palm-leaf manuscript found in a <term>Jaina<note>Followers of Jainism, an ancient Indian religion. This work was written by a Jain mathematician.</note></term> monastery at Mudbidri in South Canara, and was obtained through the kind effort of Mr. R. Krishnamacharyar, <term>M.A.<note>Master of Arts.</note></term>, the Sub-assistant Inspector of Sanskrit Schools in Madras, and Mr. U. B. Venkataramanaiya of Mudbidri. This manuscript also contains the whole work, and gives, like **K**, in <term>Kannada</term> a brief statement of the problems and their answers. The endeavour to secure more manuscripts having proved fruitless, the work has had to be brought out with the aid of these five manuscripts; and owing to the technical character of the work and its elliptical and often riddle-like language and the inaccuracy of the manuscripts, the labour involved in bringing it out with the translation and the requisite notes has been heavy and trying. There is, however, the satisfaction that all this labour has been bestowed on a worthy work of considerable historical value.

It is a fortunate circumstance about the *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics* <note>original: *Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha*</note> that the time when its author *Mahāvīrācārya* <note>The Great Hero Teacher</note> lived may be made out with fair accuracy. In the very first chapter of the work, we have, immediately after the two introductory stanzas of salutation to the *Jina Mahāvīra* <note>The 24th Tirthankara of Jainism, whom the author invokes for success.</note>, six stanzas describing the greatness of a king, whose name is said to have been *Cakrikā-bhañjana* <note>The breaker of the (enemy's) wheel or circle.</note>, and who appears to have been commonly known by the title of *Amōghavarṣa Nṛpatuṅga*; and in the last of these

six stanzas there is a benediction wishing progressive prosperity to the rule of this king. The results of modern Indian epigraphical <note>The study of ancient inscriptions.</note> research show that this king Amōghavarṣa Nṛpatuṅga reigned from A.D. 814 or 815 to A.D. 877 or 878.* Since it appears probable that the author of the *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics* <note>original: *Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha*</note> was in some way attached to the court of this Rāṣṭrakūṭa <note>A powerful royal dynasty that ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent between the 6th and 10th centuries.</note> king Amōghavarṣa Nṛpatuṅga, we may consider the work to belong to the middle of the ninth century of the Christian era. It is now generally accepted that, among well-known early Indian mathematicians, Āryabhaṭa lived in the fifth, Varāhamihira in the sixth, Brahmagupta in the seventh, and Bhāskarācārya in the twelfth century of the Christian era; and chronologically, therefore, Mahāvīrācārya comes between Brahmagupta and Bhāskarācārya. This in itself is a point of historical noteworthiness; and the further fact that the author of the *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics* belonged to the Kannada-speaking <note>original: "Kanarese"</note> portion of South India in his days and was a <term>Jaina<note>A follower of Jainism, one of the world's oldest religions, which emphasizes non-violence and asceticism.</note></term> in religion is calculated to give an additional importance to the historical value of his work. Like the other mathematicians mentioned above, Mahāvīrācārya was not primarily an astronomer, although he knew well and has himself remarked about the usefulness of mathematics for the study of astronomy. The study of mathematics seems to have been popular among Jaina scholars; it forms, in fact, one of their four <term>anuyōgas<note>original: "anuyōgas." Disciplines or auxiliary sciences used in Jainism to categorize religious and secular knowledge.</note></term> or auxiliary sciences indirectly serviceable for the attainment of the salvation of soul-liberation known as <term>moksa<note>original: "moksa." The ultimate goal in many Indian religions: liberation from the cycle of birth and death.</note></term>.

### PREFACE.

Brahmagupta <note>A prominent 7th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer who was the first to give rules to compute with zero.</note> is calculated to lead to the conclusion that, in all probability, Mahāvīrācārya was familiar with the work of Brahmagupta and endeavoured to improve upon it to the extent to which the scope of his *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics* <note>original: *Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha*</note> permitted such improvement. Mahāvīrācārya's classification of arithmetical operations is simpler, his rules are fuller and he gives a large number of examples for illustration and exercise. Pṛthūdakasvāmin, the well-known commentator on *The Correctly Established Doctrine of Brahma* <note>original: *Brahmasphuṭa-siddhānta*</note>, could not have been chronologically far removed from Mahāvīrācārya, and the similarity of some of the examples given by the former with some of those of the latter naturally arrests attention. In any case it cannot be wrong to believe, that, at the time, when Mahāvīrācārya wrote his *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics* <note>original: *Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha*</note>, Brahmagupta must have been widely recognized as a writer of authority in the field of Indian <note>original: "Hindu"</note> astronomy and mathematics. Whether Bhāskarācārya <note>Often called Bhāskara II, he was a 12th-century mathematician who headed the astronomical observatory at Ujjain.</note> was at all acquainted with the *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics* <note>original: *Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha*</note> of Mahāvīrācārya, it is not quite easy to say. Since neither Bhāskarācārya nor any of his known commentators seem to quote from him or mention him by name, the natural conclusion appears to be that Bhāskarācārya's *Crest-Jewel of Doctrines* <note>original: *Siddhānta-śirōmaṇi*</note>, including his *The Beautiful One* <note>original: *Līlāvatī*; a famous treatise on arithmetic named after a woman, possibly his daughter.</note> and *Algebra* <note>original: *Bījagaṇita*; literally "analysis of seeds," referring to the methods used to find unknown quantities.</note>, was intended to be an improvement in the main upon the *Correctly Established Doctrine of Brahma* <note>original: *Brahmasphuṭa-siddhānta*</note> of Brahmagupta. The fact that Mahāvīrācārya was a <term>Jaina<note>A follower of Jainism, an ancient Indian religion known for its significant contributions to mathematics and logic.</note></term> might have prevented Bhāskarācārya from taking note of him; or it may be that the Jaina mathematician's fame had not spread far to the north in the twelfth century of the Christian era. His work, however, seems to have been widely known and appreciated in Southern India. So early as in the course of the eleventh century and perhaps

My thanks as well as the thanks of all those who may as scholars become interested in this publication are therefore due to him for his kindness in having readily complied with my request; and I feel no doubt that his introduction will be read with great appreciation.

Although certain words forming the names of certain things are utilized in this work to represent various numerical figures, still in the numeration of numbers with the aid of such words the decimal system of notation is almost invariably followed. If we took the words *moon*, *eye*, *fire*, and *sky* to represent respectively 1, 2, 3 and 0, as their Sanskrit equivalents <note>The author uses objects to represent numbers: for example, since there is one moon, the word "moon" stands for 1; since there are two eyes, "eye" stands for 2.</note> are understood in this work, then, for instance, *fire-sky-moon-eye* would denote the number ~~2103~~ <gloss>3012</gloss>, and *moon-eye-sky-fire* would denote ~~3021~~ <gloss>1203</gloss>, since these nominal numerals <note>A system where common nouns are used as synonyms for digits to allow mathematical rules to be written as metered poetry.</note> denoting numbers are generally repeated in order from the units place upwards. This combination of nominal numerals and the decimal system of notation has been adopted obviously for the sake of securing metrical convenience and avoiding at the same time cumbrous ways of mentioning numerical expressions; and it may well be taken for granted that for the use of such nominal numerals as well as the decimal system of notation <term>Mahāvīrācārya</term> <note>A 9th-century Jain mathematician who lived in the court of the Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha; his work is one of the earliest to treat mathematics as a subject separate from astronomy.</note> was indebted to his predecessors. The decimal system of notation is distinctly described by <term>Āryabhaṭa</term> <note>Born in 476 CE, he was a foundational figure in Indian mathematics and astronomy.</note>, and there is evidence in his writings to show that he was familiar with nominal numerals. Even in his brief mnemonic method of representing numbers by certain combinations of the consonants and vowels found in the Sanskrit language, the decimal system of notation is taken for granted; and ordinarily 19 notational places are provided for therein. Similarly in <term>Brahmagupta</term>'s <note>A 7th-century mathematician and astronomer whose work *Brahmasphutasiddhanta* provided the first rules for calculating with the number zero.</note> writings also there is evidence to show that he was acquainted with the use of nominal numerals and the decimal system of notation. It is not of course meant to convey that this work is necessarily the same as what was known to <term>Āryabhaṭa</term> <note>A 5th-century mathematician-astronomer who was among the first to use a place-value system.</note> and <term>Brahmagupta</term> <note>A 7th-century scholar who defined the rules for calculating with zero.</note>; and the fact of its using nominal numerals and the decimal system of notation is mentioned here for nothing more than what it may be worth.

It is generally recognized that the origin of the conception of **zero** is primarily due to the invention and practical utilization of a system of notation wherein the several numerical figures used have place-values apart from what is called their intrinsic value. In writing out a number according to such a system of notation, any notational place may be left empty when no figure with an intrinsic value is wanted there. It is probable that owing to this very reason the Sanskrit word *śūnya*, meaning 'empty', came to denote the **zero**; and when it is borne in mind that the English word 'cipher' is derived from an Arabic word <note>The Arabic *sifr*, which is itself a translation of the Sanskrit *śūnya*.</note> having the same meaning as the Sanskrit *śūnya*, we may safely arrive at the conclusion that in this country the conception of the **zero** came naturally in the wake of the decimal system of notation: and so early as in the fifth century of the Christian era, Āryabhaṭa is known to have been fully aware of this valuable mathematical conception. And in regard to the question of a symbol to represent this conception, it is well worth bearing in mind that opera-

<page-num>xv</page-num>

## PREFACE.

Calculations with the zero cannot be carried on—not to say cannot be even thought of easily—without a symbol of some sort to represent it. <term>The Great Teacher Mahāvīra</term> <note>original: "Mahāvīrācārya"; a 9th-century mathematician who lived in the Rashtrakuta kingdom.</note> gives, in the very first chapter of his <term>Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics</term> <note>original: "Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha"</note>, the results of the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division carried on in relation to the zero quantity; and although he is wrong in saying that a quantity, when divided by zero, remains unaltered, and should have said, like <term>The Teacher Bhāskara</term> <note>original: "Bhāskarācārya"; referring to Bhāskara II, a 12th-century mathematician who clarified division by zero as infinity.</note>, that the quotient in such a case is infinity, still the very mention of operations in relation to zero is enough to show that <term>Mahāvīra</term> must have been aware of some symbolic representation of the zero quantity. Since <term>Brahmagupta</term> <note>A 7th-century astronomer and mathematician.</note>, who must have lived at least 150 years before <term>Mahāvīra</term>, mentions in his work the results of operations in relation to the zero quantity, it is not unreasonable to suppose that before his time the zero must have had a symbol to represent it in written calculations. That even <term>Āryabhaṭa</term> <note>The 5th-century pioneer of Indian mathematics and astronomy.</note> knew such a symbol is not at all improbable. It is worthy of note in this connection that in enumerating the nominal numerals in the first chapter of his work, <term>Mahāvīra</term> mentions the names denoting the nine figures from 1 to 9, and then gives in the end the names denoting zero, calling all the ten by the name of *<term>number</term>* <note>original: "saṅkhyā"</note>: and from this fact also, the inference may well be drawn that the zero had a symbol, and that it was well known that with the aid of the ten digits and the decimal system of notation numerical quantities of all values may be definitely and accurately expressed. What this known zero-symbol was, is, however, a different question.

The labour and attention bestowed upon the study and translation and annotation of the *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics*—

# Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics
## Composed by the Great Teacher Mahāvīra

### Chapter on Terminology
<note>Sanskrit: *Saṃjñā-adhikāra*. This introductory chapter defines the units of measure and the mathematical terms used throughout the book.</note>

### The Auspicious Invocation
<note>Sanskrit: *Maṅgalācaraṇa*. A traditional prayer at the beginning of a Sanskrit work to ensure its successful completion.</note>

Salutations to that Lord of the Jinas <note>A "Jina" or "Conqueror" is a liberated soul in Jainism who has overcome all inner passions.</note>, the Protector Mahāvīra, whose **Fourfold Infinity** <note>original: *ananta-catuṣṭaya*. This refers to the four infinite qualities of a perfected soul: Infinite Knowledge, Infinite Perception, Infinite Bliss, and Infinite Power.</note> is the unsurpassed essence of the three worlds. **[1]**

<gloss>1</gloss> I bow to the Lord of the Jinas, possessing great <gloss>2</gloss> splendor, by whom the entire world was illuminated with the lamp of knowledge regarding the **True Vows**. <note>The *Vratas* or vows are the ethical foundation of Jain life.</note> **[2]**

<gloss>3</gloss> The multitude of living <gloss>4</gloss> beings was delighted by that illustrious **Amoghavarṣa**, who is free from injustice and unrestrained, seeking the welfare of those dear to him. <note>Amoghavarṣa I (reigned c. 814–878 CE) was a famous Rashtrakuta Emperor and a patron of Mahāvīrācārya.</note> **[3]**

The sinful mentalities of his enemies were consumed and turned to <gloss>5</gloss> ashes; his anger <gloss>6</gloss> was never in vain. **[4]**

Subjugating the entire world, yet never coming under the control of others himself; remaining unsubdued, he is the Lord, a unique **God of Love**. <note>original: *Makaradhvaja*. Traditionally a name for Kāmadeva, the god of desire. Here, the King is praised as a "new" kind of god of love who is actually self-controlled.</note> **[5]**

He whose actions surpassed the deeds of the <gloss>7</gloss> circle of universal <gloss>8</gloss> monarchs through his heroic strides; he is truly known by the name **"Crusher of Plotters"**. <note>original: *Cakrikā-bhañjana*. This is a play on words regarding his political enemies and his royal status.</note> **[6]**

He is the foundation of the river of knowledge, a diamond pedestal of morality; a great ocean of renowned conduct, like the sea is a "womb of jewels." **[7]**

May the rule of that God-like King **Nṛpatuṅga** <note>Another name for King Amoghavarṣa I.</note> prosper—he who is a proponent of the logic of the **Doctrine of Manifold Viewpoints** <gloss>9</gloss> and who has destroyed all one-sided perspectives. <note>original: *Syādvāda*. This is the Jain system of logic which holds that truth is multifaceted and can be viewed from many valid perspectives.</note> **[8]**

# Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics

## In Praise of the Science of Mathematics

In all transactions, whether worldly, Vedic <note>Referring to the ancient sacred traditions of India</note>, or even social/canonical, the science of calculation is utilized. **[9]**

In the science of love, in the science of wealth, in music, and in drama; likewise in the culinary arts, in medicine, and in the science of architecture and similar subjects; **[10]**

In prosody <note>The study of poetic meters</note>, in the ornaments of poetry, in logic, in grammar, and in all the various arts and qualities—mathematics remains preeminent. **[11]**

In the movements of the sun and other planets, in eclipses and the conjunction of planets, in the **three problems** <term>Tri-praśna: A technical term in Indian astronomy referring to the determination of direction, place, and time</term>, and in the phases of the moon—mathematics is universally accepted as the foundation. **[12]**

The number, diameter, and circumference of the islands, oceans, and mountains; the residences of the inhabitants of the heavens, the intermediate worlds, the celestial spheres, and the higher heavens; **[13]**

And the dimensions of all the inhabitants of the hells, their tiered arrangements, their scattered clusters, and their various proportions—all these are understood through mathematics. **[14]**

The physical forms of living beings, their lifespan, their eightfold qualities, and so on; the science of journeys and the collections of omens—all these rely upon mathematics. **[15]**

What is the use of speaking at great length? In this entire universe, filled with moving and unmoving things, whatever object exists, it does not exist without mathematics. **[16]**

From the **Ford-makers** <note>original: *Tīrthakṛt*. A Tirthankara, a supreme teacher in Jainism who has crossed the ocean of rebirth</note>, who have achieved their purpose and are worshiped by the lords of the world, and from their disciples and grand-disciples, the mountain of the famous [treatise] has come. **[17]**

Just as gems are taken from the sea, or gold from stone, or pearls from an oyster shell, [so this work is taken] from the great ocean of the science of calculation. **[18]**

# Chapter on Definitions

Drawing out that essence, I shall express it according to the power of my intellect. [This is] a small <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "alpaṃ"</note> book with no small meaning, the *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics*. **[19]**

Filled with the waters of definitions <gloss>2</gloss>, with the wide altar of the fundamental operations <note>The eight basic mathematical operations</note>, and crowded <gloss>3</gloss> <gloss>4</gloss> with the lessons on fractions surfacing within it; **[20]**

Where the great sharks are the miscellaneous problems, and the Rule of Three <note>A mathematical method to find a fourth value from three known values</note> acts as the waves; where the shimmering rays of jewels are the pithy sayings regarding the calculations of mixtures; **[21]**

With the netherworld of the area of fields, full of the sands of the calculations called <gloss>5</gloss> excavations, and shining with the tides of shadow-reckoning <note>Calculating time or height using shadows</note> related to the collection of mathematical methods; **[22]**

In this ocean of the *Compendium of the Essence*, calculators <note>Mathematicians</note> filled with virtues grasp the pure jewels of its meaning through the means of calculation. **[23]**

->The Definitions<-

Since the meaning of anything cannot be understood without names, therefore, at the beginning of this science, the terminology <term>Paribhāṣā: Technical terminology or rules of interpretation</term> will be declared. **[24]**

->First, the terminology of spatial measurement.<-

Matter <term>Pudgala: In Jaina philosophy, physical substance that has form and is subject to change</term> is that which does not undergo destruction by water, fire, or other elements. An atom <term>Paramāṇu: The smallest, indivisible unit of matter in Indian physical theories</term> is declared to be the beginning of this scale, [even though it is] composed of infinite parts. **[25]**

From that comes the "mote in a sunbeam," from that the "dust of a chariot-wheel" <gloss>6</gloss>, and then a hair’s breadth. These are named <gloss>7</gloss> <gloss>8</gloss> as superior, medium, or inferior according to whether they belong to those born in the Land of Enjoyment or the Land of Action <note>Jaina cosmology divides the world into regions where inhabitants either live off "wishing trees" (Enjoyment) or must work (Action)</note>. **[26]**

A nit, a sesame seed, a mustard seed <gloss>9</gloss>, a barley grain, and a finger-breadth—each of these is eight times the size of the one preceding it in order. This is known as the "practical finger-breadth" <note>Aṅgula: a standard unit of measure roughly equivalent to 3/4 of an inch</note>. **[27]**

--- Page 36 ---
<meta>Continuing from the definition of the smallest possible physical unit (the atom), this page details the scaling of these units into human-scale measurements of distance, the Jaina division of time from the infinitesimal "instant" to the solar year, and the dry capacity measurements used for commodities like grain.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics</header>

->**Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics**<-

Those who know measurements declare that five hundred [of the previously described units] constitute the standard. The finger-breadth of the humans living in the present age is known as the "individual finger-breadth" <term>Ātma-angula: A practical unit of measure based on the proportions of a person’s own body</term>. **[28]**

The authorities recognize two types of standard measurement: the "canonical" and the "worldly" <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "rāddhānta" and "laukika". Variant manuscript M reads "others" instead of "two"</note>. The individual finger-breadth is considered in three ways; a "transverse foot" is comprised of six finger-breadths. **[29]**

Two feet make a "span" <term>Vitasti: A measure of length, roughly the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, about 9 inches</term>, and twice that amount is a "cubit" <term>Hasta: The distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches</term>. Four cubits make a "staff" <term>Daṇḍa: A pole or rod</term>, and two thousand of those make a "distance-call" <term>Kośa: A traditional unit of distance, often associated with how far the sound of a cow's lowing could reach, roughly 2 miles</term>. **[30]**

Those skilled in the measurement of areas <note>geometers or surveyors</note> say that four *kośas* make one *yojana* <note>A significant distance in ancient India; in this context, roughly 8 to 9 miles</note>. Hereafter, the terminology regarding time will be told in its proper order. **[31]**

### Now, the Terminology of Time.

The time it takes for one atom to pass by the space of another atom is called an "instant" <term>Samaya: The smallest, indivisible unit of time in Jaina philosophy</term>. An innumerable number of these instants make a "row" <note>original: "āvali"</note>. **[32]**

A numerable number of rows is called a "breath" <note>original: "ucchvāsa"</note>. Seven breaths make a "little" <note>original: "stoka"</note>. Seven "littles" make a "bit" <note>original: "lava"</note>, and thirty-eight and a half of these make a "pot-measure" <term>Ghaṭī: A 24-minute interval; the name refers to the water-clock pots used to measure time</term>. **[33]**

Two *ghaṭīs* make one "hour" <term>Muhūrta: A period of 48 minutes</term>. Thirty *muhūrtas* make a day. Fifteen days (calculated as five times three) make a "fortnight" <note>original: "pakṣa"</note>, and two fortnights are considered a month. **[34]**

Two months make a "season" <note>original: "ṛtu"</note>, and three of those make a "half-year journey" <term>Ayana: Referring to the northern or southern course of the sun</term>. Two of those journeys make a year. Next, I shall speak of the measurement of grain. **[35]**

### Now, the Terminology of Grain.

Know that there are "sixteenths" <note>original: "ṣoḍaśikā"</note>; four of these make one "cup" <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "kuḍaha"; variants K and B read "kuḍava"</note>. Four cups <gloss>3</gloss> <note>variant K reads "kuḍavān"</note> make one "measure" <term>Prastha</term>, and four *prasthas* make one "pitcher" <term>Āḍhaka</term>. **[36]**

Four *āḍhakas* make a "bushel" <term>Droṇa</term>, and four *droṇas* make a "mani". Four *maṇis* make a "khārī". Five "forward-measures" <term>Pravartikā</term> are equal to half a *khārī*. **[37]**

<meta>This page continues the "Section on Definitions" (Saṃjñādhikāraḥ) from page 4. While the previous page concluded with the beginning of dry capacity measurements for grain, this page completes those definitions and transitions into the specific weight standards for precious metals (gold and silver) and base metals (iron), often following the regional Magadha standard used in ancient Indian commerce.</meta>

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>Section on Definitions</header>

That [measure of grain] is fourfold: the *vāha*, the *kumbha*, and five *pravartikās*. Hereafter, the standard terminology for gold is discussed <note>original: "paribhāṣā vibhāṣyate"</note>. **[38]**

## Now, the Definition of Gold Weights.

Four *gaṇḍakas* make one *guñjā* <term>Guñjā: The small, red seed of the *Abrus precatorius* vine, used as a seed-weight for gold; approximately 0.12 grams</term>. Five *guñjās* make one *paṇa*, and eight of those make a *dharaṇa*. Two *dharaṇas* make one *karṣa*, and four *karṣas* make one *pala*. **[39]**

## Now, the Definition of Silver Weights.

Two grains of paddy make one *guñjā*. Two *guñjās* make one *māṣaka* <term>Māṣaka: A small unit of weight, literally "a bean"</term>. In this system, sixteen *māṣakas* are defined as one *dharaṇa*. **[40]**

Two and a half of those [dharaṇas] make a *karṣa*. Four *purāṇas* <term>Purāṇa: An ancient silver coin or its equivalent weight</term> make one *pala*. Those experts in calculation declare that these are the silver weights according to the Magadha standard <note>Magadha was a powerful ancient kingdom in eastern India known for its standardized systems of measurement</note>. **[41]**

## Now, the Definition of Base Metal Weights.

The *kalā* is said to consist of four parts (*pāda*). Eight and a quarter *kalās* make one barley-corn (*yava*). Four *yavas* make an *amśa*, and four *amśas* make a *bhāga*. **[42]**

Six *bhāgas* make one *drakṣaṇa*. A *dīnāra* <note>Derived from the Roman *denarius*, this term was commonly used in India for gold or high-value currency</note> is twice that. Two *dīnāras* make a *satera* <note>original: "sateram"; likely derived from the Greek *stater*</note>—so say the learned regarding base metals. **[43]**

> First is the *ṣoḍashika*; then the *kuḍuba*, *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, *droṇa*, *mānī*, and *khārī*—each being four times the measure of the one preceding it. 
> (The *kuḍuba* is defined as that volume which is completely filled by three thousand one hundred and twenty-six grains of rice.)

<header>Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics</header>

> Those skilled in calculation declare that twelve and a half *palas* make one *prastha*. Two hundred *palas* make one *tulā*, and ten *tulās* make one *bhāra*. **[44]**

> In the case of textiles, ornaments, and canes, twenty pairs make one *koṭi* <note>original: "koṭi"; here referring to a bundle or score rather than the numerical ten million</note>. Following this, the fundamental operations shall be discussed by name. **[45]**

## Now, the Names of the Fundamental Operations.

<term>Parikarma: Literally "preparatory work" or "purification," these are the eight basic arithmetic processes required to solve any mathematical problem.</term>

> The first of these is multiplication (*guṇakāra*), which is also known here as *pratyutpanna*. The second is named division (*bhāgahāra*), and the third is called squaring (*kṛti*). **[46]**

> The fourth is indeed called square root (*vargamūla*), the fifth is the cube (*ghana*). Thereafter, the sixth is the cube root (*ghanamūla*), and the seventh is known as the summation of a series (*citi*). **[47]**

> That [summation] is also called the "collected" (*saṅkalita*). The eighth is the "subtracted" or "separated" (*vyutkalita*), which is also termed the remainder (*śeṣa*). These eight operations apply to fractions as well. **[48]**

## Now, the General Rules Concerning Positive Numbers, Negative Numbers, and Zero.

<note>In Indian mathematics, "dhana" (wealth) refers to positive numbers, and "ṛṇa" (debt) refers to negative numbers.</note>

> A quantity multiplied by zero becomes zero. That quantity remains unchanged when zero is added to it or subtracted from it. The product of zero [and another number] is zero. In addition, zero is simply the value to be added. **[49]**

> In the multiplication and division of two negative numbers or two positive numbers, the result is positive. The result is negative when the operation involves a positive and a negative. In the addition of a positive and a negative, the result is their difference. **[50]**

> The sum of two negative numbers is negative, and the sum of two positive numbers is positive, respectively. When a quantity is to be subtracted, a positive number becomes negative and a negative number becomes positive. **[51]**

> The squares of both positive and negative numbers are positive. Their square roots are respectively positive and negative <note>Mahāvīra acknowledges that a positive square has both a positive and a negative root</note>. A negative number, by its very nature, is not a square; therefore, it has no square root. **[52]**

## Now, the Synonyms for Numbers.

<note>The author now introduces the "bhūtasaṃkhyā" system, a poetic method of recording numbers using words for objects that occur in specific quantities (e.g., "moon" for 1, "eyes" for 2).</note>

> [The following words represent the number **One**]: The hare-marked one (*śaśī*), the moon (*soma*), the moon (*candra*), the moon (*indu*), the cool-rayed one (*prāleyāṃśu*), the night-maker (*rajanīkara*), the white one (*śveta*), the cool-rayed one (*himagu*), the form (*rūpa*), the deer-marked one (*mṛgāṅka*), and the bearer of digits (*kalādhara*). **[53]**

<header>Section on Definitions</header>

# Section on Definitions

<note>The following verses list synonyms used to represent numbers in mathematical verses. This allowed mathematicians to compose technical rules in metered poetry.</note>

Two, both, a pair, a twin, a couple, and the eyes; similarly, vision, eyes, and the two sight-organs; a pair, the eyes, the pupils, and the two views. **[54]**

The eyes of Shiva <note>original: "haranetra"; Shiva is traditionally depicted with three eyes</note>, the cities, the worlds, the three jewels <note>original: "triratna"; likely referring to the Buddhist or Jain Triple Gem</note>, and the triad of realms; the qualities <note>original: "guṇa"; referring to the three cosmic properties: sattva, rajas, and tamas</note>, and the various names for fire: the crested one, the glowing one, the purifier, and the consumer of oblations. **[55]**

The ocean, the container of poisons <note>original: "viṣadhi"; likely a scribal error for "vārīdhi" or "abdhi," meaning ocean</note>, the sea, the receptacle of waters, the ocean, and the states of existence; the abyss, the bond, the four Vedas, the passions <note>original: "kaṣāya"; in Jain philosophy, there are four: anger, pride, deceit, and greed</note>, and the mine of salt-water. **[56]**

Arrows, shafts, bolts, and weapons; the elements <note>original: "bhūta"; the five elements: earth, water, fire, air, and ether</note>, the senses, and the arrows of Cupid; the five vows, the objects of the senses, that which is to be done, and the "string-arrow" <note>original: "tantu-sāyaka"; a poetic term for an arrow</note>. **[57]**

The seasons <note>referring to the six seasons of the Indian calendar</note>, living beings, the tastes, the writings, the substances <note>original: "dravya"; in Jainism, there are six fundamental substances</note>, the sextet, and the donkey; the faces of the Young Prince <note>original: "kumāravadana"; the deity Kartikeya is depicted with six faces</note>, the castes <note>note: though usually four, certain systems count six</note>, and the "feet of the bee" <note>śilīmukha-padāni; a bee has six legs</note>. **[58]**

The mountain, the crag, the earth-bearer, the immobile, the hill, the sage <note>original: "muni"; referring to the Seven Sages or Saptarishi</note>, and the mountain-peak; the horses <note>the seven horses of the Sun’s chariot</note>, the serpents, the island-continents, the bodily elements <note>dhātu; the seven tissues of Ayurveda</note>, and the vices. **[59]**

The eight, the bodies, the elephant, and karma; the Vasus <note>a group of eight elemental deities</note>, the elephant, and the lotus; the "two-tusked one," the tusker, the directions, the sins, and the elephant-host—these all represent eight. **[60]**

The nine, the Nanda kings, the apertures <note>original: "randhra"; the nine openings of the human body</note>, the categories, the attained, and Krishna; the treasures, the gems, the planets, and the names of the Goddess Durga. **[61]**

The sky, the firmament, the void, the atmosphere, the space, the heavens, and the ether; the infinite, the middle-space, and the "Footstep of Vishnu" <note>viṣṇupada; a poetic name for the sky</note> should be remembered as zero. **[62]**

### Now, the Names of the Places.

<term>Sthānanāmāni: The names of the decimal positions (units, tens, etc.) in the Sanskrit place-value system.</term>

The first place is called the "unit" (*ekam*). The second is designated as the "ten" (*daśa*). The third they call the "hundred" (*śatam*), and the fourth is the "thousand" (*sahasrakam*). **[63]**

The fifth is the "ten-thousand" (*daśa-sāhasram*), and the sixth is the "lakh" <note>one hundred thousand</note>. The seventh is the "ten-lakh" <note>one million</note>, while the eighth is called the "crore" <note>original: "koṭi"; ten million</note>. **[64]**

The ninth place is Ten Crores <note>A Crore is 10,000,000; the 9th place represents $10^8$</note>, the tenth is Hundred Crores ($10^9$); the eleventh is the *Arbuda* <note>original: "arbudaṃ rudrasaṃyuktaṃ"; the word Rudra signifies the number 11</note> ($10^{10}$), and the twelfth is the *Nyarbuda* ($10^{11}$). **[65]**

The thirteenth place is the *Kharva* ($10^{12}$), the fourteenth is the *Mahākharva* ($10^{13}$); the fifteenth is the *Padma* <note>literally "Lotus"</note> ($10^{14}$), and the sixteenth is the *Mahāpadma* ($10^{15}$). **[66]**

->Now, the description of the qualities of a mathematician.<-

A mathematician should be recognized by eight specific qualities: the ability to perform calculations quickly, the power of logical deduction, the ability to eliminate errors, lack of laziness, the capacity for quick comprehension, a strong memory, the knowledge of mathematical strategies, and excellence in expressing numbers clearly. **[69]**

These definitions have been spoken in brief by the most eminent of sages. That which remains to be said hereafter should be understood in detail through the traditional scriptures. **[70]**

Thus ends the **Chapter on Definitions** in the mathematical science titled the "Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics," the work of the Great Teacher Mahāvīra.

# First Chapter: Operations with Numbers

---

From here on, we shall describe the first topic of business, named Operations <note>original: "parikarma"; these are the fundamental mathematical procedures like addition, subtraction, multiplication, etc.</note>.

->Multiplication<-

There, <gloss>1</gloss> in the first part regarding the operation of multiplication <note>original: "pratyutpanna"; a technical term for multiplication, literally meaning "that which is produced from the components"</note>, the rule-verse is as follows:

> After placing the multiplicand and the multiplier according to the sequence of the "sliding door joint" <note>original: "kavāṭasandhikrameṇa"; this refers to a method of arranging digits where the multiplier is moved along the multiplicand like a sliding door</note>, multiply the multiplicand by the multiplier. 
> [This may be performed] through the direct or inverse methods, or by using the methods of dividing the quantity into halves, parts, or segments. [1]

->Examples here<-

> Eight lotuses were given to each Jaina temple <note>original: "jinabhavana"</note>. How many lotuses are required for one hundred and forty-four temples? <gloss>4, 5, 6</gloss> [2]

> Nine rubies <note>original: "padmarāgamaṇi"</note> were seen offered in a single Jaina temple. How many would there be in two hundred and eighty-eight temples? [3]

> Tell me, how many topazes <note>original: "puṣparājamaṇi"</note> are there in nine hundred Jaina temples if one hundred and forty <gloss>7, 8</gloss> gems are offered in each temple? <gloss>9</gloss> [4]

> Twenty-seven lotuses <gloss>10</gloss> were given to each Jaina temple. Tell me, how many are there in one thousand nine hundred and ninety-eight temples? <gloss>11</gloss> [5]

> <gloss>12</gloss> In each temple, there are one hundred and eight golden lotuses. What is the total for a group of temples numbering eighty-two million, six hundred and ninety-seven thousand, four hundred and eighty-one? <note>the Sanskrit lists the digits: 1-8-4-7-9-6-2-8</note> [6]

<term>Operations (Parikarma)</term>: The basic arithmetic procedures (multiplication, division, etc.) that form the foundation of more complex mathematics.
<term>Multiplication (Pratyutpanna)</term>: Literally "born from," referring to the product resulting from the factors.
<term>Rule-verse (Karaṇasūtra)</term>: A concise mathematical formula written in verse for easy memorization.
<term>Example (Uddeśaka)</term>: A practice problem or illustrative case used to demonstrate a rule.
<term>Jaina Temple (Jinabhavana)</term>: A place of worship for followers of the Jina; often used in this text as a context for word problems.
<term>Gemstones (Padmarāga, Puṣparāja)</term>: Rubies and topazes, commonly used in devotional imagery in Indian mathematical problems.

# Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics

After setting down the collection of the moon (1), the Vasus (8), the best (?), the oceans (4), the nine substances (9), the nine categories (9), fears (2), and policies (2) <note>This uses the "bhūta-saṅkhyā" system where words represent numbers. Indian mathematicians traditionally listed digits from right-to-left (units place first). Thus, the moon is 1, Vasu is 8, etc.</note>; what is the total amount when this is multiplied by the moon (1), the oceans (4), and the movements (4)? [7]

Set down here the moon (1), the oceans (4), the movements (4), the moon (1), the fires (3), and the collection of vows (5). Tell me the sum total after you have multiplied this by eighty-one. [8]

Setting down here the quantity of the fires (3), the Vasus (8), the best (?), fears (2), the senses (5), and the moon (1); tell me, O friend, the amount of the sum after multiplying it by the openings (9). [9]

Place here nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one <note>original: "nandā-dhṛtu-śara-catu-stri-dvandva-ekaṃ"; though the OCR is slightly garbled, this represents the sequence 12345679</note>, and multiply it by nine. This was called the **"Necklace of the Protector of Men"** <note>original: "Narpālakāṇṭhikābharaṇam"</note> by the Teacher Mahavira. [10]

Seven, six, five, six, three, and six are placed at the beginning. One should declare this to be the **"Necklace"** when multiplied by thirty-three. [11]

Setting down here the fire (3), the movements (4), the moon (1), the sages (7), the Vasus (8), policy (2), the movements (4), and the moon (1); one should state this **"Jeweled Necklace"** after multiplying it by the mountain (7). [12]

Setting down the fire (3), the oceans (4), the moon (1), the sages (7), the arrows (5), the tusker (2), the eyes (2), the oceans (4), and the moon (1); tell me the **"Royal Necklace"** after multiplying it by the mountain (7). [13]

Seven, three, two; seven, three, two; and seven, three, two; likewise multiplied by three. Know that this is further multiplied by three, starting with one and increasing up to nine. <note>This describes a recursive or iterative multiplication pattern.</note> [14]

One, five, two, two, zero, and seven are established. One should declare the **"Necklace"** when this is multiplied by seventy-three. [15]

Setting down the collection of the oceans (4), the oceans (4), the moon (1), the eyes (2), the substances (6), and the eyes (2); tell me, O knower of mathematics, what is the number when multiplied by sixty-four? [16]

->**The Operation of Multiplication**<-

Having placed here the quantity of the number consisting of the moon (1), the moon (1), the sun (12), the moon (1), zero (0), and one (1) in order <note>original: "śaśāṅkendu-ravi-kendu-śūnyai-karūpaṃ". ## Division
<note>original: "bhāgahāraḥ"</note>

In the second operation, that of division, the rule of calculation is as follows:
<gloss>1</gloss> After placing the quantity of the dividend <term>bhājya|the number to be divided</term> and, below it, the divisor <term>bhāgahāra|the number by which one divides</term>; having performed the division according to the method of reduction by a common factor <note>original: "sa-daśāpavarta-vidhinā"; this refers to simplifying fractions by dividing both numbers by a common divisor before proceeding</note>, one should state the result. [18]

Or alternatively:
One should divide the dividend by the divisor placed below it using the reverse method <note>Moving from left to right, or the opposite of the "sliding" multiplication method</note>. If the method of reduction by a common factor is applicable to them, one should perform that as well. [19]

## Here are the Problems
<note>original: "uddeśakaḥ"</note>

Eight thousand dinars <note>A gold coin</note> plus ninety-two, combined with one hundred, are divided among sixty-four men. What is the share of a single man? [20]

Where two thousand seven hundred and one gold coins <note>original: "kanakāni"</note> are divided among thirty-seven men, tell me <gloss>2</gloss> the share of one. [21]

Ten thousand dinars, joined with three hundred and the square of seven (49); divided by seventy-nine men, <gloss>3</gloss> what is the amount obtained by one? [22]

<gloss>4</gloss> Ten thousand (10,000), forty (40), and four thousand one hundred (4,100) gold coins <note>original: <gloss>5</gloss> "hemnām"</note> are given to seventy-nine houses. What is the wealth given to one? [23]

# Square
<note>original: "varga"</note>

### In the third operation, that of Squaring, the rule of calculation is as follows:

> The product of two equal numbers is a Square. Or, the product of the number minus a desired quantity and the number plus that same desired quantity, added to the square of that desired quantity, is the Square <note>This describes the algebraic identity: $(x - a)(x + a) + a^2 = x^2$</note>. Or, the sum of an arithmetic progression starting with one, having two as the common difference, and having the desired number as the number of terms, will be the Square <note>This describes the property that the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is $n^2$. For example, $1 + 3 + 5 = 9$, which is $3^2$.</note> [29]

# The Operation of Squaring

The square of a quantity consisting of two or more places is the sum of all the squares of the individual digits, combined with twice the product of those digits taken in their respective order. [30]
<note>original: "varga"; a square, or the result of a number multiplied by itself.</note>

Having squared the last digit, multiply the remaining digits by twice that last digit; then, after moving that last digit [one place over], repeat this same procedure for the remaining digits. This is the method for finding the square. [31]
<note>This describes the "shifting" method of squaring, where a mathematician processes digits one by one, shifting the partial products to maintain the correct decimal place.</note>

->Here is the example:<-

Tell me the square of the numbers from one to nine, of fifteen, and of twice eight <note>16</note>; also of the Vratas and Yugas <note>numbers 5 and 4, representing the 5 vows and 4 ages</note>, of the Rasas and Agnis <note>6 and 3, referring to the 6 tastes and 3 sacred fires; combined as 36</note>, and of the Śaras and Nagas <note>5 and 7, referring to the 5 arrows of Kama and the 7 mountain ranges; combined as 75</note>. [32]
<term>rasāgni|the number 36</term> <term>śaranaga|the number 75</term>

What would the squares be of three hundred combined with thirty-eight <note>338</note>; of four thousand sixty-one <note>4061</note>; of two hundred; and of two hundred combined with fifty-six <note>256</note>? [33]

O mathematician, if you know, tell me the square of the "Lekhyā-guṇa-iṣu-bāṇa-dravya" <note>A number represented by word-symbols: writing (1), qualities (3), arrows (5), arrows (5), and substances (6). Using the standard 'right-to-left' reading, this is 65,531</note>, of the "Śara-gati-tri-sūrya" <note>Arrows (5), movements (4), three (3), and the suns (12), resulting in 123,45</note>, and of the "Guṇa-ratna-abdhi-purāṇa" <note>Qualities (3), jewels (14), oceans (4), and the ancient texts (18), resulting in 184,143</note>. [34]

O talented mathematician, tell me the square of six thousand combined with three hundred eighty-seven <note>6,387</note>, and of seven thousand increased by one hundred thirty-five <note>7,135</note>, and of one thousand combined with twenty-two <note>1,022</note>. Having calculated the value of these three <note>original: "tantrayāṇāṃ"</note>, tell them to me. [35]

# Square Root

Regarding the fourth operation, Square Root, the rule-formula is as follows:

Subtract the square [of the root of the last odd place] from the last odd place. Divide the [next] even place by twice the root [already found]. The square of the quotient obtained must then be subtracted from the [next] odd place. Half of the twice-multiplied [divisor] is the resulting square root. [36]
<note>This describes the traditional Indian algorithm for extracting square roots, which identifies "odd" positions (units, hundreds, etc.) and "even" positions (tens, thousands, etc.) to systematically find each digit of the root.</note>
<term>vargamūla|square root</term>

## Cubing

In the fifth operation, Cubing, the rule-verse is as follows:

The product of three equal quantities is a cube. Or, it is the product of three quantities: the given number diminished by a chosen quantity, the given number increased by that same chosen quantity, and the given number itself—this product then being added to the product of the square of the chosen quantity and the given number. [43]
<note>This describes the identity: $x^3 = (x-a)(x+a)x + a^2x$</note>

Alternatively, the cube is the sum of a series where the first term is the chosen number, the common difference is twice the chosen number, and the number of terms is the chosen number. Or, the square of the chosen number, when added to the sum of a series where the first term is one, the common difference is two, and the number of terms is the chosen number minus one, that total being multiplied by the chosen number, [also results in the cube]. [44]

<insert>In a series starting from one with a common difference of one, where the number of terms is the chosen number, multiply the preceding quantity by the following one. The sum of these products, when tripled and added to the last term, becomes the cube. [45]</insert>

<page-num>15</page-num>
<header>The Operation of Basic Calculations</header>

The square of the last digit is multiplied by the digits in the remaining places and then tripled. Then, the square of the remaining digits is multiplied by the last digit and tripled. These results, along with the cubes of the individual digits, are combined in their respective places to find the **cube** <note>represented by the term 'vṛndam' or 'ghana'</note>. [46]

The cube of the last digit is set down. Then, the square of that last digit is tripled, shifted <note>to the next decimal place</note>, and multiplied by the remaining digits. Next, the square of the remaining digits is multiplied by the last digit, tripled, and shifted. This method is repeated as required. [47]

### Illustrative Examples

Tell me the cube of the numbers from one to nine; then of fifteen; and of twenty-five <note>represented by: arrows (5) and eyes (2)</note>. Find also the cube of thirty-six <note>represented by: flavors (6) and fires (3)</note> and of seventy-seven <note>represented by: mountains (7) and mountains (7)</note>, which are the sums obtained by trading goods. [48]

Tell me the cube <note>vṛndam</note> of one hundred and one <note>represented by: moon (1), sky (0), and moon (1)</note>; of one hundred and seventy-two <note>represented by: gait (2), mountain (7), and moon (1)</note>; and of five hundred and ten <note>represented by: space (0), moon (1), and arrows (5)</note>. Tell me also the cube of seven hundred and seventeen <note>represented by: sages (7), moon (1), and ascetics (7)</note>; and of one thousand three hundred and forty-four <note>represented by: four (4), oceans (4), qualities (3), and moon (1)</note>. [49]

There is a quantity that, when cubed, equals two hundred joined with thirteen <note>213</note>. Find the cube of that quantity, and then find the cube of its double, its triple, its quadruple, and its quintuple. [50]

A quantity of one hundred and sixty-eight has been observed by the most distinguished scholars. Tell me quickly the cube of that number when it is multiplied by each of the digits from one to eight. [51]

Place in order the digits represented by: a barren woman’s son <note>symbolizing zero</note>, the atmosphere <note>zero</note>, the seasons <note>six</note>, the sky <note>zero</note>, the senses <note>five</note>, and Krishna <note>represented by the number one</note>. After finding the cube of this number <note>150,600</note>, tell me the result, O you who have seen the other shore of the ocean of the profound essence of the doctrine of calculations! [52]

**Thus ends the fifth operation, Cubing, in the procedure of basic calculations.**

### Cube Root

In the sixth operation, finding the **cube root** <note>ghanamūla</note>, the rule for the procedure is as follows:

Subtract the cube of the last digit <note>from the last cube-place</note>. Divide the remainder in the next place <note>the first non-cube place</note> by three times the square of the cube root already obtained. From the next place <note>the second non-cube place</note>, subtract the square of the quotient multiplied by three times the previous root. Then, subtract the cube of the quotient <note>from the next cube-place</note>. [53]

<gloss>1</gloss> Divide the cube-place <note>the first digit of the triplet</note> by the root; then divide the two non-cube places by three times the square of the root of the cube. Subtract from the next place the square of the quotient multiplied by three times the previous root; then subtract the cube of the quotient, as done before with the obtained digits. [54]

#### Illustrative Examples

Find the cube root of the cubes of the numbers from one to nine. What is the root of four thousand nine hundred and thirteen <note>original: "ratna-śaśi-nava-abdhi," representing: jewels (3), moon (1), nine (9), and oceans (4), read from right to left</note>?
<gloss>2</gloss> And what is the root of one million, eight hundred and sixty thousand, eight hundred and sixty-seven <note>represented by: mountains (7), flavors (6), Vasus (8), sky (0), seasons (6), elephants (8), and the moon (1)</note>? [55]

Find the root of thirteen thousand, eight hundred and twenty-four <note>represented by: gait (4), logic (2), pride (8), fires (3), and the moon (1)</note>; and of three hundred and sixty-two thousand, zero hundred and thirty-seven <note>represented by: sages (7), qualities (3), sky (0), eyes (2), donkeys (6), and fires (3)</note>.
<gloss>3</gloss> Find also the root of six million, one hundred and eighty-seven thousand, zero hundred and eight <note>represented by: Vasus (8), air (0? no, 5 or 7), sky (0), sky (0), mountains (7), gait (4), elephants (8), moon (1), and seasons (6)</note>. [56]

->Four, oceans, fires, arrows, eyes, sight,<-
->horses, elephants, sky, space, three, eyes;<-
->tell the root of this, O you who have mastered<-
->the eight operations, the oceans of mathematical knowledge,<-
->along with the root of two, arms, seasons, and mountains.<- [57]

Tell the cube root of the number represented by: wealth, horses, mountains, sins, sky, fires, mountains, and fear. Also of: nine, moons, snow-rays, sages, moon, gains, sky, donkeys, and pairs. [58]

<gloss>5</gloss> Tell the root of: gait, elephants, objects of the senses, arrows, moon, sky, mountains, hands, gait, and pairs. Also of: writings, horses, mountains, nine, mountains, cities, notes, logic, lives, and moons. [59]

O calculator, skilled in the science of mathematics, find the root of the cubes represented by: gait, sounds, sins, elephants, oceans, eagles, banners, eyes, two, squares, nine, non-roots, objects, wealth, fires, moon, moon, clouds, paths, and machines. Examine them well! [60]

# The Operation of Basic Arithmetic

## Summation

In the seventh operation, regarding **Summation** <note>saṅkalita: here referring specifically to arithmetic progressions</note>, the rule of procedure is as follows:

> The number of terms <term>gaccha: the count of numbers in the series</term> is decreased by one, halved, multiplied by the common difference <term>pracaya: the constant amount added to each term</term>, increased by the first term <term>prabhava: the starting number</term>, and finally multiplied by the number of terms. This results in the **total sum** for all series. [61]

**Another rule for finding the total sum—**
> The number of terms minus one, multiplied by the common difference, is combined with twice the first term. This [sum] is multiplied by the number of terms and then divided by two. This gives the total sum including the first term. [62]

**Rule for finding the Initial Sum, the Difference Sum, and the Total Sum—**
> The first term multiplied by the number of terms is the **initial sum** <term>ādidhana</term>. The number of terms minus one, multiplied by half the number of terms and then by the common difference, is the **difference sum** <term>uttaradhana</term>. Their combined total is the sum. <gloss>¹</gloss> In a series where the difference is subtracted, the total sum is found by subtracting the difference sum from the initial sum. [63]

**Rule for finding the Last Term, the Middle Term, and the Total Sum—**
> <gloss>²</gloss> The common difference multiplied by the number of terms minus one, when added to the first term, is the **final term** <term>antyadhana</term>. The sum of that [final term] and the first term, when halved, is the **middle term** <term>madhyadhana</term>. That [middle term] multiplied by the number of terms is stated to be the **total summation**. [64]

## Illustrative Examples

> There are merchants whose first terms and common differences start from one and go up to ten. For each of these, the number of terms is ten. Calculate the total sum of their wealth. [65]

> A noble devotee <term>śrāvaka: a lay follower in Jainism</term> worshipped five shrines with gems, beginning with two and increasing by a difference of three. O scholar of mathematics, tell me the total number of these gems. [66]

> In three series, the first term is three. The number of terms are eight and twelve, and the common difference for all three is also three. Then, [the terms and differences] increase by one up to seven. O mathematician, speak the calculation for all of these. [67]

> The square of two <note>four</note> is the first term, and the common difference is eight. The sum of this series is worshipped in a thousand cities <note>meaning the number of terms is 1,000</note>. O strong-armed expert <term>bāhubalin: literally "one with strong arms," but here used as a title for a master of mathematics</term> <gloss>²</gloss> in crossing the ocean of mathematics, tell me the result. [68]

---

<gloss>¹</gloss> Manuscript M: "The sum divided by the number of terms, decreased [by the difference sum] and then increased by one... [illegible] ...is the first term."

This stanza is omitted in Manuscript M. <gloss>²</gloss> Manuscript M: "O Strong One."

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>The Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics</header>

### Rule for finding the number of terms—
> Multiply the total sum by eight and by the common difference. To this product, add the square of the difference between twice the first term and the common difference. Take the square root of this total. Add the common difference to this root, halve the result, subtract the first term, and finally divide by the common difference. This resulting value is the **number of terms** <term>gaccha</term>. [69]

### Another rule for finding the number of terms—
> To eight times the common difference multiplied by the total sum, add the square of the difference between twice the first term and the common difference. From the square root of this sum, subtract the difference between twice the first term and the common difference. This result, when halved and then divided by the common difference, gives the **number of terms**. [70]

->**Here are the problems:**<-

> The first term is 2 and the common difference is 8. For total sums of 90, 276, and 110 <note>original: "khāṅkau" (90), "rasādrinetraṃ" (276), and "khenduharā" (110). Sanskrit often uses "word-numerals" where objects represent numbers; e.g., 'netra' (eyes) means 2.</note>, what are the respective **numbers of terms**? [71]

> If the first term is 5 and the common difference is 8, what is the number of terms for a given sum <note>The text implies a problem based on the previously calculated sums</note>? Again, if the first term is 6 and the common difference is 8, what is the number of terms for the sum of 420 <note>original: "khadvicatus", literally 0-2-4 read right-to-left as 420</note>? [72]

### Rule for finding the common difference and the first term—
> Subtract the "initial sum" <term>ādidhana: the first term multiplied by the number of terms</term> from the total sum. Divide this by half the product of the number of terms minus one and the number of terms. The result is the **common difference** <term>pracaya</term>. To find the **first term** <term>prabhava</term>, subtract the "difference sum" <note>the portion of the sum generated by the additions of the common difference</note> from the total sum and divide by the number of terms. [73]

### [Another] Rule for finding the first term and the common difference—
> The first term is found by taking the total sum divided by the number of terms, and then subtracting from it the product of half the number of terms minus one and the common difference. To find the common difference, divide the total sum by the number of terms, subtract the first term, and divide the remainder by half the number of terms minus one. [74]

### Two other rules for finding the common difference and the first term—
> Twice the total sum, divided by the number of terms, minus twice the first term, and then divided by the number of terms minus one, should be known as the **common difference**. [75]

> Twice the total sum, divided by the number of terms, minus the product of the common difference and the number of terms minus one, and then divided by two, is the **first term**. [76]

# Operations with Arithmetic Progressions

->**Here are the problems:**<-

If the first term is 9, the number of terms is 25 <note>original: "tattva", representing the 25 principles of the Samkhya philosophy</note>, and the total sum is 114 <note>original: "bhāvādhika-śata", meaning 100 plus 14 (bhāva)</note>, what is the **common difference**?
If the number of terms is 8, the total sum is 156, and the common difference is [implied from context/previous calculation], tell me the **first term**. [77]

### Rule for finding the common difference and first term from a desired number of terms—

The total sum is multiplied by a chosen factor and then divided; the result is the number of terms. When the first term is subtracted from the remaining value, and the result is divided by half of the number of terms minus one, that is the **common difference**. [78]

->**Here is the problem:**<-

O crown jewel of mathematicians, the total sum is seen to be 540 <note>original: "catvāriṃśatsahitā pañcaśatī", literally five-hundred with forty</note>. Tell me the **number of terms** and the **common difference** produced here. [79]

### Three rules for separating the first term, common difference, and number of terms from a mixed sum—

Subtract the "difference-portion" <note>The portion of the sum attributed to the common difference</note> from the mixed sum, then divide by the number of terms increased by one. O crown jewel of calculators, know that this resulting value is the **first term**. [80]

The mixed sum is diminished by the first term. This is then divided by the number of terms plus one, and further by half of the number of terms minus one. This result is the **common difference**. For the number of terms, one follows the previously stated rule for finding the term-number <term>gaccha-vidhāna</term> with the first term increased by one. [81]

When the first term and number of terms are subtracted from the mixed sum, the remainder is the "difference-mixed" sum. The procedure for finding the common difference from this is the same as the method used for all combinations of terms. [82]

->**Here is the problem:**<-

The mixed sum of the first term, common difference, number of terms, and the total sum is 40. The first term, difference, and number of terms are respectively 2, 3, and 5 <note>original: "dvi-tri-ka-pañca-daśāgrā", referring to the values 2, 3, and 5</note>. Tell me the **first term**, the **common difference**, the **number of terms**, and the **total sum** for all of these. [83]

# Rule for finding the first term and common difference for a desired sum that is double, triple, half, or a third, etc., of a given sum and its parameters—

> Place the desired sum divided by the given sum in two positions. Multiply these by the [original] common difference <note>term: *pracaya* | the constant amount added to each term in a sequence</note> and the [original] first term <note>term: *prabhava* | the starting value of the sequence</note> respectively. These results will be the common difference and the first term <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: *guṇa-bhāgādya-uttarecchāyāḥ* | "for the desired first term and common difference of the multiplier or part"</note> for the desired wealth <note>The Sanskrit word *dhana* means both "wealth" and the "total sum" of a mathematical series.</note>. [84]

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

> The number of terms is 4, the first term is 60, and the common difference is twice that. O mathematician, tell me the first term and common difference for a desired sum that is double, triple, or half <gloss>2</gloss> of that [original sum]. [85]

# Rule for finding equal, double, triple, half, or third sums etc., when the first term and common difference are interchanged for two chosen numbers of terms—

> The chosen number of terms, diminished by one and multiplied by itself, is then multiplied by the desired ratio and doubled. Subtract the other number of terms from this; the result is the **first term**. The square of the other [number of terms] diminished by itself, when reduced by twice the product of the desired ratio and the chosen number of terms, is the **common difference**. [86]

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

> For two men with 5 and 8 terms in their progressions, the first term and common difference are interchanged. O calculator, after calculating, tell me when their total wealth is equal, or when one's wealth is double or triple the other's. [87]

> For two progressions with 12 and 16 terms, where the first term and common difference are interchanged, tell me when the total wealth is equal, or when it is a multiple or a fraction, O you who are a master <gloss>3</gloss> of the science of mathematics <note>original: *gaṇita-śāstra-jña*</note>. [88]

# Rule for finding the first term and common difference when the common differences are unequal but the number of terms and the total sums are equal—

> For the progression with the largest common difference, let the first term be 1 or any other chosen number. For the remaining progressions, the difference between the largest common difference and the specific common difference is multiplied by half of the number of terms diminished by one. This result, when increased by the first term of the largest progression, becomes the **first term** for each of the other common differences. [89]

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

> There are progressions where the common differences range from 1 to 6, and another set where the common differences are 1, 3, 5, and 7. The number of terms for all is 9. O friend, quickly tell me the first terms such that their total wealth is equal in each case. [90]

<header>Computational Procedures</header>

Rule for finding the common difference when the number of terms and the total sums are equal, but the first terms are unequal—

> The common difference of the progression with the largest first term is taken as one. The difference between that largest first term and any of the other remaining first terms is divided by half of the number of terms diminished by one. This [quotient], when increased by the [initial] common difference of one, becomes the common difference for each of the remaining first terms. [91]

### Here is an illustration:

> The first terms are one, three, five, seven, nine, and eleven. The number of terms for each is five, and the total sums are all equal. O calculator, you who have seen the further shore of the ocean of mathematics, tell me the common differences! [92]

Now, the rule for the value of the last term in a geometric progression and the sum of a geometric progression—

> The first term <note>term: *prabhava* | the starting value of the sequence</note> is multiplied by the common ratio <note>term: *guṇa* | the multiplier in a geometric progression</note> raised to the power of the number of terms; this gives the "multiplied wealth" <note>term: *guṇadhana* | here referring to the value of the nth term or the progression's growth</note>. That value, when diminished by the first term and divided by the common ratio minus one, should be known as the sum of the geometric progression. [93]

Another rule for the sum of a geometric progression—

> With the number of terms [as the power], the common ratio is squared when the power is even and multiplied when it is odd <note>This refers to the ancient "square and multiply" algorithm for fast exponentiation. If the exponent is even, you square the base; if odd, you subtract one to make it even and multiply by the base.</note>. The result, diminished by one, multiplied by the first term, and divided by the common ratio minus one, is the essence [of the sum]. [94]

Rule for finding the last term of a geometric progression and then the sum of that progression—

> The "multiplied wealth" <note>the value of the last term</note> for a number of terms diminished by one is first found. That result, multiplied by the common ratio, then diminished by the first term, and divided by the common ratio minus one, is the sum. [95]

### An illustration of geometric progression:

> A man starts with two pieces of gold and triples his wealth at every city he enters. Tell me, what is the wealth of that man after he has traveled through eight cities? [96]

Rule for finding the first term and common ratio of a geometric progression—

> The total "multiplied wealth" divided by the first term gives a value equal to the product of the common ratio multiplied by itself as many times as the number of terms. The first term is the "multiplied wealth" divided by the common ratio raised to the power of the number of terms. [97]

### Rule for finding the number of terms in geometric wealth —
> The "multiplied wealth" <note>term: *guṇadhana* | the value of the last term in a geometric progression</note> is divided by the first term. The resulting quotient is then divided by the common ratio <note>term: *guṇa* | the multiplier</note> as many times as possible until it is exhausted. The number of such divisions performed is the number of terms <note>term: *gaccha* | the count of steps or positions in the sequence</note> for that geometric wealth. [98]

### Example of geometric summation.
> A certain man, starting with five dinars <note>A gold coin used in ancient and medieval India</note>, earns wealth that doubles at every step. He entered eight cities; tell me, how many dinars did he have in total? [99]

> A merchant has a first term of seven, a common ratio of three, and a number of terms equal to the square of three. What is his total wealth? Also, find the wealth where the first term is three, the common ratio is five, and the number of terms is fifteen. [100]

### Rule for finding the common ratio and the first term —
> The total sum, when divided repeatedly by the common ratio minus one, and then divided by the first term... <note>The text here describes the algebraic reversal of the sum formula</note> That by which the first term, when multiplied by the wealth and diminished by one, is exactly divisible, is the common ratio. The total sum, multiplied by the common ratio minus one, and divided by the common ratio raised to the power of the number of terms minus one, results in the first term. [101]

->Here is an illustration.<-

> In a series where the first term is three and the number of terms is six <note>original: *ṛtu* | the six seasons</note>, the total wealth is forty-four thousand and ninety-five <note>original: *bāṇa-aṅka-ambara-jala-nidhi* | 5, 9, 0, 4, 4, read from right to left</note>. What is the common ratio? In another case where the common ratio is six, the number of terms is five, and the wealth is three thousand one hundred and eight, what is the first term? [102]

### Rule for finding the number of terms from the total sum —
> Multiply the total wealth by the common ratio minus one. Divide this by the first term and add one. The number of times this result can be divided by the common ratio is the number of terms. [103]

->Here is an illustration.<-

> O friend, you who are an expert in the qualities of calculation, tell me: if the first term is three, the common ratio is six, and the total sum is seven hundred and seventy-seven, what is the number of terms? [104]

In a wealth amounting to seventy-four <note>original: *shara-giri-vyeka* | 75 minus 1</note> where the first term is five and the common ratio is two; and in another where the first term is seven, the common ratio is three, and the total wealth is... 
<margin>¹</margin>...eight thousand eight hundred and eighty-seven <note>original: *naga-ibha-durita-stamberabhartu* | a complex word-numeral sequence</note>.
