### Partial Summation <note>term: *vyutkalita* | literally "subtraction"; in mathematics, it refers to calculating the sum of a specific segment of a series, or the remainder after some terms are removed</note>

The rule for the eighth operation, Partial Summation, is as follows:
> Take the chosen number of terms <note>term: *iṣṭa* | the desired or given quantity</note> and increase it by the total number of terms. Separately, take the chosen terms, subtract one, and divide by two. Multiply this by the common difference <note>term: *caya* | the amount added at each step</note> and add the first term. Then multiply the result by the remaining terms. This gives the "subtracted wealth" <note>term: *vyutkalita-dhana* | the sum of the terms being removed</note> as well as the wealth of the chosen portion. [106]

Another rule for bringing forth the partial sum and the chosen wealth:
> Add the chosen terms to the total number of terms. Take the chosen terms, subtract one, and multiply by the common difference. To this, add twice the first term and other adjustments. Multiply the half of the remaining terms by this sum. This results in the partial sum and the wealth of the chosen terms. [107]

The rule for finding the common difference in a partial sum, and for finding the remaining terms when the partial sum is known:
> Subtract the chosen wealth from the total sum. The remainder is the partial sum derived from the common difference and the multiplier. When this is divided by the total number of remaining terms, the specific remaining term is found. [108]

The rule for finding the first term of the remaining sequence:
> The first term of the remaining sequence is found by taking the common difference, multiplying it by the chosen number of terms, and adding the original first term. The common difference and the number of terms for that specific portion remain as they were before. [109]

The rule for finding the first term of a remaining sequence in a geometric progression <note>term: *guṇa-vyutkalita* | partial sum of a series where terms are multiplied rather than added</note>:
> Even when the common difference and other factors are multiplied, the method remains similar. However, there is this distinction for the remaining terms: the first term of the new sequence is the original first term multiplied by the common ratio raised to the power of the number of chosen terms. [111]

## Examples here:

Where the first term <note>term: *mukha* | the starting value</note> is two, the common difference <note>term: *caya* | the amount added to each subsequent term</note> is three, and the total number of terms <note>term: *gaccha* | the length of the series</note> is fourteen—calculate the partial sum <note>term: *vyutkalita* | the sum of a specific portion of the series</note> for the seventh, eighth, ninth, sixth, and fifth positions. [111]

The first term is six, the common difference is eight, and the number of terms is thirty-six <note>original: *ṣaṭ-kṛti* | the square of six</note>. Tell me the partial sums for the tenth, twelfth, and sixteenth positions. In another problem, where the first term and the common difference are both five, and the total terms are two hundred, tell me: what is the expenditure <note>note: "Expenditure" here is a word problem metaphor for a partial sum</note> for the one-hundredth term? [112]

The number of terms is sixty <note>original: *ṣaḍvūna* | though literally "lessened by six," in this mathematical context it likely refers to 60 as a base for the calculation</note>, the common difference is eight, and the first term <note>term: *vaktra* | literally "face," meaning the first term</note> is fourteen <note>original: *dviguṇa-saptaka* | twice seven</note>. Tell me the result for both types of summation regarding the thirty-seventh chosen term. [113]

Sixty-four <note>original: *aṣṭa-kṛti* | the square of eight</note> is the first term, the common difference is a decrease of four <note>note: this indicates a descending arithmetic progression where 4 is subtracted each time</note>, and there are sixteen terms. What is the remainder for the twenty-fifth <note>original: *tattva* | a term for the 25 principles of Samkhya philosophy</note>, the twenty-fourth <note>original: *keśava* | referring to the 24 forms of Vishnu</note>, the eleventh <note>original: *rudra* | the 11 forms of Shiva</note>, and the twelfth <note>original: *arka* | the 12 sun-deities</note> positions? [114]

### An example of Geometric Partial Summation:

Where the first term is four, and the common ratio <note>term: *uttara* | here referring to the multiplier in a geometric series</note> is two, the number of terms is sixteen <note>original: *caturṇāṃ kṛti* | the square of four</note>. The desired positions are nine, four, seven, two, five, and four <note>original: *aṅka-sindhu-giri-dvvy-endriyāmbhodhayaḥ* | Mahavira uses a list of symbolic names for these numbers</note>. O mathematician, tell me the partial sums for all these, and the total sum that pervades this forest of calculations like a rogue elephant at play! [115]

## Now, the Second Chapter: Operations with Fractions.

> <gloss>¹</gloss> I devotedly bow to the Moon among the Jinas <note>note: A title for a Tirthankara, a spiritual teacher in Jainism</note>, whose lotus feet are touched by the rays of light from the millions of crowns of the lords of the three worlds, and who has utterly uprooted the tree of karma. ->Multiplication of Fractions<-

Regarding the multiplication of fractions, the rule of operation is as follows:

> One should multiply the numerators by the numerators and the denominators <note>term: *hāra* | literally "the divider," the denominator</note> by the denominators. If it is possible for them, one should first apply the method of cross-reduction <note>term: *vajrā-pavartana-vidhi* | "thunderbolt-like reduction," referring to canceling out common factors diagonally across numerators and denominators</note> when multiplying fractions. [2]

->Examples Here:<-

> A man obtains four-ninths of a *pana* <note>term: *paṇa* | a unit of copper currency</note> for one *pala* <note>term: *pala* | a common unit of weight</note> of dry ginger. Tell me, friend, what does he get for eight-thirds of a *pala*? [3]
>

> 
> A certain person gets three-fifths of a *pala* of long pepper for one *pana*. O Mathematician, tell me after calculating, what does he get for nine halves of a *pana*? [5]
> 
> Where a merchant buys nine-tenths of a *pala* of cumin seeds for one *pana*, tell me, O person of complete intellect, what is the total for five halves of a *pana*? [6]
> 
> The numerators begin with two and increase by two <note>original: *dvya-dayo dvitaya-vṛddhyā*</note> for ten positions. The denominators begin with three and increase by an increment of two. Tell me the result of the multiplication there, taken two by two. [7]

# Division of Fractions

### The rule of operation for the division of fractions is as follows:

> Having swapped the denominator and the numerator <note>original: *aṃśī-kṛtya-chedaṃ* | literally, "making the denominator the numerator"</note> of the divisor-quantity <note>term: *pramāṇa-rāśi* | the 'measure' or standard quantity acting as the divisor</note>, the operation is then the same as in multiplication. Alternatively, in the division of fractions, the process is like that of whole numbers after the numerators have been multiplied by the alternate denominators. [8]

# Examples

> Where the price of half a *pala* <note>term: *pala* | a traditional Indian unit of weight, roughly 40-50 grams</note> of asafoetida <note>term: *hiṅgu* | a pungent resin used in medicine and cooking</note> is three-quarters of a *pana* <note>term: *paṇa* | a unit of copper currency</note>, what does a man obtain for one *pala*? [9]

> Where a man obtains twenty-thirds of a *pana* <note>original: *viṃśati-vyaṃśān* | representing the fraction 20/3</note> for three-eighths of a *pala* of aloe-wood <note>term: *agaru* | fragrant agarwood used for incense</note>, what does he get for one *pala*? [10]

> Where eighty-two sevenths of a *pala* of *nakha* <note>term: *nakha* | literally "fingernail," referring here to a fragrant dried shellfish part</note> are obtained for four-fifths of a *pana*, what is obtained for one *pana*? [11]

> The numerators start from two and increase by one until they reach eight; the denominators are those same values minus one. Tell me the result when these are divided by each other in succession. [12]

->Thus ends the Division of Fractions.<-

# Squares, Square Roots, Cubes, and Cube Roots of Fractions

### <gloss>1</gloss> The rule of operation for the squares, square roots, cubes, and cube roots of fractions is as follows: <note>original: ¹ A variant reading in manuscript M adds "of fractions" to each term individually.</note>

> Having calculated the square, square root, cube, and cube root of both the denominator and the numerator, the square or other [required] result for the fraction is formed by the [new] numerator and denominator. [13]

# Operations on Fractions

->**Here are the examples:**<-

Oh calculator <note>original: *gaṇaka* | a mathematician or expert in computation</note>, tell me the square <note>term: *varga* | the product of a number multiplied by itself</note> of five, seven, and nine, each being halved; and also the squares of sixteen, twenty, one hundred, and two hundred, each divided by three. [14]

The numerators <note>term: *aṃśa* | the upper part of a fraction</note> start from three and increase by two; the denominators <note>term: *hara* | the divisor or lower part of a fraction</note> start from two and increase by one. The number of terms <note>term: *pada* | the position or count in a sequence</note> is known to be twelve. Oh best of mathematicians, tell me quickly the squares of these. [15]

Tell me quickly, mathematician, the square root <note>term: *kṛti-mūla* | literally "the root of the action/square"</note> of one-quarter, one-ninth, one-sixteenth, one-twenty-fifth, and one-thirty-sixth. [16]

Which quantities, when squared, result in these fractional squares? Oh expert, tell me the square root of seven hundred diminished by twenty-four <note>original: *tryaṣṭonāyāḥ* | 3 times 8 = 24 subtracted from 700, resulting in 676</note> and then divided by the square of five <note>The resulting fraction is 676/25; the root is 26/5</note>. [17]

The cube <note>term: *ghana* | a number multiplied by itself twice (x³)</note> of one-half, one-third, and one-quarter; then of one-fifth, one-sixth, one-seventh, and one-eighth; and finally of one-ninth—oh mathematician, tell me these separately. [18]

The set of numerators starts with three and has a common difference of four; the denominators here start with two and have a common difference of two. There are ten terms in total. Tell me quickly their cubes, oh you of subtle intellect in mathematics. [19]

Tell me the cube root <note>term: *ghana-mūla* | the value which, when cubed, gives the original number</note> of one hundred and twenty-five divided by eight; and also of seven hundred and twenty increased by nine <note>original: *navayuta-sapta-śatānām* | 720 + 9 = 729</note>, divided by eight. [20]

# Addition of Fractions

### The Rule of Procedure for the addition of fractions is as follows:

The number of terms <note>term: *pada* | the total count of numbers in a sequence, often denoted as *n*</note> is decreased by one, then multiplied by the common difference <note>term: *pracaya* | the constant amount added to each term in a sequence</note>, then increased by twice the first term <note>term: *prabhava* | the starting value of the sequence</note>. When this result is multiplied by half of the number of terms, it becomes the sum <note>term: *phala* | the total value of the series</note> in the addition of fractions. [22]

<note>This is the standard formula for the sum of an Arithmetic Progression: $S = \frac{n}{2} [2a + (n-1)d]$</note>

### Here is an example:

In one instance, the first term is two-thirds, the common difference is one-sixth, and the number of terms is three-quarters. In another instance, the first term is two-fifths, the common difference is three-quarters, and the number of terms is two-thirds. Tell me, what is the total sum for each? [23]

The first term is three-fifths, the common difference is one-fifth, and the number of terms is three-quarters. If the numerators and denominators of all these are increased by two, three, and so on up to seven, what is the sum of the resulting sequences? [24]

### The rule for arriving at the first term, the common difference, the number of terms, the squares of those terms, and the sum of the cubes:

The chosen number of terms is one. The first term is a chosen number. The first term subtracted from the number of terms is divided by half of the chosen terms minus one; this result is the common difference. The sum of these is their square, and that sum multiplied by the number of terms is the cube-sum. [25]

### Here is an example:

¹ The chosen number of terms is two-thirds; the numerator and denominator are each increased by one. Tell me the first term, the common difference, the squares, and the sum of the cubes for these, up to the tenth term. [26]

---

<note>¹ This stanza is not found in Manuscript M.</note>

### Rule for finding the desired sum, first term, common difference, and number of terms —

The first term <note>term: *prabhava* | the starting value of the arithmetic progression</note> is taken as one-fourth of the desired sum. The common difference <note>term: *pracaya* | the constant increment between terms</note> shall be that first term multiplied by two and decreased by one. The number of terms <note>term: *gaccha* | the total count of numbers in the sequence</note> is four times the common difference. The sum of all these values is the total <note>term: *vṛnda* | the collective sum of the series components</note>. [27]

->Here is an example:<-

The numerators have 2 as the first term and 1 as the common difference. The denominators have 3 as the first term and 1 as the common difference. Both sequences consist of five terms. Tell me, O friend, the sum of their sums, as well as the first term, common difference, and number of terms for each. [28]

### <margin>¹</margin> Rule for finding a desired first term, common difference, and number of terms when they are multiples or fractions (such as double, triple, half, or one-third) of known values —

The desired sum is divided by the given factor and placed in two positions. This is then multiplied by the common difference to find the common difference <margin>³</margin> and by the first term to find the first term, in relation to the multipliers and divisors of the desired sum. [29]

<note>This rule explains how to scale an existing arithmetic progression to meet a new desired total sum by applying proportional adjustments to the initial term and the increment.</note>

->Here is an example:<-

The first term is half of one <note>i.e., 1/2</note>. The common difference is five-eighths. The sum of the series is equal to the number of terms. Tell me, friend, what are the first term and the common difference in this case? [30]

The first term is twice and a half times the common difference. The number of terms is thirteen-eighteenths. The total sum is sixty-seven divided by six. Tell me the first term and the common difference. [31]

<margin>⁴</margin> The first term is one. The common difference is two-thirds. The number of terms is eight-ninths. The desired sum is twenty-two divided by eighty-one. Tell me the first term and the common difference. [32]

### <margin>⁵</margin> Rule for finding the number of terms —

The sum <note>term: *vitta* | also called *dhana*, the total value of the series</note> is multiplied by twice the common difference. To this, add the square of the first term diminished by half the common difference. Take the square root of this result, increase it by half the common difference, and then subtract the first term. This value, divided by the common difference, is the number of terms <note>term: *gaccha*</note>. [33]

<note>This is the algebraic solution for $n$ in the sum formula $S = \frac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]$. It translates to the modern formula: $n = \frac{\sqrt{8dS + (2a-d)^2} - (2a-d)}{2d}$</note>

³ Manuscript M: "of the desired sum in relation to multipliers and parts."
⁴ This verse replaces verse No. 31 in Manuscript M and is omitted in Manuscript B.
⁵ In place of the following two verses, Manuscript M reads: "The number of terms for the desired sum is to be brought out by the rule of the multiplier of the common difference, etc.," and repeats verse No. 70 from the section on "Basic Operations."

<header>Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics</header>

The author states the same rule in another way —

The square root of the sum <note>term: *vitta* | the total value of the series</note> multiplied by twice the common difference <note>term: *caya* | the constant amount added to each step</note>, increased by the square of the difference between the first term <note>term: *mukha* | the starting value</note> and half the common difference, is taken. From this root, subtract the first term and half the common difference, then divide the remainder by the common difference; the result is the number of terms <note>term: *gaccha* | the total count of numbers in the sequence</note>. [34]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

The first term is two-fifths; the common difference is three times the first term. The sum is stated as seven times six divided by the square of three. <note>original: *ṣaḍaṃśas-sapta-ghnāstra-kṛti-vihataṃ* | this describes a complex fraction: $(7 \times 6) / (16 \times 3^2)$</note>. In another case, the common difference is five-eighths and the first term is three-eighths, while the sum is forty-three. O dear friend, tell me quickly the number of terms for both of these. [35]

### Rule for finding the first term and common difference —

<gloss>¹</gloss> The sum divided by the number of terms, decreased by the product of [the number of terms minus one] multiplied by half the common difference, is the first term <note>term: *ādi*</note>.
The sum divided by the number of terms, decreased by the first term, and then divided by half of the number of terms minus one, is the common difference <note>term: *pracaya*</note>. [36]
<note>original footnote ¹: In manuscripts K and B, the reading is: "The first term is the sum divided by the number of terms..."</note>

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

The common difference is three-fourths, the number of terms is four-fifths, and the sum is thirty-one multiplied by one hundred and fifty <note>original: *khe-pu-śaśi* | a numerical code where *kha* (space/0), *pu* (flower/5), and *śasi* (moon/1) represents 150</note>. In a second case, the first term is one-third and the number of terms is four-fifths. Tell me the first term for the first case and the common difference for the second. [37]

### Rule for finding sums that are doubled, tripled, or divided into parts (like a half or a third) where the first term and common difference of two desired series are swapped —

The desired number of terms, decreased by one and multiplied by itself, then multiplied by a chosen factor and decreased by twice the other number of terms, gives the first term. The square of the other number of terms, decreased by its own value and then further decreased by twice the product of the chosen factor and the first number of terms, gives the common difference. [38]
<note>This complex rule allows a mathematician to construct two different series that have a specific mathematical relationship (like one being double the other) by swapping their starting values and increments.</note>

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

O friend, tell me the first term and common difference for two series where the sums are multiples or fractions (such as one, two, etc.) of each other, and where the first term and difference are swapped. The number of terms for the two series are nine and eleven, or fifty, and they are mixed with fractions like two-thirds. [39]

### Rule for the geometric accumulation and the sum of a geometric series —

The first term <note>term: *prabhava* | the starting value</note> multiplied by the common ratio <note>term: *guṇa* | the constant multiplier in a geometric series</note> raised to a power equal to the number of terms <note>term: *pada* | the total count of numbers in the sequence</note> is the geometric accumulation <note>term: *guṇadhana* | the value of the final term in the series</note>. That value, diminished by the first term and then divided by the common ratio minus one, should be known as the sum of the geometric progression <note>term: *guṇasaṅkalita*</note>. [40]

### Rule for finding the last term of a geometric sum and calculating that sum —

The last term of a geometric sum is equivalent to the geometric accumulation of the series when the number of terms is reduced by one. That result, multiplied by the common ratio, diminished by the first term <note>term: *mukha*</note>, and divided by the ratio minus one, is the essence [of the sum]. [41]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

The first term is 8, the common ratio is 4, and the number of terms here is 5. Tell me quickly, O mathematician, the geometric accumulation and the sum of that progression. [42]

<insert>One may also find the first term, the common ratio, and the number of terms for both the geometric accumulation and the sum by using the inverse of the rules stated previously.¹</insert>

### Rule for finding the first term when the sum of an arithmetic progression and a geometric progression are equal —

When the number of terms and the common difference [of an arithmetic progression] are equal to the number of terms and the common ratio [of a geometric progression], and the first term of the geometric progression is one: the sum of that geometric series is divided into the product of the common difference and the sum of a series where the first term is one. This result is the first term [of the arithmetic progression] when the two sums are equal. [43]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

The number of terms are 3, 4, and 6 <note>original: *bhāva-vārdhi-bhuvana* | coded numbers for 6, 4, and 3</note>. The common differences [and ratios] are 7, 2, and 4, each multiplied by three <note>resulting in 21, 6, and 12</note>. Tell me, what are the first terms when the sums of the two types of progressions <note>arithmetic and geometric</note> are equal? [44]

->Thus ends the summation of fractions.<-

### The subtraction of series.

### The rule for calculating the subtraction of series is as follows —

Choose a desired number of terms greater than the actual number of terms; this chosen number, multiplied by the common difference, is diminished by the common difference and then increased by twice the first term. This is then multiplied by half of the remaining desired terms; the result is the "subtracted" sum and the value of one's own desired wealth <note>term: *vitta* | here meaning the total sum of the series</note>. [45]

### Rule for finding the first term of the remaining part of a series —

<gloss>1</gloss> The first term <note>term: *prabhava* | the initial value of the sequence</note>, diminished by half of the common difference <note>term: *caya* | the constant amount added to each successive term</note> and then increased by the product of the number of removed terms <note>term: *iṣṭapada*</note> and the common difference, as well as by half of that difference, becomes the first term of the remaining number of terms. The common difference, however, remains exactly as previously stated. [46]

Even in a geometric progression <note>term: *guṇaguṇita* | a sequence where each term is multiplied by a common ratio</note>, this change regarding the remaining terms is similar. The first term [of the remaining part] becomes the original first term multiplied by the common ratio raised to the power of the number of terms to be removed. [47]

->Here are the illustrative examples:<-

The common difference is one-fourth, the first term <note>term: *āsya*</note> is one-half, and the total number of terms is specified as three-fourths. The desired number of terms to be removed <gloss>2</gloss> is one-fourth. Calculate the subtracted sum <note>term: *vyutkalita* | the sum of the terms remaining after some have been removed</note>. [48]

The first term is one-half, the common difference is one-fifth, and the total number of terms is two-thirds. The desired number of terms to be removed <gloss>3</gloss> is five-eighths. O mathematician, tell me the remaining value of the calculation. [49]

The first term is one-fourth, and the common difference is one-fifth. The total number of terms is three-fifths. If the desired number of terms to be removed is one-tenth, what is the value of the subtracted sum <note>term: *vyavakalita*</note>? [50]

The first term is two-thirds, and the common difference is one-fifth. The total number of terms is three times one-fourth <note>i.e., 3/4</note>. If the number of terms to be removed is one-fifth, one-sixth, or one-seventh, tell me the expenditure <note>term: *vyaya* | here used as a synonym for the sum of the remaining series</note>, O you who are a dwelling-place of the arts and whose light of wisdom is like that of the moon! [51]

In a series of twelve terms, the common difference is four, and the first term is five diminished by one-half <note>i.e., 4.5</note>. Calculate the subtracted sums for when three, four, five, and eight terms are removed. [52]

# The Six Classes of Fraction Operations

Hereafter, we shall illustrate the six classes of operations regarding the reduction of fractions <note>term: *kalāsavarṇa* | the process of simplifying or reducing fractions to a common denominator</note>:

> Simple fractions, fractions of fractions, sub-divided fractions, associated fractions, dissociated fractions, and mixed fractions—these are declared to be the six classes in this section on the reduction of fractions. [54]

## Simple Fractions

In the case of simple fractions <note>term: *bhāgajāti*</note>, the rule of operation <note>term: *karaṇasūtra*</note> is as follows:

> The numerators and denominators are mutually multiplied by denominators that have been made equal; thus the numerators are provided with common denominators. In the procedure for simple fractions, one of these identical denominators is then dropped, and the numerators should be added or subtracted. [55]

<gloss>2</gloss> To produce a common denominator by another method, here is the following rule:

> The product of the common divisors of the denominators and the resulting quotients shall be the common denominator <note>term: *niruddha* | equivalent to the modern Least Common Multiple (L.C.M.)</note>. When the numerators and denominators are multiplied by the quotients obtained by dividing this common denominator by the original denominators, the denominators become equal. [56]

### Here Follow the Problems

<margin>1</margin>A lay worshipper <note>original: *śrāvaka* | a devoted Jain householder</note>, for the purpose of worshipping the Jina, purchased rose-apples, citrons, oranges, plantains, bananas, mangoes, and pomegranates. He bought them for 1/6, 1/12, 1/20, 1/30, 1/24, and 1/8 of a gold piece <note>original: *hema* | a unit of currency or weight of gold</note> respectively. Simplify <note>term: *saṅkṣipa* | to reduce or sum up a series of fractions</note> the following: 8/15, 1/20, 7/30, 11/63, and 1/21. [59]

The numerators are equal to their respective starting values <note>term: *mukha* | literally "face," meaning the first term of the series</note>, and are multiplied by themselves and the subsequent terms. What is the total sum of these? [60]

Denominators starting with 1, 2, 3 and those starting with 4 and so on increase by one. The numerators are equal to their respective starting values. These are multiplied by the next consecutive denominator. What is the total sum of these series when they end at 20, at the product of 6 and 7 (42), at the square of 5 (25), and at 36? [61-62]

<margin>3</margin>For the great festival of the Jina <note>term: *jinamahā* | a grand worship ceremony</note>, a man purchased sandalwood, camphor, aloe-wood, and saffron. He spent 1/4, 1/2, 1/20, and 1/5 parts of a gold piece <gloss>4</gloss>. What is the remainder of the gold? [63]

A person gave 1/4, 1/5, 1/2, three times 1/10 (3/10), and 1/27 of two gold pieces to provide a "smiling" white lotus, thickened yogurt, ghee, and milk... [64]

# Operations with Fractions

A noble lay worshipper <note>original: *śrāvaka*</note> said to me today: "Bring some sandalwood <note>original: *śrīkhaṇḍa*</note> for the purpose of worshipping in the temple of the Jina." O mathematician <note>original: *gaṇaka*</note>, tell me what the remainder is after subtracting the specified fractions? [64]

<gloss>1</gloss>The two sets of denominators start with eight and five, each increasing by one.
<gloss>2</gloss>They end at thirty, and are multiplied by the next terms, with the last terms being multiplied by four. [65]

<gloss>3</gloss>Subtract those two sets of fractions, whose numerators are the measure of their own starting values, from one <note>original: *rūpa* | literally "form," used in mathematics to represent the integer 1 or unity</note>. O friend, you who have crossed the ocean of mathematics <note>original: *gaṇitārṇava*</note>, tell me the remainder. [66]

The denominators are described as: nineteen, then twenty-three, sixty-two,
one less than thirty (29), and one hundred and twenty-three. [67]

Then thirty-five, one hundred and eighty-eight,
thirty-seven, ninety-eight, and three less than fifty (47). [68]

One hundred and forty-one, one hundred and sixteen,
thirty-one, ninety-two, and fifty-seven. [69]

Three more than seventy (73), then fifty-five, and twice that (110),
four more than the square of seven (53), seventy, and two hundred and nineteen. [70]

These are the denominators. The numerators start with one and increase by one.
<gloss>5</gloss>Add these together and tell me the result, <gloss>4</gloss>O you who have reached the opposite shore of the ocean of fractions. [71]

## Rule for deriving the numerators:

Assume the numerator to be one, then multiply those desired numerators by the same denominators.
Those intended numerators, which when multiplied and added together equal the result, are the correct ones. [72]

### ¹Rule for arriving at the numerators of fractions whose numerators increase by one, while the denominators remain unchanged:

The numerator of the first of a series of fractions increasing by one is found by taking the total sum and multiplying it by the numerator of a fraction with a common denominator. The remaining numerators are then found by multiplying the rest of the sum by the subsequent numerators in order until the end. [73]
<note>original footnote: Rule for producing numerators for fractions with similar increases.</note>

->Here is an illustration:<-

The denominators of a set of fractions are 9, 10, and 11. Their sum is 880 divided by 990 <note>original: *nyūnāśītyaṣṭaśatī* (800 + 80) and *navati-navaśatī* (900 + 90)</note>. Tell me, what are the numerators? [74]

### Rule for the production of denominators:

When the numerators of the fractions are all one <note>original: *rūpāṃśaka* | unit fractions</note>, the denominators are determined by starting with one and multiplying by three in succession. The first and last of these are then multiplied by two and one-and-a-half <note>original: *dvyaṃśa* and *tryaṃśa*</note> respectively, so that the total sum becomes one <note>original: *rūpa* | unity</note>. [75]

->Here is an illustration:<-

The sum of five fractions, each having one as its numerator, is one. O mathematician, tell me what the denominators are for those five, or for a set of six or seven fractions that also sum to one. [76]

### Rule for the production of denominators in odd positions:

To find the denominators of fractions with one as the numerator that sum to unity, start with two and increase by one. Each denominator is then multiplied by the one following it and halved; these results will be the denominators that yield a sum of one. [77]

### Rule for producing denominators for fractions with various numerators that result in a sum with one as the numerator:

The given denominator of the sum is the first denominator. This, when increased by its own numerator, becomes the next denominator. Each preceding denominator multiplied by its successor, and then divided by its own numerator, provides the final denominator when the sum is a unit fraction. [78]

->Here is an illustration:<-

For a set of fractions with the numerators 7, 9, 3, and 13, tell me the denominators such that their sum results in one <note>original: *rūpa*</note>, or one-fourth <note>original: *pāda*</note>, or one-sixth <note>original: *ṣaṣṭha*</note>. [79]

While the previous rules focused on finding numerators, Mahāvīra now turns to the "production of denominators" (chedotpatti)—essentially the reverse process where the mathematician must find the denominators required to reach a specific sum, a precursor to the modern study of Egyptian fractions.</meta>

<page-num>37</page-num>
<header>Operations on the Partition of Fractions</header>

### Rule for the production of denominators when the result is either a unit fraction or a non-unit fraction, and the numerators are unity:

A chosen divisor, divided by its own numerator without remainder, becomes the first denominator. The chosen denominator, divided by the sum of those results, provides the remainder from which the others are similarly found. [80]
<note>This rule explains how to break down a fraction into a series of unit fractions (fractions with 1 as the numerator). This was a sophisticated area of Jaina mathematics.</note>

->Here is an illustration:<-

Tell me, what are the denominators of three quantities whose numerators are one <note>original: *rūpakāṃśānāṃ* | unit fractions</note>, such that their sum <note>original: *phalam*</note> is one-fourth? Also, find the denominators of four such quantities whose sum is three-sevenths. [81]

### Rule for the production of denominators when the numerators are either unity or multiple, and the sum is a non-unit fraction:

The given numerators are multiplied by a chosen factor such that their sum equals the numerator of the resulting fraction. The denominator of that result, multiplied by the respective factors, then becomes the specified denominators. [82]

->Here is an illustration:<-

¹Tell me, what are the denominators for three quantities with unit numerators <note>original: *ekakāṃśena*</note>, such that their sum is twenty-three divided by twelve? [83]

Tell me the denominators for three quantities with numerators of three, seven, and nine, such that their sum is seventy-three divided by forty-nine. [84]

### Rule for the production of denominators for two quantities where the numerators are unity and the sum is a unit fraction:

The denominator of the sum, multiplied by a chosen number, is the first denominator. That value divided by the chosen number minus one is the other. Alternatively, the two denominators are found by taking the denominator of the sum and its factors whose sum is equal to the denominator. [85]
<note>This provides two methods for the equation 1/x + 1/y = 1/n.</note>

->Here is an illustration:<-

O you who are learned in the meaning of mathematics <note>original: *gaṇitārthavit*</note>, tell me what the two denominators are for two unit fractions whose sum is one-sixth, or again, when the sum is one-tenth. [86]

¹ <margin>Stanzas 83 and 84 are omitted in manuscript B.</margin>

## The first rule for the production of denominators in cases where the sum is either a unit fraction or a non-unit fraction, and the components are likewise unit or non-unit fractions:

> A chosen number <note>original: *iṣṭa*</note> is multiplied by the numerator of one fraction and added to the numerator of the other; this sum is then divided by the numerator of the resulting sum <note>original: *phalāṃśa*</note>. The first denominator is the denominator of the result multiplied by the chosen number. The second denominator is that same value divided by the quotient obtained from the first step. [87]

### Here is an illustration:

> Tell me, what are the two denominators for two quantities with unit numerators <note>original: *rūpāṃśakayoḥ* | where the numerators are 1</note> such that their sum is one-fourth <note>original: *pāda*</note>? Or, what are they if the sum is one-fifth? Also, tell me the denominators for two fractions whose numerators are two-sevenths and two-ninths. [88]

## The second rule:

> The numerator of the result multiplied by a chosen denominator and added to another numerator, then divided by the numerator of the result, gives the denominator of the first. This value, multiplied by the denominator of the result, becomes the denominator of the other. [89]
<note>This provides an alternative algebraic method to solve for unknown denominators in an equation of the form a/x + b/y = C/D.</note>

### Here is an illustration:

> What are the two denominators of two quantities with unit numerators such that their sum is two-sevenths? O friend, tell me also for the sum of six-eighths. [90]

> The sum of one-half, one-third, one-tenth, and one-fifteenth is unity <note>original: *rūpam* | the number 1</note>. If the one-fifteenth is removed, what two unit-numerator fractions should be added in its place to maintain the sum of one? [91]

> The sum of one-half, one-fourth, one-fifth, and one-twentieth is unity. If the one-twentieth is removed, what two fractions with numerators of seven and eleven <note>original: *sapta-ekādaśakāṃśau*</note> should be added here instead? [92]

## Rule for the production of denominators based on pairs:

> One should project the fractional parts of the resulting sum as unit-numerator fractions <note>original: *ekaikāṃśān*</note> in even numbers. From these resulting parts, the denominators are to be calculated using the method for two quantities. [93]
<note>This rule suggests a "divide and conquer" strategy: breaking a complex sum into pairs and solving each pair using the previous rules.</note>

# The Operation of Reducing Fractions to a Common Denominator

-> Here is an illustrative problem: <-

For fractional quantities with numerators of 3, 5, 13, 7, 9, and 11, what are the denominators such that the resulting sum is 1, or four-fifths <note>original: pañcāṃśo vā catur-guṇitaḥ | literally: one-fifth multiplied by four</note>? [94]

The rule for generating denominators for a unit result <note>original: phale rūpe | where the sum is 1</note> using denominators derived from one rule and denominators derived from another rule, and for finding a missing part <note>original: naṣṭa-bhāga</note>:

> The denominators produced by a chosen rule <note>original: sūtra</note> become the final denominators when multiplied by the denominators produced by another rule. The value of a desired missing part <note>to make the sum reach the target</note> is the target result minus the sum of the known fractions. [95]

-> Here is an illustrative problem: <-

By the rule of halving the product of others <note>referring to a previous algorithm</note>, let 13 be the numerator. By the rule of multiplying self and others, let there be four parts <note>numerators</note>. From these, what are the denominators when the result is 1? [96]

By the previously mentioned rule of self-and-other multiplication, there are seven numerators; by the rule of halving the product of the near-other, there are three numerators. From these, what are the denominators when the resulting sum is 1? [97]

Fractions with unit numerators <note>original: rūpāṃśakā | fractions with 1 as the numerator</note> have denominators of 2, 8, 12, and 20. Here, the fifth quantity is missing. The sum of all is 1. What is that missing quantity? [98]

-> Thus ends the Class of Simple Fractions. <-

### Rule for the Class of "Fractions of Fractions" and the Class of "Divided Fractions":

> In the class of "fractions of fractions" <note>original: prabhāga | compound fractions like 1/2 of 1/3</note>, the multiplication of the numerators and of the denominators should be performed. In the method for "divided fractions" <note>original: bhāgabhāga</note>, the numerator of the fractional quantity acts as the multiplier and its denominator acts as the divisor. [99]

-> Here is an illustration of "fractions of fractions": <-

Calculate the values of: half of one; half of one-third; half of a half of one-third; one-fifth of half of a half; one-third of half of one-fifth; and one-seventh of half of one-third. [100]

A half of a half of a half of a seventh; a third of a third of a half of a half; a half of a third of a third of a fifth; and a half of a fifth. [101]

Having bought red lotus, jasmine, screwpine, and white lily flowers with one *pana* <note>original: paṇa; a standard unit of currency, usually a copper coin</note>, these were offered to worship at the feet of the Jina <note>original: jina-caraṇa; refers to the Tirthankaras or spiritual victors of Jainism</note>. Two-fifths of a third; thirteen-sixths of a third; thirteen-eighteenths of five-eighteenths; nine-eighths of an eighth; [105]

Four-thirteenths of a ninth; and a half of three-quarters of a fifth. Simplify these and tell me the result, if you have any effort left for this class of compound fractions <term>prabhāgajāti: the "class of fractions of fractions," a specific category in Indian arithmetic</term>. [106]

### Here is the rule for finding a single unknown quantity—

Put 1 in the place of the unknown <term>avyakta: literally "the unmanifest," representing the unknown variable in an equation</term> and find the result according to the previous rule. The given result <note>the known total</note> divided by that calculated value yields the unknown quantity in the class of compound fractions. [107]

-> Here is an illustrative problem: <-

Of a certain quantity, take an eighth part, a fourth of a third, and a half of a fifth. From a sixth, take a fifth of three-quarters. If the result of these is a half, what is the unknown quantity? [108]

---

### Here is the rule for finding multiple unknown quantities—

Having assumed desired values for the unknowns so that their sum equals the target result, divide the known quantities separately by those values to find the proportions of the known quantities. [109]

### Rule for the class of addition of fractions <term>bhāgānubandhajāti: the "class of fractional increase," involving the addition of a fraction to an integer (mixed numbers) or to another fraction</term> —

> In the rule for the class of addition of fractions, add the numerators to the integers that have been multiplied by the denominators. <insert>For compound additions,</insert> multiply the numerator and denominator of the upper fraction by the denominator and the denominator-plus-numerator of the lower fraction respectively. [113]

From a half part increased by its own third, quarter, seventh, and last <margin>The 'B' manuscript reads "with its own quarter, half, and last parts"</margin> parts, a man brought flowers; from a seventh part increased by its own half, fourth, fifth, and ninth parts, he brought perfume; and from a fifth part combined with its own half, quarter, and third parts, he brought incense to worship the lords of the Jinas. ### Rule for finding unknown parts from the result <term>agrāvyakta: literally "the unknown at the beginning," a method for working backward from a known result to find initial values</term>—

The results obtained, divided by the fractions produced from a chosen unity and the results of the additions, are respectively equal to the broken parts; these are the measures of the unknown parts. [122]

# Operations on Fractions

## Examples for this Section

One part is combined with its own halves, thirds, and quarters; a second part with its own fifths, fourths, and ninths; and another with its own thirds, fifths, ninths, and halves. Their sum is one. What are the unknown parts in this case? [123]

A certain part, when joined with its own half, fifth, third, quarter, and ninth, quickly becomes one-half. O dear one, tell me the measure of that unknown quantity! [124]

### Rule for finding unknown parts in desired places from a remainder —

The assumed parts are taken from the result, made homogeneous <term>savarṇi: the process of reducing fractions to a common denominator</term>, and divided by the known quantities. When these are successively subtracted from one, they become the unknown parts in their respective desired places. [125]

->Thus ends the class of addition of fractions.<-

## Now, the rule for the class of subtraction of fractions —

In the procedure for the class of subtraction of fractions <term>bhāgāpavāhajāti: a type of problem where a fraction of a quantity is subtracted from the quantity itself, often represented as x - (x/y)</term>, subtract the numerators from their respective denominators.
¹ Multiply the numerators by the original denominators and by the denominators reduced by the numerators. [126]

<margin>¹ The 'B' manuscript reads: "One should multiply the initial numerators and denominators by the denominators minus the numerators and the [original] denominators."</margin>

## Example of subtraction of parts from a whole quantity —

Three, eight, and fourteen *karṣas* <term>karṣa: a traditional unit of weight, often for gold or silver</term>, reduced respectively by a quarter, a half, a twelfth, and a sixth, were given with humility by men to the Tīrthaṅkaras <note>original: tīrthakṛtām; refers to the "Ford-makers" or the 24 great spiritual teachers of Jainism</note>. What is the sum of those offerings? [127]

Three times a quarter and a half, [reduced by] three, eight... nine, seven, and nine were made successively...

->Examples of Subtraction of Fractions<-

Respectively take double of one-fifth, then one-ninth, one-third, one-eighth, and two-sevenths. Reduce these by their own sixth, quarter, quarter, third, and eighth parts [respectively]. Tell me the sum of these. [129]

### Rule for bringing out unknown parts from a remainder—

The assumed parts <note>The translator interprets "assumed parts" as a trial value used in the rule of three or a similar algebraic substitution</note> are divided by the results of the [fractional] subtractions derived from unity. These, equal to the individual parts, are the measures of the unknown fractions. [132]

## Operations with Fractions

Some fraction, when diminished by its own half, sixth, fifth, eighth, and seventh parts, <gloss>1</gloss> results in a sixth. O scholar of the meaning of mathematics, what is that fraction? [135]

### Rule for bringing out unknown parts from a remainder and a chosen location —
The assumed parts <note>Trial values used to solve for an unknown</note> are divided by the known quantities, which have been increased or decreased from unity. Those [assumed parts] subtracted separately from unity results in the unknown parts in those positions. [135]

->Thus ends the "subtraction of fractions" variety.<-

### Rule for bringing out all unknown parts in the "addition of fractions" and "subtraction of fractions" varieties —
Setting aside one, one should assume one's own desired parts for all the [other] unknown ones. With these, one should again bring out that [last] part using the rules previously mentioned. [136]

->Here is an illustration.<-

What part of a part, when added to five certain parts, becomes a half? Or, when subtracted, becomes a quarter? O dear one, tell me those parts! [137]

### Rule on the "Mother of Fractions" variety —
For the "Mother of Fractions" <term>original: bhāgamātṛ-jāti; a category of complex or compound fractions</term> variety, the respective rules of the first [six] varieties of fractions are applied. It has twenty-six variations; unity <term>original: rūpa; the number 1</term> is the denominator of a quantity that has no denominator. [138]

->Here is an illustration.<-

A third; a quarter; a half of a half; a fifth of a sixth; one multiplied by three-quarters; unity multiplied by five-halves; one with a sixth <note>1 + 1/6</note>; one with a fifth <note>1 + 1/5</note>; [139]
a half joined with its own third; two-sevenths joined with its own sixth; one diminished by its own ninth part; unity with a tenth part removed; and an eighth.

---

¹ The P, K, and B manuscripts read "the sum" <note>original: tadyutiḥ</note> instead of "results in" <note>original: jāyate</note>.

# III.
## Operation with Miscellaneous Problems

Having bowed down to the Jina Mahāvīra—the Lord of Conquerors who is praised for his ocean of infinite qualities, and who grants boons to the three worlds that bow before him—I shall now declare the "Miscellaneous" section of mathematics. [1] <note>Mahāvīra (c. 6th century BCE) was the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism; the author Mahāvīrācārya shares his name and begins with this traditional religious invocation.</note>

<note>Footnote 1: Manuscripts B and M omit the following stanza.</note>
May the Jina Vidyānanda be victorious—he who has destroyed the darkness of false doctrines, who is successful, whose teaching is the doctrine of "maybe" <term>original: syādvāda; the Jain theory of multifaceted reality or relative pluralism</term>, the lord of great debaters, and the best of sages. [2]

Hereafter, we shall illustrate the "Miscellaneous" section, the third operation:

The varieties of problems consist of: Part-Remainder, Square Root, Remainder-Root; two varieties known as Double-Remainder and Part-Root; Part-Multiplication, Square-of-the-Part, and then Root-Mixed. From these, including the variety with a known quantity, these are the ten varieties. [3] <note>original: bhāga, śeṣa, mūla, etc. These are technical categories of equations involving fractions of an unknown total.</note>

### Here is the rule for the Part-variety and the Remainder-variety:

In the procedure for the Part-variety, the known quantity divided by one minus the sum of the fractions is the result. In the Remainder-variety, the known quantity is divided by the product of one minus each of the fractions. [4] <note>This provides the algebraic formula for solving $x - (\frac{a}{b}x + \frac{c}{d}x...) = K$ and $x(1-\frac{a}{b})(1-\frac{c}{d})... = K$.</note>

### An example in the Part-variety:

One-eighth of a pillar was seen by me on the ground; one-third in the water; and one-fourth in the moss. What is the total height of the pillar if seven cubits <term>original: hasta; a standard unit of measure, approximately 18 inches</term> are visible in the air? [5]

One-sixth of a swarm of excellent bees was among the Trumpet-flowers; one-third in the Kadamba flowers; one-fourth among the Citron trees; and one-fifth in the full-blown Jasmine flowers. One-thirtieth part enjoyed itself in a cluster of blooming lotuses opened by the sun’s rays. One intoxicated bee wanders alone there in the sky. What is the total number of bees in that swarm? [6]

A layman, eloquent with a hundred hymns of praise, offered lotuses to the best of Tirthankaras. He gave one-third of the total to the four Vṛṣabha-Jinas; then one-third, one-fourth, and one-sixth to Sumanas-Jina; and then one-ninth and one-twelfth [to another]. To each of the remaining Jinas, he gave two lotuses with a joyful heart. What was the total number of lotuses? [7] <note>Vṛṣabha (also known as Rishabhanatha) was the first Tirthankara, and Sumanas (Sumatinatha) was the fifth. The problem asks the student to find the total quantity based on these fractional distributions and the known remainder of 2 lotuses for each of the remaining 24 Tirthankaras.</note>

Of those who have brought their senses under control, who have cast away the stains of worldly desires and passions, who are adorned with the virtues of good conduct, and whose bodies are embraced by the lady of Compassion— [8]

A pair of such holy men was seen. One-twelfth of the group are those learned in logic. The scripture-knowers are that same quantity [one-twelfth] diminished by one-third of itself. The remainder of those two are the scholars of the Vedas. [9] <term>original: sādhu; a Jain monk or holy person</term> <term>original: chāndas; here referring to those specialized in prosody or Vedic studies</term>

The preachers of Dharma are six times that [remainder]. The astrologers are the same as the preachers diminished by one-fourth of themselves. The debaters are the difference between those two, and the ascetics are six times that difference. [10] <note>This "riddle" builds a complex equation where each group of monks is a fractional function of the previous groups.</note>

->On the slope of a mountain peak, I saw<-
->lords of ascetics numbering eight multiplied by nine.<-
->Their radiant bodies were heated by the rays of the sun;<-
->tell me quickly, O Prince of Sages, the size of that group of monks. [11]<-

In a field of rice, bowed down by the weight of ripening grain, a flock of parrots sat. Suddenly disturbed by men, they all flew up in fear. [12]

Half of them went to the East; one-sixth went to the Southeast. The remainder of those from the East and Southeast, diminished by its own half and [again] diminished by its own half, went to the South. [13] <note>original: prācī (East), āgneyī (Southeast), yāmī (South). Indian mathematics frequently uses the cardinal and intermediate directions in word problems.</note>

The remainder from the South and Southeast, diminished by two-fifths of itself, went to the Southwest. The remainder from the Southwest and West went to the Western quarter. [14] <term>original: nairṛti (Southwest), vāruṇī (West)</term>

The remainder from the Northwest and West, increased by its own three-sevenths, [flew to the Northwest]. The remainder from the Northwest and North, increased by its own seven-eighths, went to the North. [15] <note>The problem continues onto the next page to provide the final known quantity of parrots to solve the equation.</note>

### The Parrots in the Sky
The sum of the fractions found in the Northwest and North directions, combined with the fraction in the Northeast increased by its own third and then diminished by its own third—when this [total fraction] is removed, ten times twenty-eight parrots remain in the sky. How many parrots are there in total? [16] <note>original: vāyavy-uttararyor-yutir-aiśānīm; This refers to a problem where parrots are distributed according to the points of the compass. The remainder is 280 (10 x 28).</note>

### The Problem of the Broken Necklace
In the month of spring, in a garden bowed down by the weight of blossoms, fruit, and hanging vines, filled with the sweet, nectar-intoxicated sounds of parrots, cuckoos, and bees— [17]

On the broad terrace of a palace, white as the moon, upon a thick, soft bed, a young woman was seen. Her body was adorned with the beauty of stainless ornaments, her eyes like the belly of a *Pathina* fish, and her slender waist bowed by the weight of her firm breasts and necklaces. [18-19] <note>original: pāṭhīna-jaṭhara-nayanā; The *Pathina* is a type of catfish (Wallago attu). In Sanskrit poetry, "fish-eyes" are a compliment, suggesting large, shimmering, and darting eyes.</note>

While she was enjoying a night of love with her husband, a lover's quarrel arose. During the struggle, the lady's pearl necklace was broken. One-third of the pearls fell upon the ground. [20]

One-sixth was found on the bed. Then [portions of] one-half, one-half of that, and so on, were scattered. Six clusters of pearls fell everywhere. [21] <note>The mathematical structure here involves a series of fractions where each is half of the preceding one, starting from the one-sixth portion.</note>

One thousand, one hundred and sixty-one pearls were seen remaining. If you understand the "Miscellaneous" method of calculation, tell me the total number of pearls in that necklace. [22]

### The Swarm of Bees
<margin>Manuscript 'M' reads "Glittering with the king of jewels" (sphurat-nendra) at the start of the verse, likely comparing the bees to sapphires.</margin>
A swarm of bees, the color of a shimmering blue sapphire, was seen in a blooming garden. One-eighth of them settled on an Asoka tree, and one-sixth on a Kutaja tree. [23] <term>original: aśoka; the Saraca asoca tree, famous for its red flowers. kutaja; the Holarrhena antidysenterica, known for white flowers.</term>

Six times the difference between the Kutaja and Asoka portions was found in a vast cluster of Patali trees. The difference between the Patali and Asoka portions, diminished by one-ninth of itself, was in a great Sal forest. [24] <term>original: pāṭalī; the Trumpet Flower tree. sāla; a large timber tree (Shorea robusta) often associated with thick forests.</term>

The difference between the Patali and Asoka portions, increased by one-seventh of itself, was in a Madhuka forest. One-fifth of the total was seen on Vakula flowers, which were heavy with blooming buds. [25] <term>original: madhuka; the Butter Tree. vakula; Mimusops elengi, known for its fragrant, star-shaped flowers.</term>

That same fraction (one-fifth) was also found on Tilakas, on Kuravakas, on Sarala trees, on the tips of lotus clusters, and even on the temples of forest elephants. [26] <note>Bees are frequently described in Sanskrit literature as being attracted to the "mada" (ichor or temple-fluid) of elephants in rut. The problem asks the student to find the total population of the swarm based on these many distributions.</note>

In a grove of lotuses, shimmering yellow with heaps of flower-pollen, thirty-three bees were seen. O mathematician, tell me the total measure of that swarm of bees! [27] <note>original: kiñjalkapuñjapiñjarakañjavane; This problem asks for the total when only a portion is visible, though here the text implies the 33 bees are the total or a specific part of a larger set to be calculated based on the previous context.</note>

Half of a herd of cows was seen on a mountain; half of that half was at the foot of the hill. In a vast forest, there were six further portions, each being half of the one preceding it. Thirty-two cows were seen standing near a city. O friend, tell me the total number of cows in that herd! [28] <note>This is a "Partitive Proportion" problem. ->This ends the section on problems of simple fractions.<-

### Problems on Remainders

A King took a sixth part of a pile of mangoes; the Queen took a fifth of the remainder. Three noble princes took a fourth, a third, and a half of the successive remainders. [29]

The three mangoes that remained were taken by the youngest child. O expert in miscellaneous calculations, tell me the total measure of that pile of mangoes! [30] <note>original: śeṣasya; This signifies a "Remainder" problem where each fraction applies only to what is left after the previous person has taken their share.</note>

One-seventh of a group of elephants roams on a mountain. Portions starting from one-sixth and decreasing down to one-half are taken from the successive remainders. Finally, six elephants were seen at a lake. How many elephants are there in total? [31]

One person received one-ninth of a treasury; others took the eighth part and so on, down to a half-part of the successive remainders. At the end, I saw twelve <term>Purāṇas</term> <note>An ancient Indian silver coin used as a standard of currency.</note> remaining. What was the total amount? [32]

->This ends the section on problems involving remainders.<-

### The Rule for Problems Involving Square Roots

Divide the visible quantity by the result of the fractions being subtracted from one. The square root of the "square-root-portion" should be added to the result of the "visible-quantity-portion," and the whole then squared. This is the method for the <term>Mūlajāti</term> <note>The "Square Root Class" of problems, which involve equations where the unknown is related to its own square root.</note> [33]

One-fourth of a herd of camels <note>original: mṛṣṭayūthasya; Variant B reads "elephants" (hasti). ## Now, the rule for the variety of problems involving square roots of the remainder:

> Take half the coefficient of the square root and square it; add this to the "visible" quantity <note>original: agra; the constant or known value in the equation</note>. Take the square root of this sum, then add half the coefficient. The square of this result is the total. If there are fractions involved, first apply the method for the variety of fractions <note>original: bhāga-jāti; referring to rules for simplifying fractions within the equation</note>. [40]

## Here are the illustrative problems:

> One-third of a herd of elephants and three times the square root of the remainder <note>original: śeṣa-pada; "pada" is often used synonymously with "mūla" or square root in this context</note> were on a mountain slope. In a lake, one male elephant <note>original: nāgo</note> was seen together with three female elephants. How many elephants are there here in total? [41]

> In a place free of insects, in a garden adorned with groves of various trees, there was an assembly of ascetics <note>original: yamīnām; self-controlled monks</note>. The square root of their total number was added to the square of the square root of those sitting at the base of the trees. [42]

> One-tenth of the remainder and its square root; then one-ninth [of the new remainder] and its square root; one-eighth and its square root; one-seventh and its square root; one-sixth and its square root; and one-fifth and its square root [are all accounted for]. [43]

> These groups of monks are skilled in the knowledge of poetry, discourse, law, logic, and philosophy; they are experts in debate, prosody, astronomy, sacred spells, rhetoric, and grammar. [44]

> Twelve possess the power of great penance; twelve others have minds skilled in the twelve-fold scriptures <note>original: dvādaśa-bhedāṅga; referring to the limbs of Jaina scripture</note>. Twelve more monks are seen. O Moon of Monks <note>original: muni-candra; a poetic address to a learned teacher</note>, how large is this assembly of ascetics? [45]

> Five times the square root of the total plus one-quarter [of the total] are on a mountain slope. Five-ninths of the remainder of the elephants are on a mountain peak. Five times the square root [of the total] are sporting in a forest of lotuses. Six elephants are seen here on the bank of the river. How many elephants are there in total? [46]

->Thus ends the variety of problems involving square roots of the remainder.<-

## Now, the rule for the variety of problems involving square roots of successive remainders:

> Divide the coefficient of the square root and the visible quantity <note>the known constant in the equation</note> by the portion remaining after the specified fractions are subtracted from one. Add any previously separated quantity to this new visible quantity. From this point, follow the previously established method for calculating the square root of a remainder. [47]

### Here are the illustrative problems:

> One bee <note>original: madhukara</note> was seen in the sky; one-fifth and one-fourth of the remainder were elsewhere. The square root of the [next] remainder [was also elsewhere], and two <gloss>1</gloss> were on a mango tree. How many bees were there in total? [48]

> Four lions were seen on a mountain. Of the successive remainders, fractions starting from one-tenth and ending in one-half [were elsewhere]. The square root [of the final remainder] and also four lions were seen in the forest. How many were they in total? [49]

> A pair of young does was seen in the forest; of the successive remainders, fractions starting from one-fifth and ending in one-half [were elsewhere]. Three times the square root of the [final] remainder of those does stayed on the bank of a lotus pond, along with exactly ten more. How large is the herd? [50]

->Thus ends the variety of problems involving square roots of successive remainders.<-

---

## Now, the rule for the variety of problems involving the square root of a part:

> Multiply the visible quantity by the fraction and set it down. By using the method for finding the square root of a known quantity, the result divided by the fraction becomes the total value <term>dhana</term><note>literally "wealth," but used here for the total quantity being sought</note> in the rule for square roots of parts. [51]

## Another rule for the same:

> Four times the visible quantity is divided by the fraction; add the square of the square-root's coefficient to this and take the square root [of the sum]. Add the coefficient to this, then halve the result, square it, and multiply it by the fraction. This will be the essence <note>the final answer</note>. [52]

## Here are the illustrative problems:

> Eight times the square root of the [total length of a] lotus stalk is submerged in the mud, one-third of it is in the water, and sixteen finger-breadths <term>aṅgula; a traditional unit of measure based on the width of a finger</term> are visible in the sky. Tell me the total height of the lotus stalk. [53]

> Nine times the square root of two-thirds of a herd of elephants, and again six times the square root of three-fifths of the remainder, were seen in the forest. Twenty-four other elephants with their temples wet with trickling musth <note>original: vigalad-dāna-dhārā; the fragrant secretion of elephants in heat</term> were also seen. How many elephants were there in total? [54–55]

> In a forest where tigers play, some wild boars were seen: one-half of the total were in the woods; twice the square root of one-tenth of the remainder went to a mountain; the square root of half of the [next] remainder, multiplied by three squared <note>original: trivarga; nine</note>, were on an embankment; and thirty-six <note>original: tat-guṇa-ṣatka; six times that multiplier of six</note> boars were also seen. Tell me the total number of them. [56]

->Thus ends the variety of problems involving square roots of a part.<-

---

## Now, the rule for the variety of problems involving the product of fractions:

> Multiply the known quantity <note>the visible constant</note> by four and by the denominator of the fraction [representing the product of parts]; subtract this from the square of the denominator <note>meaning the part of the total squared</note>. Add the square root of this result to the denominator, or subtract it, then divide by twice the denominator to find the total. [57]

<note>This rule provides a method for solving quadratic equations of the form $x - (a/b \cdot c/d) \cdot x^2 = K$, a type of problem where a portion of the total squared is considered.</note>

## Here is an illustrative problem:

> A farmer obtained twenty-four *vāhas* <term>a large measure of capacity for grain</term> from a heap of paddy <note>original: śāli-rāśi; a pile of unhusked rice</note>. This amount was what remained after one-eighth multiplied by one-sixteenth [of the square of the total] was removed. Tell me, how large was the original heap? [58]

---

<note>
¹ Another version reads: "with cheeks wet by water."
² Following this verse, all manuscripts include the following stanza, which is a simplified paraphrase of Verse 57:
</note>

**Another version of the rule:**

> Multiply the seen quantity by four and subtract it from the denominator... multiply by the denominator of the fraction... take the square root... add or subtract... half of that result, divided by the denominator, is the total value.

<header>Miscellaneous Calculations</header>

## Miscellaneous Calculations

One-sixteenth of a flock of peacocks, multiplied by its own part <note>original: svaguṇa-śrute; meaning the square of that fraction of the total</note>, stayed in a grove of Tamāla trees. Nine-sixteenths of the remainder, multiplied by itself <note>original: śeṣa-navāṃśaḥ svahṛtaḥ; interpreted in this mathematical context as the square of the remaining fraction</note>, plus ten more were also seen. How many peacocks were there in total? [59]

> One-twelfth of a pillar, multiplied by one-thirtieth part, is in the water. One-twentieth of the remainder, multiplied by sixteen and then by three, is in the mud. Twenty cubits <term>kara; a traditional unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term> are in the sky. O friend, tell me the measure of the total length of the pillar. [60]

->Thus ends the variety of problems involving the product of fractions.<-

### Now, the rule for the variety involving the square of a fractional part increased or decreased by a quantity:

Halve the denominator [of the fraction] after it has been divided by its own numerator. To this, add or subtract the given increased or decreased amount. Square that result. Subtract the known remaining quantity from that square and take the square root. That root is then added to or subtracted from the previous value <note>the halved denominator plus/minus the amount</note>. This final result, when multiplied by the denominator and divided by the numerator, gives the total quantity. [61]

->¹ This is an example of the variety involving a decrease.<- <margin>M <note>a specific manuscript reference</note> omits "decrease".</margin>

One-eighth of a herd of buffaloes, minus one, squared, is enjoying the forest. Fifteen were seen on a mountain grazing on grass. How many buffaloes are there in total? [62]

> One-tenth of a herd of elephants, minus two, multiplied by itself, plays in a forest of Sallakī <term>Boswellia serrata; Indian frankincense trees</term> trees. Six-squared <note>original: ṣaḍ-varga; thirty-six</note> elephants are wandering on a mountain. How many tuskers are there in total? [63]

->² This is an example of the variety involving an increase.<- <margin>M omits this heading as well as the following verse.</margin>

In a Jamun tree, one-fifteenth part [of a flock of peacocks] plus two, multiplied by itself, [and then] multiplied by two squared <note>original: dvikṛti-ghnāḥ; multiplied by four</note>...

Five other intoxicated peacocks are sporting in a mango tree. O friend, tell me the total measure of them all. [64]

->Thus ends the variety involving the square of a fractional part increased or decreased by a quantity.<-

### Now, the rule for the variety of the mixture of roots:

The square of the mixed sum <note>original: *miśra-kṛti*; referring to the sum of the square roots given in the problem</note>, decreased or increased by the known difference and divided by twice that same mixed sum, then squared, shall be the result. This is the procedure in the rule for the mixture of roots. [65]

->An example involving a statement of decrease:<-

The square root of a flock of pigeons, and also the square root of that same flock decreased by twelve—the sum <note>original: *yoga*</note> of these two roots is seen to be six pigeons. How large is that flock? [66]

In a group of pigeons <note>original: *pārāvatīya*</note>, the sum of the square roots of the total and of the total decreased by four cubed <term>catughana; 4³ = 64</term> is sixteen. How many birds are in that flock? [67]

->An example involving a statement of increase:<-

The square root <note>original: *pada*</note> of a group of royal swans <note>original: *rāja-haṃsa*</note> and the square root of that group increased by sixty-eight—the sum of these is the square of six diminished by two <note>6² - 2 = 34</note>. Say, how many swans <note>original: *marālaka*</note> are in that forest? [68]

->Thus ends the variety of the mixture of roots.<-

### Now, the rule for the variety of visible fractions:

When unity <term>rūpa; the number 1, representing the whole</term> is diminished by the fractional parts, and then divided by the product of the fractions, the quotient obtained becomes the essence <note>the total quantity</note> in the rule of visible fractions. [69]

## Miscellaneous Calculations

### Here are the problems:

One-eighth of a pillar is in the sand, and that portion is multiplied by one-eighteenth <note>The text suggests a nested calculation: (1/8) × (1/18) of the total</note>. Half of the pillar is seen <note>original: *dṛṣṭaṃ*. A footnote indicates that manuscripts B, M, and K read "in the sky" (*gagane*) instead of "seen"</note>. Tell me, what is the total length of the pillar? [70]

A fractional part of a herd of elephants—one-ninth divided by two and then multiplied by one-twenty-seventh—remains happily on the surface of the earth. Another third part of the herd, looking like a dark blue cloud, wanders on a mountain. O friend, tell me now the total measure of that elephant herd. [71]

Of a group of sages <note>original: *sādhūt-kṛti*; a collection or multitude of holy men</note>, the sixteenth part divided by three and then squared <note>original: *svaka-guṇitaḥ*; multiplied by itself</note> dwells in the interior of the forest. A quarter <term>pāda; literally a "foot," meaning 1/4</term> is on the mountain. Tell me quickly the total measure of them, you who have crossed the ocean-like section of miscellaneous calculations. [72]

->Thus ends the variety of visible fractions.<-

<meta>This page begins the fourth chapter of Mahāvīrācārya's *Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha*, transitioning from the complex fractions of Chapter 3 to the "Rule of Three" (Trairāśika), a foundational concept in Indian mathematics used for solving proportions.</meta>

# Chapter 4
## Practice of the Rule of Three

> Salutation to that Lord Vardhamāna <note>original: *śrī-vardhamānāya*; the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism, also known as Mahāvīra, the namesake of the author</note>, the friend of the three worlds, the sun of pure knowledge, who has shaken off all karmic bonds. [1]

From here on, we shall exemplify the Rule of Three, which is the fourth subject of treatment.

### Here is the rule-verse:

> In this Rule of Three, the fruit <term>phala; the known result associated with the argument</term> is multiplied by the requirement <term>icchā; the question or demand</term> and then divided by the argument <term>pramāṇa; the standard or measure of the initial proportion</term>. In the Inverse Rule of Three, this operation is reversed. [2]

### Problems in the first half.

> If a man travels six <term>yojanas; a unit of distance, roughly 7-9 miles</term> less a fourth part in three and a quarter days, tell me, how much does he travel in a year and a day? <note>Calculated as: (Argument: 3.25 days) -> (Fruit: 5.75 yojanas). (Requirement: 361 days) -> ?</note> [3]

> A lame man <note>original: *paṅguḥ*</note> travels one-eighth of a <term>krośa; 1/4th of a yojana</term> plus its own lash <note>original: *sva-pakṣmam*; possibly a very small unit or a poetic addition. A margin note indicates manuscripts P, K, and M read *sa* (with) instead of *swa* (own)</note> in seven and a half days <note>original: *vyardhāṣṭābhir*; literally "eight minus a half"</note>. Tell me here, what does he travel in three years divided into seven parts? [4]

> An insect travels one-fourth of an <term>aṅgula; a "finger-breadth" unit, approx 1.9 cm</term> in one-eighth of a day. In how many days will he reach the summit of Mount Meru from its base? <note>Mount Meru is the mythological axis of the world; in Jain cosmography, its height is often cited as 99,000 or 100,000 yojanas</note> [5]

> If a man earns one and a quarter <term>kārṣāpaṇa; a standard silver or copper coin</term> in three and a half days, in what time will that man earn a hundred <term>purāṇas; an old silver coin</term> and one <term>paṇa; a smaller unit of currency</term>? [6]

> A block of black aloe wood <note>original: *kṛṣṇāguru-taru-khaṇḍaṃ*; highly valued for incense</note> is twelve cubits <term>hasta; the length of a forearm</term> long and three cubits wide. It wears away by one *aṅgula* per day. What is the time required for this round block to be exhausted? <margin>B reads "with black aloe wood section"</margin> [7]

> If a load <term>vāha; a heavy measure of weight</term> of excellent royal beans <note>original: *rājamāṣa*; black-eyed peas or similar legume</note> mixed with a <term>droṇa</term>, an <term>āḍhaka</term>, and a <term>kuḍuba</term> <note>Units of volume: 1 drona = 4 adhaka = 16 kuduba</note> is bought for ten and a half gold coins, what can be bought for a hundred and a half gold coins? [8]
