# Rule of Three Practice

If one and an eighth <term>pala; a unit of weight, approx. 40 grams</term> of saffron are obtained for three and a half <term>purāṇas; an ancient silver coin</term>, what [amount] would be obtained there for one hundred <term>purāṇas</term>? [9]

For seven <term>palas</term> and a half of two <note>interpreted as 9.5 palas</note> of ginger, fourteen and a half <term>paṇas; a copper coin, usually 1/16th of a kārṣāpaṇa</term> <gloss>¹</gloss> were received. Tell me, friend, what [is the cost] for thirty-two and one-fifth <term>palas</term> of ginger? [10]

A man obtains sixteen and a half <term>palas</term> of silver for four and one-fifth <term>kārṣāpaṇas; a standard silver or copper currency unit</term>. What does he get for a myriad of <term>karṣas; a weight unit, 1/4th of a pala</term>? [11]

In this case, for eight <term>palas</term> of camphor less one-third [7 and 2/3 palas], one obtains five <term>dīnāras; a gold coin</term> along with various fractional parts. What does one get for a thousand <term>palas</term>? [12]

If a man buys five and one-fifth <term>palas</term> of ghee for three and a half <term>paṇas</term>, what [does he get] for a hundred <term>karṣas</term> plus one-eighth? [13]

Sixteen and a half pairs of cloth are obtained for five and a half <term>purāṇas</term>. Friend, tell me, what is obtained for sixty-one <term>karṣas</term>? [14]

There is a square cistern, eight cubits <term>hasta; the length of a forearm, approx. 18 inches</term> in depth, but empty of water. A mountain <gloss>²</gloss> has risen from its bank; and from the peak of that [mountain]— [15]

—a stream of water, clear as crystal and with a diameter of one <term>aṅgula; a finger-breadth, approx. 1.9 cm</term>, falls. [The stream] fills the interior of the cistern with water. What is the height of the mountain and the quantity of the water? [16]

<gloss>³</gloss> Two <term>droṇas; a measure of capacity or volume</term> of mung beans, nine <term>kuḍuvas; 1/4th of a prastha</term> of ghee, six <term>droṇas</term> of rice, eight pairs of clothes, six cows with their calves, and three [units] of gold... <note>This verse is continued on the next page.</note>

---

<gloss>¹</gloss> Manuscripts M and B read "to be obtained" <note>original: *labhyāḥ*</note> instead of "received."
<gloss>²</gloss> Manuscript B reads "has risen from the [bank]" <note>original: *samutthitā śi°*</note> with a slight spelling variation.
<gloss>³</gloss> Manuscripts B and K provide an entirely different verse for this stanza:

> Two <term>droṇas</term> of milk, nine <term>kuḍuvas</term> of ghee, six <term>droṇas</term> of sugar, eight *coca* fruits, six <term>khārīs; a large volume measure</term> of thick curd, and three <term>purāṇas</term>. O friend, tell me [the total of] that milk and other items [given] for three hundred and thirty-six [offerings] by the King giving to six temples of the Jinas <note>original: *jināgārake*; temples dedicated to the Jinas, the spiritual victors of Jainism</note> for the sake of a sacrificial rite.

<page-num>60</page-num>
# Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics

On the occasion of the solstice <note>original: "saṅkrānti"; a festival marking the sun's transition into a new zodiac sign, often a time for charity</note>, a king gave [gifts] to six Brahmins <term>dvija; literally 'twice-born', referring to the priestly class</term>. O friend, tell me quickly, what is the amount given in coins and such to three hundred and thirty-six [Brahmins]? [17]

->Thus ends the Rule of Three.<-

->An illustration of the Inverse Rule of Three.<-

With gold of ten <term>varṇaka; a unit of gold purity, similar to a karat</term> and a <term>guñjā; a tiny weight based on a seed, approx. 0.1 gram</term> in weight, there are one hundred pieces. How many pieces of gold will there be if the purity is nine <term>varṇaka</term>? [18]

There are three hundred pieces of Chinese silk <term>cīnāmbara</term>, each measuring six cubits <term>kara; the length of a forearm, approx. 18 inches</term> in width and [six] in length. O you who are learned in the method of inverse proportion, tell me: how many [pieces] would there be if the dimensions were three cubits and five cubits? [19]

->Thus ends the Inverse Rule of Three.<-

->An illustration of the Inverse Rule of Five.<-

In a collection of seventy pieces of Chinese cloth, each is nine cubits long and five cubits wide. Tell me, how many pieces of cloth would there be if the width and length were two and three cubits? [20]

->An illustration of the Inverse Rule of Seven.<-

From a large ruby <term>māṇikya</term> measuring four, nine, and eight cubits in width, length, and height [respectively], how many statues of the <term>Tīrthankaras; the 24 supreme teachers of Jainism</term> can be fashioned, each measuring two, six, and one cubit [in those same dimensions]? [21]

->An illustration of the Inverse Rule of Nine.<-

There is a stone slab measuring thirty-six, eight, and nine in width, length, and height. How many [smaller] slabs, suitable for a temple <term>caitya</term>, can be made from it, if each measures two, six, and one, and [the count is increased by] five and a half? [22]

->Thus end the Inverse Rules of Five, Seven, and Nine.<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of mathematical operations, moving from the Inverse Rule of Three to a specific application of the Rule of Three involving "progress and regress" (relative motion or net gain/loss). The previous page concluded the general Inverse Rules, and we now apply these principles to dynamic problems like a boat fighting a current or a lotus growing in a drying pond.</meta>

<page-num>61</page-num>

## Operations on the Rule of Three

### Rule for progress and regress— <note>original: "gati-nivṛttau sūtram"; literally "rule on movement and return"</note>

Divide the distance traveled and the distance returned by their respective times, and find the difference between them. Having established this "purified" daily movement <note>the net speed per day</note>, one should then proceed according to the method of the Rule of Three. [23]

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

A boat travels one-fifth of a *krośa* <term>krośa; a measure of distance, roughly 2 miles or 3.2 km</term> in three-sevenths of a day. Blown by the wind in the ocean <margin>¹ B and K manuscripts read: "At that time in the ocean"</margin>, it is pushed back one-ninth of a *krośa*. [24]

In what time will it travel one hundred *yojanas* <term>yojana; a long-distance measure, equal to 4 krośas, roughly 8-9 miles</term> reduced by three-fifths? O you who are as strong as Bāhubali <note>A figure of immense strength and wisdom in Jain tradition; here used as a respectful address to the student</note> in solving calculations for crossing the ocean, tell me! [25]

A man earns one and a quarter gold pieces in three and one-fifth days, but he spends one-fourth of a gold piece [during that time]. Additionally, he loses one-eighth of his own [total earnings] in five days reduced by two-fifths. In what time will he have a net gain of seventy? [26]

A scent-elephant <term>gandhebha; an elephant in its prime whose scent is said to attract bees and intimidate rivals</term>, whose temples are troubled by bees greedy for the scent of its rut-fluid, travels one-fifth of a *yojana* plus a half in six days reduced by two-fifths. It returns two-fifths of a *krośa* in three and a half days. Tell me, in what time will it reach one hundred *yojanas* reduced by half a *krośa*? [27]

In a pond filled with water, a lotus has grown ten *danḍas* <term>danḍa; literally 'a staff', a unit of length equal to 4 cubits or about 6 feet</term> high. It grows two and a half fingers <term>aṅgula; a finger-breadth, roughly 3/4 of an inch</term> in one and a half days. [28]

The water is discharged from the pond by a machine at the rate of two and one-twentieth fingers in one and a half days. The water also dries up due to the rays of the sun at the rate of one and one-fifth fingers per day. [29]

A turtle at the bottom pulls the stalk down five and a quarter fingers in three and a half days. In what time will the lotus be level with the water? [30]

---

<meta>This page concludes the "Motion and Return" section (relative speed and net gain) and introduces the Rule of Five, Seven, and Nine—what modern mathematicians call compound proportion. The snake problem on this page is a famous variation of the "snail in a well" puzzle, where progress is countered by the physical growth of the object itself.</meta>

<page-num>62</page-num>

<header>Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics</header>

A black king of snakes <note>original: "kṛṣṇāhīndro"</note>, thirty-two cubits <term>hasta; a cubit, approximately 18 inches or 45 cm</term> in length, enters a hole. In five-fourteenths <note>original: "pañcabhis saptamārdhaiḥ"; literally "five of half-sevenths"</note> of a day, it moves seven and a half digits <term>aṅgula; a digit or finger-breadth, roughly 3/4 of an inch</term> into the hole. But in one-quarter of a day, its tail grows by two and three-quarter digits. O crown-jewel of mathematicians <note>original: "gaṇakottaṃsa"</note>, tell me: in what time will the snake completely enter the hole? [31]

->Thus ends the section on Motion and Return.<-

### Rule for the Compound Proportion of Five, Seven, and Nine Quantities —

<note>1</note> After exchanging the "fruits" <note>phala; the results, such as interest or profit, are swapped between the two sets of data to solve for the unknown</note> between the two sides, one should multiply the quantities in each row. Divide the row containing the larger number of quantities by the row containing the fewer <note>original: "pṛthupaktimalpayā paṅktyā"</note>. For problems involving the buying and selling of living beings <note>such as livestock</note>, the same procedure applies to those quantities. [32]

### Here are the illustrative problems:

If for principals of two hundred, three hundred, and four hundred, the profits are fifty, sixty, and seventy *purāṇas* <term>purāṇa; an ancient Indian silver coin</term> [respectively in a certain time], what will be the total interest for one seeking profit over ten months? [33]

If the interest on eighty and a half gold pieces for one-third of a month is one and a half, what is the interest on ninety and three-quarters gold pieces for six months reduced by one-quarter <note>i.e., five and three-quarters months</note>? [34]

If a person obtains twenty gems for one hundred gold pieces of sixteen-point fineness <term>varṇaka; a unit of gold purity, similar to karats</term>, what will he obtain for two hundred and eighty-eight gold pieces of ten-point fineness? [35]

---

$^1$ The P manuscript reads the following variations:
**An alternative rule—**
> After swapping the result, divide the row with many quantities by the smaller row. For the buying and selling of horses and other animals, apply the same to their specific quantities.

**Another rule—**
> After swapping the result, divide the product of the larger row by the smaller row. In cases of buying and selling horses, swap the horses and the other factors accordingly.

The B manuscript gives only the latter of these stanzas with the following variation in the second quarter:

->...by multiplying the product of the larger row with the smaller row.<-

### Operations involving the Rule of Three

A man carrying nine *mānīs* <term>mānī; a measure of capacity or weight</term> of wheat for a distance of three *yojanas* <term>yojana; a measure of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles</term> receives sixty *paṇas* <term>paṇa; a copper coin</term> as his wage. What would be the wage for carrying one *kumbha* <term>kumbha; a large measure, typically equal to 20 mānīs</term> along with its container for a distance of ten *yojanas*? [36]

### Problems on Barter

If three *karṣas* <term>karṣa; a weight approximately equal to 12 grams</term> of musk <note>original: "kastūrī"</note> are obtained for eighteen gold coins <note>original: "kanakaiḥ"</note>, and two *karṣas* of camphor <note>original: "karpūra"</note> [are valued against something else], then for three hundred *karṣas* of musk, how many [gold coins] <gloss>1</gloss> <gloss>2</gloss> are obtained? [37]

If sixty jackfruits <note>original: "panasāni"</note> are obtained for eight [units], and eighty citrons <note>original: "mātuluṅgāni"</note> are obtained for ten *māṣas* <term>māṣa; a small weight or coin, usually 1/16th of a larger unit</term>, then for nine hundred jackfruits, how many citrons will be received? [38]

### Problems on the Sale and Purchase of Living Beings

Twenty horses <note>original: "turagā"</note>, each sixteen years of age, cost one hundred thousand gold coins. O leader of mathematicians, tell me: what is the cost here for seventy-seven horses that are each ten years old? [39]

If the price of nine young women <note>original: "aṅganānāṃ"</note>, each ten years of age, is three hundred gold pieces <note>original: "svarṇa"</note>, what would be the price for thirty-six women who are each sixteen years old? [40]

What is the interest on six hundred and ninety for ten months? Or, if two of these values are known, O mirror to the face of mathematicians, tell me: what is the time, and what is the principal? [41]

### Problem on the Rule of Seven

Two pieces of sandalwood <note>original: "śrīkhaṇḍa"</note>, with a width and length of three and four [units respectively], are worth eight gold pieces. How many [gold pieces] are for fourteen pieces that are six [units] in width and nine in length, with a thickness of one cubit <term>hasta; a cubit, approx. 18 inches</term>? [42]

### Thus ends the Rule of Seven.

## Fifth Chapter
## Mixed Operations <note>original: "mishraka-vyavahāra"</note>

> I bow for the sake of spiritual merit to the Jinas, the authors of the sacred path <term>tīrthakaras; enlightened teachers who establish the Jain faith</term> who have attained the four infinite perfections; to the Siddhas <term>perfected souls</term> of pure qualities, honored in the three worlds; to the venerable teachers <term>ācāryas</term>; to the preceptors <term>upādhyāyas</term> who have reached the far shore of the ocean of scripture and lead all worldly beings; and to the monks <term>sādhus</term>, who are a mine of all virtues and doers of good. [1]

Hereafter, we shall illustrate the fifth chapter, titled Mixed Mathematics <note>original: "mishra-gaṇita"</note>. It is as follows:

### Rule for the terms 'Conjunction' and 'Unequal Conjunction'—

> The operation of halving the sum and the difference of two quantities is known as Conjunction <term>sankramana; a method for finding two unknown numbers when their sum and difference are known</term>. Those who have reached the end of the ocean of mathematics call this Unequal Conjunction <term>vishama-sankramana</term> when it involves the division of remainders. [2]

### An Illustration here:

> Given a set of numbers where the sum is twelve and the difference is two, what are the two values? From that set, tell me what is the resulting Conjunction or Unequal Conjunction? [3]

### The Rule of Five <note>original: "pañcarāśika-vidhi"</note>

### Rule for calculating interest using the Rule of Five—

> The desired principal <term>icchā-rāśi</term> is multiplied by its own time and then by the known fruit <term>pramāṇa-phala; the known interest amount</term>. This product, when divided by the known time and the known principal <note>this refers to the standard units used to define the interest rate</note>, results in the desired interest in mathematics. [4]

### An Illustration here:

> If the interest on one hundred *purāṇas* <term>purāṇa; an ancient Indian silver coin</term> for three, five, or six months is [respectively] fifty, sixty, or seventy; then what is the interest to be gained for a period of six months <note>The student is expected to solve for each interest rate provided</note>? [5]

Three hundred <term>kārṣāpaṇas; a standard silver coin of ancient India</term> less half of eight [i.e., 296], and eight <term>paṇas; a copper coin usually valued at 1/16th of a kārṣāpaṇa</term>, are lent out. ### Rule for finding the Principal <note>original: "mūlānayana-sūtram"</note>—

The known principal <term>pramāṇa</term> multiplied by its own time and divided by its own fruit <note>the interest earned</note> should be divided by the desired time; the result, when multiplied by the desired fruit, shall be the desired principal. [10]

### Examples here:

In a loan of one hundred less half of five [97.5], someone receives five <term>purāṇas</term> as interest in two months less half a month [1.5 months]. Tell me, what is the principal required to get that interest? [11]

The interest on seventy for one and a half months is five and a half. In eight months less half a month [7.5 months], what is the principal that results in two and a half as interest? [12]

In three cases where the interest is nine, eighteen, and twenty-five <note>original: "pañca-kṛti"; the square of five</note> combined with one-fifth respectively, and the time for all is six months; what are the various principals [if the rate is based on the previously stated rule]? [13]

### Rule for finding the Time <note>original: "kālānayana-sūtram"</note>—

The principal <term>pramāṇa</term> multiplied by its time and divided by its own fruit and the desired [interest]; then, this result multiplied by the desired fruit and divided by the [desired] principal is called the Time by the wise. [14]

## Miscellaneous Problems

### Examples Here:

If the interest on seven hundred and fifty is twenty-eight over a period of eighty <note>This likely refers to a base unit of 80 months or a specific rate per 80</note>, tell me, friend, after calculating carefully, what is the time required to earn this? [15]

If for six hundred the interest is seen to be ninety-six, what is the time required for the sum of fifty-seven and three-fifths [57 3/5]? [17]

### Rule for the Exchange of Commodities <term>bhāṇḍa-pratibhāṇḍa-sūtram; literally "the rule for goods and counter-goods," used to calculate barter values</term>—

The quantity of the first commodity is divided by its own price, multiplied by the price of the exchange commodity, and then multiplied by the quantity of the desired commodity; this result gives the value for the exchange of goods. [18]

### Examples Here:

Eight <term>palas; a traditional Indian unit of weight, roughly 48 grams</term> of ginger were bought for six and a quarter <term>paṇas</term>. Five <term>palas</term> of long pepper were bought for nine <term>paṇas</term> less a quarter [8.75 <term>paṇas</term>]. [19]

If someone has eighty <term>palas</term> of ginger, O you who are learned in mathematics, think and tell me quickly: how many <term>palas</term> of long pepper can be bought in exchange? [20]

## Rules for Interest

Henceforth, we shall explain the specific rules for interest within the section on Miscellaneous Problems.

### Rule for Separating Principal and Interest from the Combined Sum <note>original: "mūla-vṛddhi-miśra-vibhāgāyana-sūtram"</note>—

Divide the combined sum <note>the total of principal plus interest</note> by one <term>rūpa; here meaning the integer one</term> added to the interest for the unit time. The result of this division is the principal; the combined sum minus that principal is the interest. [21]

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

If, at a rate of five percent <note>original: "pañcaka-śata", meaning 5 per 100</note>, one invests capital for twelve months, and the combined sum of the principal and its interest is forty-eight <note>original: "sāṣṭā catvāriṃśan", which literally means 48 with 8 (possibly 48 and 1/8); in this mathematical context, it refers to the "mixed sum" or total amount</note>, tell me, what are the principal and the interest? [22]

->**Again, the rule for separating the principal and interest from their combined sum—**<-

Multiply the interest for the given time <term>phala; the interest earned on the base principal</term> by the desired time and divide by the product of the base time and base principal. Add one to this result. Divide the total mixed sum <term>miśra; the combined total of principal and interest</term> by this value; the quotient should be known as the principal. [23]

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

If, at a rate of interest of two and a half per hundred, a certain amount of capital is lent for four months, and the lender receives a total combined sum of thirty-three, what would the original principal be? [24]

->**The rule for separating the time and the interest from their combined sum—**<-

Multiply the principal by its own base time, and divide by the product of the base interest and the desired principal. To this, add one. Divide the combined sum of time and interest by this result; the quotient is indeed the interest. [25]

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

At a rate of five percent, a capital of sixty is invested by someone seeking profit. Here, the time added to its own interest is twenty. What is the time? [26]

At a rate of three and a half per seventy <note>original: "ardha-trika-saptatyāḥ", likely meaning 3.5 per 70</note>, a principal of seven hundred and five <note>original: "pañcottara-sapta-śataṃ"</note> is invested. The sum of the time and the interest is eighty. What are the time and interest? [27]

At a rate of four less a half <note>3.5</note> per eighty-four, for two and a half months, the principal is four hundred. The combined sum of the time and the interest is thirty-six. Find the time and the interest. [28]

->**The rule for separating the principal and the time from their combined sum—**<-

Divide the base principal by its interest, then multiply by four times the combined sum <term>kāla-catur-vṛddhi; this refers to a specific step in solving quadratic equations</term>. This is subtracted from the square of the mixed sum. Take the square root of that result and perform the process of "concordant transformation" <term>saṅkramaṇam; a mathematical technique for finding two unknown quantities when their sum and another relationship—usually their difference—are known</term> with the mixed sum. [29]

# Mixed Operations

## Here is an illustration:

If the interest on 70 <note>original: "saptatyā"</note> is 4 <term>purāṇas; an ancient Indian denomination of silver coin</term>, and the time is 25 <note>original: "pañca-kṛti", the square of five</note>; if the combined sum <term>miśra; the total of principal and interest</term> is 45 and a quarter, tell me, what is the principal? [30]

On an investment of 63, what is the principal and for what time was it lent, if the interest obtained was 18 and the combined sum of the time and the principal is 66? [31]

The interest on 60 for one and a half months is seen to be 2 and a half <note>original: "pañcārdha", five-halves</note>. If the interest earned [on a separate loan] is 24, and the sum of the principal and the time is 60, [find the principal and the time]. [32]

## The rule for separating the principal, interest, time, and combined sum from their distribution:

The principal, multiplied by the interest of its own time and divided by the given time, is then multiplied by the interest-rate and divided by the other principal. From the square of the mixed sum, the square root of the remainder is taken, and the process of "symmetrical separation" <term>saṅkramaṇa; a mathematical process used to find two quantities when their sum and difference, or other related values, are known</term> is performed on the mixed sum. [33]

## Here is an illustration:

For a principal of 100 lent for one and a half months, [the rate is unknown]. However, for a principal of 30, the combined sum of the interest <note>original: "phala"</note> and the time <note>original: "kāla"</note> is 12 and a half. The interest itself is 5. [Find the time and the interest-rate]. [34]

## The rule for separating the principal, time, and interest from their combined sum:

Subtract the known quantity from the mixed sum to find the time; then, by adding one to the profit of that same amount <note>the interest on a unit of capital</note>, divide the principal. The mixed sum, when diminished by the principal and the time, results in the interest. [35]

## Here is an illustration:

In an investment at a rate of five percent <note>original: "pañcaka-śata", 5 per 100</note>, the specific amounts for time, principal, and interest are unknown. Their combined sum is 82 <note>original: "dvāśīti"</note>. What is the principal, and what are the time and interest? [36]

---

<note>original: "dvāśīti" (82). This form is found in the manuscripts, though the mathematically correct value for the problem should likely be 80 ("aśīti"); however, "aśīti" does not fit the poetic meter of the verse.</note>

# Rule for separating individual interests from a collective sum, given multiple principals and times:
One should divide the total sum of the interest <note>original: "phala-samāsa"</note> by the sum of the various principals each multiplied by its own time. Then, this quotient should be multiplied by each individual principal and its respective time to find the interest <term>vṛddhi; the "growth" or interest earned on a specific loan</term> for each. [37]

### Here is an illustration:
The principals lent out are 40, 30, 20, and 50. The periods of time <note>usually measured in months</note> are respectively 5, 4, 3, and 6. The total interest earned from all of these together is 34. [Calculate the interest for each loan.] [38]

# Rule for separating individual principals from a collective sum:
Multiply the total mixed sum of the principals by each individual interest and divide by its own time. Then, divide each of these by the sum of all such quotients to find the individual principals. <note>The text suggests dividing the mixed sum by the sum of the ratios of interest to time, then multiplying the parts.</note> [39]
<note>Footnote from original: The manuscripts read *छिन्द्यादंशान्* (divide the parts), which does not seem to be correct according to the commentator.</note>

### Here is an illustration:
The interests earned are 10, 6, 3, and 15; the time periods are 5, 4, 3, and 6 months respectively. The total sum of the principals <note>original: "mūla-samāsa"</note> is seen to be 140. [Find the individual principals.] [40]

In another case, the interests are 5, 8, 6, 10, and 16 and a half. The months are 5, 6, 7, 8, and 10 respectively. The total sum of the principals is 80. [Find the individual principals.] [41]

# Rule for separating individual time periods from a collective sum:
Divide the total mixed sum of the time periods <term>kāla-miśra; the combined total of several different durations</term> by the sum of the interests, each having been divided by its own principal. Multiply each quotient by the corresponding parts to find the individual durations of time. [42]

### Here is an illustration:
The principals are 40, 30, 20, and 50. The interests are 10, 6, 3, and 15. The total mixed sum of the time periods is 18. [Find the individual times.] [43]

When the interest <note>phala</note> on a known standard principal <note>pramāṇa-rāśi</note> is known, the interest on any desired principal <note>icchā-rāśi</note> [is calculated accordingly]...

<meta>This page continues the "Mixed Operations" section (Miśrakavyavahāra) of Mahāvīrācārya’s treatise. This page introduces more complex quadratic-style problems where the principal and its interest have been merged into a single "mixed sum," requiring the mathematician to work backward to find the original components using square roots.</meta>

<page-num>71</page-num>
<header>Operations on Mixed Quantities</header>

And having combined them, here is the rule for bringing about the separation of the interest <term>vṛddhi-vibhāga; the division or separation of the earned interest from the total amount</term> from that mixed sum of the standard quantity:

**The standard principal multiplied by its time is multiplied by the other time. To the mixed sum multiplied by that same [first product], add the square of half the other. The square root [of this sum], diminished by half the other and divided by the principal-time product, is the interest on the principal.** [44]
<note>This verse provides a geometric/algebraic solution to find the rate of interest when the sum of the principal and interest is known. In modern terms, it is solving a quadratic equation of the form $x^2 + px - q = 0$.</note>

### Here is an illustration:

The interest on a standard principal of one hundred for four months is unknown. That unknown interest, when added to its own principal <note>the "mixed sum"</note>, becomes twelve. The time for this transaction is twenty-five <note>five squared</note> months. [Calculate the interest and the principal.] [45]

The interest on a standard principal of eighty for three months is unknown. The mixed sum of the principal and its interest is eight less than its fifth part <note>original: "pañcama-bhāgena-ūna-aṣṭau", meaning $80 - (80/5) = 64$</note>. The time is one year. What are the principal and the interest? [46]

## Rule for separating components from a mixed sum when the interest earned is the same:

**The mixed sums are multiplied by each other's time. These are called the "parts." These parts, divided by the difference in time and multiplied by the difference in the mixed sums, allow one to know the principal.** [47]
<note>This rule applies to cases where different principals are lent for different times, but the resulting interest earned is identical for each.</note>

### Here is an illustration:

The mixed sums <note>principal + interest</note> are fifty, fifty-eight, and sixty-six. The periods of time are five, seven, and nine months respectively. Find the interest. [48]

A mathematician says that the mixed sums are thirty, thirty-one and two-thirds, and thirty-three and one-third. Another is thirty-five. [49]

A certain man lent to four people for periods of three, four, five, and six months. What would be the principal for each? O calculator, tell me quickly! [50]

## Rule for separating components from a mixed sum when the principal and time are the same:

**The mixed sums are multiplied by each other's interest. These are called the "parts." The wise say that the principal is obtained when these are divided by the difference in interest.** [51]

### Here is an illustration:

In three separate instances, the mixed sums of the time and the principal are twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-six. The interests earned in these cases are six, ten, and fourteen respectively. What is the principal here, assuming the rate of interest remains the same? [52]
<note>The Sanskrit "eka-tri-ṣañ-miśrita-viṃśatiḥ" literally means "one, three, and six mixed with twenty," representing the values 21, 23, and 26.</note>

The mixed sums of the time and principal are thirty-five, thirty-seven, and thirty-nine <note>original: "nava-yuta-triṃśat", meaning nine joined with thirty</note>. The interests earned on these are twenty, twenty-eight, and thirty-six respectively. What is the principal? [53]

**Rule for finding the principal in two separate investments:**

Calculate the two interests <term>phala; the result or fruit of an investment</term> for a single unit of money <term>rūpa; literally 'form,' representing the number one or a single coin</term> over the desired periods of time. Divide the [difference between the two] given principals by the difference between those two interests. The result is the principal [originally sought]. [54]

### Here is an illustration:

A certain principal was lent out at an interest rate of six per hundred, and then again at nine per hundred. Over three months, the total interest obtained was eighty-one. What was the principal in each case? [55]

A principal was lent out at a rate of three percent per month. After eight months, the interest was eighty. What would the principal be for a duration of two months [to earn the same interest]? [56]

**Rule for finding the time for the discharge of principal and interest:**

The principal multiplied by its own time and then by the interest, then divided by the standard principal and standard time, gives the interest for the installment <term>skandha; literally 'shoulder' or 'section,' here referring to a portion or installment of a debt</term>. The principal and the time are then found from the interest as explained previously. [57]

### Here is an illustration:

One must pay five for every seventy <note>as interest</note> per month. In two months, eighteen must be paid...

**Another rule for finding the principal in two separate investments:**
> Having calculated the interest of the two investments from the desired time, the wise man should know the principal by dividing the difference [of the mixed sums] by the difference [of the interests].

# Mixed Operations
<note>original: "Miśraka-vyavahāra"; this chapter deals with complex interest, combinations of principal and interest, and problems involving multiple stakeholders.</note>

The total amount <term>skandha; the combined sum of principal and interest</term> is eighty-four. What then is the principal, and what is the time of discharge? [58]

The monthly interest on sixty is five. The principal is thirty-five. In three months, the total amount <note>original: "skandha"</note> becomes fifteen. What is the time required for this? [59]

## Rule for separating various principals when the interests are equal

One should divide the mixed sum — which has been multiplied by its own time — by the sum of the various principals as multiplied by their respective times and divided by their respective interests. The results are the principals and interests as determined before. [60]
<note>This rule provides a method for dividing a total sum of money into different investments such that each portion earns the same amount of interest over a specific period.</note>

->Here is an illustration:<-

The interest rates on three separate investments are two, six, and four per hundred respectively. The mixed sum of the capitals is four thousand four hundred. If the interests earned on these over two months are equal, what are the respective principals? [61]

The interests on three sums are three per hundred, five per hundred, and seventy-five divided by four <note>original: "pāda-ūna-catuṣ-ṣaṣṭi", literally 64 less a quarter, but mathematically interpreted in this context as part of a fractional rate</note> per hundred. Their total sum is nine hundred thousand. Over three months, they earn equal interest. [What are the principals?] [62]

## Rule for arriving at the principal from the time of discharge

Divide the total amount <note>original: "skandha"</note> by its own time, then multiply by the discharge time. Divide this by the interest on one unit <term>rūpa; the number one, representing a single coin</term> for the discharge time, increased by one. The result is the principal. [63]

->Here is an illustration:<-

In a transaction where the interest is five per hundred, a total amount <note>original: "skandha"</note> of eight was given after two months. If the debt was discharged over sixty months, what would the principal be? [64]

One person gives a total amount of twelve in twelve days, where the interest rate is two and two-fifths...

If the interest on one hundred is three, what is the principal that is released after ten months? [65]

## Rule for dividing a mixed sum when the final amounts (principal plus interest) are to be equal

The mixed sum <note>The total capital to be distributed among various borrowers.</note> should be divided by the sum of the quotients obtained by dividing one by [one] increased or decreased by its own interest <note>original: "sva-phala"; the interest earned on a unit principal for the given time.</note>. The results are the equal final amounts. These, when multiplied by the respective quotients mentioned before, give the individual principals. [66]
<note>This rule is used when a lender wants to distribute a sum of money among different people at different interest rates such that, after a set time, every borrower returns the exact same total amount (Principal + Interest).</note>

->Here is an illustration:<-

A total sum of eight thousand five hundred and twenty is lent out at interest rates of three, five, and eight per hundred. If the amounts to be returned after five months are equal, [what are the three individual principals?] [67]

[Four thousand two hundred and fifty] is divided into three parts. The monthly interest rates on sixty are three, six, and eight respectively. After two months, the amounts <note>Principal plus interest.</note> are found to be equal. [What are the principals?] [68]

A mixed sum of thirteen thousand seven hundred and forty is lent out at rates of two, five, and nine per hundred respectively. After four months, the amounts—consisting of the principal along with the interest—are equal. [Find the portions.] [69]

The interest rates are one and a half, two and a half, and three per eighty <note>original: "sa-ekārdhaka" (1.5), "pañcārdhaka" (2.5), and "ṣaḍardhaka" (3.0).</note>. In eight months, the total sum of three thousand six hundred and forty-six <note>original: "ṣaḍ-adhikā catvāriṃśac-ca ṣat-kṛti-śatāni"; 6 plus 40 plus (6 squared times 100) = 46 + 3600 = 3646.</note> is to be divided such that the principals plus interest are equal. [70]

## Rule for finding the time and the sum in a debt involving a series of payments

The principal is found by multiplying the sum of the series by the principal [of the rate] and dividing by the total sum <term>skandha; here referring to the total of a specific series of interest payments</term>... <note>This verse describes a complex calculation for debt discharge when interest is paid in installments or follows an arithmetic progression.</note> [71]

->Here is an illustration:<-

Someone lends sixty at an interest rate of five per hundred. [The payments are made in installments] starting from the seventh day of the first month, increasing by fractions of three-fifths of a month... [72]

...the sum of that series, measured by one-seventh of sixty, having been given, he also gave the interest on that seventh part. [Find the time and the total.]

## Mixed Operations

What is that <term>interest</term><note>Sanskrit: *vriddhi*</note>, what would be the <term>time</term><note>Sanskrit: *kala*</note>, and when would the discharge of that debt occur? [73½]

Someone lent an amount of eighty at a rate of five percent [per month].
The installments paid toward the debt follow an <term>arithmetic progression</term><note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.</note> starting with eight and increasing by eight, with the number of payments being one-eighth of that eighty <note>This implies 10 installments (80 / 8 = 10).</note>.
Having paid the principal, and from that money starting at eight and increasing by eight, for every half-month... [75]
...he pays the interest. O friend, after calculating, tell me the exact measure of the principal, the interest, and the time of discharge. [76]

### Rule for Unified Calculation

Divide the sum of the total interests by the sum of the monthly interests; the result is the <term>desired time</term>. 
The result obtained by multiplying the standard time by the total interest, and then dividing by the total principal [gives the interest rate]. [77½]

### Here is an illustration:

A total of four hundred is increased by two, three, and five [per hundred] <gloss>as stated</gloss> for that four hundred.
The months [of the loans] are five, four, and two or three respectively. What is the single, unified time for this collection of loans? [78½]

Thus ends the regulation of interest in the chapter on Mixed Operations.

### Proportional Distribution 

From here on, we shall explain the mathematics of <term>proportional distribution</term><note>Sanskrit: *prakṣepa-kuṭṭīkāra*; the method of dividing a whole into parts based on specific proportions or fractions.</note> within Mixed Operations.

The rule for distribution is this: The mixed sum <note>The total amount to be divided.</note> is divided by the sum of the various fractions [representing the shares]. The result is then multiplied by each individual fraction to find the specific shares. This is what the wise call the method of distribution. [79½]

### Here is an illustration:

A quantity of gold weighing twice sixty <note>120 units.</note> is to be divided into shares of one-half, one-third, one-fourth, and one-sixth.
O mathematician, tell me quickly: what are the individual shares for these four servants? [80½]

->**The Offering of Lotuses**<-

Having taken lotuses, a pious <term>Shravaka</term><note>A Jain layperson; literally "a listener."</note> then entered the temple of the <term>Jinas</term><note>Also known as Tirthankaras, the 24 great spiritual teachers of Jainism who have "conquered" the cycle of rebirth.</note>. ### Rule for calculating the result of desired multipliers—

The principal is divided by the remaining parts and multiplied by the multipliers; these results are then added together to form the <term>sum of the parts</term>. The total wealth is multiplied by each individual part and divided by that sum; the result is the individual share. [87½]

### Another rule for this same purpose—

Multiply the individual shares by their respective multipliers. Having taken the sum of these results, use the <term>Rule of Three</term><note>Sanskrit: *Trairāśika*; a mathematical method for finding an unknown fourth value (x) when three values (a, b, c) are known, such that a/b = c/x.</note> to declare the final fruit. [88½]

### Another rule for this same purpose—

The shares are multiplied by their own results and their own multipliers; with these, the remainder is calculated as before. The desired result is correctly determined through the Rule of Three. [89½]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

A man who understands the meaning of mathematical calculations bought fruits—pomegranates, mangoes, and wood-apples—at the rates of three for two, five for three, and seven for five <term>Manakas</term><note>A specific unit of weight or measure used in ancient India.</note> respectively. [90 ½]

The number of mangoes bought is triple that of the wood-apples, and the pomegranates are six times the wood-apples. O friend, having bought them for seventy-six <term>Panas</term><note>A copper coin used as a standard currency unit.</note>, bring them here quickly! [91 ½]

->**The Anointment of the Exalted Jina**<-

A devotee performed the ritual anointment of the image of the <term>Jina-pungava</term><note>Literally "Bull among the Jinas," a title of great respect for the Tirthankara.</note> with pots of curd, clarified butter, and milk. the respective amounts of curd, clarified butter, and milk. Here, there are twenty-four palas of clarified butter, sixteen palas of milk, and thirty-two palas of curd distributed among them. [94 ½]

->**The Wages of the Horsemen**<-

The daily wage for a man who is a horseman is three <term>Puranas</term><note>An ancient silver coin.</note>. There were sixty-five such men in total, but some of them deserted the troop. The total money [to be distributed among those remaining] is given. [95 ½]

Ten units were given to each of the men who remained present. O friend, consider and tell me: how many remained present, and how many deserted? [96 ½]

### The Rule for Proportional Distribution with Added or Subtracted Quantities:

The total sum is to be decreased by the "additional" values or increased by the "deficient" values. From the remainder, the operation of <term>Praksepaka</term><note>Proportional distribution or "alligation"; a method for dividing a whole into parts based on specific ratios.</note> is to be performed. Then, the previously subtracted amounts are added back, or the added amounts are subtracted. [97 ½]

---

The first man has one share; then the subsequent men have shares that increase in a doubled progression <note>i.e., 1, 2, 4, 8...</note>. There are four such men. If the total sum to be distributed among them is sixty-seven, what is the share of each? [98 ½]

Starting from the first, multiplied by one and a half, then by three, and with one as the common difference <term>Rūpottara</term><note>The fixed amount added to each successive term in a mathematical sequence.</note>, a total is to be divided. Tell me the shares of these four people which sum to seventy-eight. [99 ½]

The shares are multiplied by one and a half starting from the first, with two and a half as the common difference. The sum of the five shares is fifty-one and three-quarters <note>Original: "fifty-one increased by one and three-quarters of a part."</note>. [100 ½]

The shares are multiplied by two and a half from the first, with a common difference of four. A total of four hundred less fifteen <note>385</note> is divided among four men. [101 ½]

### Rule for finding the price, the equal amount of wealth, and the wealth of the eldest person ---

The wealth of the eldest person should be increased by one; this is then multiplied by the selling rate and decreased by one. To find the wealth of the eldest in a purchase scenario, one should perform the calculation in reverse. [102 ½]

->**Here is an illustrative problem:**<-

The initial capitals of several men are two, eight, and thirty-six. There are six men in total, and the final remainder for each is six. Having bought and sold at the rate of one and a half, they all became possessed of equal wealth. [103 ½]

Three men possessed one and a half, a half, and two <term>Dinars</term><note>A gold coin or unit of currency.</note> respectively. Having conducted buying and selling at a rate of five-halves <gloss>divided by</gloss>, they became possessed of equal wealth. [104 ½]

The amount of equal wealth is forty-one, and the final remainder is six. O mathematician, tell me quickly: what is the wealth of the eldest, and what were the initial capitals? [105 ½]

Where the equal wealth amounts to thirty-five <term>Dinars</term>, and the final remainder is four, O mathematician, tell me what the wealth of the eldest is. [106 ½]

### Rule for finding the price and equal wealth when the final remainder is a fraction ---

Using the equal wealth and the final remainder, the selling and buying rates are found as before. When the final remainder is a fraction, the results are multiplied by the square of the denominator to find the equal wealth through proportion. [107 ½]

->**Again, here is the rule for arriving at equal wealth when the final portion is a different fraction:**<-

The denominator of the eldest person's share is multiplied by two. This is then increased by the denominator of the final portion. The selling price is multiplied by the final value. Subtract one, multiply by all the denominators, and this provides the ratio for the purchase quantity. [109 ½] <note>This technical rule provides a method for solving indeterminate equations where participants start with different fractional amounts of a commodity and must end with equal cash after selling their stock.</note>

->**Here is an illustrative problem:**<-

Taking a half, two-thirds, and three-quarters as their respective shares, and having bought and sold, they all ended with equal wealth amounting to five and a half and one-third <note>5 + 1/2 + 1/3, or 5 5/6</note>. [110 ½]

->**Rule for arriving at a desired number when there is a given multiplier and a given quantity to be given away:**<-

Multiply the last term by its own multiplier and add the penultimate term. Divide the result by that penultimate term; the value obtained shall be the original quantity. [111 ½] <note>This rule describes a reverse-calculation method used for problems where a quantity changes at several stages (like doubling or tripling) and a fixed amount is removed at each stage.</note>

The number of flowers became double at the first face, triple at the second, fourfold at the third, and fivefold at the fourth. At each face, he offered five lotuses. What was the initial number of lotuses? [113 ½]

The multipliers are fractions of two, three, and four, as well as five and a half; the flowers given to the <term>Arhats</term><note>The "Worthy Ones" or enlightened beings in Jainism.</note> by the devotees with devotion are three, five, seven, and eight. [114 ½]

# The Chain-Pulverizer Method <note>original: "Vallikā-kuṭṭīkāraḥ." A 'pulverizer' (kuṭṭaka) is a mathematical method for solving indeterminate equations by breaking numbers down into remainders. 'Vallikā' refers to a 'creeper' or 'chain' because the quotients are written in a vertical column resembling a climbing vine.</note>

Henceforth, we shall explain the mathematics of the Chain-Pulverizer. Regarding this Pulverizer:

## The Rule-Verse for the Chain Method—

> Having divided the quantities by each other, discard the first quotient. Place the remaining quotients one below the other in a column. Below these, place an "optional multiplier" <term>mati</term> <note>original: "mati-guṇam"; an auxiliary number chosen by the mathematician to help solve the equation</note> and then the remainder, which is added or subtracted depending on whether the number of quotients is even or odd. Multiply the number above by the one below and add the one below that. By this process of "moving upward," the results for the two unknowns are found. The divisor of the larger remainder is used to find the final values. [115 ½]

->**Here is an illustrative problem:**<-

> The branches are bent low with the weight of many fruits and flowers: Jambu, lime, plantain, betel-nut, jackfruit, date, palm, <term>hintāla</term> <note>a species of marshy palm</note>, <term>tālī</term> <note>the corypha palm</note>, <term>punnāga</term> <note>the nutmeg tree</note>, and mango. The air is filled with the buzzing of wandering bees and the various calls of parrots and cuckoos near the lotus ponds. Exhausted travelers, seeking relief from their weariness, have entered this pure forest grove with delighted hearts. [116 ½]

> There were 63 heaps of plantains <note>original: "kadali-phalānām"</note>. After seven fruits were taken from each heap and the remainder was divided among 23 travelers, nothing remained. Tell me, you who know the truth, what was the quantity in a single heap? [117 ½]

> Again, there were 12 heaps of pomegranates <note>original: "dāḍimānāṃ"</note>. After five fruits were taken from each heap and the remainder was divided among 20 travelers (less one, i.e., 19), nothing remained. Tell me the quantity in a single heap. [118 ½]

Seeing the heaps of fruits, a traveler makes a group of 31 heaps, then removes three...

## Miscellaneous Calculations <note>original: "Miśraka-vyavahāraḥ." This section deals with a variety of mathematical problems that do not fall into a single category, often presented as riddles.</note>

-> If the remainder is multiplied by seventy and then [something] by three mixed <note>The text here is slightly fragmented in its mathematical expression</note>, tell me the single quantity that is cleanly divisible. [119 ½] <-

In a forest, there were piles of pomegranates. When divided by twenty-one travelers <note>original: "trayassaptabhiḥ," literally three-times-seven</note>, the remainder is one. When divided by nine, the remainder is seven. When divided by five or eight, the remainder is two. Oh mathematician <note>term: "guṇaka," literally a calculator or multiplier</note>, tell me the quantity of these piles. [128 ½]

A quantity is divided by nine and increased by two; then [that part is] multiplied by five and increased by four; then divided by six and eight. When seven travelers each take one, four [of something] remain. Tell me the measure of this. [129 ½]

## Rule for arriving at the original quantity from the divisions of the remaining parts—

The product of the remainder and the part is added to its own remainder, and this sum is multiplied by the denominator. This process is repeated for as many parts as there are, and the results are the divisors of those remainders. [130 ½] <note>This rule describes the "reverse" method for solving problems where fractions of a remainder are taken repeatedly.</note>

-> Here is an illustrative example: <-

A man brought mango fruits. First, he took one for himself, and then [took] half of what remained. After his eldest son had gone, the youngest son took half of what was left there. Then another person [did the same]. [131 ½]

A pure man, having entered a Jain temple <note>original: "Jaina-bhavana"</note> of three stories, first worshipped at the foot <note>original: "pāde." The translator notes that some manuscripts say "pādau" (feet) or "keśān" (hair)</note> of the Jina <note>term: "Jina," meaning "Conqueror," an epithet for the great spiritual teachers of Jainism</note> with one flower. He then offered one-third of the remainder in the first section, and similarly in the second and third sections. [132 ½]

From the two-thirds of the remainder [after those offerings], he took two-thirds of those two parts, and then from those thirds, having worshipped the twenty-four Tirthankaras <note>term: "Tirthankaras," the twenty-four supreme Ford-makers or spiritual guides of the Jain faith</note>, he departed, purified of spirit. [133 ½]

## The Complex Pulverizer

Henceforth, we shall explain the Complex Pulverizer <note>term: "Viṣama-kuṭṭīkāra"; a variation of the pulverizer method used when the conditions or the remainders are non-uniform.</note>.

**Rule** for the Complex Pulverizer—

> The two denominators, multiplied by a chosen number <note>term: "mati"; an auxiliary number chosen by the mathematician's own intelligence to facilitate the division</note>, are added to or subtracted from the additive, and then multiplied by the quantity. When the pulverizer is fractional, this is declared to be the multiplier. [134 ½]

-> Here is an illustrative example: <-

> A quantity is multiplied by six and increased by ten; when divided by nine, there is no remainder. Likewise, [the quantity multiplied by the multiplier] is decreased by ten [and divided by nine with no remainder]. Tell me quickly, what are those two multipliers? <note>note: original: "guṇakau"; manuscript variant B reads "guṇakārau," both meaning multipliers.</note> [136 ½]

## The General Pulverizer

**Rule** for the General Pulverizer <note>term: "Sakala-kuṭṭīkāra"; the complete or universal method for solving linear indeterminate equations of the form ax + c = by.</note>—

> Divide the dividend, the divisor, and the remainder mutually <note>This refers to the Euclidean algorithm of successive division.</note>. The first quotient is to be set aside. At the end of the chain, having placed the chosen number and the remainder, multiply from the bottom upwards by the quotient above it and add the number below. Whether the number of quotients is even or odd, multiply by the positive or negative signs. For the positive and negative remainders, multiply the divisor of the greater remainder by the difference between the remainders and add the greater remainder... [131 ½]

-> Here is an illustrative example: <-

> One hundred increased by seventy is the additive; thirty-eight is the number to be added <note>note: This word problem involves solving for a multiplier that satisfies a specific remainder when divided by 201.</note>. When divided by two hundred and one, what would the multiplier be in this case? [137 ½]

> Thirty-five is the first number, and there are sixteen terms increasing by three which serve as divisors. The remainders, starting from thirty-two, increase by one and then by three. What are the multipliers for the positive and negative cases? [138 ½]

### Rule for separating the roots and mixed quantities of larger and smaller amounts—

> Subtract the product of the smaller result and the larger divisor from the larger quantity. The remainder divided by the square of the result is the larger portion; the other is the inverse of the multiplier. [139 ½]

***

<note>1: Manuscript B reads "multipliers" (guṇakārau).</note>

### Here is an illustrative example:

> The combined price of nine citrons <note>term: "mātuluṅga"; the *Citrus medica*, a large fragrant citrus fruit</note> and seven fragrant wood-apples <note>term: "kapittha"; the *Limonia acidissima*, often used in rituals and medicine</note> is one hundred and seven. [140 ½]
> 
> Furthermore, the combined price of seven of the same citrons and nine wood-apples is one hundred and one. [141 ½]
> 
> O mathematician <note>term: "gaṇaka"; a traditional title for a person skilled in calculation and astronomy</note>, tell me quickly the prices of the citron and the wood-apple after correctly calculating them separately. [142 ½]

### Rule for distributing the mixture of multiple quantities and their mixed prices—

> From the given total value, subtract the results of multiplying the chosen quantities [by their rates]. The remainder is divided by the result of the chosen multiplier. These values, when combined with the denominators and halved, shall be the individual prices. <note>This rule describes a method for solving simultaneous linear equations of the form $ax + by = c$.</note> [143 ½]

### Here is an illustrative example:

> Here, citrons, plantains, wood-apples, and pomegranates are mixed together. The first group contains twenty-one [fruits]; the second has twice as many [as a chosen number]; [144 ½]
> 
> The third group has twenty fragrant fruits, and the fourth has twenty-three. The sum of their prices is seventy-three. What is the quantity of each fruit and what is the price? [145 ½]

### Rule for finding combined quantities when the smallest price is used—

> Subtract the smallest quantity [at its rate] from the total price. Divide the remaining value by the difference of the rates of the commodities. Having created as many parts as desired, the price less that amount will be the price of the lowest commodity. <note>This rule pertains to the "Hundred Fowls" problem type, an indeterminate equation where one must find integer solutions for buying a fixed number of items for a fixed total cost.</note> [146 ½]

### Here is an illustrative example:

> Three peacocks are bought for two [coins]; four pigeons for three; five swans for four; and eight cranes <note>term: "sārasa"; the Indian Sarus crane, often referenced in poetic and mathematical contexts</note> for five. [147 ½]

# Calculations regarding Mixtures <note>original: "Miśrakavyavahāraḥ"; this chapter deals with "alligation" or the mathematics of mixing quantities with different values.</note>

O friend, in a case where there is a half-rate, after buying birds for fifty-six <term>paṇas</term> <note>a copper coin used as a standard denomination of currency</note> and being told to bring seventy-two [birds], he gave only the principal. Quickly calculate and tell me: how many birds were bought for how many <term>paṇas</term>? [149]

Five <term>palas</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 40-50 grams</note> of ginger are obtained for three <term>paṇas</term>, eleven of long pepper for four, and one of black pepper for eight. From sixty <term>paṇas</term>, quickly bring sixty-eight [of these items in total]. [150]

**Rule for finding the quantities of desired objects using desired parts and desired prices—**

The prices are multiplied by the results [quantities], and then the difference between the desired multipliers is calculated. This is then swapped and placed in two positions, multiplied by one's own wealth and the chosen multiplier. The remaining operation is the calculation of the projected parts. [151]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

Five pigeons are bought for three <term>paṇas</term>, seven cranes for five, nine swans for seven, and three peacocks for nine. [152]

For the sake of the prince’s amusement, bring one hundred [birds] for one hundred [coins]. Being thus commanded and sent, what must be given for which [bird]? [153] <note>This is a variation of the famous "hundred birds" problem found in many ancient mathematical traditions.</note>

**Rule for finding the quantities of commodities using the inverse of the prices¹—**

Take the difference between the sum of the prices and the sum of the commodities. Then, divide by the differences between the specific commodity prices. When the transition is made, the two prices are found. These commodities, when placed in the difference of the commodity-sum, result in the inverse of those two prices. This rule, which delights learned men who ask questions, was spoken by the Lord of the Jinas <note>original: "Jinendroditam"; likely referring to Mahavira, the 9th-century Jain mathematician who wrote this text.</note>. [154]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

What is the individual price of one [unit] of sandalwood and one of aloe-wood? The mixture of both is twenty <term>palas</term>, and the [total] price is one hundred and four <term>paṇas</term>. [155]

In a certain time, through an exchange of rates, the total becomes sixteen hundred <term>paṇas</term> <note>a copper coin used as a standard denomination of currency</note>. Tell me separately the products of those two rates, six and eight. [156]

### Rule for calculating the distance in yojanas traveled by the horses of the Sun's chariot in a desired combination—

The total distance <note>original: "yojanas"</note> divided by the total number of horses provides the base distribution; these, when multiplied by the number of horses in a harness, give the distance traveled by each individual horse. [157]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

The Sun's chariot is said to have seven horses, yet only four horses pull the yoke at any one time. If the chariot travels a total distance of seventy <term>yojanas</term> <note>a Vedic measure of distance, roughly 8–15 kilometers</note>, how far has each horse actually traveled? [158]

### Rule for finding the wealth in each person's hand from the sum of the remainders after subtracting each person's individual wealth—

One should divide the sum of the reported values by the total number of men minus one. The result is the total wealth of all the men combined. From this total wealth, subtract the amounts stated by each person to find the wealth held in each individual's hand. [159]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

Four merchants were once asked separately by a tax collector <note>original: "śāulkika," an official who collects customs or tolls</note>, "What is the value of your goods?" To hide the true value of their own wealth, the first of these excellent merchants spoke thus: [160]

"Excluding my own wealth, the sum of the others' is twenty-two." The next said, "Twenty-three." Then the third said, "Twenty-four," and the fourth said, "Twenty-seven." O friend, if they all have their own specific wealth, tell me the individual value of the goods held by each merchant. [161-162]

### Rule for arriving at equal wealth by exchanging a desired number of gems with one another—

Multiply by the total number of men and give that amount; after subtracting that from the goods, the remainder—multiplied mutually and setting aside one's own—gives the price of the gems. [163]

### Here is an illustrative example:

The first person has six sapphires <term>śakranīla</term> <note>literally "Indra’s blue," a high-quality sapphire</note>; the second has seven emeralds <term>marakata</term>; and the third has eight diamonds <term>vajra</term>. Each gives one of their own gems to each of the other two men, and as a result, they all come to possess equal wealth. [164]

In another instance, the first has sixteen sapphires; the second has ten emeralds; and the third has eight diamonds. If they each give two of their gems to the others, they achieve equality in wealth. [165]

Tell me, for these three men in both cases, what are the respective prices of those sapphires, emeralds, and diamonds? [166]

## Rule for finding the original capital based on purchase, sale, and profit—

Multiply the purchase rate by the combined value and divide by the sale rate. From the resulting figure, subtract one. The profit divided by this value gives the original capital <term>mūlyam</term>. [167]

### Here is an illustrative example:

A merchant buys seven units <term>prasthas</term> <note>a dry measure of capacity</note> for three coins, and sells five units for nine coins. What would be the profit, or indeed the loss, relative to the original wealth? [168]

# Calculations Regarding Gold

From here on, we shall explain the "Gold Distribution" <term>suvarṇa-kuṭṭikāra</term> <note>The term "kuṭṭikāra" refers to a "pulverizer" or algebraic method used here to solve for unknown values in gold alloys</note>.

## Rule for calculating the fineness of a mixture from various grades of gold—

The sum of the products of each piece of gold's weight and its fineness <term>varṇa</term> <note>a measure of gold purity, similar to the modern "carat"</note> should be divided by the total weight of the combined gold. The result is known as the resulting fineness of the gold <term>heman</term>. [169]

## Here is an illustrative example:

There is one piece of gold of weight one, one of weight two, one of purity three <term>varṇa</term> <note>varṇa refers to the "color" or purity of gold, similar to the modern carat system</note>, two pieces of purity four, four pieces of weight five, seven pieces of purity fourteen, and eight pieces of purity fifteen <note>original: tri-guṇita-pañca, or "three times five"</note>. [170]

When all these are combined and cast into the fire, what is the resulting purity of the mixture? And when this mixed gold is distributed based on the original weights, what is the value for each individual piece? [171 ½]

### Formula for determining the desired purity of various gold pieces—

Multiply each individual weight of gold by its respective purity. Divide the sum of these products by the total weight of the mixed gold. The resulting quotient should be understood as the purity for each part respectively. [172 ½]

## Here is an illustrative example:

If twenty <term>paṇas</term> <note>a unit of weight or currency</note> of sixteen-purity gold are exchanged for gold of ten-purity, tell me, how many <term>purāṇas</term> <note>a standard silver coin or weight unit</note> does this amount to now? [173 ½]

One hundred and eight pieces of gold are combined with a purity fraction of three-eighths. If this, along with gold of eleven-purity, is converted into fourteen-purity gold, what is the resulting quantity of gold? [174 ½]

### Formula for finding an unknown purity—

Multiply the known weights by their respective purities and subtract this sum from the total value of the mixture. This remainder, divided by the weight of the gold whose purity is unknown, gives the required purity. [175 ½]

### Another formula for an unknown purity—

The wise state that the sum of the products of each known gold weight and its purity should be subtracted from the product of the total weight and the total mixed purity. This result, divided by the weight of the gold with the unknown purity, reveals the purity. [176 ½]

## Here is an illustrative example:

Six, four, and three pieces of gold possess purities of thirteen, eight, and six respectively... <note>original: ṣaḍ-jaladhi-vahni-kanaka; where jaladhi (oceans) represents 4 and vahni (fire) represents 3</note>

<header>Procedures Relating to Mixtures</header>

# Procedures Relating to Mixtures

O friend, you who are an expert in the essence of mathematics, tell me the unknown purity <term>varṇa</term> <note>varṇa literally means "color," used here as a measure of gold purity similar to carats</note> of five pieces of gold, given that the total purity of the mixture is eleven. [178]

There are seven pieces of gold of fourteen-purity. If a mixture of these results in gold of ten-purity, tell me the unknown loss <note>original: kṣayaka; this refers to the decrease in purity or weight during the alloying process</note> that occurred. [179]

**Formula for determining the unknown weight of gold—**

Multiply each known weight of gold by its respective purity and find the sum of these products. Subtract this sum from the total weight of the gold multiplied by the desired average purity. Divide the remainder by the difference between the average purity and the purity of the unknown gold piece to find the weight of that piece. [180]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

There are three pieces of gold with purity levels <note>original: kṣaya-māna, literally "measures of loss" or "purity values"</note> of two, three, and four. If the total weight of the gold is ten, and the resulting purity of the mixture is thirteen, O friend, tell me the weight of each piece of gold. [181]

**Formula for finding the weights of gold pieces of two different purities—**

The difference between the higher purity and the average purity, and the difference between the lower purity and the average purity, should be calculated. These differences, when swapped and used as proportions for the distribution, allow one to find the quantities of gold. This process may be repeated many times to solve for multiple components. [182]

**Another formula for finding the weights of gold pieces of two different purities—**

Calculate the difference between the desired purity and the higher purity, as well as the difference between the desired purity and the lower purity. Place these two values in reverse order <note>meaning the difference from the high purity becomes the proportion for the low-purity gold, and vice versa</note>. The resulting values represent the proportions of gold to be mixed. [183]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

Gold of ten-purity is mixed with gold of sixteen-purity. If the resulting mixture weighs one hundred and has a purity of twelve, tell me the individual weights of the two different types of gold separately. [184]

**Formula for finding the weights of many gold pieces—**

For all positions except one, choose desired weights for the gold pieces as you wish. Then, the weight of the remaining piece should be calculated using the method for finding an unknown weight of gold as described previously. [185]

### Formula for determining two unknown purity levels

Multiply the two weights of gold by a chosen unit. Separately, multiply the weights by the average purity. By subtracting and adding these values in reverse order <note>This refers to a method of cross-variation common in Indian algebra to solve indeterminate equations</note> and then dividing by the respective weights, the resulting purities are found. [187]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

The individual purities of two pieces of gold weighing sixteen and ten are not known. However, if the average purity of the mixture is eleven, what would be the respective purity levels of those two pieces of gold? [188]

### Another formula for determining unknown purity levels

Assume a desired purity for one piece of gold and calculate the remainder as before. In the case of many pieces of gold, assume desired purities for all except one <note>This "rule of assumption" allows the mathematician to solve for multiple unknown variables by fixing all but one of them</note>, then proceed as described previously. [189]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

When two gold pieces weighing twelve and fourteen are mixed together, the resulting purity is ten. Think carefully and tell me what the individual purity levels of those two pieces were. [190]

->An example for the second half of the rule:<-

When gold pieces weighing seven, nine, two, and ten are combined, the resulting purity is twelve. Tell me, what is the individual purity level for each of these pieces? [191]

### Formula for calculating the testing sticks

Divide the gold weights by the maximum purity loss to determine the testing sticks <term>śalākā</term> <note>śalākā refers to small rods or sticks used as standardized samples for comparison in the assaying process</note>; these are to be added together separately. The resulting gold value should be subtracted from the total sum of the sticks to find the filler <note>original: prapūraṇikā; likely a corrective value used to balance the assaying equation</note>. [192]

<header>Procedures for Mixtures</header>

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

Merchants who are experts in the colors <note>original: varṇa; here referring to the degree of purity</note> of gold desire to make gold testing sticks <note>original: śalākā; needles of known purity used by goldsmiths to determine the quality of unknown gold by comparing the streaks they leave on a touchstone</note>. They made gold testing sticks where the first is of twelve-karat purity, [193]

the second is of fourteen-karat, and the third is of sixteen-karat. The amount of gold <note>original: kanaka</note> available is: for the first, one minus one-ninth; for the second, [194]

one minus half-of-a-half <note>i.e., 1 - 1/4 = 3/4</note>; and for the third person, one minus one-quarter. Starting from the next purity level, the first stick uses the last purity, and the second uses the last two. [195]

The third merchant also uses the last two purities. All the testing sticks are to weigh exactly one māṣa <note>A traditional unit of weight, approximately 0.6 grams</note>. What is the pure gold and what is the required additive <note>original: prapūraṇī; the base metal or alloy used to reach the desired weight/purity</note> for each? O mathematician, tell me quickly the calculation of gold if you truly know it! [196 $^1/_2$]

### Formula for determining weight and purity in the exchange of gold

Multiply the weight of the gold being purchased by the purity levels of the exchange gold; then set down the differences. The result obtained by dividing by the difference in purity levels, when applied inversely, gives the weight of the gold. [197 $^1/_2$]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

A man obtains seven hundred units of sixteen-karat gold in an exchange. If this was exchanged for gold of twelve and ten-karat purity, and the total weight of the gold was eight thousand, what were the individual amounts of each? [198 $^1/_2$]

### Formula for the procedure of exchanging gold with multiple components

Multiply the weight of the gold by its purity and divide by the desired purity; there is a fixed reduction. By proceeding as before, the weights of the gold for the various components of the exchange are determined. [199 $^1/_2$]

->Here is an illustrative example:<-

Exchanging three hundred units of fourteen-karat gold, [merchants] obtain five hundred units of gold with purities of twelve, ten, eight, and seven. [Determine the individual weights].

What is the weight and the purity <note>original: varṇa; literally "color," a unit measuring the fineness of gold on a scale of 1 to 16</note> of each of these pieces of gold? [201]

### Formula for determining the gain, the purities, and the quantities of gold in an exchange —

The sum of the purities of the gold pieces exchanged is divided by the sum of the products of the quantities and their purities. When this is multiplied by the root loss and subtracted from one, the result is divided into the capital. The quotient is then subtracted from the original capital to find the remaining wealth. [202]
That result is then added to the original capital and divided by the sum of the exchange values. When this quotient is multiplied by the respective proportions, it gives the quantity of gold for each exchange and its purity. [203]

### Here is an illustrative example:

A certain merchant, seeking profit, possesses two hundred units of gold of sixteen-karat purity. He exchanges portions of it—starting with one part and doubling each subsequent part—for gold of other qualities. [204]
The purities of the exchanged gold are twelve, eight, nine, and ten <note>original: vasu; a word-numeral representing the eight Vasu deities, used here to mean the number 8</note> respectively. The loss in the process results in a profit of two hundred. Tell me, what is the remainder of the gold, and what were the individual quantities exchanged? [205]

### Formula for finding the original capital from the visible gold and the exchanged portions —

The visible gold <note>original: dṛśya; the known quantity remaining or resulting from a calculation</note> is divided by one minus the sum of the fractions. This result is further modified by the loss factors associated with the exchange purities. The final result obtained here is the original capital. [206]

### Here is an illustrative example:

A merchant took a certain quantity of gold of sixteen-karat purity. He exchanged one-third, one-fourth, and one-fifth parts of it respectively. [207]
These parts were exchanged for gold of twelve, ten, and nine-karat purity. After these transactions, and excluding the original capital, one thousand units of gold are seen. What was the original amount of his capital? [208]

### Formula for finding the required purity by giving a desired part, and for finding the quantity of gold from the desired parts and purities —

The reciprocal of the given parts is increased by one and then multiplied by the desired value; this gives the weight of the gold. From that, the gold corresponding to the mutual parts can also be determined. [209]

One should assume the purities <note>original: varṇa; the measure of gold fineness</note> based on one’s own established loss, just as before. If, by doing so, the results for both pieces of gold are equal, then the calculation is correct. [210]

If the purities and the testing sticks <note>original: gulikā; small beads or sticks of gold used as standards for testing</note> assumed at the start are not certain, then one should make a slight adjustment—either an increase or a decrease—to the loss. [211]

Taking the difference between this adjusted loss and the previous loss, and placing the remainder here, the two purities are accurately determined through the <term>Rule of Three</term> <note>original: trairāśika; a mathematical proportion where three known values are used to find a fourth</note> by adding or subtracting the result. ### Miscellaneous Pulverization

Henceforth, we shall explain the section on Miscellaneous <term>Pulverization</term> within the chapter on mixtures.

**The Rule for Truth and Falsehood —**

The number of men plus one is multiplied by a chosen number, then diminished by twice that same chosen number; the results are the false statements. The square of the number of men, when diminished by those false statements, gives the true statements. [216]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

There are five men who are lovers of a certain courtesan, but only three of them are truly dear to her. To each of them, she says, "You alone are my favorite." Tell me, how many of her words are true and how many are false? [217]
