## Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics

### Rule for the variations in combinations:

Place the numbers beginning with one in increasing order, and then in decreasing order, one above the other. Multiply the terms in reverse order and divide that by the product of the terms in the original order. This gives the essence of the variations. [218]
<note>This describes the formula for combinations, often written as $nCr$. To find how many ways one can choose $r$ items from $n$, you multiply $n \times (n-1) \times ...$ and divide by $1 \times 2 \times ...$</note>

### Here is an illustrative problem:

O mathematician, tell me now the variations that can be made from the different flavors—astringent, bitter, sour, pungent, and salty—when they are combined with the sweet flavor. [219]
<note>original: rasānām; refers to the six primary tastes of Indian pharmacology</note>

Tell me quickly and correctly, my friend: how many variations are there in a necklace composed of diamonds, sapphires, emeralds, corals, and pearls, based on the different ways they can be combined? [220]

O friend, you who know the reality of mathematics, tell me: how many variations are there in a garland made of Ketaki, Ashoka, Champaka, and Blue Lotus flowers, based on their possible combinations? [221]

### Rule for finding the capital investment from known and unknown profits:

Having calculated the individual profits from the known total sum of the investments, the profit of the unknown person is divided by that result. The quotient obtained is the value of the investment for the unknown person. [222]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

At one time, three merchants were engaged in buying and selling. The first merchant’s investment was six <term>purāṇas</term> <note>a type of silver coin used in ancient India</note>, and the investment of the second was eight. [223]

The investment of the third merchant is not known, but the total profit gained by these men was ninety-six. The unknown merchant alone received a profit of forty. [224]

What was his investment, and what were the individual profits of the other two merchants? Calculate and tell me, friend, if you understand the method of investment. [225]

### Rule for calculating carriage-hire:

Subtract the product of the weight carried and the distance traveled from the square of the weight multiplied by half the distance. Subtract the square root of that from the original weight, then divide by the distance to be traveled. This gives the result. [226]
<margin>M and B add 'ta' here; metrically it is faulty.</margin>
<note>This rule deals with calculating the cost of rent or hire (bhāṭaka) for transporting loads over distances, specifically when the weight or distance changes during the journey.</note>

<header>Miscellaneous Problems</header>

## Miscellaneous Problems

### Here is an illustrative problem:

A man, having carried thirty-two jackfruits over a distance of one <term>yojana</term> <note>a traditional measure of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles</note>, receives a <term>bhāṭaka</term> <note>wage or hire-price</note> of seven and a half <note>original: "dalo-na-aṣṭau", literally eight diminished by a half</note>. If he becomes exhausted <note>original: "magno", literally sunk or stuck</note> halfway through the journey, what wage should be given to him? [227]

### Rule for calculating the distance for second and third carriers:

The product of the load and the hire-price is divided by the square of the second person’s wage. The speed <note>or distance traveled</note> of the second person is then found by taking the difference between their wages and the movement of the load, divided by the rate of wages. [228]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

A man, carrying twenty-four jackfruits over a distance of five <term>yojanas</term>, receives nine as his wage. If the second man's speed is reduced by a wage of six, what is the distance traveled by that second man? [229]

### Rule for calculating wages for many stages <gloss>1</gloss>:
<insert>¹ Manuscript B omits the word "stage" (pada) here.</insert>

Divide the distances traveled by the number of men present during those specific stages. Combine these results for the preceding and succeeding segments of the journey. When multiplied by the number of men who have left the group, the values calculated through this proportional distribution give the individual wages. [230]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

Twenty men carry a <term>shivika</term> <note>a palanquin or litter</note> over a distance of two <term>yojanas</term>. The total wage for all of them is seven hundred and twenty <term>dinaras</term> <note>a type of gold coin</note>. [231]

Two men leave after the first two <term>kroshas</term> <note>a unit of distance equal to one-fourth of a yojana</note>. Three other men leave after the next two <term>kroshas</term>. Finally, five more men leave after half of the remaining distance is covered. What is the individual wage for each of these groups of men? [232]

### Rule for calculating the value of bundles <note>original: "pottalaka", referring to purses or bundles of money</note> when multiplied by a desired factor:

Add one to the multiplier and multiply it by the desired amount. Subtracting the others from this product gives the remainder. After simplifying by a common factor, the "roots" are added together. Then, by subtracting one from this sum of roots... [233]

...multiply the simplified quantities from the first step. By taking the sum of these simplified quantities and subtracting each one individually, the result will be the specific amount of wealth held in each person's hand. [234]

Subtract each person's own wealth from the total sum of all wealth, and place these results separately. These results, when multiplied by their respective multipliers and then reduced by the amounts held in hand, will give the total value of the "bundles" <note>the shared purses</note>. [235]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

On the road, three merchants saw a <term>purse</term> <note>original: "pottalaka", a bundle or bag of money</note>. One of them said: "If I obtain this purse, I will have twice the wealth [of you two combined]." [236]

### Rule for finding the value of the purse and the money in hand when the multipliers are given:

The sum of the [reciprocals of the] fractions, diminished by the product of the chosen fractions and the number of positions minus one, [provides the basis]. The <term>money in hand</term> <note>original: "hastagata", the wealth already possessed by the individual</note> and the purse are then found as before, divided by the chosen fractions. [238]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

Five merchants saw a single purse and each spoke in turn. Each claimed that by obtaining exactly one-sixth, one-seventh, one-ninth, one-eighth, and one-tenth part of the purse respectively, [239]

and adding it to what is in their own hand, they would have three times the wealth of the remaining merchants. O mathematician, tell me quickly the amount held in each hand and the value of the purse. [240]

### Rule for finding the purse with chosen fractions and chosen multipliers:

The parts multiplied by the chosen multipliers, increased by the chosen parts and multiplied by the multiplier increased by one, are added. When diminished by the chosen parts multiplied by the number of positions minus one, and multiplied by the chosen multiplier increased by one, the <term>money in hand</term> is found. [241]

### Here is an illustrative problem:

Two travelers on a road saw a purse. One of them said: "By obtaining half of this, I will have twice the wealth [that you have]." [242]

The other said: "By obtaining two-third parts, I will have three times the wealth of what is in your hand when added to mine." What is the amount in each hand and the value of the purse? [243]

Two travelers on the road saw a purse and took it. The first became twice as wealthy [as the other] with his own hand-money and [the purse]...

**Rule for bringing about equal wealth by giving to a person wealth equal to what that person already possesses:**

One divided by the "desire" <note>Here, "desire" refers to the specific ratio or multiplier used in the problem.</note> is multiplied by the multiplier of the preceding person and then increased by one. # Miscellaneous Problems

Five merchants, after each gives half of his own wealth to the person preceding him, become equal in wealth. After thinking it over, tell me: what was the amount held in each of their hands? [263 ½]

There are six merchants. The eldest of them gives, in order, two-thirds of his own wealth to his younger brother. Having done this, they all become equal in wealth. What was the amount held in their hands? [264 ½]

## Rule for bringing about equal wealth after giving to another an amount of money equal to what that person already holds in his hand:

Take one divided by the "desired" multiple <note>original: "vāñchā" – the ratio or specific number chosen for the calculation</note> and add one to it. Place this at the beginning. To find the values for the others, multiply by the "desired" multiple plus one, and then subtract one. [265 ½]

### An Illustration

Three merchants mutually give to one another the amount of wealth already held in the other's hand. They then become equal in wealth. What was the money held in their hands? [266 ½]

There are four merchants. They each take half of the wealth from one another and thereby become equal in wealth. How much was the wealth held in their hands? [267 ½]

## Rule for arriving at the gain or loss (in betting):

Place the sums of the respective numerators and denominators <note>original: "chedāṃśa-yuti"</note> one above the other, in both direct and inverse order. These are to be multiplied by the denominators and numerators of the others through the process of <term>cross-reduction</term> <note>original: "vajrāpavartana" — a mathematical method involving diagonal or crosswise operations to simplify ratios or fractions</note>. [268 ½]

The results are divided by the difference between the numerator and denominator (arranged in order). Then, the other denominators, multiplied by their own numerators and denominators, and further multiplied by the "desired" amount, give the amount held in the hand in inverse order. [269 ½]

### An Illustration

While watching a cockfight, the two owners of the cocks were each addressed in secret with mysterious words by a great man who possessed the power of <term>mantras and medicinal herbs</term> <note>original: "mantrauṣadhi" — it was a common historical belief that spiritual spells (mantras) and specialized herbs could influence the strength or luck of animals in competitive fights</note>. [270 ½]

### Rule for the division of a mixed sum consisting of the quantity, the quotient, and the divisor:

Subtract the given number <note>The "given number" refers to the value used to divide the original quantity</note> from the mixed sum. The divisor is then found by taking the remainder and dividing it by the quotient increased by one. The original quantity is simply the remainder minus the profit <note>original: "lābha" — here meaning the quotient</note>. [273 ½]

#### An Illustration

A certain quantity was divided by an unknown divisor. The sum of the quantity, the quotient, and the divisor is fifty increased by three (53). What is the divisor and what is the quotient? [274 ½]

### Rule for arriving at a quantity which, when a desired number is added to or subtracted from it, yields a square root:

The sum of the number to be added <term>yojya</term> and the number to be subtracted <term>tyājya</term> is multiplied by the remainder of a division involving an odd number increased by one. This result is halved, then diminished, then multiplied by the "bond" <note>original: "bandha" — a specific multiplier or constraint in the calculation</note> and increased by one. This process applied to the differences and sums of the added/subtracted values, when halved and adjusted, gives the desired quantity. This quantity, when the larger of the added or subtracted values is applied, will indeed yield a square root. [275 ½]

#### An Illustration

O calculator, tell me quickly: what is that quantity which, when increased by ten or decreased by seventeen, yields a perfect square root? [276 ½]

What is that quantity which, when decreased by seven or increased by eighteen, yields a perfect square root? Calculate and tell me, O calculator. [277 ½]

# Miscellaneous Procedures

A certain quantity is diminished by two-thirds of itself and then increased by three-sevenths of that same quantity. This resulting value yields its own square root. O calculator, think quickly and tell me: what is that number? [278 ½]

## Rule for arriving at a square root when a desired number is added to or subtracted from a quantity —

Take the desired quantity <note>This refers to the number to be added or subtracted to make the result a square</note>, halve it, and square the result. Then, add one <term>rūpa</term> <note>original: "rūpa" — in Indian mathematics, this usually signifies the integer 1 or a concrete unit</note> to it. This process yields the root when the quantity is either increased by or diminished by its own desired number. [279 ½]

->Here is an illustration:<-

This number, when combined with ten, or when ten is subtracted from it, yields a perfect square root. O calculator, reflect on this and tell me the quantity. [280 ½]

## Rule for arriving at a desired number from the square root of the difference between two quantities that have been squared as desired —

Take two quantities: the desired number increased by one, and the desired number decreased by one. Halve both of these, then square them. When these are multiplied by the desired multiplier, the square root of their difference will be the desired value. [281 ½]

->Here is an illustration:<-

There are two quantities which, when squared and then multiplied by seventy-one, result in a difference whose square root is seventy-one plus one (72). If you truly understand the "wonderful pulverizer" <term>citra-kuṭṭaka</term> <note>The "pulverizer" (kuṭṭaka) is a method for solving indeterminate equations, often compared to the modern Euclidean algorithm or continued fractions</note> branch of mathematics, O calculator, tell me what those two quantities are. [283]

## Rule for arriving at the multiplier and the additive or subtractive quantity —

Multiply the remainder by the desired value in two places. With the unit <note>the number 1</note> and the desired multiplier, perform the operations of addition and subtraction. Then divide by the reverse of those two. These will be the additive <term>prakṣepa</term> and subtractive <term>hāni</term> values. [285]

->Here is an illustration:<-

The product of three and five is fifteen; eighteen is also given. In this case, fourteen is the desired result. What is the additive quantity <term>prakṣepa</term> <note>original: "prakṣepa" — a value added to an equation to make it solvable in integers</note> or the subtractive quantity <note>original: "hāni"</note> here? [286]

# Rule for the Procedure of Inversion —

In this method, where there was multiplication, use division; for division, use multiplication. In the case of an increase (addition), perform subtraction; for subtraction, perform addition. To reverse a square, take the square root; and for a square root, perform a squaring. This is known as the procedure of inversion. [286]

## An Illustration:

What is that quantity which, when divided by seven, multiplied by three, squared, increased by five <note>original: "śara" — the word "arrow" is a common Sanskrit numerical symbol for the number 5</note>, then multiplied by three times fifty, divided by three, halved, and the square root taken, results in the number five? [287]

# Rule for Calculating the Circumference of a Bundle of Arrows —

Take the circumference of the bundle of arrows, add three to it, and square the result. To this, add three again. When the resulting sum is divided by twelve, the quotient shall be the desired number of arrows in the bundle. [288]

## An Illustration:

If there are eighteen arrows forming the outer circumference of a bundle in a quiver, tell me, O mathematician, how many arrows are there in total? Speak if you have exerted yourself in the "curious pulverizer" <term>vicitra-kuṭṭīkāra</term> <note>The "pulverizer" is a method for solving indeterminate equations; here applied to a specific arrangement of items</note>. [289]

# Summation of Series

From here on, we shall explain the summation of series within the context of miscellaneous mathematics.

## Rule for Finding the Sum of a Series with Increase or Decrease —

The number of terms <term>pada</term> <note>original: "pada" — the number of terms in a series</note> is diminished by one and halved. This is then multiplied by the common difference <term>caya</term> <note>original: "caya" — the amount by which each term in the series increases or decreases</note>, which may be negative or positive. The first term <term>prabhava</term> <note>original: "prabhava" — the starting value of the series</note> is then added or subtracted accordingly. Finally, this result is multiplied by the number of terms to find the sum of the series. [290]

### An Illustration:

What is the sum when the first term is ten, the common difference is a decrease of three, and the number of terms is five? Again, what is the sum where the first term is two, the common increase is two, the number of terms is six, and an additional eight is added to the total? [291]

### Rule for obtaining the first term and the common difference when the sum of a series is given—

The sum of the series is divided by the number of terms. From this, subtract the product of the common difference and half of the number of terms as diminished by one. The result is the **first term** <term>ādi</term>.
To find the **common difference** <term>pracaya</term>: subtract the first term from the sum divided by the number of terms, then divide this remainder by half of the number of terms as diminished by one. [292]

### An Illustration:

The sum of a series <term>gaṇita</term> is 40, the number of terms <term>gaccha</term> is 5, and the common difference is 3. The first term is currently unknown; find it. Also, [in a second case] tell me the common difference if the first term is 2. [293]

### Rule for finding the number of terms in the summation of a series—

The last term <term>lābha</term> <note>literally "gain" or "profit," referring here to the value of the final term in the progression</note> is diminished by the first term and divided by half of the common difference; this result is then increased by one to provide the **number of terms**. The number of terms multiplied by the [average] gain results in the **total sum** of the series. [294]

### An Illustration:

Three is the common difference, two is the first term, and blue water-lilies have been distributed among several women. If the share of the last woman is eight, how many women are there and how many flowers were there in total? [295]

### Rule for calculating the sum of squares—

The chosen number <note>the number of terms, $n$</note> is increased by one, then squared, and multiplied by two. This same chosen number, increased by one, is then subtracted [from that product]. When this result is multiplied by half of the chosen number and the product is divided by three, it results in the **sum of the squares** <term>varga-saṅkalita</term>. [296]

### An Illustration:

O friend, tell me quickly the sum of the squares of 8, 18, 20, 60, 81, and 6. [297]

### Rule for the sum of squares of a series with a given first term, common difference, and number of terms—

Twice the common difference is multiplied by the number of terms diminished by one. To this, add six times the first term. Multiply this sum by the common difference and the number of terms as diminished by one. Then, add six times the square of the first term. Finally, multiply the whole by the number of terms and divide by six. This gives the sum of the squares of the chosen series. [298]

## Again, a rule for calculating the sum of squares of a series with a given first term, common difference, and number of terms—

Twice the number of terms diminished by one, multiplied by the square of the common difference, and further multiplied by the number of terms diminished by one, then divided by six <note>The original uses "aṅga" (limbs) to denote the number 6</note>; this is then added to the product of the first term, the common difference, and the number of terms diminished by one, and also added to the square of the first term. The entire sum, when multiplied by the number of terms, is the result. [299]

### An Illustration:

The first term is 3, the common difference is 5, and the number of terms is 5. Tell me the **sum of squares** <term>varga-saṅkalita</term> for this. Also, tell me the sum of squares where the first term is 5, the common difference is 3, and the number of terms is 7. [300]

## Rule for finding the sum of cubes—

The square of the number representing half the number of terms, multiplied by the square of the number of terms increased by one, is declared by the experts of the essence of mathematics to be the **sum of cubes** <term>ghana-saṅkalita</term> in this science. [301]
<note>This provides the formula for the sum of the first *n* cubes: $(n(n+1)/2)^2$</note>

### An Illustration:

Tell me the total sum of cubes for 6, 8, 7, and 25 terms; and also for 56 and 256 terms. [302]

## Rule for finding the sum of cubes of a series with a chosen first term, common difference, and number of terms—

The product of the sum [of the arithmetic series] and the first term is multiplied by the first term minus the common difference. This is then added to the product of the common difference and the square of the sum [of the series] if the first term is greater than the common difference; however, if the first term is less than the common difference, it is subtracted. This gives the **sum of cubes of the series** <term>ghana-citikā</term>. [303]

### An Illustration:

The first term is 3, the common difference is 2, and the number of terms is 5; find the sum of cubes for this. Also, what would the sum of cubes be if the first term is 5, the common difference is 7, and the number of terms is 6? [304]

## Rule for finding the sum of sums—

Twice the number of terms diminished by one, multiplied by the square of the common difference, divided by six, and increased by half of the common difference; then the product of the first term and the common difference is subtracted; then multiply the result by the number of terms diminished by one. This result, when increased by the first term and its square, and finally multiplied by half the number of terms, becomes the **sum of sums** <term>citi-citikā</term>. [305]
<note>The "sum of sums" refers to the summation of the partial sums of an arithmetic progression.</note>

### An Illustration:

The first term is six, the common difference is five, and the number of terms is also seen to be eighteen. What is the **sum of the series** <note>original: "citi-saṅkalita"; this refers to the second-order summation or the "sum of sums"</note> for a series of eighteen terms, where the first term is one and the common difference is one? [306 ½]

## Rule for calculating the fourth-order summation—

The product of half the number of terms and the number of terms increased by one, multiplied by seven <note>The original uses "aśva" (horses) to denote the number 7</note>, then diminished by the number of terms, and again multiplied by the number of terms increased by one, results in the **fourth-order summation** <term>catuḥ-saṅkalita</term> <note>This represents a higher-order summation process often involving the sums of powers</note>. [307 ½]

### An Illustration:

For seven, eight, nine, and ten; and for sixteen, fifty-six, and sixty-one; tell me the **fourth-order summation** separately by applying the rules to each. [308 ½]

## Rule for calculating the combined summation—

The number of terms increased by three, multiplied by one-fourth of the number of terms, and then increased by one; this, when multiplied by the number of terms and the square of the number of terms, becomes the **combined summation** <term>saṅghāta-saṅkalita</term>. [309 ½]

### An Illustration:

For the square of seven (49), for sixty-six, for thirteen and fourteen, and for twenty-five; what would be the **combined summation**? [310 ½]

## Rule for calculating the summation of a geometric progression with fractional terms—

[The procedure involves] the even and odd positions [of the power], multiplied by the common ratio, and further multiplied by the square, and placed in two positions. Diminished by one and divided by the numerator, the result is then multiplied by the first term and the other terms, and divided by the common ratio minus one. [311 ½]
<note>This rule describes the sum of a geometric progression (GP) where the ratio or terms are fractions.</note>

### An Illustration:

Half a *dinara* <note>A gold coin or unit of currency</note> was [distributed] in five cities; the common difference was one-third. The first term was one-third, and the common ratio was one-fourth; tell me the **fractional geometric summation** <term>bhinnaguṇa-citikā</term> for seven terms.

### Rule for calculating the sum of geometric series with an added or subtracted constant —

> The geometric sum <note>original: "guṇa-citi"; the standard sum of a geometric progression</note> is multiplied by the first term, then multiplied by the amount of excess or deficiency and divided by the common ratio minus one. This result is subtracted from the total sum in the case of a deficiency, and added in the case of an excess. [314]

->Here is an illustration:<-

> The common ratio is five, the first term is two, the additive amount is three, and the number of terms is four. O knower of the essence of mathematics, calculate quickly the sum of this geometric series with an added constant. [315]

> The first term is three, the common ratio is eight, the subtractive amount is two, and the number of terms is ten. O calculator, reflect and tell me quickly what the sum of this geometric series with a subtracted constant becomes. [316]

### Rule for finding the first term, common difference, and number of terms from their combined sum —

> Divide the mixed sum <note>original: "miśra"; the total sum of the first term, common difference, number of terms, and the sum of the series itself</note> by the number of terms increased by one, then by the intended sum minus one... the result is the **common difference** <term>pracaya</term> and the remainder, when divided by the number of terms plus one, is the **first term** <term>prabhava</term>. [317]

->Here is an illustration:<-

> The combined sum of the first term, common difference, number of terms, and the total wealth <note>original: "dhana"; here referring to the sum of the arithmetic progression</note> is seen to be fifty. O mathematician, tell me quickly the first term, the common difference, and the number of terms. [318]

### Rule for finding the time of meeting for one in accelerated motion and another in constant motion —

> The **constant speed** <term>dhruva-gati</term> minus the first term, divided by half the common difference, and then increased by one, is the **time** <term>kāla</term>. Double the distance is the time of meeting when multiplied by the sum of their speeds. [319]

->Here is an illustration:<-

> A certain man travels with a first term of three and a common difference of eight. Another man has a constant speed of twenty-one. At what time will they have traveled the same distance? [320]

# Miscellaneous Procedures

## An Illustration of Motion.

A certain man travels six *yojanas* <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8 or 9 miles</note>, and another man travels three. If both move toward each other and the total distance to be traveled is one hundred and eight *yojanas*, O mathematician, tell me quickly: what would be the time for each of them to meet? [321 ½]

## Rule for calculating the time and distance of meeting in an arithmetic progression—

The difference between the two initial terms is multiplied by the difference of the common differences, then multiplied by two and increased by one. This provides the time of meeting on the path for those who started their journey simultaneously. [322 ½]

## Here is an illustration.

One man travels with an initial speed <term>ādi</term> of four and an acceleration <term>pracaya</term> <note>literally "accumulation" or common difference in an arithmetic progression</note> of eight. A second man travels with an initial speed of ten and an acceleration of two. At what time will they meet? [323 ½]

## Rule for finding the time of meeting for those with increasing and decreasing speeds—

The difference between the two initial terms is divided by half the sum of the common differences and then increased by one. This shall be the time of meeting on the road for those whose journeys were performed simultaneously. [324 ½]

## Here is an illustration.

The first man starts with an initial speed of five and an acceleration of eight. The second man has an initial speed of forty-five <note>original: "pañca-ghna-nava", meaning five times nine</note> and a decreasing common difference <term>hīna-pracaya</term> of eight. What is the time of their meeting? [325 ½]

## Rule for finding the time of meeting for a fast traveler and a slow traveler—

Regarding the motion of a slow traveler and a fast traveler in the same direction: the distance already traveled <note>the "lead" or gap between them</note> is divided by the difference between their speeds. The resulting days are the time in which the fast traveler overtakes the slow one. [326 ½]

## Here is an illustration.

A certain man travels at a rate of nine *yojanas* per day, and he has already traveled a distance of one hundred *yojanas*. A messenger <term>pratidūta</term> follows him, traveling at a rate of thirteen *yojanas* per day. In how many days will he overtake him? [327 ½]

# Rule for calculating the circumference of arrows in a quiver with unequal arrows—

The circumference is increased by three, halved, squared, and then divided by three. When one is added to this result, it gives the number of arrows. To find the circumference from the number of arrows, the process is reversed. [328 ½]

->Here is an illustration.<-

The circumference of a quiver is nine, but the number of arrows within is unknown. Again, if there are thirteen arrows in another, tell me, O mathematician, what is their circumference? [329 ½]

# Rule for calculating the number of bricks in a series-built structure—

The number of layers <term>tara</term> squared, decreased by one, and divided by three, is then multiplied by the number of layers. This is added to the sum of the layers multiplied by the desired dimensions of the base; the result is the essence of the total mixture. [330 ½]

->Here is an illustration.<-

If a square-series structure starts with one brick at the top and increases by five in each subsequent layer, O expert in mathematics, tell me: how many bricks are there in total? [331 ½]

In a structure shaped like a *Nandyāvarta* <note>an auspicious, labyrinthine symbol or "turning-joy" diagram often found in Indian art</note>, there are four layers made of sixty equal pieces. Tell me the total number of bricks in this tiered series. [332 ½]

# Rules for the six variations mentioned in the Science of Prosody—

The number of syllables <term>pada-saṅkhyā</term> in a meter is doubled or squared depending on whether the form is even-syllabic or uneven. To find the total variations, if the number is odd, add one and halve it; a heavy syllable <term>guru</term> <note>a long syllable in Sanskrit meter</note> is placed when the number is even. [333 ½]

A light syllable <term>laghu</term> <note>a short syllable</note> is placed sequentially; this is the method for expansion <term>prastāra</term> <note>the systematic enumeration of all possible metrical combinations</note>. In the "lost" calculation <term>naṣṭa</term> <note>finding the specific form of a meter given its rank</note>, a light syllable is placed if the number can be halved; otherwise, add one, halve it, and place a heavy syllable. [334 ½]

Beginning from one and doubling each subsequent term, the sum of those numbers corresponds to the specific variations. One is added at the end. The combinations of light and heavy syllables are arranged from top to bottom in regular and reverse order. [335 ½]

Place the essence <term>sāram</term>, multiplied by the inverse and divided by the inverse. This is the procedure for determining short and long syllables <term>laghu-guru-kriyā</term>. The number is to be calculated by doubling and then subtracting one. [336 ½]

->Here is a problem.<-

Quickly tell me the total number <term>saṅkhyā</term>, the method of expansion <term>prastāra</term>, the "hidden" <term>naṣṭa</term> and "specified" <term>uddiṣṭa</term> forms, and the two paths of short and long syllable calculations—including all six variations <term>ṣat-pratyaya</term> <note>these are the six standard combinatorial tools used in Sanskrit prosody to analyze meters</note>—for a meter consisting of three syllables. [337 ½]

---

<header>Sixth Chapter</header>

# Calculation of Areas
<term>kṣetra-gaṇita-vyavahāra</term>

Having paid respectful homage to the most excellent among those who have attained the final goal <note>original: *siddhebhyaḥ*, referring to the liberated beings in Jain tradition</note>, I bow again and again so that the desired purpose of this work may be successfully accomplished. [1]

From this point forward, we shall describe the sixth branch of mathematics, known as the calculation of areas <term>kṣetra-gaṇita</term>. It is as follows:

The study of areas was first taught by the Jinas <note>the Great Teachers or "Conquerors" of the Jain faith</note>. It is considered to be of two kinds: the "Practical" <term>vyāvahārika</term> and the "Precise" <term>sūkṣma</term>, based on the intended result. Having considered these two divisions, I shall clearly explain the practical operations here. [2]

Triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles exist in various distinct types. These have been correctly described by those great teachers who have crossed to the other shore of the ocean of mathematics. [3]

The triangle is divided into three types, the quadrilateral into five, and the circle into eight. All other remaining shapes are merely variations derived from these. [4]

Wise men say that a triangle may be equilateral <term>sama</term>, isosceles <term>dvisama</term>, or scalene <term>viṣama</term>. Similarly, a quadrilateral may be equilateral (a square), possess two pairs of equal sides (a rectangle), possess only two equal sides (an isosceles trapezoid), possess three equal sides, or be entirely unequal (scalene). [5]

The eight types of "circles" include: the perfect circle, the semicircle, the elongated circle (ellipse), the conch-enclosed circle, the sunken or raised circle <note>referring to concave or convex shapes</note>, and the "wheel" circle which includes both outer and inner boundaries <note>an annulus or ring-shape</note>. [6]

## Practical Mathematics
<term>vyāvahārika-gaṇita</term>

### Rule for calculating the area of triangles and quadrilaterals:

For triangles and quadrilaterals, the area <note>original: *gaṇitam*</note> is found by multiplying half the sum of the sides by half the sum of the opposite sides. In the case of the crescent moon <note>original: *bālendu*, referring to a segment of a circle</note>, the area is half of the product of the diameter and half the sum of the boundary lines. [7]

## Here is a problem:

There is a triangular area where the sides and the opposite base are all eight rods <term>daṇḍas</term> in length. Having calculated its practical area <term>avyāvahārika-phalam</term> <note>the text uses "avyāvahārika" here, but in the context of this chapter's "practical" focus, it refers to the approximate area calculated by the rule above</note>, tell it to me quickly. [8]

<summary>This page introduces the sixth chapter on geometry, classifying plane figures into triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles. It provides the "Surveyor's Rule" for calculating the approximate area of these shapes by averaging opposite sides.</summary>

## Rule for arriving at the area of a circular area—

The diameter multiplied by three is the circumference. The square of the radius multiplied by three is the calculated area. The teachers say that for a semi-circle, the result is half of that. <note>original: "triguṇīkṛtaviṣkambhaḥ paridhir..." This rule uses the practical approximation of pi (π) as 3, which was common in early Indian mathematical traditions for simplified calculations.</note> ॥ 19 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

For a circle with a diameter <term>vyāsa</term> <note>literally "width" or "extension"</note> of eighteen, what is the circumference and what is the area? For a semi-circle with a diameter of eighteen, tell me quickly what the calculation is. ॥ 20 ॥

## Rule for arriving at the area of an elongated circular area—

The length added to the radius and then doubled is the circumference of an elongated circle <term>āyata-vṛtta</term> <note>likely referring to an ellipse or an oval-like shape</note>. One-fourth of the diameter multiplied by the circumference shall be the area. <note>original: "āyātavṛttasya paridhirāyāmaḥ..." This provides an approximation for the perimeter and area of elongated circular shapes.</note> ॥ 21 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

For an elongated circular area, the diameter is exactly twelve, and the length there is thirty-six. What is the circumference and what is the area? ॥ 22 ॥

## Rule for arriving at the area of a conch-shaped area—

In a conch-shaped circle <term>kambuka-vṛtta</term> <note>a "shell-shaped" figure, possibly a spiral or a specific curved segment</note>, the diameter minus the width of the mouth, multiplied by three, is the circumference. One-third of the square of half the ring, added to three-quarters of the square of half the mouth [is the area]. ॥ 23 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The diameter is eighteen cubits <term>hastas</term>, and the width of the mouth is four. Tell me, what is the circumference and what is the calculated area in this conch-shaped circle? ॥ 24 ॥

## Rule for arriving at the area of concave and convex circles—

Know that one-fourth of the circumference multiplied by the diameter is the calculated area for a sacrificial pit <term>catvāla</term> <note>representing a concave or sunken area</note> and for a turtle-like area <term>kūrma-nibha</term> <note>representing a convex or raised area</note>, which are concave and convex respectively. ॥ 25 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

For a sacrificial pit area <term>catvāla-kṣetra</term> <note>original: "catvāla-kṣetrasya"; a catvāla is a specific hole or pit used in Vedic rituals, treated here as a geometric shape</note>, the diameter is the number *bha* <note>original: "bha-saṅkhyakaḥ"; in the Sanskrit alphanumeric system, 'bha' represents the number 27</note> and the circumference is [given]. If the area is seen to be 568, what are the [exact dimensions]? ॥ 26 ॥

**An example of a convex circular area resembling a tortoise shell—**

The diameter is seen to be 15, and the circumference is 36. In this tortoise-shaped area <term>kūrma-nibha</term>, what is the area resulting from the practical calculation? <note>A "tortoise-like" area refers to a convex surface, such as a dome or a segment of a sphere.</note> ॥ 27 ॥

**Rule for arriving at the practical area of an inner annular circle and an outer annular circle—**

The diameter added to the width of the ring, then tripled and multiplied by that same width, gives the area of the outer ring. In the case of an inner annular circle <term>cakravāla</term> <note>literally "a range or circle"; in geometry, it refers to an annulus or the space between two concentric circles</note>, the width is instead subtracted from the diameter [before proceeding with the calculation]. ॥ 28 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The diameter is 18 hands <term>hasta</term> <note>a standard unit of measurement, approximately the length of a forearm</note>, and there is a projection outward of 3 hands. In another case, the diameter is 18 hands and there is an inward encroachment of 3 hands. What would the areas be? ॥ 29 ॥

**Rule for separately arriving at the values of the circumference, diameter, and area from the total sum of these three measures, by taking this combined sum as the given quantity—**

The combined sum is multiplied by 12, and 64 is added to it. After taking the square root of this result, the circumference is found by subtracting 8 <note>original: "prakshepaka-padonaḥ"; literally, "less the square root of the additive factor," where the additive was 64, so its root is 8</note> from that root. ॥ 30 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The combined sum of the circumference, the diameter, and the area is 1,116 <note>original: "ṣoḍaśa-śataṃ sahasrayutam"; literally "sixteen, a hundred, and a thousand joined together"</note>. Tell me, what is the circumference, what is the area, and what is the diameter? ॥ 31 ॥

### Rule for calculating the practical area of fields shaped like a grain of barley, a drum, a double-headed drum, and a thunderbolt—

For those shapes established as the grain of barley <term>yava</term>, the drum <term>muraja</term>, the small drum <term>paṇava</term>, and the weapon of Indra <term>śakrāyudha</term> <note>original: "śakrāyudha"; literally "Indra's weapon," another name for the thunderbolt or *vajra*</note>; half the sum of the width of the mouth <note>the ends of the shape</note> and the width of the middle, when multiplied by the length, becomes the area. ॥ 32 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

For a field shaped like a barley grain <term>yava-saṃsthāna</term>, the length is 80 and its middle width is 40. Tell me, what would the area be? <note>original: "yava-saṃsthāna-kṣetra"; in this calculation, a barley-shape is treated as an elongated diamond or lens where the "mouths" at the tips are zero.</note> ॥ 33 ॥

The length is 80 rods <term>daṇḍa</term> <note>a unit of length</note>; its mouth width is 20 and in the middle it is 40. Tell me the area for the field in the shape of a drum <term>mṛdaṅga</term>. ॥ 34 ॥

The length of a field shaped like a double-headed drum <term>paṇava</term> <note>an hourglass-shaped drum</note> is 77 rods. The width of the two mouths is 8, while the width in the middle is 4 rods. ॥ 35 ॥

The length of this thunderbolt-shaped <term>vajra</term> field is 96. The middle is a point <note>original: "sūci"; literally "a needle," indicating the width narrows to zero in the center like two triangles joined at their apexes</note> and the width at the two mouths is 13 rods plus one-third. ॥ 36 ॥

### Rule for calculating the area of fields with deductions on both sides and similar shapes—

From the width multiplied by the length, subtract the product of half the width and the length <note>this refers to calculating areas where the sides are curved inward or outward</note>. You should state that the area for a "deduction" <term>niṣedha</term> <note>original: "niṣedha"; literally a "prohibition" or "exclusion," referring here to a segment or cutout from a rectangular area</note> on both sides is decreased by that amount, and for a deduction on one side, it is decreased by half of that. ॥ 37 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The length is 36 rods and the width is 18 rods. What is the area when there is a deduction on both sides, and what is the calculation for a deduction on one side? ॥ 38 ॥

### Rule for calculating the practical area of various types of thunderbolt-shaped fields—

One-third of the square of half the rope <note>original: "rajju"; here referring to the perimeter or a specific linear measurement used in the construction</note>, divided by the number of sides and multiplied by the number of sides minus one, is the area for all many-sided figures. In the space between the circles, it is one-fourth. ॥ 39 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

Tell me the area of a sixteen-sided figure, given that the diameter of one six-sided figure <term>ṣaḍbāhuka</term> is 5, and for another, the width is 3. ॥ 40 ॥

A triangle has one side of 5, the other side of 7, and its base <term>dharā</term> <note>literally "the earth," a common term for the base of a geometric figure</note> is 6. Find the area of the middle space between four circles <term>maṇḍala-catuṣṭaya</term> that each have a diameter of 9. Then, find the middle area for three circles with diameters of 6, 5, and 4. <note>original: "madhya-phalam"; the "middle fruit" or the area of the empty space enclosed when circles are placed edge-to-edge.</note> ॥ 42 ॥

### Rule for calculating the practical area of a bow-shaped field—

Having added the chord <term>jyā</term> and the arrow <term>iṣu</term> <note>the "arrow" or "bāṇa" refers to the height of the arc (the versed sine)</note> together, multiply that sum by half the arrow; this is the area for a bow-shape <term>śarāsana</term>. The square root of the sum of five times the square of the arrow and the square of the chord is the arc length <term>kāṣṭham</term> <note>literally "wood," referring to the wooden body of the bow/arc</note>. ॥ 43 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The chord is 26 and the arrow <term>iṣu</term> is 13; this is the bow that is seen. O mathematician <term>gaṇaka</term>, tell me quickly: what is its area and what is its arc length? ॥ 44 ॥

### Rule for finding the measurements of the arrow and the chord—

The square root of the difference between the square of the arc <term>capa</term> and the square of the chord, when divided by five, is said to be the arrow. The square root of the square of the bow minus five times the square of the arrow is the chord <term>jīvā</term>. ॥ 45 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

In this bow-shaped field, the arrow is not known; in the next, the chord <term>maurvī</term> <note>another term for the bowstring or chord</note> is not known. O expert in mathematics, tell me those two values! ॥ 46 ॥

### Rule for calculating the practical area of a square outside and inside a circle—

For the area of a square outside a circle, it is three times the square of the radius <note>Mahāvīra uses the "practical" value of Pi as 3. In this approximation, the area of a circle is $3r^2$, while the circumscribed square would be $4r^2$. This verse sets up the proportional relationships used by surveyors.</note>. Inside, it is half of that. The reverse applies when the square is the primary figure. ॥ 47 ॥

## Now begins Accurate Geometry.

Hereafter, we shall illustrate the practice of accurate geometry <term>sūkṣma-gaṇita</term> <note>literally "subtle calculation," referring to mathematically precise results rather than rough approximations used in trade</note> within the measurement of areas. It is as follows:

### Rule for calculating the segments and the perpendicular:

In a triangle, the two segments of the base <term>ābādhā</term> <note>the two parts into which the base is divided by the perpendicular height</note> are found by the "proportional transition" <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> of the base and the difference of the squares of the sides divided by the base. The teachers say that the square root of the difference between the square of a side and the square of its segment is the perpendicular <term>avalambaka</term>. ॥ 49 ॥

### Rule for calculating the accurate area:

The square root of the product of four terms—the semi-sum of the sides diminished by each of the sides in turn—is the accurate area. Alternatively, [the area is] half the sum of the top and the base multiplied by the perpendicular; but this [latter rule] does not apply to irregular quadrilaterals <term>viṣama-caturaśra</term>. ॥ 50 ॥ <note>This is a version of what is known today as Heron’s Formula for the area of a triangle, though Mahāvīrāchārya presents it as a general rule for shapes where the "fourth side" in the calculation is the semi-perimeter itself.</note>

### Here is a problem:

O mathematician, you who know how to find perpendiculars and base-segments: tell me the accurate area of a triangular field where the base is 8 rods <term>daṇḍa</term> and the two sides are also 8. ॥ 51 ॥ <note>An equilateral triangle with side 8.</note>

In an isosceles triangular field, the two sides are 13 rods each and the base is 10. Tell me the segments of the base, the perpendicular, and the accurate area. ॥ 52 ॥

The side of a scalene triangle is 13, and the opposite side is 15. Its base is 14. What are the results for the calculation of the area, the perpendicular, and the segments of the base? ॥ 53 ॥

---

<insert>After this, the manuscript 'M' adds the following definition: The line starting from the point where the two sides of a triangular field meet and touching the base below is called the perpendicular <term>avalambaka</term>.</insert>

### Hereafter is the rule for calculating the diagonals of the five types of quadrilaterals:

The two sides that meet at the base are multiplied by the base in reverse order; these results are then added to the products of the opposite sides and the top face. These two sums serve as the multiplier and the divisor. The square root of the product of these [two sums] multiplied by the sum of the products of the opposite sides gives the two diagonals. ॥ 54 ॥ <note>This complex rule describes a method for finding the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral, a hallmark of Indian geometry often associated with Brahmagupta and Mahāvīrāchārya.</note>

-> Here is a problem: <-

O friend, you who are well-versed in the essence of mathematics, tell me quickly the diagonal and the accurate area <term>sūkṣma-phala</term> of a square <term>sama-caturaśra</term> whose four sides are each 5 units long. ॥ 55 ॥

In the case of a rectangle <term>āyata-caturaśra</term>, the side <term>bāhu</term> <note>the horizontal side</note> is 12 and the upright <term>koṭi</term> <note>the vertical side</note> is 5. Tell me quickly: what is the diagonal and what is the accurate area? ॥ 56 ॥

In a quadrilateral with two equal sides <term>dvisama-caturaśra</term> <note>an isosceles trapezoid</note>, the base is 36 and the two sides are 61. The other side—the top face—is 14. What is the diagonal and what is the accurate calculation of the area? ॥ 57 ॥

In a quadrilateral with three equal sides <term>trisama-caturaśra</term>, the top face is the square of 13 <note>169</note>, and the base is 7 added to 400 <note>407</note>. What is the measurement of the diagonals, the base segments <term>ābādhā</term>, and the perpendicular altitude <term>avalambaka</term>? ॥ 58 ॥

In an irregular quadrilateral <term>viṣama-caturaśra</term>, the sides are 13 multiplied by 15 <note>195</note> and 13 multiplied by 20 <note>260</note>. The top face is the cube of 5 <note>125</note> and the base is 300. What are the diagonals, the face-perpendiculars, and the area? ॥ 59 ॥

---

### Hereafter are the rules for calculating the accurate areas of circular figures. First, the rule for calculating the accurate area of a perfect circle:

The diameter <term>vyāsa</term> of a circular figure multiplied by the square root of ten becomes the circumference <term>parikṣepa</term>. The circumference multiplied by one-fourth of the diameter is the area. ॥ 60 ॥ <note>Mahāvīrāchārya uses $\sqrt{10}$ (approx. 3.162) as the value for $\pi$, which was standard in Jaina mathematics for "accurate" calculations, as opposed to the "practical" value of 3.</note>

-> Here is a problem: <-

The diameter of one perfect circle is 18; the diameter <term>viṣkambha</term> of another is 60; and yet another is 22. What are the circumferences and areas of these three figures? ॥ 61 ॥

In the case of a semicircle <term>ardha-vṛtta</term> with a diameter of 12, and another with a diameter of 36, what is the circumference and what is the area? ॥ 62 ॥

## Rule for calculating the accurate area of an elongated circular area:

The square of the diameter <term>vyāsa</term> multiplied by six, added to twice the square of the length, [and the square root of this sum] is the circumference. The circumference multiplied by one-quarter of the diameter is the accurate area of the elongated circle <note>This "elongated circle" or *āyata-vṛtta* refers to an ellipse-like shape</note>. ॥ 63 ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The length of an elongated circle is thirty-six, and its diameter <term>viṣkambha</term> is twelve. Calculate and tell me: what is the circumference and what is the accurate area? ॥ 64 ॥

## Rule for calculating the accurate area of a conch-shaped area:

The diameter diminished by half the width of the mouth and multiplied by the square root of ten <note>original: *daśa-pada-guṇita*; Jaina mathematicians frequently used $\sqrt{10}$ (approx. 3.162) as a precise value for $\pi$</note> is the circumference. ॥ 65 ॥
Square the half of the diameter which has been reduced by half the mouth; then add the square of one-quarter of the mouth. This sum, multiplied by the square root of ten, is the accurate area for a figure resembling a conch shell <term>kambu-nibha</term>. ॥ 66½ ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The diameter is eighteen rods <term>daṇḍa</term>, and the width of the mouth is four. What is the circumference and what is the accurate area for that conch-shaped circle? ॥ 67½ ॥

## Rule for calculating the accurate area of an external ring-shaped area and an internal ring-shaped area:

The diameter increased by the width of the projection <note>original: *nirgama*; the width of the ring extending outward</note> and then multiplied by the square root of ten and the width of the projection is the area of the external ring <term>bahir-gaṇita</term>. For the internal ring-shaped area <term>abhyantara-cakravāla</term>, the diameter is diminished by the width of the encroachment. ॥ 68½ ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The diameter is eighteen rods, and there is an external projection of three rods. Tell me the accurate area of the external and internal ring-shaped circles. ॥ 69½ ॥

The diameter is eighteen rods, and there is an internal encroachment of four rods. Tell me the accurate area of the internal ring-shaped circle. ॥ 70½ ॥

### Rule for calculating the accurate area of a barley-shaped area and a bow-shaped area:

The product of the chord <term>guṇa</term> and the arrow <term>iṣu</term>, multiplied by the square root of ten <note>original: *daśa-pada-guṇita*; in this context, the formula for these areas is understood as $\frac{\sqrt{10} \times \text{chord} \times \text{arrow}}{4}$</note>, becomes the calculated area. This should be known for fields in the shape of a barley-corn <term>yava</term> and for those in the shape of a bow. ॥ 70½ ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

The length of a barley-shaped field is twelve rods, the two ends are pointed like a needle <term>sūchi</term>, and the width in the middle is four. What is its area? ॥ 71½ ॥

In a bow-shaped arrangement, the chord <term>jyā</term> is twenty-four; moreover, its arrow <term>iṣu</term> is said to be four. What would be the accurate area? ॥ 72½ ॥

### Rule for calculating the measure of the bow-arc and the arrow in a bow-shaped field:

The square of the arrow multiplied by six, increased by the square of the chord; the square root of that sum is the arc of the bow <term>dhanus</term>. In finding the chord or the arrow, the process is reversed. ॥ 73½ ॥

### Rule for the inverse operation:

The square of the arrow is declared to be the square root of the difference between the square of the arc and the square of the chord, divided by six <note>original: *tarka-hata*; the word 'tarka' is a numerical code for 6</note>. The chord <term>jīvā</term> is the square root of the square of the arc <note>original: *dhanuṣaḥ kṛteḥ*</note> diminished by six times the square of the arrow. ॥ 74½ ॥

-> Here is a problem: <-

In a bow-shaped field, the chord is twelve and the arrow is six. The arc-measure <term>kāṣṭha</term> is not known. Oh friend, tell me, what is that arc? And [in another instance], what is its chord and what is its arrow? <note>This asks the student to solve the problem forward to find the arc, and then backward to verify the chord and arrow.</note> ॥ 75½ ॥

### Rule for calculating the accurate area of a field resembling a drum, a cymbal-shaped area, and a thunderbolt-shaped area:

In the case of a field resembling a drum <term>mṛdaṅga</term>, the area is the length multiplied by the width of the face, added to the area of its own two bow-segments <note>The drum is treated as a central rectangle with two segmental caps</note>. In the case of the cymbal-shaped <term>paṇava</term> and thunderbolt-shaped <term>vajra</term> areas, the area is that same calculation diminished by the area of the two bow-segments. ॥ 76½ ॥

### Here is a problem regarding these:

In a field shaped like a barrel-drum <term>mṛdaṅga</term> <note>A traditional Indian drum that is wider in the middle and narrows at the two ends</note>, the length is twenty-four, the width at each of the two faces is eight, and the width in the middle is sixteen. What is the area? ॥ 77 ½ ॥

The length is twenty-four, and likewise the width at the two faces is eight; the middle width is four. What is the area in a field shaped like a small hourglass-drum <term>paṇava</term>? ॥ 78 ½ ॥

The length is twenty-four, and likewise the width at the two faces is eight; in the middle, it is like a needle <term>sūchi</term> <note>meaning the width tapers to a single point or zero</note>. Tell me, what is the area of this thunderbolt-shaped <term>vajra</term> field? ॥ 79 ½ ॥

### Rule for bringing out the accurate area of a rim-shaped field, a young-crescent-moon-shaped field, and an elephant-tusk-shaped field:

The sum of the outer side <term>pṛṣṭha</term> and the inner side <term>udara</term> is divided by six, then multiplied by the width, and then multiplied by the square root of ten <note>original: *daśamūla*; Jaina mathematicians frequently used $\sqrt{10}$ (approx. 3.16) as the value for $\pi$</note>. This is the area for the rim <term>nemi</term>. For the crescent moon and the elephant tusk, the area is half of that. ॥ 80 ½ ॥

### Here is a problem regarding these:

The outer side is fourteen, the inner side is eight, and the width is four. What is the area for a field in the shape of a rim? Likewise, what would it be for the young crescent moon <term>bālendu</term> and for the elephant tusk <term>ibhadanta</term>? ॥ 81 ½ ॥

### Rule for bringing out the accurate area of the space situated in the middle of four circles:

From the square of the diameter <term>viṣkambha</term>, subtract the accurate area of a single circle. The remainder shall be the area of the interval between four equal circles <note>This refers to the gap created in the center when four identical circles are placed so that each touches two others</note>. ॥ 82 ½ ॥

### Here is a problem regarding these:

What would be the accurate calculation for the middle of four spheres <term>golaka</term> <note>here used interchangeably with circles in a 2D plane</note> which are touching one another, when each is possessed of a diameter of four? ॥ 83 ½ ॥

### Rule for bringing out the accurate area of the space situated within three touching circles:

> The area of an equilateral triangle whose side is equal to the diameter [of the circles], diminished by half the area of one circle, shall be the area of the space generated in the middle of the three [circles]. ॥ 84 ½ ॥

### An illustration regarding this:

> There are three circular fields, each with a diameter of four, which are touching one another. What is the accurate calculation of the area of the space born in their midst? ॥ 85 ½ ॥

### Rule for bringing out the accurate area, the diagonal, and the perpendicular of a six-sided (hexagonal) field:

> The square of the side, the square of that square, and the square of that [the fourth and eighth powers] are multiplied by two, three, and three respectively. These results are, in order, the squares of the diagonal, the perpendicular, and the area in a six-sided field. <note>The author uses a specific Jaina mathematical convention where the diagonal and height of a hexagon are related to the side by these simplified square-root factors</note> ॥ 86 ½ ॥

### An illustration regarding this:

> In a six-sided field, there are two <term>daṇḍas</term> <note>A unit of measurement, literally a "staff," usually four cubits long</note> for each side. In this field, what are the squares of the diagonal, the perpendicular, and the accurate area? ॥ 87 ½ ॥

### Rule for finding the sum of quantities that are in the form of square roots (surds), and for finding the remainder after the mutual subtraction of those same square-root quantities:

> Divide the quantities by a common factor <term>apavartana</term> <note>a divisor that makes the quantities perfect squares</note>. Take the square roots of these quotients and either add or subtract them. The square of that sum or difference, multiplied by the common factor, is the square of the total sum or remainder. This is the calculation for surds <term>karaṇi</term>. ॥ 88 ½ ॥

### An illustration regarding this:

> Tell me the sum of the square roots of the surds sixteen, thirty-six, and one hundred. Also, O friend who knows the essence of mathematics, tell me the remainder [the result of the subtraction] of these roots. ॥ 89 ½ ॥

## Operations on Generated Figures

Henceforth, we shall describe the operations on "generated" <term>janya</term> <note>This refers to figures—specifically right-angled triangles or rectangles—derived or "born" from two chosen numbers called "seeds"</note> figures in the calculation of areas. Here is the rule for bringing out a rectangular field from two chosen "seed" numbers:

->The difference of the squares [of the seeds] shall be the upright side; their product, doubled, shall be the horizontal side.<-
->The sum of the squares [of the same seeds] is the diagonal of the generated rectangle. ॥ 90 ½ ॥<-

->Here is an illustration:<-

->After setting down the numbers one and two as the seeds for a generated field,<-
->O friend, calculate and tell me quickly the measures of the upright side, the horizontal side, and the diagonal. ॥ 91 ½ ॥<-

->After setting down the numbers two and three as the seeds, O friend, for a generated field,<-
->tell me quickly, after calculating, the measures of the upright side, the horizontal side, and the diagonal. ॥ 92 ½ ॥<-

Furthermore, here is another rule for the construction of a rectangular field from those known as seed numbers:

->The product of the sum and the difference of the seeds is the upright side. Through the <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> <note>A mathematical process for finding two unknown quantities when their sum and difference are known</note> of their squares,<-
->the horizontal side and the diagonal are found. This is also a method in the operations of generated figures. ॥ 93 ½ ॥<-

->Here is an illustration:<-

->Having constructed a generated field from the seed numbers three and five, O friend,<-
->tell me quickly the numbers for the upright side, the horizontal side, and the diagonal, O you who know the essence of mathematics. ॥ 94 ½ ॥<-

The rule for bringing out the two quantities known as seed numbers from a given generated field:

->The upright side, divided by a chosen number, is subjected to the <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> process with that same divisor; the results are then halved to give the seeds. Alternatively,<-
->the seeds are the square roots of half the sum and half the difference of the diagonal and a chosen square. ॥ 95 ½ ॥<-

->Here is an illustration:<-

->In a certain field, the upright side is sixteen; what are the two seeds?<-
->Or else, the other side [the base] is thirty and the diagonal is thirty-four; what are those two seeds? ॥ 96 ½ ॥<-

<summary>This page introduces the algebraic construction of right-angled triangles and rectangles using "seed" numbers (u, v), providing formulas for the sides (u²-v², 2uv) and diagonal (u²+v²). It also includes the inverse operation: finding the original seeds when the dimensions of the figure are already known.</summary>

The rule for finding the measures of the horizontal side and the diagonal when the vertical side is known; for finding the vertical side and the diagonal when the horizontal side is known; and for finding the vertical and horizontal sides when the diagonal is known:

->Through the <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> <note>A mathematical process for finding two quantities when their sum and difference are known</note> of a chosen divisor and the quotient obtained by dividing the square of the vertical side <term>koṭi</term> by that divisor, the diagonal and the horizontal side are found. The same may be done with the square of the horizontal side <term>bhujā</term>.<-
->Alternatively, the square root of the difference between the squares of the diagonal <term>śruti</term> and a chosen [side] is the measure of the other [side, whether] vertical or horizontal. ॥ 97 1/2 ॥<-

### Here is an illustration:

->The vertical side of a certain [triangle] is 11; the horizontal side of another is 60; the diagonal of yet another is 61. Tell me the unknown measures in each case. ॥ 98 1/2 ॥<-

The rule for the method of calculating an isosceles quadrilateral <term>dvisamachaturashra</term> <note>A "twice-equal" quadrilateral, or an isosceles trapezoid, where the two non-parallel sides (flanks) are equal</note> field:

->The sum of the products of the generated horizontal side, the vertical side, and the seeds <note>This verse describes a complex geometric construction where sides of the trapezoid are derived from the seed numbers of right-angled triangles</note> results in the base and the top side; their difference is the horizontal side. The diagonal is the hypotenuse. The altitude <term>avalambaka</term> is the vertical side. In an isosceles four-sided figure, the base <term>bhū</term> is the largest, the top side <term>mukha</term> is the smallest, and the segments of the base <term>ābādhā</term> are determined accordingly. The area <term>phala</term> is the product of the altitude and half the sum of the top and base. ॥ 99 1/2 ॥<-

### Here is an illustration:

->In a quadrilateral with two equal sides, where the seed numbers are 5 and 6, tell me the measures of the top side, the base, the flank sides, the altitude, the diagonals, the segments of the base, and the area. ॥ 100 1/2 ॥<-

The rule for calculating the top side, base, flank sides, altitude, diagonals, segments of the base, and area of a trilateral quadrilateral <term>trisamachaturashra</term> <note>A "thrice-equal" quadrilateral, where three sides (the top and the two flanks) are equal in length</note> <margin>field:</margin>

->By using the products of the seeds and their differences, and the values derived from the generated sides, one should calculate the dimensions for a trilateral quadrilateral in the same manner as was done for the isosceles quadrilateral. ॥ 101 1/2 ॥<-

### Here is an illustration:

->In a quadrilateral where three sides are equal, and the seed numbers are 2 and 3, tell me the measures of the top side, the base, the flank sides, the altitude, the diagonals, the segments of the base, and the area. ॥ 102 1/2 ॥<-

### The rule for arriving at the top side, flank sides, perpendicular altitude, diagonals, segments of the base, and the area of a scalene quadrilateral field:

> The horizontal side and the vertical side [of the first generated triangle] are multiplied by the diagonal of the other; these become the base and the top side <note>original: *mukha-bhū*; the top and bottom parallel-ish sides</note>. The horizontal and vertical sides of the second triangle, multiplied by the diagonal of the first, become the two flank sides. The diagonals of the quadrilateral are the products of the vertical side of one and the diagonal of the other, added to the product of the horizontal side of the first and the diagonal of the second. The two altitudes <note>original: *lambaka*; the perpendicular heights</note> are the products of the diagonals and the vertical/horizontal sides. The segments of the base <note>original: *ābādhā*; the distances from the corners of the base to the points where the altitudes land</note> and the area <note>original: *dhana*; literally 'wealth', meaning the calculated area</note> are found through the product of the diagonals. ॥ 103 1/2 ॥

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

> Tell me the top side, the flank sides, the perpendicular altitude, the diagonals, the base segments, and the area of a scalene quadrilateral <note>original: *viṣama-chaturashra*; a quadrilateral with unequal sides</note> generated from the seed pairs of (1, 2) and (2, 3). ॥ 104 1/2 ॥

### Another rule for arriving at a scalene quadrilateral:

> The larger horizontal side multiplied by the square of the smaller diagonal becomes the base, and the vertical side becomes the top side. The two flank sides are the horizontal and vertical sides of the smaller triangle multiplied by the larger diagonal. ॥ 105 1/2 ॥

> The difference between the larger horizontal and vertical sides is doubled and multiplied by the smaller sides; this is used to find the diagonals. The diagonals are also found by multiplying the sum of the smaller horizontal and vertical sides by the larger sides and then by the smaller diagonal. ॥ 106 1/2 ॥

> The products of the smaller diagonal, the larger diagonal, and the smaller sides individually give the two altitudes. The square root of the difference between the squares of the flanks and the altitude gives the segments. Half the product of the diagonals is the area. ॥ 107 1/2 ॥

### The rule for arriving at an isosceles triangle from a single rectangle:

> In an isosceles triangle <note>original: *dvisama-tribhuja*; a "twice-equal" triangle</note>, the diagonal [of the generating rectangle] becomes the two flank sides. The horizontal side, when doubled, becomes the base. The vertical side is the perpendicular altitude. The area is calculated as the product of the altitude and half the base. ॥ 108 1/2 ॥

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

> O mathematician, calculate and tell me quickly the two flank sides, the base, and the altitude of an isosceles triangle generated from the seed numbers 3 and 5. ॥ 109 1/2 ॥

# Formula for the method of constructing a scalene triangle:

By dividing half of the side of a <term>generated triangle</term><note>A right-angled triangle constructed from two "seed" numbers.</note> by any chosen divisor, the base of the scalene triangle is the sum of the side and the result of that division. The two diagonals [of the generated triangles] become the two flank sides, and the vertical sides of the original generated triangles become the perpendicular altitudes in the resulting scalene triangle. ॥ 110 1/2 ॥

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

O friend, after calculating the sides of a triangle using the seeds 2 and 3, and then generating another from them, tell me the sides, the base, and the perpendicular altitude <note>original: *avalambaka*</note> for that scalene triangle. ॥ 111 1/2 ॥

->Thus ends the section on Generated Operations.<-

## "Paisa-chika" Operations <note>The term 'Paisachika' usually refers to something ghostly or demonic; here it likely denotes a class of 'recreational' or 'extraordinary' problems where different units—like area and length—are treated as numerically equal.</note>

From here on, we shall explain the "Paisa-chika" operations.

In the case of a <term>square</term><note>original: *samachaturashra*</note> or a <term>rectangle</term><note>original: *āyatachaturashra*</note>, when the area is numerically equal to the <term>perimeter</term><note>original: *rajju*; literally 'rope'</note>; or when the area is equal to the measure of the side; or the area is equal to the measure of the diagonal; or the area is equal to half the perimeter; or the area is equal to one-third of the side; or the area is equal to one-fourth of the diagonal; or when the area is equal to twice the sum of twice the diagonal, three times the side, four times the altitude, and the perimeter—for all such cases where two chosen quantities are equal, or where one is equal to a result multiplied by a desired factor, the formula for arriving at the measure of the sides and altitudes is as follows:

The mathematician should multiply the chosen quantities by the given factors and divide by the desired multipliers. The results of these multiplications become the measures of the sides for the figures generated, such as squares and others. ॥ 112 1/2 ॥

->**Here is an illustration:**<-

If the perimeter of a square is equal to its calculated area, what is the measure of its side? And for another square, tell me the side when the area is equal to its side. ॥ 113 1/2 ॥

If the <term>area</term><note>original: *gaṇita*; in this context, it refers to the calculated area</note> is equal to the diagonal of a square, what would the side be? In another figure, if the area is twice the <term>perimeter</term><note>original: *rajju*; literally 'rope'</note>, tell me the [side] from its area. ॥ 114 ½ ॥

In the case of a <term>rectangle</term><note>original: *āyatachaturashra*</note>, the area here is equal to the perimeter. In another figure, the area is equal to the diagonal; what is the side? ॥ 115 ½ ॥

In a certain figure, the side is three times the area; what is that side? In another square, the diagonal is four times the area. ॥ 116 ½ ॥

In a rectangle, twice the diagonal, three times the side, and four times the <term>perpendicular</term><note>original: *koṭi*; the vertical side of a right-angled triangle or rectangle</note>, when added to the perimeter, equals twice the area. ॥ 117 ½ ॥

The perimeter of a rectangle here is equal to one <note>original: *rūpa*; a unit or the number one</note>. Quickly calculate and tell me the perpendicular or the side. ॥ 118 ½ ॥

Twice the diagonal, three times the side, and four times the perpendicular, combined with the perimeter of that rectangle, is equal to one. ॥ 119 ½ ॥

### Again, a formula for finding the "seed" numbers for a given generated rectangle:

The square roots of [1] half the difference between the diagonal and the perpendicular, and [2] the difference between the diagonal and that [half-difference], are the two <term>seeds</term><note>original: *bīja*; the two numbers used to generate the sides of a Pythagorean triple using the formulas $m^2-n^2$, $2mn$, and $m^2+n^2$</note>. This is the operation for a generated rectangle. ॥ 120 ½ ॥

->**Here is a problem:**<-

The perpendicular of a rectangle is fifty-five <note>original: *pañcāśadadhikapañca*</note>, the side is forty-eight, and the diagonal is seventy-three. What are the two seeds here? ॥ 121 ½ ॥

### A formula for producing a figure with a diagonal of a desired size using chosen seed numbers:

Having established whatever figure is produced by the seeds, divide the desired diagonal by the diagonal of that [produced figure]. The perpendicular, the side, and the diagonal [of the first figure] multiplied by the quotient [become the required dimensions]. ॥ 122 ½ ॥

->**Here is a problem:**<-

O mathematician, quickly calculate the perpendiculars and sides generated by the seeds (1 and 2), (2 and 3), (4 and 7), and (1 and 8). ॥ 123 ½ ॥

<header>Calculations on Areas</header>

# Calculations on Areas

For <term>rectangles</term><note>original: *āyatachaturashra*</note> and figures with <term>unequal sides</term><note>original: *vishama-bāhu*; often referring to scalene quadrilaterals or triangles</note>, if the <term>diagonal</term><note>original: *karṇa*</note> here is sixty-five, tell me what the [dimensions of the] figures would be. ॥ 124 ½ ॥

A formula for finding the numbers for the <term>base</term><note>original: *bhuja*</note> and <term>perpendicular</term><note>original: *koṭi*</note> of a rectangle generated from desired "seeds," when the <term>perimeter</term><note>original: *rajju*; literally 'rope'</note> and the diagonal are known:
Subtract the square of half the perimeter from twice the square of the diagonal. The square root of that, when processed through <term>concurrence</term><note>original: *saṅkramaṇa*; an operation to find two values when their sum and difference are known: $x = (sum + diff) / 2$ and $y = (sum - diff) / 2$</note> with half the perimeter, gives the base and the perpendicular. ॥ 125 ½ ॥

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

The perimeter is thirty-four, and the diagonal here is seen to be thirteen. Calculate and tell me the perpendicular and the base of this generated figure. ॥ 126 ½ ॥

A formula for finding the numbers for the base and the perpendicular when the <term>area</term><note>original: *gaṇita*</note> and the diagonal are known:
Take the square of the diagonal and both decrease and increase it by twice the area. The square roots [of these two results] are the sum and difference of the perpendicular and base; through concurrence, the larger and smaller sides are found. ॥ 127 ½ ॥

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

The area of a rectangle is sixty, and its diagonal is thirteen. I wish to hear the measurements of its perpendicular and base. ॥ 128 ½ ॥

A formula for finding the numbers for the base and the perpendicular of a rectangle when the area and the perimeter are known:
Subtract four times the area from the square of half the perimeter. The square root of that, when processed through concurrence with half the perimeter, results in the base and the perpendicular. ॥ 129 ½ ॥

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

The perimeter is one hundred and seventy, and the desired <term>wealth</term><note>original: *dhana*; here meaning the area</note> is one thousand five hundred. Tell me the perpendicular and the base for this generated rectangle. ॥ 130 ½ ॥

In a case where there are two <term>rectangles</term><note>original: *āyatachaturashra*</note>, and their <term>perimeters</term><note>original: *rajju-saṅkhyā*; literally 'the number of the rope'</note> are equal, but the <term>area</term><note>original: *kṣetraphala*</note> of the first is twice the area of the second; OR, where the areas of both figures are equal, but the perimeter of the second figure is twice the perimeter of the first; OR, where the perimeter of the second figure is twice that of the first, and the area of the first figure is twice that of the second—here is the formula for calculating the dimensions of those two figures:

The square of the difference between the perimeter and the area, multiplied by a chosen factor, shall be the <term>perpendicular</term><note>original: *koṭi*; the vertical side of a right-angled triangle or rectangle</note>. The <term>base</term><note>original: *dos* or *bhuja*</note> is that same value decreased by one, in the case of equal areas; in other cases, it is multiplied by the specified factor. ॥ 131 ½ ॥
One less than that is the reduced perpendicular; three times the base shall be the base of the other. From the square of half the perimeter, using the previously stated formula, one should bring forth the base and the perpendicular according to that area and perimeter. ॥ 133 ॥
