In two rectangles, the area of the first is double that of the second. The perimeter of the second is also twice that of the first. Tell me the base and the perpendicular for both. ॥ 136 ॥

The formula for finding two <term>isosceles triangles</term><note>original: *dvisamatribhuja*; literally 'two-equal-sides triangle'</note> whose perimeters and areas are equal, or where the perimeters and areas are modified by a chosen multiplier:

The square of the perimeter multiplied by the reciprocal of the area; six times the base decreased by one; the remainder doubled is called the "seed." From that seed, the sides and other dimensions are generated as before. ॥ 137 ॥

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

There are two isosceles triangles. The area of these two figures is equal. The perimeters of the two are also equal. What is the side and what is the base? ॥ 138 ॥

<header>Operations in Geometry</header>

# Operations in Geometry

## Example of a Trapezoid with Three Equal Sides

The accurate area <term>accurate area</term><note>original: *sūkṣma*; the precise mathematical area calculated using rigorous geometric rules</note> is five, and the practical area <term>practical area</term><note>original: *vyāvahārika*; a simplified approximation often used by craftsmen or surveyors, such as multiplying the average of the sides by the height</note> is thirteen. O friend, think and tell me the lengths of the sides of this three-equal-sided quadrilateral <term>three-equal-sided quadrilateral</term><note>original: *trisama-caturaśra*; a trapezoid where the two slanted sides and the top side are equal in length</note>. ॥ 167 ½ ॥

Having understood the practical rough area and the accurate area, this is the **formula** for finding the side of a three-equal-sided quadrilateral or the diameter of a circle that possesses those same areas:

> Find the difference between the squares of the areas; take the square root of that. From that result, take the square root again and multiply it by two. This is the side in a three-equal-sided quadrilateral and the diameter of an equal circle. ॥ 168 ½ ॥

## Here is an Illustrative Problem:

The practical area <term>practical area</term><note>original: *sthūla-dhana*; "gross wealth" or area</note> is eighteen. The accurate area is the square root <term>square root</term><note>original: *karaṇi*; a term used for roots, especially those that result in irrational numbers</note> of three cubed multiplied by nine <note>This calculates to $\sqrt{27 \times 9} = \sqrt{243}$</note>. Calculating this, O friend, tell me the measure of the three-equal-sided quadrilateral. ॥ 169 ½ ॥

The square of five squared <note>$(5^2)^2$, which is 625</note> multiplied by ten is the square root of the accurate area <note>$\sqrt{6250}$</note>. The practical area is seventy-five. What is the diameter of this circle? ॥ 170 ½ ॥

Having understood the practical rough area and the accurate area, this is the **formula** for finding the measure of the base and the sides of an isosceles triangle <term>isosceles triangle</term><note>original: *dvisama-tribhuja*; "two-equal-triangle"</note> that possesses those areas:

> The square root of the difference between the squares of the areas, when doubled, is the practical base. The same root, when divided by the square root of half the base, gives the side of the isosceles triangle. ॥ 171 ½ ॥

## Here is an Illustrative Problem:

The accurate area is given as sixty, and the practical area is sixty-five. After calculating, O friend, tell me the length of the sides of this isosceles triangle. ॥ 172 ½ ॥

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

> The base is fourteen <note>original: *indra*; referring to the fourteen Indras of a cosmic age</note>, the two sides are thirteen <note>original: *viśve*; referring to the thirteen deities called the Visvedevas</note>, the face is five <note>original: *gati*; referring to the five types of motion or states of being</note>, and the height is twelve <note>original: *ravi*; referring to the twelve solar deities or suns</note>. Having understood the practical rough area <term>practical area</term><note>original: *vyāvahārika-sthūla-phala*; an approximation of area used for quick surveying</note> of a scalene quadrilateral, when that area is to be divided into a desired number of parts, the **formula** for finding the measurement of the base of each part within that quadrilateral, and also for finding the height of each respective part:

> The square of the face of a section is multiplied by the difference between the squares of the base and the face of the whole, then divided by the sum of the shares. To this, add the square of the face of the whole. The square root of this, divided by the result of half the sum of the base and face, gives the height respectively. ॥ 175 ½ ॥

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

> The face is said to be seven, the base below is twenty-three, and the sides are thirty. This area is divided into two equal parts; what is the length of the base at the point of division? ॥ 176 ½ ॥

> The base is one hundred and sixty-two, the face is stated to be eighteen, and the height is four hundred. This field is divided among four men. ॥ 177 ½ ॥

> The shares received by each man are respectively one, two, three, and four parts. In this distribution, tell me the area, the base of each section, and the height of each section. ॥ 178 ½ ॥

> The base is eighty, the face is forty, and the height is sixty <note>original: *catur-guṇā ṣaṣṭi*; literally "four times fifteen," a common way of expressing sixty</note>. The parts to be divided are three, eight, and five sections. ॥ 179 ½ ॥

Knowing the measurements of the heights of two pillars, having tied two ropes to the tops of those two pillars, and having stretched those two ropes diagonally <term>diagonally</term><note>original: *karṇikāreṇa*; literally "acting as a diagonal or ear-line"</note> so that they touch either the base of the opposite pillar or a point beyond that base; then, starting from the point where those two diagonal ropes intersect and stretching a single rope vertically down to the ground: the measurement of that rope is known as the **intermediate perpendicular** <term>intermediate perpendicular</term><note>original: *antarāvalambaka*; the height of the intersection point above the ground</note>.

Starting from the point where that intermediate perpendicular touches the ground, the distances on that ground toward both sides up to where the diagonal ropes touch the base are known as the **segments** <term>segments</term><note>original: *ābādhā*; the horizontal distance from the base of a pillar to the point directly beneath the intersection of the ropes</note>. The formula for calculating the value of the intermediate perpendicular and the value of the segments is as follows:

->The pillars, multiplied by the distance on the ground between the ropes and divided by their own sum, result in the two segments. The product of the pillars divided by their sum is the intermediate perpendicular. ॥ 180 ½ ॥<-

->Here is an illustrative problem:<-

> Two pillars are each sixteen cubits <term>cubit</term><note>original: *hasta*; a unit of measurement approximately the length of a forearm</note> in height, and the ground between them is also specified as sixteen. Tell me the measurements of the segments here, and also the intermediate perpendicular. ॥ 181 ½ ॥

> The height of one pillar is thirty-six, and that of the second is twenty. The ground between them is twelve cubits. What are the two segments, and what is this intermediate perpendicular? ॥ 182 ½ ॥

> Two pillars are twelve and fifteen cubits high, and the ground between the pillars is four cubits. A rope is dropped from the top of the twelve-cubit pillar to a point four cubits beyond the base of the other; ॥ 183 ½ ॥

> and similarly, another rope is dropped from the top of the other pillar to a point one cubit beyond the base of the first. In this case, what is the segment, and what is the intermediate perpendicular? ॥ 184 ½ ॥

> The two sides are thirteen each, the base is fourteen, and the top face is four cubits. Tell me the segments and the intermediate perpendicular <note>In this context, the "intermediate perpendicular" refers to the height where the diagonals of the trapezoid intersect</note>. ॥ 185 ½ ॥

> In a figure where the face and the base are each reduced by one, and ropes are dropped from the opposite tops to the bases: tell me the perpendicular and the segments. ॥ 186 ½ ॥

Having known the measure of the height of a pillar, and if that pillar is broken and fallen due to some cause, and having known the distance on the ground between the root of the pillar and its tip; this is the rule for calculating the measure of the standing part starting from the root of that pillar:

Having known the height of a taller pillar and the height of a shorter pillar, and having known the distance on the ground between the two pillars; when the taller pillar is broken such that the top of the taller pillar touches the top of the shorter pillar, the rule for calculating the height of the break and the height of the remaining standing portion is as follows:

> From the square of the taller pillar, subtract the sum of the square of the distance and the square of the shorter pillar; half of this result, divided by the difference between the heights of the pillars, becomes the height of the break <note>This calculates the "fallen" part of the pillar. Subtracting this from the original height gives the standing part.</note>. ॥ 196 ½ ॥

Having imagined two-thirds of the height of a mountain to be the base of a rectangular field, this is the rule for calculating the distance of the city from the mountain and the length of the diagonal path <term>hypotenuse</term><note>original: *karṇa*; the diagonal path of the flying ascetic</note> based on that mountain’s height:

> Twice the height of the mountain is the distance between the mountain and the city; half of the mountain's height is the leap into the sky. The hypotenuse is the sum of the distance and the leap. <note>This rule provides a specific case where the leap and distance are fixed proportions of the height for equal path lengths.</note> ॥ 198 ½ ॥

The rule for arriving at equal numerical values for the two hypotenuses of two rectangular fields, by taking the two segments of the base <term>ābādhā</term><note>The *ābādhā* refers to the segments into which the base of a triangle is divided by the altitude.</note> and swapping them to serve as the two vertical sides <term>koṭi</term> of two rectangles:

Take the two vertical heights of the two pillars in a swing-shaped figure <note>original: *dolākāra-kṣetra*; a figure resembling a swing or trapeze where paths meet at a central point</note> and imagine them to be the two sides <term>arms</term> of a triangle. ॥ 201 ½ ॥

From the numerical value of the ground distance between these two, calculate the two base segments as previously described; then, swap their positions and set them as the two vertical sides <term>koṭi</term>. ॥ 202 ½ ॥

In those two rectangular fields, from those horizontal sides and vertical sides, two hypotenuses are produced; as before, they shall be of equal numerical value. ॥ 203 ½ ॥

Being sky-travelers, they have both come to a city to seek alms. They have traveled at an equal speed <note>This implies the distance traveled—the hypotenuse—is the same for both.</note>. O mathematician, what are the numerical values of the base segments in this swing-shaped figure? ॥ 207 ½ ॥

### The rule for arriving at the measurement of the diameter of the circumcircle for eight types of figures—namely, five types of quadrilaterals and three types of triangles:

In a quadrilateral, the diagonal <term>śruti</term> divided by the altitude <term>avalambaka</term> and then multiplied by the lateral side <term>pārśva-bhuja</term> [gives the diameter]. In a triangle, the product of the two sides divided by the altitude becomes the diameter of the circumcircle. ॥ 213 ½ ॥

The square root of the difference between the squares of the diameter and the chord should be subtracted from the diameter. ### The rule for arriving at the measurement of the central diameter of a circle, knowing the measurement of the chord and the measurement of the "arrow":

The square of the chord is divided by four times the height <note>original: *śara*; another term for "arrow"</note>; this value, when added to the height itself, is declared to be the diameter situated in the middle of a perfect circle. ॥ 229 ½ ॥

## Calculations Regarding Excavations <term>original: *Khāta-vyavahāra*; the branch of mathematics dealing with volumes of earth, pits, and foundations</term>.

->I bow my head in devotion to Jina Vardhamāna <note>Vardhamāna is the given name of Mahāvīra, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism</note>,<-
->Whose footstool is honored by the crowns of all the lords of the gods,<-
->Who is all-knowing, eternal, inconceivable, and infinite in form,<-
->The morning sun to the lotus-garden of those beings seeking liberation. ॥ 1 ॥<-

The various areas which have been described previously,
When their results are multiplied by their depths <gloss>by the depth</gloss>,
For the purpose of estimating labor, the results of field-work, and subtle variations,
I shall now speak of this seventh subject, the calculation of excavations. ॥ 2 ॥

### Precise Calculation <term>original: *Sūkṣma-gaṇita*; here referring to the exact mathematical volume as opposed to rough estimation</term>.

In this context, here is the defining verse regarding density:

In a cubic cubit <term>original: *hastaghana*; a unit of volume measuring 1 cubit on each side</term> of solid earth, there are exactly three thousand two hundred *pala* units <note>a unit of weight</note>.
When that earth is dug out and loosened, it is reckoned as three thousand six hundred *pala* units in this world. ॥ 3 ॥

**The rule for arriving at the mathematical result of an excavation:**

The area of the figure multiplied by the depth is the practical calculation in a uniform excavation.
Where dimensions vary, the sum of the top and bottom faces divided by two, or divided by the appropriate count, results in the equalization of the measurements. ॥ 4 ॥

->**Here are the problems:**<-

In a square excavation, the side is eight, the opposite side is eight, and the depth is also eight.
What would the volume of this excavation be in a uniform pit? ॥ 5 ॥

In a triangular field where the side is thirty-two and the depth is thirty-six,
The height is seen as eight and its remaining part is six digits <term>original: *aṅgula*; a finger’s width, 24 of which make a cubit</term>. What is its volume? ॥ 6 ॥

In a circle with a diameter of one hundred and eight, its depth is one hundred and sixty-five.
Tell me, what is the result of the volume for this circle in a uniform excavation? ॥ 7 ॥

In an elongated rectangle, the width is five and the length is twenty-five.
The depth is one hundred and sixty. Tell me quickly the volume of this uniform excavation. ॥ 8 ॥

In these calculations regarding excavations, after determining the results known as the **Approximate** <term>original: *Karmāntika*; a volume estimation derived by averaging the linear dimensions (length and width) of the top and bottom before calculating the area</term> and the **Regional** <term>original: *Auṇḍra*; a volume estimation derived by averaging the areas of the top and bottom faces</term>, the following rule is used to arrive at the **Precise** <term>original: *Sūkṣma*; the exact geometric volume</term> volume of the excavation using those two values:

The lengths and widths of the respective faces situated at the exterior <gloss>the top</gloss> and the interior <gloss>the bottom</gloss> are added to their respective opposite sides and then divided by the number of faces <note>i.e., averaged</note>. ॥ 9 ॥

When these are multiplied together and then multiplied by the depth, the result is the **Approximate** <term>Karmāntika</term> volume. Separately, calculate the areas of the respective faces situated at the exterior <gloss>top</gloss> and interior <gloss>bottom</gloss>, add them together, and divide by their number; then multiply this by the depth to find the **Regional** <term>Auṇḍra</term> volume. To the Approximate volume, add one-third of the difference between these two results; this indeed becomes the **Precise** volume. ॥ 10–11½ ॥

->**Example Problems**<-

There is a square step-well <term>original: *Vāpī*; a large well or tank often with steps</term> that is twenty units wide at the top and sixteen at the bottom. The depth is nine. O mathematician, tell me quickly, what is the volume? ॥ 12½ ॥

A step-well is an equilateral triangle, measuring twenty at the top and sixteen at the bottom. The depth is nine. What is the Approximate volume, the Regional volume, and the Precise volume? ॥ 13½ ॥

There is a circular step-well, twenty units in diameter at the top and sixteen at the bottom. The depth is twelve *daṇḍas* <note>a unit of length equal to 4 cubits</note>. What would be the Approximate, Regional, and Precise volumes? ॥ 14½ ॥

A rectangular excavation has a length of sixty and a width of twelve at the mouth <gloss>the top</gloss>; at the bottom, these dimensions are half as much. The depth is eight. What is the volume? ॥ 15½ ॥

The lengths at the top, middle, and base are ninety, eighty, and seventy respectively. The widths are twenty-two, sixteen, and ten. The depth is seven. <note>The student is expected to apply the averaging method across three levels here</note>. ॥ 16½ ॥

The diameter at the mouth of a circular well is sixty, in the middle it is thirty, and at the bottom it is fifteen. If the depth is sixteen, what is its mathematical volume? ॥ 17½ ॥

# Calculations Regarding Excavations

In a triangular excavation, the width at the top is 80, in the middle it is 60, and at the bottom it is 50. In all three sections, the depth is 9. What is the calculated volume for that? ॥ 18 ½ ॥

A rule for calculating the volume of a moat <term>original: *khātikā*; a ditch or moat</term>, and for calculating the volume of a moat when the depth follows a needle-shaped taper <term>original: *sūcī-mukha*; literally "needle-mouthed," referring to a shape that narrows to a point or edge</term>:

The width of the moat is added to the diameter of the circular or triangular area and then multiplied by three. In the case of a quadrilateral area, the length is multiplied by four and then by the width of the moat. ॥ 19 ½ ॥

When the depth is like a needle-taper, the middle of the moat is used, but for the actual moat calculation, use half the depth. Then, after adding the width at the top, the calculation is performed as before for the bottom and the "needle" depth. ॥ 20 ½ ॥

### An Illustration

A triangle, a quadrilateral, and a circle—as previously described—are each surrounded by a moat. The diameter of the inner area is 80 rods <term>original: *daṇḍa*; a unit of measurement roughly equal to 6 feet</term>. The moats are 4 units wide and 3 units deep. ॥ 21 ½ ॥

There is a rectangular area with a length of 120 and a width of 40. The moat surrounding it is 4 units wide and 3 units deep. <note>The student is expected to find the volume of the earth removed to create these moats based on the rules provided above.</note> ॥ 22 ½ ॥

A rule for calculating the volume when there are many different depths, and for finding the depth of one excavation from the known volume of another:

The sum of the depths at various points is divided by the number of locations <gloss>to find the average depth</gloss>; this depth is then multiplied by the area of the top to find its own volume. For triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles, the volume divided by the area of the other field gives its depth. ॥ 23 ½ ॥

### An Illustration

In a square field with a width of exactly four cubits <term>original: *hasta*; a cubit, the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term>, various points are dug to the depths of one, two, three, and four cubits. What is the uniform average depth? ॥ 24 ½ ॥

A square water tank <term>original: *vāpikā*; a small stepped well or tank</term> has sides of 18 cubits <term>original: *hasta*; a unit of length roughly 18 inches</term> and a depth of 4. There is another tank filled with the water from that first one; its side is 9 cubits. What is its depth? ॥ 25 ½ ॥

For any excavation, once the measurements of the top side, the bottom side, and the height (depth) are known, this is the rule for finding the side length at a desired depth and for finding the "needle-depth" <term>original: *sūcī-vedha*; the depth to the imaginary vertex if the sloping sides met at a point like a needle</term>:

The top side multiplied by the depth, and then divided by the difference between the top and bottom sides, results in the needle-depth. To find the width at a specific point, the top and bottom sides are multiplied by the "reverse depth" <note>the distance from the bottom to the point in question</note>, and the sum is divided by the total height. ॥ 26 ½ ॥

->Here is an illustration:<-

A square tank is 20 units wide at the top and 14 units wide at the bottom. The total depth is 9 units. What is the side length at a depth of 3 units from the top, and what is the needle-depth? ॥ 27 ½ ॥

The rule for calculating the volume <term>original: *phala*; literally "fruit" or result</term> of a spherical area <term>original: *golaka-ākāra-kṣetra*</term>:

Half the cube of the radius multiplied by nine is the "practical" <term>original: *vyāvahārika*; for everyday trade and use</term> volume of a sphere. Nine-tenths of that practical result becomes the "accurate" <term>original: *sūkṣma*; precise or subtle</term> volume. ॥ 28 ½ ॥
<note>Mahāvīra’s "practical" formula is $V = 4.5 r^3$. His "accurate" formula is $V = 0.9 \times 4.5 r^3 = 4.05 r^3$. This differs from the modern formula $4/3 \pi r^3$.</note>

->Here is an illustration:<-

Calculate the volume for a sphere with a diameter of 16. Tell me both the practical result and the accurate result. ॥ 29 ½ ॥

The rule for calculating the practical volume and the accurate volume of a "horn-shaped" excavation <term>original: *śṛṅgāṭaka-kṣetra*; a triangular pyramid, named after the water chestnut</term>:

Half the square of the side is cubed, then multiplied by the square root of ten and divided by nine; this is the practical calculation. Three times that result, divided by the square root of ten, is the accurate volume for the triangular pyramid. ॥ 30 ½ ॥

->Here is an illustration:<-

Calculate the volume of a triangular pyramid <term>original: *tryasra-śṛṅgāṭaka*</term> where the sides are 6 units. Tell me what the practical volume and the accurate volume would be. ॥ 31 ½ ॥

# Calculations on Excavations

This is the rule for calculating the time required to fill a water tank <term>original: *vāpī*; a stepped well or rectangular reservoir</term> when various desired pipes <term>original: *praṇālikā*; a channel, conduit, or pipe</term> are opened and connected to it:

The units representing the time taken by each individual pipe to fill the tank are turned into fractions by placing one over them. The sum of these fractions is then divided into one; the resulting fraction of a day is the time required for all the pipes combined to fill the tank. The denominators of those fractions represent the "velocity" <note>the rate of flow</note> of the water from each pipe into the tank. ॥ 33 ॥

### Here is an illustration:

There are four pipes. Each one, acting alone, can fill a tank in 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/5 of a day, respectively. In what fraction of a day will they fill the tank if all four are opened together? ॥ 34 ॥

In the fourth chapter of this mathematical treatise, titled "The Rule of Three," only a brief indication of such problems was given. Here, they will be explained and described in full detail:

A square water tank, measuring nine cubits <term>original: *hasta*; approximately 18 inches</term> in each dimension (length, width, and depth), sits at the foot of a mountain. From the peak of that mountain, a stream of water falls; the stream has a square cross-section with a width of one digit <term>original: *aṅgula*; a finger-breadth, roughly 3/4 of an inch</term>. ॥ 35 ॥

The stream is continuous from the peak to the tank, and the water contained within that column in the air exactly fills the tank. Tell me, what is the height of the mountain <term>original: *utseḍha*</term>, and what is the total volume of water <term>original: *jala-pramāṇa*</term>? ॥ 36 ॥

A square water tank, measuring nine cubits in each dimension, sits at the foot of a mountain. A stream of water falls from the peak, having a circular cross-section with a diameter of one digit. ॥ 37 ॥

This stream is suspended in the air between the peak and the mouth of the tank, and it exactly fills the tank. My friend, calculate and tell me the height of that mountain and the volume of the water. ॥ 38½ ॥

A square water tank, measuring nine cubits in each dimension, sits at the foot of a mountain. A stream of water falls from the peak, and its cross-section is a triangle with a side of one digit. ॥ 39½ ॥

It enters the mouth of the tank, and the water contained in that suspended column fills the tank. My friend, after calculating, tell me both the height of the mountain and the volume of the water. ॥ 40½ ॥

# Calculations on Piles of Bricks

From here on, we shall describe the calculations related to piles of bricks <term>original: *citi-gaṇita*; masonry or stacking</term> within the context of excavations. Here are the definitions of measurements:

->A standard brick is known to be one cubit in length, half a cubit in width,<-
->and four digits in height. All calculations should be performed using these units.<- ॥ 43 1/2 ॥

The rule for arriving at the volume of a desired area and the number of bricks required for it:

->Multiply the area of the face <note>the cross-section</note> by the height. Divide that result<-
->by the volume of a single brick. The result is the volume of the pile,<-
->and that same value represents the total number of bricks.<- ॥ 44 1/2 ॥

### Here are the illustrations:

> A square altar <term>original: *vedi*; a sacrificial platform or pedestal</term> has eight cubits on each side and a height of nine cubits. If it is constructed using the standard bricks mentioned before, O mathematician, tell me how many bricks are there? ॥ 45 1/2 ॥

> An equilateral triangular altar is built with sides of eight cubits and a height of nine cubits. Using the previously described bricks, calculate and tell me how many bricks are in this structure. ॥ 46 1/2 ॥

> A circular altar has a height of nine cubits and a diameter of eight cubits. O mathematician, tell me how many bricks were used to build this. ॥ 47 1/2 ॥

> A rectangular structure has a length of sixty cubits and a width of twenty-five <note>literally "the square of five"</note>. Its height is six cubits. Describe the number of bricks in the pile here. ॥ 48 1/2 ॥

The width of a wall at the top is 6, and at the bottom it is 8. Its length is [unspecified, implying continuity] <note>likely referring to the previous length of 24</note> and its height is 20. How many finished bricks would there be in this case? ॥ 50 1/2 ॥

There are three walls with heights of 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Their widths at the bottom are 7, 6, and 5, while their widths at the face <note>the top</note> are 4, 3, and 2. The length of each is 24. [Calculate the bricks for each]. ॥ 51 1/2 ॥

When a brick altar <term>original: *vedi*</term> has partially fallen, the rule for bringing out <note>calculating</note> the number of bricks remaining in the standing portion and the number of bricks in the fallen portion:

->The difference between the top <term>original: *mukha*</term> and the bottom <term>original: *tala*</term> widths is multiplied by the height of the fallen part, then divided by the total height. Add this to the top width. With this new top width and the existing bottom width <note>for the standing part</note>, or with the new bottom width and the existing top width <note>for the fallen part</note>, the previously mentioned calculation <note>for trapezoidal volumes</note> should be performed.<- ॥ 52 1/2 ॥

### Here is an illustration:

A wall is 12 in length. Its width is 1 at the top and 5 at the bottom, and its height is 10. A portion of it, measuring 5 cubits in height, has broken off and fallen. How many bricks are in that fallen part? ॥ 53 1/3 ॥

When a wall is broken in the shape of a diagonal <term>original: *karṇa*</term>, the rule for finding the bricks in the standing part and the fallen part:

->Multiply the bottom and top widths by two, then add the top and bottom widths respectively. Add twice the bottom width of the unbroken part and subtract... <note>The text describes a proportional adjustment for the slanted break</note>. Multiplying by one-sixth of the length and height, the bricks for the standing and fallen parts are found in order.<- ॥ 54 1/2 ॥

### Here is an illustration:

This wall has been struck from its base by a whirlwind <term>original: *madhyāvartena vāyunā*</term>. It is broken in the shape of a diagonal. How many bricks remain standing and how many have fallen? ॥ 55 1/2 ॥

This wall, having been struck by a whirlwind starting one cubit up from the base, is broken in the shape of a diagonal. How many bricks are there in the standing part, and how many in the fallen part? ॥ 56 1/2 ॥

### The rule for calculating the increase of layers when the height of the middle of a wall is known, and for calculating the decrease of layers on both sides of a wall:

**The mathematical rule for calculating the volume of a structure made of bricks where there is both a bottom width and a top width:**

> Double the width of the base and add it to the length; then double the length and add it to the width of the base. Multiply these by the width and the height respectively. In a rectangular structure <term>original: "āyatacaturaśre"</term>, this gives the [volume/brick count]. ॥ 61 ॥

# Operations regarding Sawing.

Henceforth, **we shall illustrate the operations regarding sawing** <term>original: "Krakacikā-vyavahāra"</term>. Here are the definitions:

> A length of two cubits <term>original: "hasta"</term> minus six finger-breadths <term>original: "aṅgula"</term> is known as a <term>Kishku</term> <note>A 'Kishku' is a specific unit of measure used in timber work, roughly equivalent to 42 finger-breadths, or about 31.5 inches</note>. > The numerical values of the diameter, the height, and the number of paths <note>cuts</note>, when multiplied together, [give the result]. ॥ 64 ॥

### Calculations of Excavations

The measure of a plank produced by sawing <note>original: "krakacike"</note> is determined by the product of its dimensions in cubits and fingers. In the case of trees such as the Teak <note>original: "Śāka"</note> and others, the number of cubits in circumference and length are multiplied by each other. ॥ 65 ॥

This product is then multiplied by the number of saw-paths <note>the number of cuts made through the timber</note>. The resulting figure represents the total quantity of work completed by the sawyer in terms of the finished planks. ॥ 66 ॥

For the Teak, Arjuna, Sour Dock <note>original: "Amlavetasa"</note>, Pine <note>original: "Sarala"</note>, Ebony <note>original: "Asita"</note>, Sal <note>original: "Sarja"</note>, and Dunduka trees, as well as the Sriparni and Laksha trees, the standard for a single saw-path is ninety-six inches in length and one cubit <term>original: "kiṣku"; a traditional unit of length often equal to 24 fingers or one cubit</term> in width. ॥ 67½ ॥

->Here is an illustration:<-

In a Teak tree, the length is sixteen cubits and the circumference is three and a half cubits. If there are eight saw-paths, tell me, what is the measure of the work performed? ॥ 68½ ॥

# Chapter Eight.
## Calculations using Shadows. <note>original: "Chāyā-vyavahāra"</note>

---

Peace is the Jina <note>original: "Jina"; referring here to the Tirthankara Shantinatha</note>, the giver of peace to all beings, the lord of the world who has perceived all things as they are <note>original footnote ¹: M reads "as the essence"</note>. I bow to him, who grows through the eight auspicious miraculous powers <term>original: "prātihārya"; eight marks of divine presence surrounding a Jina</term> and who has conquered the host of internal enemies. ॥ 1 ॥

First, I shall explain the method for determining the eight directions, beginning with the East:

On a ground surface as level as the surface of water, one should draw a circle. The radius of this circle should be twice the height of the chosen gnomon <term>original: "śaṅku"; a vertical pillar or stick used to cast a shadow for astronomical or geometric calculations</term>. ॥ 2 ॥

Place the gnomon in the center of that circle. Its shadow at the beginning of the day <note>sunrise</note> and at the end of the day <note>sunset</note> will touch the circumference of the circle in sequence. The point in the West and the point in the East are thus indicated <note>The morning shadow points west; the evening shadow points east</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

By using a string stretched between those two points, one should draw a "fish-like" figure <note>the intersection of two arcs, known today as a vesica piscis</note> oriented toward the South and North. From the center and the corners, the intermediate directions are established. The shadow itself determines the South and North and the mid-points between the directions. ॥ 4 ॥

One-half of the sum of the midday shadows on the days the sun enters Aries <note>the spring equinox</note> and Libra <note>the autumnal equinox</note> is known as the Equinoctial Shadow <term>original: "viṣuvadbhā"; the length of the midday shadow of a gnomon when the sun is on the celestial equator</term>. ॥ 4 ½ ॥

In Lanka, Yavakoti, Siddhapura, and Romaka-puri <note>legendary cities located on the earth's equator in ancient Indian geography</note>, there is no equinoctial shadow at all. For that reason, the day is always thirty ghatikas <term>original: "ghaṭikā"; a unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 30 ghatikas equal 12 hours</term> in duration. ॥ 5 ½ ॥

In other countries, the day length may be more or less than thirty units of time. However, on the days when the sun enters Aries and Libra, the day length is indeed thirty ghatikas everywhere. ॥ 6 ½ ॥

Having determined the duration of the day and the length of the midday shadow according to the methods taught in the science of astronomy <term>original: "jyotiṣa-śāstra"</term>, one should learn the calculations of shadows through the collection of formulas that will be stated hereafter. ॥ 7 ½ ॥

# Calculations using Shadows. <note>original: "Chāyā-vyavahāra"</note> 153

In regions where there is no equinoctial shadow <note>original: "viṣuvacchāyā"; this refers to regions on the equator where the sun is directly overhead at noon during the equinox, casting no shadow</note>, here is the formula for calculating the time of day once the shadow of a chosen gnomon <term>original: "śaṅku"; a vertical rod used to cast shadows</term> is known:

> Increase the length of the shadow by one and double the result. In the forenoon, the measure of the day divided by this value is the time passed. In the afternoon, the same calculation gives the time remaining. This is known in the *Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics* <note>original: "Sārasaṅgraha"; the title of this treatise</note>. ॥ 8 ½ ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

> In the forenoon, the "man-shadow" <term>original: "pauruṣī chāyā"; the shadow cast by a person, or a shadow measured in units relative to the height of the caster</term> is three times the height. Tell me, dear friend, what part of the day has passed? In the afternoon, tell me the corresponding remaining part of the day. ॥ 9 ½ ॥

The rule for calculating *ghatikas* <term>original: "ghaṭikā"; a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> once the fraction of the day is known:

> When the fraction of the day is determined, the total measure of the day is divided by the denominator of that fraction. This gives the *ghatikas* passed in the forenoon, or the *ghatikas* remaining in the afternoon. ॥ 10 ½ ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

> In a land without an equinoctial shadow, one-eighth of the day has passed. Another eighth remains in the afternoon. How many *ghatikas* would these be, given that the day consists of thirty *ghatikas* <note>original: "khāgni-nāḍyaḥ"; literally 'sky-fire' (0 and 3) units, a poetic way to say 30</note>? ॥ 11 ½ ॥

The rule for calculating the duration of a wrestling match:

> The duration is the difference between the time passed [at the start] and the time remaining [at the end] as calculated from the time-finding rule. The "man-shadow" is found by dividing the shadow of a pillar by the height of that same pillar. ॥ 12 ½ ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

> In the forenoon, a wrestling match began when the shadow of the pillar was [a certain length]. It ended in the afternoon when the shadow had doubled. What was the duration of the match? ॥ 13 ½ ॥

->**An example for the second half of the rule:**<-

> The shadow of a twelve-cubit <term>original: "hasta"; a unit of length roughly 18 inches</term> pillar is twenty-four. At that moment, O mathematician, what would the "man-shadow" be? ॥ 14 ½ ॥

<summary>This page provides mathematical formulas for converting shadow lengths into time of day and vice versa, specifically for equatorial regions. It also includes practical word problems, such as determining the duration of a wrestling match and normalizing pillar shadows into "man-shadow" units.</summary>

# The Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics <note>original: "Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha"</note>

In a region where there is an equinoctial shadow <note>original: "viṣuvacchāyā"; the shadow cast by a gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox, used here to account for the observer's latitude</note>, here is the formula for calculating the time of day once the current shadow is known:¹

> The current shadow increased by the height of the gnomon <term>original: "śaṅku"; a standard vertical rod of 12 units</term> and then diminished by the midday shadow <note>original: "madhyacchāyā"</note> must be doubled. The measure of the gnomon divided by this result gives the fraction of the day passed in the forenoon or remaining in the afternoon. ॥ 16 ½ ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

> For a gnomon of twelve digits <term>original: "aṅgula"; a unit of measure roughly equal to a finger-breadth</term>, the midday shadow is two digits. If the current shadow is eight digits, what fraction of the day has passed or remains? If the total day consists of thirty *nadikas* <term>original: "nāḍika"; a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term>, how many *ghatikas* <note>equivalent to a nadika</note> does that fraction represent? ॥ 17 ॥

The formula for calculating the shadow length from the desired number of *nadikas*:

> The height of the gnomon is multiplied by the fraction of the day <note>expressed as the time passed/remaining doubled</note> and then reduced by the height of the gnomon. This result, when increased by the midday shadow, becomes the shadow length for that specific time. ॥ 18 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

> For a gnomon of twelve digits, the midday shadow is two digits. What is the shadow length when ten *ghatikas* have passed, assuming the total day is thirty *nadikas*? ॥ 19 ॥

In the characterization of "foot-shadows" <note>original: "pādacchāyā"; measuring time by the length of one's own shadow measured in "feet"</note>, here is the definitional formula for the measure of a man’s foot:

> One-seventh of a man's height is the length of that man's foot. If a man's proportions follow this, he is considered fortunate; his foot-shadow will be accurate. ॥ 20 ॥

The formula for calculating the measure of a shadow cast upon a wall <note>original: "ārūḍhacchāyā"; literally 'ascended shadow'</note>:

> The height of the gnomon <note>here referring to a pillar or tall object</note> is multiplied by a man's shadow and then divided by the distance between the wall and the pillar. The result is the height of the shadow that has "ascended" the wall. ॥ 21 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

> A pillar is twenty cubits <term>original: "hasta"; the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term> high, and the distance between the wall and the pillar is eight cubits. If a man's shadow <note>of a standard 12-digit gnomon</note> is doubled, what will be the shadow of the pillar cast upon the wall? ॥ 22 ॥

# Calculations using Shadows <note>original: "chāyā-vyavahāra"</note>

### A rule for finding the distance between a wall and a pillar, having known the height of the pillar and the measurement of the shadow climbing the wall:

->The difference between the two <note>the pillar's height and the height of the shadow on the wall</note> is multiplied by the human shadow. This gives the distance between them.<-
->The distance between them divided by that same difference is the measure of the human shadow. ॥ 23 ॥<-

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

A pillar is twenty cubits <term>original: "hasta"; a standard unit of length roughly 18 inches</term> high, and the shadow climbing the wall is sixteen cubits. If the human shadow <note>original: "puruṣacchāyā"; the shadow cast by a standard vertical gnomon of 12 units</note> is double the height of the gnomon, what would be the distance between the wall and the pillar? ॥ 24 ॥

->**An example for the reverse calculation:**<-

A pillar is twenty cubits high, and the shadow climbing the wall is sixteen. What is the length of the human shadow if the distance between the wall and the pillar is eight? ॥ 25 ॥

### A rule for finding the height of a pillar, having known the measurement of the climbing shadow, the distance of the ground between the wall and the pillar, and the length of the human shadow:

->The shadow climbing the wall is divided by the human shadow <note>specifically, the ratio of the human shadow to the 12-unit gnomon</note> and added to the distance between the wall and the pillar. Wise men know that the result of this, divided by the human shadow <note>ratio</note>, gives the measurement of the height of the pillar. ॥ 26 ॥<-

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

The shadow climbing the wall is sixteen cubits, and the human shadow is exactly double. What would be the height of the pillar if the distance between the wall and the pillar is eight? ॥ 27 ॥

### A rule for separating the measurement of the gnomon and the shadow when they are mixed together:

->The sum of the gnomon's height and the gnomon's shadow is divided by the human shadow increased by one. The result is the measure of the gnomon; the shadow is that same sum diminished by the gnomon's measure. ॥ 28 ॥<-

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

The sum of the gnomon's height and the gnomon's shadow is fifty. What would be the height of the gnomon if the human shadow is four times its height? ॥ 29 ॥

### Rule for separating the combined sum of the gnomon’s shadow and the human shadow—

The sum of the gnomon's shadow and the human shadow is divided by the measure of the gnomon's height increased by one. The result is the length of the human shadow <note>original: "puruṣacchāyā"; this refers to the shadow cast by a standard vertical gnomon of 12 units, often used as a reference ratio</note>. The gnomon's shadow is the combined sum minus that result. ॥ 30 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

The height of a <term>gnomon</term> <note>original: "śanku"; a vertical rod used to measure the sun's altitude</note> is ten. The sum of the human shadow and the gnomon's shadow is fifty-five. What is the human shadow, and what is the gnomon's shadow? ॥ 31 ॥

### Rule for calculating the measure of the inclination of a pillar—

Subtract the square of the gnomon's height multiplied by the square of the human shadow from the square of the shadow <note>of the pillar</note>. From the square of the shadow, subtract the square of the human shadow increased by one. ॥ 32 ॥

The square root of that <note>the first result</note> should be subtracted from the shadow, and then divided by the square of the human shadow <note>original: "narabhāna"; referring to the ratio of the human shadow</note>. The resulting value will be the inclination of the pillar. ॥ 33 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

The human shadow is twice <note>the gnomon height</note>. The shadow of a pillar thirteen cubits high is twenty-nine. What is the inclination of the pillar in that instance? ॥ 34 ॥

A certain prince, staying inside his palace in the forenoon, is curious to know the time of day and the length of the human shadow. ॥ 35 ॥

At a height of thirty-two cubits <term>original: "hasta"; a unit approximately 18 inches</term> in a lattice-window in the middle of the eastern wall, the sunlight enters. It falls upon the western wall at a height of thirty-one cubits. ॥ 36 ॥

The distance between those two walls is twenty-four cubits. Oh mathematician, if you have put effort into the calculation of shadows, calculate and tell me the time of day and the human shadow! ॥ 37$\frac{1}{2}$ ॥

In a square room that is ten cubits deep <note>literally "ten cubits thick," referring to a cubic space or pit</note>, the human shadow is twice the height of a man. <note>Calculate</note> the shadow on the eastern floor in the forenoon. ॥ 38$\frac{1}{2}$ ॥

In that instance, what would the shadow cast behind be, O student? If you know how to calculate the climbing shadow <note>original: "ārūḍha-chāyā"; this likely refers to the shadow cast upon a vertical surface or a shadow that "climbs" an object</note>, tell me. ॥ 39.5 ॥

## Rule for calculating the shadow of a gnomon cast by a lamp—

The height of the lamp diminished by the height of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>original: "śanku"; a standard vertical measuring rod, usually 12 units high</note> is to be divided by the measure of the gnomon. The distance between the lamp and the gnomon, when divided by that resulting quotient, gives the length of the shadow. ॥ 40.5 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

The distance between a gnomon and a lamp is ninety-six <term>angulas</term> <note>original: "aṅgula"; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's width</note>. For a gnomon of twelve angulas, tell me quickly the length of the shadow cast by the lamp. The height of the lamp-flame is sixty angulas, O you who have crossed to the other shore of the ocean of mathematics! ॥ 42 ॥

---

## Rule for calculating the distance between the lamp and the gnomon—

The height of the lamp diminished by the height of the gnomon is to be divided by the measure of the gnomon. That resulting quotient, multiplied by the length of the gnomon’s shadow, shall be the distance between the gnomon and the lamp. ॥ 43 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

The shadow of the gnomon is eight angulas and the height of the lamp-flame is sixty. Tell me the distance between the gnomon and the lamp, O you who have crossed to the other shore of the ocean of mathematics! ॥ 44 ॥

---

## Rule for calculating the measure of the lamp's height—

The distance between the lamp and the gnomon is divided by the shadow of the gnomon, and then increased by one. This result, multiplied by the measure of the gnomon, becomes the height of the lamp. ॥ 45 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

The shadow of the gnomon is exactly two <note>angulas</note>, and the distance between the gnomon and the lamp is two hundred. In this case, where the gnomon is twelve <note>angulas</note>, what is the height of the lamp? ॥ 46 ॥

In this context as well, the measure of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>original: "śanku"; a vertical rod used to measure shadows</note> is twelve digits. Having correctly understood the examples, one should know the system of rules. ॥ 47 ॥

The following is the rule for finding the height of a tree by knowing the length of a man’s shadow in terms of his own feet and the tree’s shadow in terms of those same feet; and also for finding the length of a tree’s shadow by knowing the height of the tree and the length of the man’s shadow in terms of his own feet:

The shadow of the desired tree, when divided by one's own shadow <note>meaning the shadow cast by the observer, measured in the units of their own foot-length</note> and then multiplied by seven, results in the height of the tree. That height, when multiplied by one's own shadow and divided by seven <note>original: "adri"; literally "mountain," a Sanskrit numerical code for the number 7, representing the traditional proportion that a man's height is seven times his foot-length</note>, shall surely be the shadow of the tree. ॥ 48 ॥

->**Here is an example problem:**<-

One's own shadow is four feet long, and the shadow of a tree is one hundred feet. Tell me, what would be the height of the tree according to the measure of one's own feet? ॥ 49 ॥

### Example for calculating the length of a tree's shadow

One's own shadow is four feet long. If the height of a tree is one hundred and seventy-five, what would be the length of the tree's shadow at that time? ॥ 50 ॥

Going eight <term>yojanas</term> <note>original: "yojana"; a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles</note> forward from a city, there stands a mountain ten units high. Another mountain is situated eighty yojanas further from there. ॥ 51 ॥

At night, the lamps on the peaks of these mountains are visible to those standing in the city. The shadow of the mountain standing in the middle has its tip and its base joined <note>This implies a line-of-sight calculation where the nearer mountain perfectly obscures the base or a specific point of the further light source</note>. O mathematician, quickly tell me the height of this second mountain. ॥ 52<gloss>1/2</gloss> ॥

### CHAPTER I.

### ON TERMINOLOGY.

### Salutation and Benediction.

-> 1. Salutation to <term>Mahāvīra</term> <note>Literally "Great Hero," the title of the 24th and final Tirthankara, the primary spiritual teacher of the Jain faith</note>, the Lord of the <term>Jinas</term> <note>meaning "Conquerors," those who have attained ultimate victory over the cycle of rebirth</note>, the protector (of the faithful), whose four * infinite attributes, worthy to be esteemed in (all) the three worlds <note>In Indian cosmology: the heavens, the earth, and the netherworld</note>, are unsurpassable (in excellence). <-

-> 2. I bow to that highly glorious Lord of the <term>Jinas</term>, by whom, as forming the shining lamp of the knowledge of numbers <note>the study of mathematics</note>, the whole of the universe has been made to shine. <-

-> 3. That blessed <term>Amōghavarṣa</term> (<gloss>meaning "one who showers down truly useful rain"</gloss>) <note>A reference to King Amoghavarsha I of the Rashtrakuta Dynasty, who reigned in the 9th century and patronized the author, Mahāvīrācārya</note>, who (ever) wishes to do good to those whom he loves, and by whom the whole body of animals and vegetables, having been freed from (the effects of) pests and drought, has been made to feel delighted : <-

-> 4. He, in whose mental operations, conceived as fire, the enemies in the form of sins have all been turned into the condition of ashes, and who in consequence has become one whose anger is not futile : <-

-> 5. He, who, having brought all the world under his control and being himself independent, has not been overcome by (any) opponents, and is therefore an absolute lord (like) a new God of Love <note>Referring to the deity of desire, Manmatha</note> : <-

-> 6. He, to whom the work (of service) is rendered by a circle of kings, who have been overpowered by the progress of (his) heroism, and who, being <term>Cakrikābhañjana</term> <note>A royal title meaning "the breaker of circles" or military formations</note> by name, is in reality a <term>*cakrikābhañjana*</term> (<gloss>meaning "the destroyer of the cycle of recurring re-births"</gloss>) : <-

---

\* These four attributes of <term>Jina Mahāvīra</term> <note>Known as the "Ananta Chatushtaya" in Jain philosophy</note> are said to be his faith, understanding, blissfulness and power.

8. May (his rule)—the rule of that sovereign lord who has destroyed in philosophical controversy the position of single conclusions and propounds the logic of the *predication of possibilities* <term>syādvāda</term> <note>original: "syādvāda"; a Jain logical system holding that truth and reality are perceived differently from different points of view</note> —(may the rule) of that Nṛpatuṅga <note>A title of King Amoghavarsha I, meaning "High among Kings"</note> prosper!

### An Appreciation of the Science of Calculation.

9. In all those transactions which relate to worldly, Vedic <note>Referring to the ancient sacred scriptures of India</note> or (other) similarly religious affairs, calculation is of use.

10. In the science of love, in the science of wealth, in music and in the drama, in the art of cooking, and similarly in medicine and in things like the knowledge of architecture:

11. In prosody <note>the study of poetic meters</note>, in poetics and poetry, in logic and grammar and such other things, and in relation to all that constitutes the peculiar value of (all) the (various) arts: the science of computation is held in high esteem.

12. In relation to the movements of the sun and other heavenly bodies, in connection with eclipses and the conjunctions of planets, and in connection with the <term>three questions of astronomical direction, position, and time</term> <term>tripraśna</term> <note>original: "tripraśna"; literally "three questions"</note> and the course of the moon—indeed in all these (connections) it is utilised.

13-14. The number, the diameter and the perimeter of islands, oceans and mountains; the extensive dimensions of the rows of habitations and halls belonging to the inhabitants of the... <note>Sentence continues on the following page</note>

---

* The <term>theory of conditioned predication</term> <term>syādvāda</term> is a process of reasoning adopted by the Jainas in relation to the question of the reality or otherwise of the totality of the perceptible objects found in the phenomenal universe. The word is translatable as the "may-be-argument"; and this "may-be-argument" declares that the phenomenal universe (1) may be real, (2) may not be real, (3) may and may not be real, (4) may be indescribable, (5) may be real and indescribable, (6) may be unreal and indescribable, and (7) may be real and unreal and indescribable. The position represented by this argument is not, therefore, one of a single conclusion.

† The <term>three questions</term> <term>tripraśna</term> is the name of a chapter in Sanskrit astronomical works; and the fact that it deals with three questions is responsible for that name. The questions dealt with are <term>direction</term> <gloss>Dik</gloss>, <term>position</term> <gloss>Deśa</gloss> and <term>time</term> <gloss>Kāla</gloss> as appertaining to the planets and other heavenly bodies.

->**GAṆITASĀRASAṄGRAHA**<-

...shadows, which concern the practical application of calculation in the study of astronomy—from this vast ocean, mathematicians who possess the necessary skills in abundance will, by using the tools of calculation, obtain the pure gems of knowledge they desire.

24. Because it is impossible to understand the meaning of any subject without the proper technical terms, the required terminology is set forth at the very beginning of this science.

### Terminology relating to the measurement of Space <note>In this context, "Space" refers to linear distance and surface area.</note>

25–27. That infinitely small particle of matter which cannot be destroyed by water, fire, or any other force is called an **ultimate atom** <term>paramāṇu</term>. An infinite number of these atoms makes a **minute particle** <term>aṇu</term>, which is the first measurable unit here. 

The units that follow are:
* the **mote** <term>trasareṇu</term> <note>literally "a moving particle," like a speck of dust in a sunbeam</note>, 
* the **chariot-dust** <term>rathareṇu</term>, 
* the **hair-measure**, 
* the **louse-measure**, 
* the **sesame-measure** (which is the same as the **mustard-seed-measure**), 
* the **barley-measure**,
* and the **finger-breadth** <term>aṅgula</term>.

Among the inhabitants of the "worlds of enjoyment" and the "worlds of work" <note>Jain cosmological regions where life is either purely blissful or requires labor and action</note>—which are classified as superior, middling, or inferior—each of these measures is exactly eight times the size of the one preceding it in the order listed. This finger-breadth is known as the **practical finger-breadth** <term>vyavahārāṅgula</term>.

28. Those who are experts in the systems of measurement state that five hundred of these **practical finger-breadths** constitute one **standard finger-breadth** <term>pramāṇāṅgula</term>. The actual finger-width of a person living today forms their own **personal finger-breadth** <term>ātmāṅgula</term>.

29. In the established customs of the world, they hold that the finger-breadth is of three kinds: the **practical** <term>vyavahāra</term>, the **standard** <term>pramāṇa</term>, and the **personal**. Furthermore, six finger-breadths make one **foot-measure** <note>measured across the width of the feet</note>.

30. Two such feet make one **span** <term>vitasti</term> <note>the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger when the hand is fully extended</note>; and twice that length is one **cubit** <term>hasta</term> <note>the length of the forearm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note>. Four cubits make one **rod** <term>daṇḍa</term>, and two thousand of those make one **Indian mile** <term>krōśa</term>.

31. Those well-versed in the measurement of distances say that four such miles form one **league** <term>yōjana</term>. Following this, I shall describe in the proper order the terminology relating to the measurement of time.

<summary>Mahāvīrācārya defines the units of linear measurement, starting from the indivisible atom (paramāṇu) up to the yōjana. He distinguishes between different types of finger-breadths (aṅgula) used for practical, standard, and personal measurements.</summary>

->CHAPTER I—TERMINOLOGY.<-

### Terminology relating to (the measurement of) Time.

32. The time in which an atom (while moving) passes beyond another atom immediately next to it is called a **moment** <term>samaya</term> <note>original: "samaya"; the smallest indivisible unit of time in Jain physics</note>; an innumerable number of **moments** <term>samayas</term> make a **blink** <term>āvali</term> <note>original: "āvali"</note>.

33. A <unclear>*</unclear>measured number of **blinks** <term>āvalis</term> makes a **respiration** <term>ucchvāsa</term> <note>original: "ucchvāsa"; roughly the duration of a single breath</note>; seven **respirations** <term>ucchvāsas</term> make one **drop** <term>stoka</term> <note>original: "stoka"</note>; seven **drops** <term>stokas</term> make one **particle** <term>lava</term> <note>original: "lava"</note>, and thirty-eight and a half of these make up the **Indian hour** <term>ghaṭī</term> <note>original: "ghaṭī"; a unit of approximately 24 minutes</note>.

34. Two **Indian hours** <term>ghaṭīs</term> make one **portion of the day** <term>muhūrta</term> <note>original: "muhūrta"; a standard period of 48 minutes</note>; thirty **portions of the day** <term>muhūrtas</term> make one full day; fifteen days make one **fortnight** <term>pakṣa</term> <note>original: "pakṣa"</note>; and two **fortnights** <term>pakṣas</term> are taken to be a month.

35. Two months make one **season** <term>ṛtu</term> <note>original: "ṛtu"</note>; three of these are understood to make one **half-year** <term>ayana</term> <note>original: "ayana"; referring to the movement of the sun between solstices</note>; two of these form one year. Next, I give the grain-measure.

### Terminology relating to (the measurement of) Grain.

36. Know that four **sixteenths** <term>ṣoḍaśikas</term> <note>original: "ṣoḍaśika"</note> form here one **cup** <term>kuḍaba</term> <note>original: "kuḍaba"</note>; four **cups** <term>kuḍabas</term> one **handful-measure** <term>prastha</term> <note>original: "prastha"</note>; and four **handful-measures** <term>prasthas</term> one **quart** <term>āḍhaka</term> <note>original: "āḍhaka"</note>.

37. Four **quarts** <term>āḍhakas</term> make one **bucket** <term>droṇa</term> <note>original: "droṇa"</note>, and four times one **bucket** <term>droṇa</term> make one **measure** <term>mānī</term> <note>original: "mānī"</note>; four **measures** <term>mānīs</term> make one **bushel** <term>khārī</term> <note>original: "khārī"</note>; five **bushels** <term>khārīs</term> make one **load** <term>pravartikā</term> <note>original: "pravartikā"</note>.

38. Four times that same (**load** <term>pravartikā</term>) is a **cartload** <term>vāha</term> <note>original: "vāha"</note>; five **loads** <term>pravartikās</term> make one **pot-measure** <term>kumbha</term> <note>original: "kumbha"</note>. After this the terminology relating to the measurement of gold is described.

### Terminology relating to (the measurement of) Gold.

39. Four **bits** <term>gaṇḍakas</term> <note>original: "gaṇḍaka"</note> make one **berry-weight** <term>guñjā</term> <note>original: "guñjā"; the weight of the Abrus precatorius seed</note>; five **berry-weights** <term>guñjās</term> make one **coin-weight** <term>paṇa</term> <note>original: "paṇa"</note>, and eight of these (**coin-weights** <term>paṇa</term>) make one **stamp** <term>dharaṇa</term> <note>original: "dharaṇa"</note>; two **stamps** <term>dharaṇas</term> make one **unit** <term>karṣa</term> <note>original: "karṣa"</note>, and four **units** <term>karṣas</term> make one **weight** <term>pala</term> <note>original: "pala"</note>.

### Terminology relating to (the measurement of) Silver.

40. Two grains make one **berry-weight** <term>guñjā</term> <note>original: "guñjā"</note>; two **berry-weights** <term>guñjās</term> make one **bean-weight** <term>māṣa</term> <note>original: "māṣa"</note>; sixteen **bean-weights** <term>māṣas</term> are said here to make one **stamp** <term>dharaṇa</term> <note>original: "dharaṇa"</note>.

41. Two and a half of that (**stamp** <term>dharaṇa</term>) make one **unit** <term>karṣa</term> <note>original: "karṣa"</note>; four **ancient coins** <term>purāṇas</term> <note>original: "purāṇa"</note> (or **units** <term>karṣas</term>) make one **weight** <term>pala</term>—so say persons well versed in calculation in respect of the measurement of silver according to the standard current in **Magadha** <term>Magadha</term> <note>An ancient Indian kingdom known for its influence on weights and measures</note>.

### Terminology relating to (the measurement of) Other Metals.

42. What is known as a **fractional part** <term>kalā</term> consists of four **quarters** <term>pādus</term>; six and a quarter **fractional parts** <term>kalās</term> make one **barley-grain** <term>yava</term>; four **barley-grains** <term>yavas</term> make one **part** <term>aḿśa</term>; four **parts** <term>aḿśas</term> make one **division** <term>bhāga</term>.

43. Six **divisions** <term>bhāgas</term> make one **drachma** <term>drakṣūṇa</term> <note>original: "drakṣūṇa"; a term derived from the Greek "drachma," showing the influence of Indo-Greek trade on Indian coinage</note>; twice that weight is one **denarius** <term>dīnāra</term> <note>original: "dīnāra"; derived from the Roman "denarius"</note>; two **denarii** <term>dīnāras</term> make one **stater** <term>satēra</term> <note>original: "satēra"; another term of Greek origin</note>. Thus say the learned men in regard to the measurement of other metals.

44. Twelve and a half **palas** <term>pala</term> make one **measure** <term>prastha</term>; two hundred **palas** <term>palas</term> make one **balance-weight** <term>tulā</term>; ten **balance-weights** <term>tulās</term> make one **load** <term>bhāra</term>. Thus say those who are clever in calculation.

45. In this matter of measurement, twenty pairs of cloths, of jewels, or of canes are called a **score** <term>kōṭikā</term>. Next, I give the names of the principal operations in arithmetic.

### Names of the Operations in Arithmetic.

46. The first among these operations is **multiplication** <term>guṇakāra</term>, which is also called **the produced** <term>pratyutpanna</term>; the second is what is known as **division** <term>bhāgahāra</term>; and **squaring** <term>kṛti</term> is said to be the third.

47. The fourth, as a matter of course, is **square root** <term>varga-mūla</term>, and the fifth is said to be **cubing** <term>ghaṇa</term>; then **cube root** <term>ghanamūla</term> is the sixth, and the seventh is known as **summation** <term>citi</term>.

48. This is also spoken of as **addition of a series** <term>saṅkalita</term>. Then the eighth is **subtraction of a series** <term>vyutkalita</term> <note>specifically, the subtraction of a part of a series, taken from the beginning, from the whole series</note>, and this is also spoken of as **the remainder** <term>śēṣa</term>. All these eight operations appertain to fractions also.

### General rules in regard to zero and positive and negative quantities.

49. A number multiplied by zero is zero, and that number remains unchanged when it is divided by zero, combined with zero, or...

<note>Translator's note: Mahāvīrācārya incorrectly states here that a number remains unchanged when divided by zero. In contrast, the later mathematician Bhāskara (12th century) calls the quotient of such zero-divisions "that which has zero as its divisor" <term>khahara</term> and correctly identifies it as having the value of infinity. Mahāvīrācārya likely viewed division by zero as a "null" operation that leaves the value untouched.</note>

...diminished by zero remains unchanged. Multiplication and other operations in relation to zero result in zero; and in the operation of addition, the zero becomes the same as what is added to it. <note>In modern terms: x - 0 = x; x * 0 = 0; and 0 + x = x.</note>

50. In multiplying as well as dividing two negative or two positive quantities, the result is a positive quantity. But it is a negative quantity when the two quantities consist of one positive and one negative. In adding a positive and a negative quantity, the result is their difference.

51. The addition of two negative quantities or of two positive quantities results in a negative or positive quantity respectively. A positive quantity which has to be subtracted from a given number becomes negative, and a negative quantity which has to be so subtracted becomes positive. <note>This describes the rule of signs: subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive.</note>

52. The square of a positive as well as of a negative quantity is positive; and the square roots of those square quantities are positive and negative respectively. As in the nature of things a negative quantity is not a square quantity, it has therefore no square root. <note>Mahāvīrācārya correctly identifies that within the system of real numbers, negative numbers cannot have square roots—a sophisticated observation for the 9th century.</note>

### **The Names of Notational Places.**

63. The first place is what is known as the **unit** <term>ēka</term>; the second place is named **ten** <term>daśa</term>; the third they call **hundred** <term>śata</term>, while the fourth is **thousand** <term>sahasra</term>.

*   A strong power of memory;

*   The skill to find unknown numbers from those already known <note>This refers to the basics of algebraic reasoning—deriving the value of a variable.</note>.

70. Great sages have briefly established these technical terms. Whatever else needs to be explained in more detail should be learned directly from the study of the science of mathematics.

# CHAPTER II.
## ARITHMETICAL OPERATIONS.

### The First Subject of Treatment.

Hereafter we shall expound the first subject of treatment, which is named *<term>Parikarman</term>* <note>literally "preliminary work" or "purification"; in a mathematical context, these are the fundamental operations that "prepare" or "process" numbers, usually numbering eight: multiplication, division, squaring, square-root extraction, cubing, cube-root extraction, and two types of series summation</note>.

### Multiplication.

The rule of work in relation to the operation of multiplication, which is the first (among the *parikarman* operations), is as follows:—
1. After placing (the multiplicand and the multiplier one below the other) in the manner of the hinges of a door <note>original: *kapāṭa-sandhi*. This refers to a method where the digits are aligned vertically and shifted horizontally as the calculation progresses, much like how a folding door or hinge moves</note>, the multiplicand should be multiplied by the multiplier, in accordance with (either of) the two methods of normal (or) reverse working, by adopting the process of (i) dividing the multiplicand and multiplying the multiplier by a factor of the multiplicand, (ii) of dividing the multiplier and multiplying the multiplicand <note>This describes the "method of factors," where numbers are simplified into their divisors to make multiplication easier</note>

<insert>
1. Symbolically expressed, this rule works out thus:—
* In multiplying $ab$ by $cd$, the product is (i) $\frac{ab}{a} \times (a \times cd)$; or (ii) $(ab \times c) \times \frac{cd}{c}$; or (iii) $ab \times cd$. Obviously the object of the first two devices here is to facilitate working through the choice of suitable factors.
</insert>

The *<term>anulōma</term>* <note>literally "with the hair" or "with the grain," referring to the natural or forward order, starting with the highest place value and moving down to the units</note> or normal method of working is the one that is generally followed. The *<term>vilōma</term>* <note>literally "against the hair" or "against the grain," referring to the reverse order, starting from the units and moving to the higher values</note> or the reverse method of working is as follows:—
To multiply 1998 by 27:

## Division.

The rule of work in relation to the operation of division, which is the second among the <term>parikarman</term> <note>original: "parikarman" — these are the fundamental mathematical operations or "tools" used in calculation.</note> operations, is as follows:—

18. Put down the dividend and divide it by the divisor, which is placed below the dividend. This should be done in accordance with the process of removing common factors <note>The text suggests simplifying the fraction before dividing, a process known as reduction.</note>. Then, provide the resulting quotient.

Or:

19. The dividend should be divided in the reverse way <note>In ancient Indian mathematics, the "reverse way" usually refers to performing division from left to right, starting with the highest place value, which is the opposite of how many scribal traditions handled addition.</note> by the divisor placed below, after performing the operation of removing common factors if that is possible.

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

20. <term>Dīnāras</term> <note>A gold coin, the name of which is derived from the Roman denarius.</note> amounting to 8,192 have been divided between 64 men. What is the share of one man? <note>In the original Sanskrit verse, the number 8,192 is described as 8,000 + 92 + 100.</note>

21. Tell me the share of one person when 2,701 pieces of gold are divided among 37 persons.

22. <term>Dīnāras</term> amounting to 10,349 have been divided between 79 persons. What is the amount obtained by a single person? <note>In the original, 10,349 is presented as 10,000 + 300 + 7² (49).</note>

23. Gold pieces amounting to 14,141 are given to 79 temples. What is the money given to each temple? <note>In the original, 14,141 is phrased as 10,000 + (40 + 4,000 + 1 + 100).</note>

24. <term>Jambū</term> fruits <note>The rose-apple or Indian blackberry, a common fruit in South Asia.</note> amounting to 31,317 have been divided between 39 persons. Tell me the share of each. <note>In the original, 31,317 is given as 17 + 300 + 31,000.</note>

25. <term>Jambū</term> fruits amounting to 31,313 have been divided between 181 persons. Give out the share of each. <note>In the original, 31,313 is given as 13 + 300 + 31,000.</note>

26. Gems amounting to 36,261 in number are given to 9 persons equally. What does one man obtain here? <note>In the original, 36,261 is given as 30,000 + 1 + (60 + 200 + 6,000).</note>

27. O friend, gold pieces to the value of the number wherein the figures in order from the units' place upwards are— <note>The dividend described here is a "palindrome" number: 12,345,654,321.</note>

### Squaring.

The rule of work in relation to the operation of squaring, which is the third (among the <term>parikarman</term> operations), is as follows:—

29. The multiplication of two equal quantities: or the multiplication of the two quantities obtained (from the given quantity) by the subtraction (therefrom), and the addition (thereunto), of any chosen quantity, together with the addition of the square of that chosen quantity (to that product): or the sum of a series in arithmetical progression, of which 1 is the first term, 2 is the common difference, and the number of terms wherein is that (of which the square is) required: gives rise to the (required) square. <note>This verse provides three methods for squaring a number (n): 1. n × n; 2. (n + x)(n - x) + x²; 3. The sum of the first 'n' odd numbers.</note>

30. The square of numbers consisting of two or more places is (equal to) the sum of the squares of all the numbers (in all the places) combined with twice the product of those (numbers) taken (two at a time) in order. <note>This is the geometric expansion of a square, similar to (a+b)² = a² + b² + 2ab.</note>

---

28. Here, 28,483 is given as 83 + 400 + (4000 × 7). <note>This describes how the number is structured in the original verse, likely to fit the poetic meter.</note>
29. The rule given herein, expressed algebraically, comes out thus:
    (i) a x a = a²; (ii) (a + *x*) (a - *x*) + *x*² = a²; (iii) 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + . . . up to a terms = a².
30. The word translated by place here is <term>sthāna</term> <note>original: "स्थान" (sthāna)</note>; it obviously means a place in notation. Here, as a commentary interprets it, it may also denote the component parts of a sum, as each such part has a place in the sum. According to both these interpretations the rule works out correctly.
    For instance, (1234)² = (1000² + 200² + 30² + 4²) + 2 × 1000 × 200 + 2 × 1000 × 30 + 2 × 1000 × 4 + 2 × 200 × 30 + 2 × 200 × 4 + 2 × 30 × 4.
    Similarly (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)² = (1² + 2² + 3² + 4²) + 2(1 × 2 + 1 × 3 + 1 × 4 + 2 × 3 + 2 × 4 + 3 × 4).

31. Get the square of the last figure (in the number, the order of counting the figures being from the right to the left <note>In modern terms, the "last figure" here refers to the highest place value, such as the hundreds or thousands digit.</note>,) and then multiply this last (figure), after it is doubled and pushed on (to the right by one notational place), by (the figures found in) the remaining places. Each of the remaining figures (in the number) is to be pushed on (by one place) and then dealt with similarly. This is the method of squaring.

->*Examples in illustration thereof.*<-

32. Give out the squares of (the numbers from) 1 to 9, of 15, 16, 25, 36 and 75.
33. What will 338, 4661 and 256 become when squared?
34. O arithmetician, give out, if you know, the squares of 65536, 12345 and 3333.
35. (Each of the numbers) 6387, and then 7135, and (then) 1022 is squared. O clever arithmetician, tell me, after multiplying well, the value of those three (squares).

->Thus ends squaring, the third of the operations known as <term>Parikarman</term> <note>original: "parikarman" — the basic or "preparatory" operations of arithmetic.</note>.<---

## Square Root.

The rule of work in relation to the operation of extracting the square root, which is the fourth of the <term>parikarman</term> <note>original: "parikarman" — the fundamental or "preparatory" operations of arithmetic, which traditionally include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, squaring, and square roots.</note> operations, is as follows:

36. From the number represented by the figures up to the last odd place <note>Counting from right to left, the 1st, 3rd, and 5th digits are "odd" places; the 2nd, 4th, etc., are "even" places.</note> of notation counted from the right, subtract the highest possible square number; then multiply the root of this number by two, and divide with this product the number represented by taking into position the figure belonging to the next even place; and then the square of the quotient so obtained is to be subtracted from the number represented by taking into position the figure belonging to the next odd place. If it is so continued till the end, the half of the last doubled quantity comes to be the resulting square root.

### Examples in illustration thereof.

37. O friend, tell me quickly the roots of the squares of the numbers from 1 to 9, and of 256 and 576.
38. Find out the square root of 6561 and of 65536.
39. What are the square roots of 4,294,967,296 and 622,521?
40. What are the square roots of 63,664,441 and 1,771,561?
41. Tell me, friend, after considering well, the square roots of 1296 and 625.

### Cubing.

The rule of work in relation to the operation of cubing, which is the fifth (of the <term>parikarman</term> operations), is as follows:—

43. The product of (any) three equal quantities; or the product obtained by the multiplication of any (given) quantity by that (given quantity) as diminished by a chosen quantity and (then again) by that (given quantity) as increased by the (same) chosen quantity, when combined with the square of the chosen quantity as multiplied by the least (of the above three quantities) and (combined) also with the cube of the chosen quantity: gives rise to a cubic quantity.

44. Or, the summing up of a series in arithmetical progression <note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.</note>, of which the first term is the quantity (the cube whereof is) required, the common difference is twice this quantity, and the number of terms is (equal to) this (same given) quantity, (gives rise to the cube of the given quantity). Or, the square of the quantity (the cube whereof is required), when combined with the product (obtained by the multiplication) of this given quantity diminished by one by the sum of a series in arithmetical progression in which the first term is *one*, the common difference is *two* and the number of terms is (equal to) the given quantity, (gives rise to the cube of the given quantity).

---

<insert>
43. Symbolically expressed, this rule works out thus:
(i) $a \times a \times a = a^3$ : (ii) $a (a+b) (a-b) + b^2 (a-b) + b^3 = a^3$.
44. Algebraically, this rule means—
(i) $a^3 = a + 3a + 5a + 7a + \dots$ to $a$ terms.
(ii) $a^3 = a^2 + (a-1) (1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + \dots$ to $a$ terms).
</insert>
