<page-num>71</page-num>

## CHAPTER IV—MISCELLANEOUS PROBLEMS (ON FRACTIONS).

The varieties of **Two-fold Remainder-Root** <note>original: *Dviragraśēṣamūla*</note> and **Fractional Root** <note>original: *Amśamūla*</note>, then **Product of Parts** <note>original: *Bhāgābhyāsa*</note>, then **Square of a Fraction** <note>original: *Amśavarga*</note>, **Mixed Roots** <note>original: *Mūlamiśra*</note>, and **Fractional Visible Portion** <note>original: *Bhinnadr̥śya*</note>.

The rule relating to the <term>Portion</term> <note>original: *Bhāga*</note> and the <term>Remainder</term> <note>original: *Śēṣa*</note> varieties therein (that is, in these miscellaneous problems on fractions):

4. In the operation relating to the **Portion** variety, the required result is obtained by dividing the given quantity by *one* as diminished by the known fractions. In the operation relating to the **Remainder** variety, the required result is the given quantity divided by the product of the quantities obtained respectively by subtracting the known fractions from *one*.

->Examples in the <term>Portion</term> variety.<-

5. Of a pillar, 1/8 part was seen by me to be buried under the ground, 1/3 in water, 1/4 in moss, and **7** <term>hastas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of length, approximately 18 inches or the length of a forearm (a cubit).</note> thereof was free in the air. What is the total length of the pillar?

---

In the **Product of Parts** <note>original: *Bhāgābhyāsa* or *Bhāgasamvarga*</note> variety, the numerical value is given of the portion remaining after removing from the whole the product or products of certain fractional parts of the whole taken two by two.

The **Square of a Fraction** <note>original: *Amśavarga*</note> variety consists of problems wherein the numerical value is given of the remainder after removing from the whole the square of a fractional part thereof, this fractional part being at the same time increased or decreased by a given number.

The **Mixed Roots** <note>original: *Mūlamiśra*</note> variety consists of problems wherein is given the numerical value of the sum of the square root of the whole when added to the square root of the whole as increased or diminished by a given number of things.

In the **Fractional Visible Portion** <note>original: *Bhinnadr̥śya*</note> variety, a fractional part of the whole as multiplied by another fractional part thereof is removed from it, and the remaining portion is expressed as a fraction of the whole. Here it will be seen that, unlike in the other varieties, the numerical value of the last remaining portion is not actually given, but is expressed as a fraction of the whole.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;4. Algebraically, the rule relating to the **Portion** variety is $x = \frac{a}{1 - b}$, where *x* is the unknown collective quantity to be found out, *a* is the <term>visible part</term> <note>original: *dr̥śya* or *agra*</note>, and *b* is the **portion** <note>original: *bhāga*</note> or the fractional part (or the sum of the fractional parts) given.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It is obvious that this is derivable from the equation $x - bx = a$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The rule relating to the **Remainder** <note>original: *Śēṣa*; the OCR "Śēṣu" is likely a typo</note> variety, when algebraically expressed, comes to:

$x = \frac{a}{(1 - b_1) (1 - b_2) (1 - b_3) \times \dots}$ 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;where $b_1$, $b_2$, $b_3$, etc., are fractional parts of the successive remainders. This formula also is derivable from the equation:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$x - b_1x - b_2 (x - b_1x) - b_3 \{ x - b_1x - b_2 (x - b_1x) \} - \dots = a$.

<note>Vocabulary used on this page: **Bhāga** (Portion/Part), **Śēṣa** (Remainder), **Dviragraśēṣamūla** (Two-fold Remainder-Root), **Amśamūla** (Fractional Root), **Bhāgābhyāsa** (Product of Parts), **Amśavarga** (Square of a Fraction), **Mūlamiśra** (Mixed Roots), **Bhinnadr̥śya** (Fractional Visible Portion), **hastas** (cubits), **dr̥śya** (the known/visible quantity), **agra** (the tip or known remainder).</note>

6. Out of a collection of excellent bees, 1/5 took delight in <term>pāṭalī</term> trees <note>The Trumpet Flower tree (*Stereospermum chelonoides*).</note>, 1/3 in <term>kadamba</term> trees <note>A tropical tree with fragrant, orange, globe-shaped blossoms (*Neolamarckia cadamba*).</note>, 1/4 in mango trees, and 1/5 in a <term>campaka</term> tree <note>A tree famous for its strongly scented yellow or orange flowers (*Magnolia champaca*).</note> with blossoms fully opened; 1/30 was in a collection of full-blown lotuses, opened by the rays of the sun; and finally, a single intoxicated bee was seen circling in the sky. What is the total number of bees in that collection?

7. A certain <term>śrāvaka</term> <note>A lay follower of Jainism.</note>, having gathered lotuses and loudly uttering hundreds of prayers, offered those lotuses in worship: 1/3 of the lotuses were offered, and of that 1/3, he gave 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6 respectively to four <term>tīrthaṅkaras</term> <note>The 24 "ford-makers" or great spiritual teachers of Jainism who have conquered the cycle of rebirth.</note> commencing with the excellent <term>Jina Vṛṣabha</term> <note>The first Tīrthaṅkara, also known as Lord Rishabhanatha.</note>; then to <term>Sumati</term> <note>The fifth Tīrthaṅkara.</note> he offered 1/6 as well as 1/12 of that same initial 1/3 of the lotuses; thereafter, he offered in worship to the remaining 19 <term>tīrthaṅkaras</term> 2 lotuses each with a mind well-pleased. What is the numerical value of all those lotuses?

8 to 11. * this last quantity multiplied by 6 was made up of the preachers of the rules of conduct; 
* and this very same quantity diminished by 1/4 of itself was made up of astrologers; 
* the difference between these two last-mentioned quantities was made up of controversialists; 
* this quantity multiplied by 6 was made up of penitent ascetics; 
* and 9 $\times$ 8 leading ascetics <note>Totaling 72 individuals.</note> were further seen by me near the top of a mountain with their shining bodies highly heated by the rays of the sun. 
Tell me quickly the total measure of this collection of prominent sages.

# CHAPTER IV—MISCELLANEOUS PROBLEMS (ON FRACTIONS).

32. Of the contents of a treasury, one man obtained 1/3 part; others obtained from 1/3 in order to 1/2, in the end, of the successive remainders; and at last 12 <term>purāṇas<note>An ancient Indian silver coin mentioned frequently in historical mathematical texts.</note></term> were seen by me to remain. What is the numerical measure of the <term>purāṇas</term> contained in the treasury?

Here end examples in the <term>Śēṣa<note>original: "Śēṣa" means "remainder". These are problems where fractions are taken from successive remaining amounts rather than the whole.</note></term> variety.

The rule relating to the <term>Mūla<note>original: "Mūla" means "root". This variety involves the square root of the unknown quantity within the equation.</note></term> variety of miscellaneous problems on fractions:—

33. Half of the coefficient of the square root of the unknown quantity and then the known remainder should be each divided by *one* as diminished by the fractional coefficient of the unknown quantity. The square root of the sum of the known remainder so treated, as combined with the square of the coefficient of the square root of the unknown quantity dealt with as above, and then associated with the similarly treated coefficient of the square root of the unknown quantity, and thereafter squared as a whole, gives rise to the required unknown quantity in this <term>mūla</term> variety of miscellaneous problems on fractions.

<insert>
33. Algebraically expressed, this rule comes to:
x = { (c/2)/(1-b) + √[ a/(1-b) + ((c/2)/(1-b))^2 ] }^2
This is easily obtained from the equation x — (bx + c √x + a) = 0. This equation is the algebraical expression of problems of this variety. Here *c* stands for the coefficient of the square root of the unknown quantity to be found out, *b* for the fractional part of the total, and *a* for the constant remainder.
</insert>

46. Five and one-fourth times the square root of a herd of elephants are sporting on a mountain slope; 5/9 of the remainder sport on the top of the mountain; five times the square root of the remainder (after deducting this) sport in a forest of lotuses; and there are 6 elephants then left on the bank of a river. ->Here ends the <term>Śeṣamūla<note>Sanskrit: "Root of the remainder." These problems involve finding a total quantity where various parts and square roots of remainders are subtracted until a final known constant is reached.</note></term> variety of miscellaneous problems on fractions.<-

### The rule relating to the Root of the Remainder variety involving two known quantities constituting the remainders:

47. The coefficient of the square root of the unknown collective quantity and the final quantity known to remain should both be divided by the product of the fractional proportional quantities, as subtracted from *one* in each case; then the first known quantity should be added to the other known quantity treated as above. Thereafter, the operation relating to the <term>Śeṣamūla</term> variety of miscellaneous problems on fractions is to be adopted.

---

<note>The following section provides an algebraic commentary on the preceding rule, explaining how Mahāvīrācārya's verbal rule translates into modern mathematical notation.</note>

47. Algebraically, this rule enables us to arrive at the expressions $\frac{c}{(1-b_1) (1-b_2) \times \&c.}$ and $\frac{a_2}{(1-b_1) (1-b_2) \times \&c.} + a_1$, which are required to be substituted for *c* and *a* respectively in the formula for <term>śeṣamūla</term>, which is $x - bx = \{ \frac{c}{2} + \sqrt{(\frac{c}{2})^2 + a} \}^2$. In applying this formula, the value of *b* becomes zero, as the <term>mūla<note>Sanskrit: "root." In this context, it refers specifically to the square root operation.</note></term> or square root involved in the <term>dviragra-śeṣamūla<note>Sanskrit: "Root of the remainder with two remainders." This refers to a specific sub-class of problems where there are two distinct constant quantities (*a1* and *a2*) left over at different stages of the problem.</note></term> is that of the total collective quantity and not of a fractional part of that quantity. Substituting as desired, we get $x = \{ \frac{c}{2 (1-b_1) (1-b_2) \times \&c.} + \sqrt{(\frac{c}{2 (1-b_1) (1-b_2) \times \&c.})^2 + (\frac{a_2}{(1-b_1) (1-b_2) \times \&c.} + a_1)} \}^2$. This result may easily be obtained from the equation $x - a_1 - b_1 (x - a_1) - b_2 \{ x - a_1 - b_1 (x - a_1) \} - . . . . . . - c \sqrt{x} - a_2 = 0$, where $b_1, b_2$, etc., are the various fractional parts of the successive remainders; and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are the first known quantity and the final known quantity respectively.

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

48. A single bee (out of a swarm of bees) was seen in the sky; 1/5 of the remainder (of the swarm), and 1/4 of the remainder (left thereafter), and (again), 1/3 of the remainder (left thereafter), and (a number of bees equal to) the square root (of the numerical value of the swarm, were seen) in lotuses; and two (bees remaining at last were seen) on a mango tree. How many are those (bees in the swarm)?

49. Four (out of a collection of) lions were seen on a mountain; and fractional parts commencing with 1/6 and ending with 1/2 of the successive remainders (of the collection), and (lions equivalent in number to) twice the square root (of the numerical value of the collection), as also (the finally remaining) four (lions), were seen in a forest. How many are those (lions in the collection)?

multiplied by the (given proportional) fraction; then that result which is arrived at by means of the operation of finding out (the unknown quantity) in the <term>Root of the Remainder<note>Sanskrit: *Śēṣamūla*. A category of problems where the square root of a specific fraction of the total is part of the equation.</note></term> variety (of miscellaneous problems on fractions).

### Another rule relating to the Root of a Fraction variety.

52. The known quantity given as the (ultimate) remainder is divided by the (given proportional) fraction and multiplied by **four**; to this the square (of the coefficient) of the square root (of the given fraction of the unknown collective quantity) is added; then the square root (of this sum), combined with (the above mentioned coefficient of) the square root (of the fractional unknown quantity), and (then) halved, and (then) squared, and (then) multiplied by the (given proportional) fraction, becomes the required result.

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

53. Eight times the square root of 1/3 part of the stalk of a lotus is within water, and 16 <term>finger-breadths<note>Sanskrit: *aṅgulas*. An ancient Indian unit of length, approximately 0.75 inches.</note></term> (thereof are) in the air (above water); give out the height of the water (above the bed) as well as of the stalk (of the lotus).

54-55. (Out of a herd of elephants), nine times the square root of 2/3 part of their number, and six times the square root of 3/5 of the remainder (left thereafter), and (finally) 24 (remaining) elephants with their broad temples wetted with the stream of the exuding <term>ichor<note>The original refers to *mada*, a secretion from an elephant's temples during a period of high testosterone known as "musth."</note></term>, were seen by me in a forest. How many are (all) the elephants?

---

<note>In reference to stanza 47, $x - bx$ becomes $x$ here also. After substituting as desired, and dividing the result by $b$, we get $x = \left\{ \frac{cb}{2} + \sqrt{(\frac{cb}{2})^2 + ab} \right\}^2 \div b$. This value of $x$ may be easily arrived at from the algebraic equation $x - c\sqrt{bx} - a = 0$.</note>

The rule relating to the <term>Product of Fractions<note>Sanskrit: *Bhāgasamvarga*. This category deals with problems where the unknown quantity is multiplied by fractional parts of itself.</note></term> variety (of miscellaneous problems on fractions):—

57. From the (simplified) denominator (of the specified compound fractional part of the unknown collective quantity), divided by its own (related) numerator (also simplified), subtract four times the given known part (of the quantity), then multiply this (resulting difference) by that same (simplified) denominator (dealt with as above). The square root (of this product) is to be added to as well as subtracted from that (same) denominator (so dealt with); (then) the half (of either) of these (two quantities resulting as sum or difference is the unknown) collective quantity (required to be found out). <note>In modern algebraic terms, if $x$ is the total and $a$ is the remainder, and the fractions are $\frac{m}{n}$ and $\frac{p}{q}$, the formula provided is $x = \frac{\frac{nq}{mp} \pm \sqrt{(\frac{nq}{mp} - 4a)\frac{nq}{mp}}}{2}$. This is derived from the quadratic equation $x - (\frac{m}{n} \cdot \frac{p}{q})x^2 - a = 0$.</note>

Give out what the measure of the heap is.

The rule relating to the <term>Square of a Fraction<note>Sanskrit: *Aṁśavarga*</note></term> variety (of miscellaneous problems on fractions), characterized by the subtraction or addition of known quantities:—

**61.** Take the half of the denominator (of the specified fractional part of the unknown collective quantity), as divided by its own related numerator, and as increased or diminished by the given known quantity which is subtracted from or added to the specified fractional part of the unknown collective quantity. The square root of the square of this resulting quantity, as diminished by the square of the above known quantity to be subtracted or to be added and also by the known remainder of the collective quantity, when added to or subtracted from the square root of the square quantity mentioned above and then divided by the specified fractional part of the unknown collective quantity, gives the required value of the unknown collective quantity.

$x = \{ \pm \sqrt{ (\frac{n}{2m} \pm a )^2 - a^2 - a } + ( \frac{n}{2m} \pm a ) \} \div \frac{m}{n}$. This value
is obtained from the equation $x - ( \frac{m}{n} x \mp a )^2 - a = 0$, where $a$ is the
given known quantity.

### *Examples of the "minus" variety.*

66. After adding together a number of pigeons equal to the square root of the whole collection, and another number equal to the square root of that same collection minus 12, the result is exactly 6 pigeons. What is the numerical value of that collection of pigeons?

67. The sum of two quantities—the first being the square root of a whole collection of pigeons, and the second being the square root of that same collection minus 64 <note>The original text uses "the cube of 4."</note>—amounts to 16. How many birds are in that collection?

### *An example of the "plus" variety.*

68. There is a collection of superior swans. The sum of the square root of their total number and the square root of that same total number *plus* 68 amounts to 34 <note>The original text states "6 squared minus 2."</note>. Tell me, how many swans are in that collection?

->Here ends the <term>Mixed Roots<note>original: *Mūlamiśra*</note></term> variety.<-

### The rule relating to the <term>Visible Fractions<note>original: *Bhinnadṛśya*</note></term> variety (of miscellaneous problems on fractions):—

69. When one, diminished by the given fractional remainder, is divided by the product of the specified fractional parts, the result reached is the required answer for problems in the <term>Visible Fractions<note>original: *Bhinnadṛśya*</note></term> category.

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

70. A portion of a pillar was found buried in the sand; this buried portion was equal to one-eighth of the pillar's total length multiplied by one-eighteenth of that same length. One-half of the pillar was visible above ground. Say, what is the vertically measured length of the pillar?

---

<note>
69. In modern algebraic terms, the total length $x$ is found by $x = ( 1 - \frac{r}{s} ) \div (\frac{m}{n} \times \frac{p}{q})$. This is derived from the equation $x - (\frac{m}{n}x \cdot \frac{p}{q}x) - \frac{r}{s}x = 0$, where $x$ represents the whole, the middle term is the product of fractions of that whole, and the final term is the remaining fractional part.
</note>

# CHAPTER V.

## THE RULE OF THREE.

### The fourth subject of treatment.

1. Salutation to that blessed <term>Vardhamāna<note>Another name for Mahāvīra, the 24th Tirthankara (spiritual teacher) of Jainism, to whom the author is devoted.</note></term>, who is like a helpful relative to all the three worlds, and is resplendent like the sun in the matter of absolute knowledge, and has cast off the taint of all <term>karmas<note>In Jain philosophy, *karma* is viewed as a physical substance that attaches to the soul; "casting it off" refers to achieving spiritual liberation.</note></term>.

Next we shall expound the fourth subject of treatment, namely, the <term>rule-of-three<note>original: *trairāśika*</note></term>.

The rule of operation in respect thereof is as follows:

2. Here, in the rule-of-three, the <term>Fruit<note>original: *Phala* — the known result or output.</note></term> multiplied by the <term>Requisition<note>original: *Icchā* — the "desire," or the quantity for which we want to find a result.</note></term> and divided by the <term>Measure<note>original: *Pramāṇa* — the initial standard or reference quantity.</note></term>, becomes the required answer, provided that the Requisition and the Measure are similar (meaning they are in direct proportion); and in the case of this proportion being inverse, this operation involving multiplication and division is reversed, so as to have division in the place of multiplication and multiplication in the place of division.

->Examples relating to the former half of the above rule, that is,<-
->on the direct rule-of-three:<-

3. A man who in $3\frac{1}{4}$ days travels $5\frac{3}{4}$ <term>yojanas<note>A *yojana* is a traditional Indian measure of distance, roughly equal to 8 or 9 miles.</note></term>—calculate what distance he goes over in a year and a day.

4. A lame man walks over $1/2$ of a <term>krośa<note>A *krośa* is a measure of distance, traditionally one-fourth of a *yojana* (about 2 miles).</note></term> together with $1/3$ thereof in $7\frac{1}{2}$ days. Say what distance he covers in $3\frac{1}{2}$ years at this rate.

5. A worm travels $1/4$ of an <term>aṅgula<note>An *aṅgula* is a unit of length based on the width of a finger, roughly 3/4 of an inch.</note></term> in $1/8$ of a day. In how many days will it reach the top of the <term>Meru mountain<note>In Indian cosmology, Mount Meru is the sacred golden mountain at the center of the universe.</note></term> from its bottom?

6. The man who in $3\frac{1}{2}$ days uses up $1\frac{1}{4}$ <term>kārṣāpaṇas<note>An ancient Indian silver or copper coin.</note></term>—in what time will he use up 100 <term>purāṇas<note>A type of silver coin, often equal in value to a *kārṣāpaṇa*.</note></term> along with 1 <term>paṇa<note>A copper coin, usually 1/16th of a *kārṣāpaṇa* or *purāṇa*.</note></term>?

***

<note>2. The Measure (*Pramāṇa*) and Fruit (*Phala*) together establish the rate. The Requisition (*Icchā*) is the new quantity we are curious about. For example, in Problem 3: the Measure is $3\frac{1}{4}$ days, the Fruit is $5\frac{3}{4}$ yojanas, and the Requisition is 1 year and 1 day. The formula is (Fruit × Requisition) / Measure.</note>
<note>5. The height of the Meru mountain is traditionally calculated here as 99,000 *yojanas*, which translates to 76,032,000,000 *aṅgulas*.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the Rule of Three, a fundamental mathematical principle for solving proportions. It provides the core formula (Result = [Fruit × Requisition] / Measure) and applies it to various practical and mythological problems involving distance, time, and currency.</summary>
<keywords>Rule of Three, Vardhamāna, karma, proportion, yojana, krośa, aṅgula, Mount Meru, kārṣāpaṇa, purāṇa, currency, ancient Indian mathematics</keywords>

### *An example on inverse quadruple rule-of-three.*

## The rule in regard to problems bearing on associated forward and backward movement.

**23.** Write down the net daily movement, as derived from the difference of the given rates of forward and backward movements, each of these rates being first divided by its own specified time; and then in relation to this net daily movement, carry out the operation of the rule-of-three. <note>This rule explains how to find the "net rate" (velocity) by subtracting the rate of retreat from the rate of progress before solving for the total time or distance.</note>

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

**24-25.** In the course of 3/7 of a day, a ship goes over 1/4 of a <term>krōśa<note>original: *krōśa*; a traditional unit of distance, roughly 2 miles.</note></term> in the ocean; being opposed by the wind she goes back (during the same time) 1/9 of a *krōśa*. Give out, O you who have powerful arms in crossing over the ocean of numbers well, in what time that ship will have gone over 99 2/3 <term>yōjanas<note>original: *yōjana*; a large distance measure, usually considered to be about 8 or 9 miles (consisting of 4 *krōśas*).</note></term>.

**26.** A man earning at the rate of 1 1/4 of a gold coin in 3 1/3 days, spends in 4 1/2 days 1/4 of the gold coin as also 1/5 of that 1/4 itself; by what time will he own 70 of those gold coins as his net earnings?

**27.** That excellent elephant, which, with temples that are attacked by the feet of bees greedy of the flowing <term>ichor<note>original: *mada*; a fragrant, honey-like fluid that secretes from the temples of an elephant in rut, often described in poetic Sanskrit literature as attracting bees.</note></term>, goes over 1/5 as well as 1/2 of a *yōjana* in 5 1/2 days, and moves back in 3 1/2 days over 3/5 of a *krōśa*: say in what time he will have gone over a net distance of 100 *yōjanas* less by 1/2 *krōśa*.

**28-30.** A well completely filled with water is 10 <term>daṇḍas<note>original: *daṇḍa*; literally a 'staff' or 'rod,' a unit of length approximately equal to 6 feet.</note></term> in depth; a lotus sprouting up therein grows from the bottom—

### The rule of operation relating to double, treble and quadruple rule-of-three.

**32.** Transpose the <term>Phala<note>original: *phala*; literally "fruit," referring to the result or "output" of the problem (e.g., the price or the quantity produced).</note></term> from its own place to the other place (wherein a similar concrete quantity would occur); (then, for the purpose of arriving at the required result), the row consisting of the larger number (of different quantities) should be, (after they are all multiplied together), divided by the row consisting of the...

---

<note>32. The transference of the <term>Phala</term> and the other operations herein mentioned will be clear from the following worked out example.</note>

The data in the problem in stanza No. 36 are to be first represented thus:—

| | |
|---|---|
| 9 <term>Mānīs<note>A unit of volume for grain.</note></term>. | 1 <term>Vāha<note>A larger unit of volume; 1 vāha = 20 kumbhas.</note></term> + 1 <term>Kumbha<note>A unit of volume.</note></term>. |
| 3 <term>Yōjanas<note>original: *yōjana*; a measure of distance, roughly 7 to 9 miles.</note></term>. | 10 <term>Yōjanas</term>. |
| 60 <term>Paṇas<note>original: *paṇa*; a copper coin used as a unit of currency.</note></term>. | |

When the <term>Phala</term> here, viz., 60 <term>paṇas</term>, is transferred to the other row we have—

| | |
|---|---|
| 9 <term>Mānīs</term>. | 1 <term>Vāha</term> + 1 <term>Kumbha</term> = 1¼ <term>Vāha</term>. |
| 3 <term>Yōjanas</term>. | 10 <term>Yōjanas</term>. |
| | 60 <term>Paṇas</term>. |

Now the right hand row, consisting of a larger number of different quantities, should be, after they are all multiplied together, divided by the smaller left hand row similarly dealt with.

Then we have
->1¼ x 10 x 60<-
->-------------<-
->9 x 3<-

The result here gives the number of <term>paṇas</term> to be found out.

# CHAPTER VI.

## MIXED PROBLEMS.

### The Fifth Subject of Treatment.

1. For attaining the supreme good, we worshipfully salute the holy <term>Jinas<note>original: *Jina*; literally "Conquerors," the enlightened beings of the Jaina faith who have overcome the cycle of rebirth.</note></term>, who are in possession of the fourfold infinite attributes, who are the makers of <term>tīrthas<note>original: *tīrtha*; literally a "ford" or "crossing-place." In Jaina tradition, these are the teachers who provide the means to cross the river of worldly suffering.</note></term>, who have attained self-conquest, are pure, are honoured in all the three worlds and are also excellent preceptors—the <term>Jinas</term> who have gone over to the (other) shore of the ocean of the <term>Jaina</term> doctrines, and are the guides and teachers of (all) born beings, and who, being the abode of all good qualities, are good in themselves and do good to others.

Hereafter we shall expound the fifth subject of treatment known as mixed problems. It is as follows:

->Statement of the meaning of the technical terms <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> and <term>viṣama-saṅkramaṇa</term>:<-

2. Those who have gone to the end of the ocean of calculation say that the halving of the sum and of the difference (of any two quantities) is known as <term>saṅkramaṇa<note>This operation is used to find two individual numbers when their sum and difference are known. If the sum is *a* and the difference is *b*, the numbers are (a+b)/2 and (a-b)/2.</note></term>, and that the <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> of two quantities which are respectively the divisor and the quotient is that which is <term>viṣama</term> <note>meaning "complex" or "non-equilateral"</note> (i.e., <term>viṣama-saṅkramaṇa<note>This refers to finding two numbers when their product and their difference—or their sum—are known.</note></term>).

->*Examples in illustration thereof.*<-

3. What is the <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> where the number 12 (is associated) with 2; and what is the divisional <term>viṣama-saṅkramaṇa</term> of that same number (12 in relation to 2)?

***

1 <term>Tīrtha</term> is interpreted to mean a ford intended to cross the river of mundane existence which is subject to <term>karma<note>The law of cause and effect regarding actions.</note></term> and reincarnation. The <term>Jinas</term> are conceived to be capable of enabling the souls of men to get out of the stream of <term>saṁsāra<note>The continuous cycle of birth, death, and rebirth.</note></term> or the recurring cycle of embodied existence. The <term>Jinas</term> are therefore called <term>tīrthankaras<note>The "ford-makers" who establish the path to liberation.</note></term>.

2. Algebraically the <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> of any two quantities *a* and *b* is finding out $\frac{a + b}{2}$ and $\frac{a - b}{2}$; their <term>viṣama-saṅkramaṇa</term> is arriving at $\frac{b + \frac{a}{b}}{2}$ and $\frac{b - \frac{a}{b}}{2}$. <note>original: the symbol $\sim$ used in the OCR denotes the difference between two values.</note>

## Double Rule-of-three.

The rule for arriving at the value of interest through the operation known as the <term>Double Rule-of-three<note>Also known as compound proportion, this method is used when more than three quantities are involved in a proportional relationship—in this case, capital, time, and interest.</note></term>:

4. The number representing the <term>Desired Quantity<note>original: *Icchā*; in a proportion, this is the specific value the mathematician is trying to solve for, as opposed to the "standard" or given rate.</note></term>—that is, the amount for which the interest is sought—is multiplied by the time associated with it, and is then multiplied by the number representing the given rate of interest for the standard capital. This resulting product is then divided by the standard time and the standard capital quantity associated with the rate of interest. This quotient is, in the science of calculation, the interest of the desired amount. <note>In modern algebraic terms, this is expressed as: Interest = (Desired Capital × Desired Time × Given Interest Rate) / (Standard Time × Standard Capital).</note>

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

5. Sums of 50, 60, and 70 <term>Purāṇas<note>original: *Purāṇa*; an ancient Indian silver coin.</note></term> were lent out on interest at the rate of 3, 5, and 6 per cent per month respectively. What is the total interest for a period of 6 months?

6. A sum of 30 <term>Kārṣāpaṇas<note>original: *kārṣāpaṇa*; a common unit of currency in ancient India, often made of copper or silver.</note></term> and 8 <term>Paṇas<note>original: *paṇa*; a smaller copper coin denomination; 16 *paṇas* typically equaled one *kārṣāpaṇa*.</note></term> were lent out on interest at the rate of 7 1/2 per cent per month. What is the interest produced in exactly 7 1/2 months?

7. The interest on 60 for 2 months is seen to be 5 <term>Purāṇas</term> and 3 <term>Paṇas</term>. What would be the interest on 100 for a duration of 1 year?

8. The interest for 1 1/2 months on a loan of 150 is 15. What would be the interest obtained at this same rate on a sum of 300 for 10 months?

9. A merchant lent out 63 <term>Kārṣāpaṇas</term> at the rate of 8 for every 108 per month. What is the interest for a period of 7 1/2 months?

The rule for finding out the capital that was lent out:

10. The standard capital quantity involved in the rate of interest is multiplied by its own associated time and is then divided by the interest of that standard rate. This result is then multiplied by the interest of the desired amount and divided by the time associated with that desired amount. <note>This is the inverse of the previous rule, used to find the principal (c) when interest (i), time (t), and the standard rate (C, T, I) are known: Capital = (Standard Capital × Standard Time × Desired Interest) / (Standard Interest × Desired Time).</note>

### The rule for finding out the time (during which interest has accrued):

14. Take the capital amount (involved in the given rate of interest) as multiplied by the time (connected therewith); then cause this to be divided by its own (connected) rate-interest and by the capital lent out; then this (quotient) here is multiplied by the interest that has accrued on the capital lent out. Wise men say that the resulting (product) is the time (for which the interest has accrued). <note>This rule provides the formula for Time (t) when the other five variables of the Double Rule-of-three are known.</note>

17. It is 96 that is lent out at the rate of 6 per cent per month <note>original: "per mensem"</note>; the interest thereon is seen to be 57 3/5. What is the time (for which interest has accrued)?

### The rule regarding barter or exchange of commodities:

18. The quantity of the commodity taken in exchange is divided by its own price as well as by the quantity of the commodity given in exchange. (It is then) multiplied by the price of the commodity given in exchange, and thereafter multiplied by the quantity of the commodity intended to be exchanged. This (resulting) product is the required quantity corresponding to the prices of the commodity given in exchange as well as of the commodity taken in exchange. <note>This rule explains how to determine the amount of a new good one should receive when trading a specific quantity of one good for another, based on their relative market prices.</note>

Think out and tell me quickly, O you who know arithmetic, how many <term>palas</term> of long pepper have been purchased by one (at the above rate) by means of 80 <term>palas</term> of dried ginger?

### Another rule for the separation of the capital and the interest from their combined sum:

23. Multiply the given time by the interest rate. Divide this by the product of the time-unit and the principal-unit used in the rate. Add **one** to this result. This value acts as the divisor for the combined sum of capital and interest; the resulting quotient is understood to be the required **capital**. <note>This formula allows a person to determine the original loan amount (principal) if they only know the total amount repaid after a set period. In modern terms: $Principal = \frac{Total}{1 + (\frac{Time \times Rate}{100 \times 1})}$.</note>

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

### The rule for the separation of the time and the interest from their combined sum:

25. Take the rate-capital multiplied by the rate-time, then divide it by the interest rate and the given capital. Combine this result with **one**. The quotient obtained by dividing the combined sum of the **time** and the **interest** by this resulting sum is indeed the required **interest**. <note>This problem is a mathematical exercise where two different units—time (months) and money (interest)—are added together into a single "combined sum." While not a common business practice, it was used to test the student's ability to manipulate algebraic proportions.</note>

### The rule for arriving at the separation of the rate-interest and the required time from their sum:

33. The rate-capital <note>the standard principal used to define a rate, typically 100</note> is multiplied by its own rate-time, by the given interest, and by four; this product is then divided by the other (the actual) capital. The square root of the remainder—obtained by subtracting this quotient from the square of the given mixed sum—is then used in relation to that mixed sum to perform the process of **reconciliation** <term>saṅkramaṇa; a mathematical procedure to find two individual values when their sum and difference are known</term>.

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

### The rule for arriving separately at the capital, time, and the interest from their mixed sum:

35. Any quantity chosen by the mathematician <note>an "optionally chosen" value used as a starting point for trial and error</note> is subtracted from the given mixed sum; this may be taken as the required time. Then, calculate the interest on **one** unit of capital for that same time. Add **one** to this interest value, and divide the remainder of the mixed sum (after the chosen time was subtracted) by this total. The resulting quotient is the required capital. Finally, the mixed sum, when diminished by its own corresponding time and capital, becomes the required interest.

### The rule for determining individual amounts of interest from a combined total of interest earned on different principals over different periods of time:

37. Multiply each individual capital amount by its corresponding time and then by the given total of the various amounts of interest. Divide each of these results separately by the sum of all products obtained by multiplying each capital amount by its own corresponding time. The resulting figures are declared to be the specific interest amounts for each capital.

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

38. In this problem, the given capitals are 40, 30, 20, and 50; and the months for which they were lent are 5, 4, 3, and 6 respectively. The total sum of the amounts of interest earned is 34. Find out each of these individual amounts of interest.

### The rule for separating individual capital amounts from their combined total sum:

39. Divide the quantity representing the total sum of the various capitals lent out by the sum of the quotients obtained by dividing each individual amount of interest by its corresponding period of time. Then, multiply the resulting quotient respectively by the specific quotients obtained by dividing each interest amount by its time to find each original capital.

42. The rule for finding the specific interest rate and the <term>rate-capital|the standard principal amount (like 100) used to define a rate of interest</term> when given a <term>mixed sum|the total value of the capital plus the interest earned</term> where the capital lent out is equal to the interest rate:—

44. The <term>rate-capital</term> is multiplied by the <term>rate-time|the standard unit of time (like one month) used to define a rate of interest</term> and then divided by the actual time (for which interest has accrued). The square root of the following: this quotient multiplied by the given mixed sum, then added to the square of half that same quotient; this square root, when diminished by half of that same quotient, becomes the required interest rate (which is also equal to the capital lent out).

### Examples in illustration thereof.

45. The interest rate per 100 for 4 months is unknown. That unknown quantity is also the amount of capital lent out; this capital, when combined with its own interest, results in a total of 12 after 25 months. Find the interest rate that is equal to the capital lent out.

46. The interest rate per 80 for 3 months is unknown; 7 1/3 is the mixed sum of that unknown capital and the interest earned on it for 1 year. What is the capital here and what is the interest?

The rule for separating the capital (which remains the same in all cases) and the interest (which varies based on time) from their combined mixed sums:—

47. Know that when the difference between any two of the given mixed sums—each having been multiplied by the other's period of interest <margin>The "period of interest" here means the specific time for which interest has accrued for any of the given total mixed sums.</margin>—is divided by the difference between those two time periods, the result is the capital.

---

44. <note>In modern algebraic terms, this formula is: $\sqrt{\frac{C \cdot T}{t} \cdot m + \left(\frac{C \cdot T}{2 \cdot t}\right)^2} - \frac{C \cdot T}{2 \cdot t} = I$, where $I$ is the interest rate and $c$ is the capital.</note>

47. <note>In modern algebraic terms, the capital is found by: $\frac{m_1 \cdot t_2 \sim m_2 \cdot t_1}{t_1 \sim t_2} = c$. The $\sim$ symbol represents finding the difference between the two values.</note>

**49 and 50.** O arithmetician, a certain man paid out to 4 persons 30, 31⅔, 33⅓ and 35, (these) being the mixed sums (of the same capital and the interest due thereon) at the end of 3, 4, 5 and 6 months (respectively). Tell me quickly, what may be the capital here?

The rule for separating the capital, which is of the same value in all cases, and the time (during which interest has accrued), from their mixed sum:—

**51.** Wise men say that that is the (required) capital, which is obtained as the quotient of the difference between (any two of) the (given) mixed sums as multiplied by each other's interest, when this (difference) is divided by the difference between the (two chosen) amounts of interest. <note>This rule is used when the specific interest amounts are known rather than the time periods. Formula: (Sum1 × Interest2 - Sum2 × Interest1) / (Interest2 - Interest1)</note>

**51.** <note>original: "$\frac{m_1 i_2 \backsim m_2 i_1}{i_1 \backsim i_2} = c$"</note> In modern notation, the Capital ($c$) equals the difference between the first mixed sum ($m_1$) multiplied by the second interest amount ($i_2$) and the second mixed sum ($m_2$) multiplied by the first interest amount ($i_1$), all divided by the difference between the two interest amounts. Here, $m$ represents the <term>miśras|the Sanskrit term for mixed sums or combined totals</term>.

...optionally chosen (representing the maximum available amount of an installment) by (whatever happens to be) the outstanding (the fractional part of the number of terms in the series), then add to that the amount of the (first) installment as multiplied by the sum of that series in arithmetical progression—which has one for the first term, one for the common difference, and has for the number of terms the integral value of the quotient obtained by dividing (the above optionally chosen maximum) amount of debt (discharged at an installment) by the (above amount of the first) installment. The interest thereon is that which accrues for the period of an installment. ->Examples in illustration thereof.<-

**72 and 73 1/2.** A certain man utilized, (for the discharge of a debt) bearing interest at 5 per cent per month, 60 (as the available maximum amount) with 7 as the first installment amount, increasing it by 7 in successive installments due every 2/3 of a month. He thus gave in discharge of the debt the sum of a series in arithmetical progression consisting of 60/7 terms, and gave also the interest accruing on those multiples of 7. What is the debt amount corresponding to the sum of the series, what is that interest (which he paid), and (what is) the time of discharge of that debt?

**73 1/2 to 76.** A certain man utilized for the discharge of a debt, bearing interest at 5 per cent per month <note>original: "per mensem"</note>, 80 (as the available maximum amount) with 8 as the first installment amount, increasing it by 8 in successive installments due every 1/2 of a month. He thus

---

<note>In this problem, the number 8 represents the number of full terms in the mathematical series, starting at 1 and increasing by 1 each time. The fraction 4/7 is the <term>agra</term> <note>The "remainder" or the outstanding fractional part of a term.</note>. To find the total capital, we take the sum of the first 8 terms (which is 36), multiply it by the first installment of 7, and add the product of the fractional remainder 4/7 and the maximum installment of 60. Calculation: (36 x 7) + (4/7 x 60) = 286 2/7. This is the total debt amount. The interest on this total for 2/3 of a month at 5% per month is then calculated. The total time for repayment is found by (2/3 ÷ 7) x 60 = 40/7 months.</note>

## CHAPTER VI—MIXED PROBLEMS.

...gave in discharge of the debt the sum of a series in <term>arithmetical progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where each number increases by the same amount, such as 7, 14, 21...</note> consisting of 80/8 terms and gave also the interest accruing on those multiples of 8. The debt amount (corresponding to the sum of the series), the interest (which he paid), and the time of discharge (of that debt)—tell me, friend, after calculating, what the (respective) value of these quantities is.

The rule for arriving at the <term>average common interest</term>:—

**77 and 77½.** Divide the sum of the (various accruing) interests by the sum of the (various corresponding) interests due for a month; the resulting quotient is the required time. The product of the (assumed) rate-time and the rate-capital is divided by this required time, then multiplied by the sum of the (various accruing) interests and then divided again by the sum of the (various given) capital amounts. This gives rise to the (required) rate-interest.

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

**78½.** In this problem, four hundreds <note>Four separate investments of 100 units each.</note> were (separately) invested at the (respective) rates of 2, 3, 5 and 4 per cent per month <note>original: "per mensem"</note> for 5, 4, 2 and 3 months (respectively). What is the average common time of investment, and what the average common rate of interest?

Thus end the problems bearing on interest in this chapter on mixed problems.

---

**77 and 77½.** The various accruing interests are the various amounts of interests accruing on the several amounts at the various rates for their respective periods.

Symbolically, { (c₁ × t₁ × I₁) / (T × C) + (c₂ × t₂ × I₂) / (T × C) + . . . } ÷ { (c₁ × 1 × I₁) / (T × C) + (c₂ × 1 × I₂) / (T × C) + . . . } = tₐ or average time;

and (T × C) / tₐ × { (c₁ × t₁ × I₁) / (T × C) + (c₂ × t₂ × I₂) / (T × C) + . . . } ÷ (c₁ + c₂ + . . .) = iₐ or average interest.

<note>In these formulas, c represents capital, t represents time, I represents interest rate, T represents the standard time unit for the rate, and C represents the standard capital unit for the rate.</note>

## Proportionate Division.

Hereafter we shall expound in this chapter on mixed problems the working of proportionate division:—

**79½.** The operation of proportionate division is that wherein the given collective quantity to be divided is first divided by the sum of the numerators of the common-denominator-fractions <note>Fractions that have been converted to have the same bottom number.</note> representing the various proportionate parts, the denominators of which fractions are struck off out of consideration; and then it has to be multiplied respectively in each case by these proportional numerators. This is called <term>kuṭṭīkāra</term> <note>original: "kuṭṭīkāra"; while this term usually refers to algebra or "pulverizing" equations, here it refers specifically to the process of breaking down a whole into proportional parts.</note> by the learned.

->*Examples in illustration thereof.*<-

**80½.** Here, in this problem, 120 gold pieces are divided among 4 servants in the respective proportional parts of 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and 1/6. O arithmetician, tell me quickly what they obtained.

**81½.** The sum of 363 <term>dīnāras</term> <note>A type of gold coin or currency.</note> was divided among five, the first one among them getting 3 parts, and 3 being the common ratio successively in relation to the shares of the others <note>This implies a geometric progression where each person gets three times as much as the person before them.</note>. What was the share of each?

**82½ to 85½.** A certain faithful <term>śrāvaka</term> <note>A lay follower of Jainism.</note> took a number of lotus flowers, and going into the <term>Jina</term> <note>A "Conqueror" or Tirthankara, one of the 24 great spiritual teachers of Jainism.</note> temple conducted therein with devotion the worship of the chief <term>Jinas</term> that were worthy of worship. He offered 1/4 part to <term>Vṛṣabha</term> <note>The first Tirthankara.</note>, 1/6 to worthy <term>Pārśva</term> <note>The 23rd Tirthankara.</note>, and 1/12 to <term>Jinapati</term> <note>Meaning "Lord of Jinas," likely referring to another Tirthankara or a title for the primary deity of that temple.</note>, and 1/3 to sage <term>Suvrata</term> <note>Munisuvrata, the 20th Tirthankara.</note>; he devotedly gave 1/8 to <term>Ariṣṭanémi</term> <note>The 22nd Tirthankara.</note> who destroyed all the eight kinds of <term>karmas</term> <note>In Jainism, karma is viewed as physical particles that bind the soul; there are eight specific types that must be shed to achieve liberation.</note> and who was beloved by the world; and 1/6 of 1/4 to <term>Jinaśānti</term> <note>Śāntinātha, the 16th Tirthankara.</note>: 480 lotuses were brought for this purpose. By adopting the operation known...

---

**79½.** <note>This is a translator's or commentator's mathematical walkthrough of the rule.</note> In working the example in stanza 80½ according to this rule we get: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6 = 6/12, 4/12, 3/12, 2/12. After removing the denominators here, we have 6, 4, 3 and 2. These are also called <term>prakṣēpas</term> <note>original: "prakṣēpas"; meaning additions or proportional parts.</note> or proportional numerators. The sum of these is 15, by which the amount to be distributed, viz., 120, is divided; and the resulting quotient 8 is separately multiplied by the proportional numerators 6, 4, 3 and 2. Then the amounts thus obtained are 6 × 8 or 48, 4 × 8 or 32, 3 × 8 or 24, 2 × 8 or 16. It is worthy of note that <term>prakṣēpa</term> means both the operation of proportionate division and a proportional numerator.

**86½.** (A sum of) 480 was divided among five men in the proportion of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6; O friend, give out the share of each.

->**The rule for arriving at results in required proportions:**<-

**87½.** The number representing the rate-price is divided by the number representing the thing purchasable therewith; it is then multiplied by the given proportional number. By means of this, we find the sum of the proportionate parts through the process of addition. Then, the given total amount multiplied by the respective proportionate parts and then divided by this sum of the proportionate parts gives the value of the various things in the required proportion.

->**Another rule for this same purpose:**<-

**88½.** Multiply the numbers representing the rate-prices respectively by the numbers representing the given proportions of the various things to be purchased; then divide the result by the respective numbers measuring the things purchasable for that rate-price. The resulting quantities happen to be the requisite multipliers in the operation of *<term>prakṣēpaka</term>*. The intelligent man may then give out the required answer by adopting the <term>rule-of-three</term> <note>A mathematical method to find an unknown fourth value when three values are known, based on their ratios.</note>.

->**Again a rule for this same purpose:**<-

**89½.** The numbers representing the various rate-prices are respectively divided by their own related numbers representing the things purchasable therefor, and are then multiplied by their related proportional numbers. With the help of these, the remainder of the operation should be carried out as before.

---

<note>
**Notes on verses 87½ to 89½:** In working the example in stanza 90½ and 91½ according to these rules: the prices 2, 3, and 5 are divided by 3, 5, and 7 respectively, and are similarly multiplied by the proportions 6, 3, and 1. Thus we have (2/3 x 6), (3/5 x 3), and (5/7 x 1), which equals 4, 9/5, and 5/7. These are the "proportional parts." The rules in stanzas 88½ and 89½ require thereafter the operation of *prakṣēpa* (distribution) to be applied in relation to these proportional parts; however, the rule in stanza 87½ explicitly describes the full process.
</note>

## The rule for the operation of proportionate division, wherein there is the addition or the subtraction of certain optionally chosen integral quantities:—

**97½.** The given total quantity is diminished by the integral quantities that are to be added, or is combined with the positive integral quantities that are to be subtracted; then, with the help of this resulting quantity, the operation of <term>proportionate division</term> <note>The process of dividing a whole into parts based on specific ratios.</note> is to be conducted. The resulting proportionate parts are then respectively combined with those quantities that were to be added, or they are diminished by those quantities that were to be subtracted.

---

**97½.** The operation of proportionate division to be conducted here is according to any of the rules found in stanzas 87½ to 89½.

...purchasing rate. By reversing the processes, one may arrive at the valuation of the highest capital <note>The "capital" here refers to the quantity of a commodity held by the traders.</note> invested in the transaction.

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

**103 1/2.** The capital amounts invested by three men are respectively 2, 8, and 36; 6 is the price at which the remnants of the commodity are to be sold. Having purchased and sold at the same rates, they became possessors of equal wealth. Find out the buying and selling prices.

**104 1/2.** Those three persons took up 1 1/2, 1/2, and 2 1/2 as their respective capital amounts and conducted the operations of buying and selling the same commodity at the same rates of price; by selling the remnant in the end at a price represented by 6, they became possessors of equal wealth. Find out their buying and selling prices.

**105 1/2.** The quantity measuring the equal wealth is 41, and the price at which the remnants of the commodity are sold is 6. O arithmetician, tell me quickly what the <term>largest capital</term> <note>original: "ज्येष्ठधन" (jyeṣṭhadhana)</note> invested is, and what the various other capitals are.

**106 1/2.** In the case where 35 <term>dīnāras</term> <note>A dīnāra is a contemporary gold coin used as a standard unit of currency.</note> give the numerical measure of the equal wealth, and 4 is the price at which the remnant is to be sold, you tell me, O arithmetician, what the largest capital invested is.

---

The quantity left over after selling at the primary rate is spoken of as the remnant, and the price at which this remnant is sold is the <term>remnant-price</term> <note>original: "चरमार्घ" (caramārgha)</note>.

Symbolically, let *a*, *a* + *b* and *a* + *b* + *c* be the capitals, where the last is the <term>largest capital</term> <note>original: "ज्येष्ठधन"</note>, and let *p* be the <term>remnant-price</term> <note>original: "चरमार्घ"</note>; then, according to the rule, *a* + *b* + *c* + 1 = the vending rate; and (*a* + *b* + *c* + 1) *p* — 1 = the purchasing rate.

From these, it can be easily shown that the sum of the amounts realized by selling the commodity at the vending rate and the remnant at the remnant-price turns out to be the same in each case.

It may be noted that the purchasing rate happens in problems bearing on this rule to be the same in value as the <term>equal wealth</term> <note>original: "समधन" (samadhana)</note> or the equal sale-proceeds.

**105 1/2.** It may be noted here that, according to the rule, it is only the largest capital that is found out; while the other capitals required in the problem are optionally chosen, so as to be less than the largest capital.

# CHAPTER VI—MIXED PROBLEMS.

The rule for arriving at the value of the prices producing equal sale-proceeds when the price of the remnant is fractional in character:—

**107½.** When the remnant-price <note>The "remnant-price" is the secondary, usually higher, rate at which the leftover portion of a commodity is sold after the bulk has been sold at the primary rate.</note> is fractional in character, the selling and the buying rates are to be derived as before with the invested capitals and the remnant-price reduced to the same denominator, which is however ignored for the time being; these selling and buying rates are then respectively to be multiplied by this denominator and the square of this denominator to find the required selling and buying rates. The value of the equal sale-proceeds is then obtained by means of the <term>rule-of-three</term> <note>original: "त्रैराशिक" (trairāśika). This is a classical mathematical method for finding an unknown value using three known values based on proportions.</note>.

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

**108½.** In a transaction, 1/2, 1/3, and 1/4 are the capital amounts invested respectively by three persons; the remnant-price is 5/6. By purchasing and selling at the same prices, they became possessed of equal sale-proceeds. What is the buying price, what the selling price, and what the equal sale-amount?

Again, another rule for arriving at the value of the equal sale-proceeds, when the remnant-price is fractional:—

**109½.** The continued product of the highest numerator, of *two*, and of all the denominators to be found in the values of the capital amounts invested, when combined with the last denominator belonging to the value of the remnant-price, gives rise to the selling rate. This multiplied by the remnant-price, and then diminished by *one*, and then multiplied successively by *two* and all the denominators, becomes the purchasing rate. Then the <term>rule-of-three</term> is to be used for arriving at the common value of the sale-amounts.

The rule for arriving at the solution of a problem wherein optionally chosen quantities are bestowed in optionally chosen multiples for an optionally chosen number of times: —

### <term>Creeper-like Pulverizer</term> <note>original: "Vallikā-kuttikāra"</note>

Hereafter we shall explain the process of calculation known as the <term>Creeper-like Pulverizer</term> * :—

The rule underlying the process of calculation known as the <term>Creeper</term> <note>original: "Vallikā"</note> in relation to the <term>Pulverizer</term> <note>original: "Kuttikāra," a method for solving indeterminate equations by "grinding" or breaking down numbers through successive division</note> (which is a special kind of division or distribution):—

**115½.** Divide the (given) <term>group-number</term> <note>original: "rāśi"</note> by the (given) <term>divisor</term> <note>original: "chēda"</note>; discard the first quotient; then put down one below the other the (various) quotients obtained by the successive division (of the various resulting divisors by the various resulting remainders; again), put down below this the optionally chosen number,

In this chain, the sum obtained by adding the lowermost number to the product of the number above it and the number immediately above that upper number—this process of multiplication and addition being continued in the same way until the whole chain is exhausted—results in a sum. This sum is then to be divided by the originally provided divisor.

### The Rationale

The mathematical reasoning behind the rule is shown by the following algebraic representation:
<note>This section explains how the ancient Indian method solves for "x" in equations of the type (Bx + b) / A = y.</note>

(B*x* + *b*) / A = *y* (an integer) = *q₁x* + *p₁*, where *p₁* = ((B - A*q₁*) *x* + *b*) / A.
Therefore *x* = (A*p₁* - *b*) / *r₁*, (where *r₁* = B - A*q₁*, which is the first remainder)
= *q₂ p₁* + *p₂*, where *p₂* = (*r₂ p₁* - *b*) / *r₁*, and *q₂* is the second quotient and
*r₂* the second remainder.
Hence, *p₁* = (*r₁ p₂* + *b*) / *r₂* = *q₃ p₂* + *p₃*, where *p₃* = (*r₃ p₂* + *b*) / *r₂* and *q₃* is the
third quotient and *r₃* the third remainder.
Similarly, *p₂* = (*r₂ p₃* - *b*) / *r₃* = *q₄ p₃* + *p₄*, where *p₄* = (*r₄ p₃* - *b*) / *r₃*;
*p₃* = (*r₃ p₄* + *b*) / *r₄* = *q₅ p₄* + *p₅*, where *p₅* = (*r₅ p₄* + *b*) / *r₄*.

Thus we have:
*x* = *q₂ p₁* + *p₂*;
*p₁* = *q₃ p₂* + *p₃*;
*p₂* = *q₄ p₃* + *p₄*;
*p₃* = *q₅ p₄* + *p₅*.

<note>The following section explains the mathematical logic behind the "Pulverizer" method, which we today recognize as the Euclidean Algorithm or the method of Continued Fractions.</note>

---

->The rationale of this process will be clear from the following considerations:<-

We have:
(i) **(B₁ x + b₁) / A₁** is an integer; 
(ii) **(B₂ x + b₂) / A₂** is an integer; and
(iii) **(B₃ x + b₃) / A₃** is an integer.

In (i) Let the lowest value of *x* = *s₁*.
In (ii) Let the lowest value of *x* = *s₂*.
In (iii) Let the lowest value of *x* = *s₃*.

(iv) When both (i) and (ii) are to be satisfied, *dA₁* + *s₁* has to be equal to *kA₂* + *s₂*, so that *s₁* - *s₂* = *kA₂* - *dA₁*. 
That is, **[A₁ d + (s₁ - s₂)] / A₂** = *k*.

From (iv), which is an <term>indeterminate equation</term> <note>An equation that has more than one set of possible solutions, often requiring whole numbers.</note> with the values of *d* and *k* unknown, we arrive, according to what has been already proved, at the lowest positive integral value of *d*. This value of *d* multiplied by *A₁*, and then increased by *s₁*, gives the value of *x* which will satisfy both (i) and (ii).

Let this be *t₁*; and let the next higher value of *x* which will satisfy both these equations be *t₂*.

(v) Now, *t₁* + *nA₁* = *t₂*;
(vi) and *t₁* + *mA₂* = *t₂*.

Therefore, **A₁ / A₂ = m / n**. Thus *A₁* = *mp*, and *A₂* = *np*, where *p* is the <term>highest common factor</term> <note>Also known as the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD); the largest number that divides into two or more numbers without leaving a remainder.</note> between *A₁* and *A₂*.

Therefore, *m* = **A₁ / p**, and *n* = **A₂ / p**.
Substituting in (v) or (vi), we have:
*t₁* + **(A₁ A₂) / p** = *t₂*.

From this it is obvious that the next higher value of *x* satisfying the two equations is obtained by adding the <term>least common multiple</term> <note>The smallest positive integer that is divisible by both A₁ and A₂.</note> of *A₁* and *A₂* to the lower value.

Now again, let *v* be the value of *x* which satisfies all the three equations.
Then *v* = *t₁* + **(A₁ A₂) / p** × *r*, (where *r* is a positive integer) = (say) *t₁* + *lr*;
and *v* = *s₃* + *cA₃* = *t₁* + *lr*.
Therefore, *r* = **(c A₃ + s₃ - t₁) / l**.

---

<note>This concluding section applies the theory to a specific word problem about dividing a heap of fruit.</note>

By choosing a value for *p₄* such that **(r₅ p₄ + b) / r₄**, which is, as shown above, the value of *p₅*, becomes an integer, and by arranging in a chain *q₂*, *q₃*, *q₄*, *q₅*, *p₄* and *p₅* we get at the value of *x* by proceeding as stated in the rule. This involves the processes of multiplication by the upper quantity and the addition of the lower quantity in the chain, which are carried up to the topmost quantity. The value of *x* so obtained is divided by *A*, and the remainder represents the least value of *x*; for the values of *x* which satisfy the equation, **(Bx + b) / A = an integer**, are all in an arithmetical progression wherein the common difference is *A*.

**Problem:** It is given that a heap of fruits when diminished by 7 is exactly divisible among 8 men, and the same heap when diminished by 3 is exactly divisible among 13 men.

#### The rule for arriving at the original quantity distributed (as desired), after obtaining the remainder due to (the removal of certain specified) known quantities:—

**130½.** (Obtain) the product of the (given) <term>fixed quantity</term> <note>original: *agra*; a known number or "tip" added or subtracted from the total</note> (to be removed), as multiplied by the <term>remaining fractional proportion</term> <note>original: *śeṣāṁśa*; the fraction left over after a part has been taken away</note> of what is left (after a specified <term>fractional part removed</term> <note>original: *agrāṁśa*; the portion subtracted from the remainder</note> of what remains on the removal of the given known quantity has been given away). The next quantity is (obtained by means of) this (product), to which

---

<note>130½. Here the known quantity to be removed is called the *agra*. What remains after the removal of the *agra* is the remainder. That fraction of this remainder which is given or taken away is the *agrāṁśa*, and what is left of the remainder after the *agrāṁśa* is given or taken away is the *śeṣāṁśa* or the remaining fractional proportion of the remainder. For example, where *x* is the quantity to be found out, and *a* is the *agra* in relation to the first distribution with ⅓ as the fractional proportion distributed, (x — a) / 3 happens to be the *agrāṁśa*, and (x — a) — (x — a) / 3 to be the *śeṣāṁśa*.</note>

### **Complex Pulverizer** <note>original: *Viṣama-kuṭṭīkāra*</note>

Hereafter we shall expound **complex pulverizer**.

The rule relating to **complex pulverizer**:—

**134½.** The given divisor, written down in two places, is to be multiplied in each place by an optionally chosen number; and the known quantity given in the problem for the purpose of being added is to be subtracted from the product in one of these places; and the quantity given in the problem for the purpose of being subtracted is to be added to the product noted down in the other place. The two quantities thus obtained are to be divided by the known coefficient multiplier of the unknown quantity...

---

<note>The words *Viṣama* (uneven/complex) and *Bhinna* (broken/fractional) used here in relation to the **pulverizer** method obviously have the same meaning and refer to the fractional character of the dividend quantities occurring in the problems contemplated by this rule.</note>

# **The Pulverizer of Whole Numbers** <note>original: *Sakala-kuṭṭīkāra*</note>

## *The rule in relation to the pulverizer of whole numbers.*

**136½.** The quotient in the first among the divisions, carried on by means of the <term>dividend-coefficient</term> <note>the number by which the unknown variable is multiplied</note> (of the unknown quantity to be distributed), as well as by means of the divisor and the (successively) resulting remainders, is to be discarded. The other quotients obtained by means of this mutual division (carried on until the divisor and the remainder become equal) are to be written down (in a vertical chain along with the ultimately equal remainder and divisor); to the lowermost figure (in this chain), the remainder (obtained by dividing the given known quantity in the problem by the divisor therein), is to be added. (Then by means of these numbers in the chain), the sum, (which has to be) obtained by adding (successively to the lowermost number) the product of the two...

---

</note>

Below the lowermost quotient in this chain, the optionally chosen multiplier of the least remainder in the odd position of order in this last successive division is to be put down.

---

The principle underlying the process given in the rule is the same as that explained in the rule regarding the <term>Vallikā-kuṭṭīkāra [Creeper-Pulverizer]</term>—but with this difference, namely, that the last two figures in the chain here are obtained in a different way.

Again, from the rationale given in the footnote to rule in 115½, Chapter VI, it will be seen that the <term>agra [remainder/additive]</term> <note>original: "agra"; the constant term added to or subtracted from the dividend.</note>, *b*, associated with the remainder in the odd position of order, has the same algebraic sign as is given to it in the problem; while the sign of the *agra*, *b*, associated with the remainder in the even position of order is opposite to its sign as given in the problem. Hence, when the continued division is carried up to a remainder in the odd position of order, the value of *x* arrived at therefrom is in relation to such an *agra* as has its sign unchanged; on the other hand, when the continued division is carried up to a remainder in the even position of order, the value of *x* arrived at therefrom is in relation to an *agra* that has its sign changed. 

When the number of remainders obtained is odd, the number of quotients in the chain is even; and when the remainders are even, the quotients are odd in number. As the *agra* associated with the last remainder is in this rule always taken to be positive, the value of *x* arrived at is in relation to the positive *agra*, if the last remainder happens to be in the odd position of order. And it is in relation to the negative *agra*, if the last remainder happens to be in the even position of order. In other words, if the number of quotients be even, the value is in relation to the positive *agra*; and if the number of quotients be odd, it is in relation to the negative *agra*.

The value of *x* in relation to the positive or the negative *agra* being thus found out, the other value is arrived at by subtracting this value from the divisor in the problem. How this turns out will be clear from the following representation:

(Ax + b) / B = an integer. 
Here, let x = c; then (Ac + b) / B = an integer. 
We know that (AB / B) is also an integer. 
Hence, (AB / B) - (Ac + b) / B, or [A(B - c) - b] / B, is an integer.

It has to be noted here that the common factor, if any, of the three given numerical quantities is to be removed before the operation of continued division is begun. The last divisor and the last remainder being required to be equal, it will invariably happen that these come to be 1.

The <term>mati [chosen multiplier]</term> <note>original: "mati"; an optional number chosen by the mathematician to help solve the equation.</note>, required to be chosen in the rule relating to the *Vallikā-kuṭṭīkāra* and required to be written below the chain of quotients, is in this rule always 1, the last divisor being 1. Therefore, the last divisor here takes the place of the *mati* in the *Vallikā-kuṭṭīkāra*. It will be seen further that the last figure of the chain obtained according to this rule—that is, 1 + *agra*—is the same as the last figure in the chain obtained in the *Vallikā-kuṭṭīkāra* by dividing by the last divisor the sum of the *agra* and the product of the *mati* as multiplied by the last remainder.

### The rule for separating the prices of two different things when their larger and smaller quantities are swapped, given the total mixed price for each case:

**139 1/2**. From the larger total price, multiplied by the corresponding larger number of one of the two kinds of things, subtract the smaller total price as multiplied by the smaller number relating to the other of the two kinds of things. Then divide the result by the difference between the squares of the quantities of these things. This gives the price of the item that is larger in number. The other—that is, the price of the item smaller in number—is obtained by swapping the multipliers. <note>This rule provides a formula for solving simultaneous equations of the form ax + by = m and bx + ay = n. By cross-multiplying and subtracting, the author isolates one variable without needing modern symbolic notation.</note>

...are to be divided (one after another) by an optionally chosen number <note>The term "optionally chosen number" refers to the "iṣṭa-rāśi," a common technique in Indian mathematics where a trial value is used to initiate a calculation.</note> (and the remainders again are to be divided by an optionally chosen number, this process being repeated) over and over again. The given (mixed) quantities of the different things are to be (successively) diminished by the corresponding quotients in the above process. (In this manner the numerical values of the various things in the mixed sums are arrived at). The optionally chosen divisors (in the above processes of continued division) combined with the optionally chosen multiplier as also that multiplier constitute (respectively) the prices (of a single thing in each of the varieties of the given different things).

Choose any optional number, say 2, and multiply with it these total numbers; we get 42, 44, 46. Subtract these from 73, the price of the respective heaps. The remainders are 31, 29, and 27. These are to be divided by another optionally chosen number, say 8. The quotients are 3, 3, 3, and the remainders are 7, 5 and 3. These remainders are again divided by a third optionally chosen number say 2. The quotients are 3, 2, 1, and the remainders are 1, 1, 1. These last remainders are in their turn divided by a fourth optionally chosen number which is 1 here. The quotients are 1, 1, 1 with no remainders. The quotients derived in relation to the first total number are to be subtracted from it. Thus we get 21 - (3 + 3 + 1) = 14; this number and the quotients 3, 3, 1 represent the number of fruits of the different sorts in the first heap. Similarly we get in the second group 16, 3, 2, 1, and in the third group 18, 3, 1, 1, as the number of the different sorts of fruits.

The prices are the first chosen multiplier, viz., 2, and its sums with the other optionally chosen multipliers. Thus we get 2, 2 + 8 or 10, 2 + 2 or 4, and 2 + 1 or 3, as the price of each of the four different kinds of fruits in order.

The principle underlying this <unclear>method</unclear> will be clear from the following algebraic representation:

*ax* + *by* + *cz* + *dw* = *p* ... ... ... ... ... ... I
*a* + *b* + *c* + *d* = *n* ... ... ... ... ... ... II

Let *w* = *s*. <note>Here, "s" represents the initial multiplier chosen by the mathematician.</note>
Multiplying II by *s*, we have *s* (*a* + *b* + *c* + *d*) = *sn* ... ... ... III
Subtracting III from I, we get *a* (*x* - *s*) + *b* (*y* - *s*) + *c* (*z* - *s*) =
*p* - *sn* ... ... ... ... ... ... ... IV

Dividing IV by *x* - *s*, we get *a* as the <term>quotient</term> <note>The result of a division.</note>, and *b* (*y* - *s*) + *c* (*z* - *s*) as the <term>remainder</term> <note>The amount left over after division.</note>, where *x* - *s* is a suitable integer.

Similarly we proceed till the end.

Thus it will be seen that the successively chosen <term>divisors</term> <note>The numbers by which a total is divided.</note> *x* - *s*, *y* - *s*, and *z* - *s*, when combined with *s*, give the value of the various prices, *s* by itself being the price of the first thing; and that the successive quotients *a*, *b*, *c*, along with *n* - (*a* + *b* + *c*) are the numbers measuring the various kinds of things.

It may be noted that, in this rule, the number of divisions to be carried out is one less than the number of the kinds of things given, and that there should be no remainder left in the last division.

### The rule for arriving at the numerical value of the prices of dearer and cheaper things respectively from the given mixed value of their total price:

146½. Divide the rate-quantities <note>The "rate-quantity" is the number of items offered for a set price.</note> of the given things by their rate-prices. Diminish these resulting quantities separately by the least among them. Then multiply by the least of the above-mentioned quotient-quantities the given mixed price of all the things; and subtract this product from the given total number of the various things. Then split up this remainder optionally into as many bits as there are remainders of the above quotient-quantities left after subtraction; and then divide these bits by those remainders of the quotient-quantities. Thus the prices of the various cheaper things are arrived at. These, separated from the total price, give rise to the price of the dearest article of purchase.

---

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

147½ to 149. In accordance with the rates of 3 peacocks for 2 <term>paṇas</term> <note>original: "paṇa"; an ancient Indian unit of currency, typically a copper coin.</note>, 4 pigeons for 3 <term>paṇas</term>, 5 swans for 4 <term>paṇas</term>, and 6 <term>sārasa</term> <note>original: "sārasa"; the Indian Sarus Crane, a large non-migratory crane.</note> cranes for 5 <term>paṇas</term>...

---

<note>This footnote provides a step-by-step mathematical demonstration of the rule described in stanza 146½, applying it to the bird problem starting in stanza 147½.</note>

146½. The rule will be clear from the following working of the problem given in 147½—149:
Divide the rate-quantities 3, 4, 5, 6 by the respective rate-prices 2, 3, 4, 5; thus we have 3/2, 4/3, 5/4, 6/5. Subtract the least of these, 6/5, from each of the other three. We get 3/10, 2/15, and 1/20. By multiplying the given mixed price, 56, by the above-mentioned least quantity, 6/5, we have 56 x 6/5. Subtract this from the total number of birds, 72. Split up the remainder 24/5 into any three parts, say 3/5, 9/5, and 12/5. Dividing these respectively by 3/10, 2/15, and 1/20, we get the prices of the first three kinds of birds: 2, 13½, and 48. The price of the fourth variety of birds can be found out by subtracting all these three prices from the total of 56.

### CHAPTER VI—MIXED PROBLEMS.

[...The buyer] was told to bring at these rates 100 birds for 100 <term>panas<note>An ancient Indian copper coin used as a standard unit of currency.</note></term> for the amusement of the king’s son, and was sent to do so. What amount does he give for each of the various kinds of birds that he buys?

**The rule for arriving at the measure of two given commodities whose prices are interchanged:—**

154. Let the numerical value of the sum of the total selling and buying money-prices of the two given commodities be divided by the numerical measure of the sum of the commodities put together; then let the difference between the above-mentioned buying and selling prices be divided by the numerical measure of any such difference as may be obtained by subtracting any optionally chosen commodity-quantity from the given measure of the sum of the given commodities. If the operation of <term>saṅkramaṇa<note>original: "saṅkramaṇa" — a mathematical process for finding two unknown quantities when their sum and difference are known. If $x+y = A$ and $x-y = B$, then $x = (A+B)/2$ and $y = (A-B)/2$.</note></term> is conducted in relation to these—namely, the quotient obtained in the first operation above and any one of the many quotients that may be obtained in the second operation—the rates at which those commodities are purchased is obtained. Then if the same operation of *saṅkramaṇa* as relating to the sum of the commodities and to their difference is carried out, it of course gives rise to the numerical measure of the commodities in question. The alternation of these above-mentioned purchase-rates gives rise to the sale-rates. This is the solution of this kind of problems as propounded by the learned; and the rule itself has been declared by the great <term>Jina<note>Literally "The Victorious One," a title for a liberated teacher in Jainism. Here it refers to Mahavira, the 9th-century mathematician and author of this text.</note></term>.

***

154. *The algebraical representation of the method described in the rule may be given thus in relation to the problem proposed in stanzas 155 and 156—*

| | | |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| Let *ax + by* = 104 | ... | I |
| *ay + bx* = 116 | ... | II |
| *a + b* = 20 | ... | III |
| Adding I and II, we have (*a + b*) (*x + y*) = 220 | ... | IV |
| Therefore *x + y* = 11 | ... | V |
| Again subtracting I from II, we get (*a - b*) (*y - x*) = 12 | | |
| Now 2*b* is optionally chosen to be equal to 6. | | |
| *a + b* - 2*b* or *a - b* = 20 - 6 or 14 | ... | VI |
| Therefore *y - x* = 12 / 14 | ... | VII |

*Carry out the operation of saṅkramaṇa with reference to VII and V, and VI and III; and the values of x, y, a and b are all made out.*
