**The rule for arriving at the distance in <term>yōjanas</term> <note>A measure of distance roughly equivalent to 8 or 9 miles, or the distance a chariot can travel in a day.</note> travelled by the horses of the sun's chariot when yoked as desired:**

157. The number representing the total *<term>yōjanas</term>*, divided by the total number of horses, gives the *<term>yōjanas</term>* (which each has at a stage to travel) in turn. These *<term>yōjanas</term>*, as multiplied by the optionally chosen number of horses to be yoked, give the measure of the distance to be travelled over by each horse. <note>This rule addresses proportional work. If 7 horses share the burden of pulling a chariot that only requires 4 horses at a time, each horse only works for a fraction of the total distance.</note>

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

**The rule for arriving at the value of the commodity to be found in the hands of each (of a body of joint proprietors), from the conjoint remainder left after subtracting whatever is desired from the total value of all the commodities:**

159. Let the sum (of the values of the conjoint remainders) of the commodities be divided by the number of men lessened by one; the quotient will be the total value of all the commodities (owned in common). This total value as diminished by the specified values gives (in the corresponding cases) the value of commodity in the hands (of each of the proprietors in turn). <note>A "conjoint remainder" in this context refers to the sum of the values of the goods held by all partners except one. This is a system of linear equations.</note>

**The rule for arriving at equal amounts of wealth, as owned in precious gems, after mutually exchanging any desired number of gems:**

163. The number of gems to be given away is multiplied by the total number of men taking part in the exchange. This product is separately subtracted from the number of the gems for sale owned by each. The continued product of the remainders so obtained gives rise to the value of the gem in each case, provided the remainder relating to that specific gem is excluded from the product. <note>This rule provides a method for finding the relative values of different types of gems so that after the men trade a certain number, they all end up with the same total wealth.</note>

165 and 166. The first man has 16 azure-blue gems, the second has 10 emeralds, and the third man has 8 diamonds. Each among them gives to each of the others 2 gems of the kind owned by himself; and then all three men come to be possessed of equal wealth. O mathematician, tell me the value of those (different) gems.

**The rule for arriving at the value of the invested capital by means of the rate of purchase, the rate of sale, and the profit obtained:**

167. The buying rate and the selling rate of the commodity are each multiplied alternately by the unit prices; the product obtained from the buying rate is then divided by the product obtained from the selling rate. The profit, divided by the resulting quotient after it has been reduced by *one*, gives the amount of the capital originally employed. <note>This formula helps a merchant determine how much money they started with if they know their buying/selling rates and their total profit. Mathematically, if buying is $a$ units for $b$ price, and selling is $c$ units for $d$ price, and profit is $p$, the capital is $p \div (\frac{ad}{bc} - 1)$.</note>

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

168. A merchant buys grain at the rate of 7 dry-measures <note>original: "prastha," a unit of volume roughly equivalent to a quart.</note> for 3 copper coins <note>original: "paṇa," a common currency unit.</note>, and sells it at the rate of 9 dry-measures for 5 copper coins, and makes a profit of 72 copper coins. What is the capital employed in this transaction?

The mixed gold gives rise to the resulting <term>purity</term> <note>original: "varṇa," literally meaning "color," used here as a measure of the fineness or purity of gold, similar to the modern "karat."</note>. The original <term>purity</term> of any component part, when divided by the final <term>purity</term> of the whole mixture and then multiplied by the original weight of gold in that part, gives the corresponding weight of the mixed gold that is equal in value to that original component.

->An example in illustration thereof.<-

170 to 171½. There are: 
- 1 part of gold of 1 <term>degree of purity</term> <note>original: "varṇa"</note>, 
- 1 part of 2 <term>degrees</term>, 
- 1 part of 3 <term>degrees</term>, 
- 2 parts of 4 <term>degrees</term>, 
- 4 parts of 5 <term>degrees</term>, 
- 7 parts of 14 <term>degrees</term>, 
- and 8 parts of 15 <term>degrees</term>. 

Throwing these into the fire, melt them all into one mass. Tell me, what is the <term>purity</term> of the resulting mixed gold? If this mixed gold is then distributed back among the owners of the original parts, how much does each owner receive?

**The rule for arriving at the required weight of gold (of any desired purity equivalent in value to given quantities of gold) of given purities:**

172½. The given quantities of gold are all separately multiplied by their respective <term>purities</term>, and the products are added together. The resulting sum is divided by the total weight of the mixed gold; the quotient is understood as the resulting average <term>purity</term>. This same sum of the products is to be separately divided by any desired <term>purity level</term> to find the required equivalent weight of that gold.

->Examples in illustration thereof.<-

Twenty <term>weight units</term> <note>original: "paṇas," a standard weight or currency unit.</note> of gold of 16 <term>degrees of purity</term> have been exchanged for gold of 10 <term>degrees</term> in quality. You must determine how many <term>weight units</term> <note>original: "purāṇas," here used as a unit of weight equivalent to the paṇa.</note> they become now.

174½. One hundred and eight units of gold of 11$\frac{3}{8}$ <term>degrees of purity</term> are exchanged for gold of 14 <term>degrees</term>. What is the equivalent quantity of this new gold?

...the products obtained by multiplying the several component quantities of gold by their respective <term>purities</term> <note>original: "varṇas," referring to the color or fineness of the gold.</note> is to be subtracted. The remainder, when divided by the known component quantity of gold (the <term>purity</term> of which is to be found out), gives rise to the required <term>purity</term>; and when divided by the difference between the resulting <term>purity</term> and the known <term>purity</term> (of an unknown component quantity of gold) gives rise to the required weight of that gold.

### ->Another rule in relation to the unknown purity:—<-

176½. The sum of the products of the various component quantities of gold as multiplied by their respective <term>purities</term> is to be subtracted from the product of the total quantity of gold as multiplied by the resulting <term>purity</term>. Wise people say that this remainder, when divided by the weight of the gold of the unknown <term>purity</term>, gives rise to the required <term>purity</term>.

### ->Examples in illustration thereof.<-

179. Seven in weight of a given specimen of gold has exactly 14 as the measure of its <term>purity</term>; then 4 in weight of another specimen of gold is added to it. The resulting <term>purity</term> is 10. Give out the unknown <term>purity</term> of this second specimen of gold.

### ->The rule for arriving at the unknown weight of gold:—<-

180. Subtract the sum, obtained by adding together the products of the various component quantities of gold as multiplied by their respective <term>purities</term>, from the product of the sum of the known weights of gold as multiplied by the now durable resulting <term>purity</term>; the remainder divided by the difference between the known <term>purity</term> of the unknown quantity of gold and the resulting durable <term>purity</term> of the mixed gold gives rise to the weight of gold.

### The rule for arriving at the weights of gold (corresponding to two given purities) from the known weight and purity of the mixture of two given specimens of gold:

182. Find the differences between the resulting <term>purity</term> <note>The final purity of the mixture.</note> and the known higher and lower <term>purities</term> of the component parts. Divide the number one by each of these differences in order; then perform the operation of <term>proportionate distribution</term> <note>original: "prakṣēpaka," a mathematical method for dividing a total into parts according to a specific ratio.</note> as described previously. In this manner, it is possible to determine the values for many component quantities of gold as well.

### Again, the rule for arriving at the weights of gold (corresponding to two given purities) from the known weight and purity of the mixture of two given specimens of gold:

183. Write down in inverse order the difference between the resulting <term>purity</term> and the higher of the two component <term>purities</term>, and the difference between the resulting <term>purity</term> and the lower of the two component <term>purities</term>. The results reached by using these inversely arranged differences in the process of <term>proportionate distribution</term> will give the required weights for the different gold components.

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

If, however, these answers do not tally, the <term>purity levels</term> belonging to the first set of answers must be made a little less or a little more as the case may be; then the average <term>purity level</term> corresponding to these modified component <term>purity levels</term> must be further obtained. Thereafter, the difference between this average <term>purity level</term> and the previously obtained average <term>purity level</term> that did not tally is written down; and the required proportionate quantities are derived from there by means of the operation of the <term>Rule of Three</term> <note>A mathematical method of finding a fourth value from three known values based on proportions</note>. The <term>purity levels</term> arrived at according to the option chosen before—when respectively diminished by one of these two quantities and increased by the other—turn out to be evidently the required <term>purity levels</term> here.

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

**213—215.** Two merchants well-versed in estimating the value of gold asked each other for an exchange of gold. Then the other said: "If I only obtain one-third of your gold, I shall likewise make the whole gold in my possession become...

Thus, in the second exchange, we see an increase of 40—35 or 5 in the sum of the products of weight and <term>purity level</term>, while the decrease and the increase in relation to the originally chosen <term>purity levels</term> are 9—8 or 1 and 16—13 or 3. 

But the required increase in the sum of the products of weight and <term>purity level</term> in the second exchange is 36—35 or 1. Applying the <term>Rule of Three</term>, we get the corresponding decrease and increase in the <term>purity levels</term> to be 1/5 and 3/5. 

Therefore, the <term>purity levels</term> are 9 minus 1/5 (which is 8 4/5) and 13 plus 3/5 (which is 13 3/5).

### **<term>Complex Algebraic Variations</term>** <note>original: "Vicitra-kuṭṭīkāra"</note>

Hereafter we shall expound the **<term>Complex Algebraic Variations</term>** in the chapter on mixed problems.

The rule in regard to (the ascertaining of) the number of truthful and untruthful statements (in a situation like the one given below wherein both are simultaneously possible):

216. The number of men, multiplied by the number of those liked (among them) as increased by *one*, and (then) diminished by twice the number of men liked, gives rise to the number of untruthful statements. The square of the number representing all the men, diminished by the number of those (untruthful statements), gives rise to the statements that are truthful.

---

<note>
216. The logic of this rule is explained through this algebraic breakdown of the problem:
Suppose *a* is the total number of people, and *b* is the number of people who are "liked." Each person makes a statement about everyone in the group, including themselves. Therefore, the total number of statements is the total number of people squared (*a*²).
Of these *a* people, *b* are liked and the rest (*a - b*) are not liked. 
1. When a person who is "liked" says to each of the other "liked" people, "You alone are liked," they are lying about everyone except the person they are speaking to. This results in *b - 1* lies for each "liked" person. For all *b* people, the total lies are *b* multiplied by (*b - 1*).
2. When the same statement is made to the people who are "not liked" (*a - b*), the number of lies increases because even the "liked" status is false. This results in (*a - b*) multiplied by (*b + 1*) lies.
By adding these together and simplifying the math: *b*(*b* - 1) + (*a* - *b*)(*b* + 1) = *a*(*b* + 1) - 2*b*.
This gives the total number of untruthful statements. Subtracting this from the total statements (*a*²) reveals how many statements were actually true.
</note>

The rule to arrive at the unknown capital with the aid of certain known and unknown profits in a given transaction:

222. By means of the operation of proportionate distribution <note>This refers to the method of sharing gains or losses based on the ratio of the original investments.</note>, the unknown profits are to be determined from the mixed sum of all the profits *minus* the known profit. Then the capital of the person whose investment is unknown results from dividing his profit by that same common factor which has been used in the process of proportionate distribution above.

->An example in illustration thereof.<-

223-225. According to agreement, some three merchants carried out the operation of buying and selling. The capital of the first of them consisted of six <term>purāṇas</term> <note>An ancient Indian silver coin used as a standard of currency.</note>, that of the second of eight <term>purāṇas</term>, but that of the third was not known. The profit obtained by all those three men was 96 <term>purāṇas</term>. In fact, the profit obtained by this third person on the unknown capital happened to be 40 <term>purāṇas</term>. What is the amount thrown by him into the transaction, and what is the profit of each of the other two merchants? O friend, if you know the operation of proportionate distribution, tell me this after making the necessary calculation.

The rule for arriving at the wages due in kind for having carried certain given things over a part of the stipulated distance according to a given rate:

226. From the square of the product of the numerical value of the weight to be carried and half of the stipulated distance—

<insert>
226. Algebraically, the formula given in the rule is:
x = [ (a * D / 2) - √((a * D / 2)² - a * b * d * (D - d)) ] / (D - d)
where:
*x* = the wages to be found out,
*a* = the total weight to be carried,
*D* = the total distance,
*d* = the distance already traveled,
and *b* = the total wages promised.
It may be noted here that the rate of the wages for the two stages of the journey is the same, although the amount paid for each stage of the journey is not in accordance with the promised rate for the whole journey. This formula is easily derived from the following equation containing the data in the problem:
x / (a * d) = (b - x) / ((a - x) * (D - d))
</insert>

The rule for arriving at the distances in <term>yojanas</term> to be traveled by the second or the third weight-carrier, after the first or the second of them breaks down:

228. From the product of the whole weight to be carried multiplied by the value of the stipulated wages, subtract the square of the wages already given to the first carrier. This allows the user to find how much further the next laborer must go to earn the rest of the payment.

The rule for arriving at the value of the wages corresponding to the various stages over which varying numbers of persons carry a given weight:

230. The distances traveled over by the various numbers of men are respectively to be divided by the number of men doing the work of carrying at that stage. The quotients so obtained are to be combined in a cumulative fashion: the first quotient is taken alone, then the second is added to it, then the third to that sum, and so on. These resulting sums are then respectively multiplied by the number of men who leave the journey at each corresponding stage. By then applying the process of proportionate distribution (<term>prakṣēpaka</term>) <note>A method in Indian mathematics for dividing a whole into parts according to given ratios.</note> to these products, the wages due to the men leaving at the different stages may be found.

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

231–232. Twenty men are hired to carry a palanquin <note>A covered litter or seat carried on poles by laborers.</note> over a distance of 2 <term>yōjanas</term> <note>A unit of distance; 1 yōjana is approximately 8 or 9 miles.</note>, and 720 <term>dīnāras</term> <note>A type of gold coin used as currency.</note> are set as their total wages. Two men drop out after traveling two <term>krōśas</term> <note>A unit of distance equal to 1/4 of a yōjana.</note>; after traveling two more <term>krōśas</term>, three others drop out; after traveling half of the remaining distance, five more men drop out. What wages do these various groups of bearers receive?

The rule for arriving at the value of the money contents of a purse which, when added to the money on hand with each of certain persons, becomes a specified multiple of the sum of the money held by the others:

233–235. The quantities obtained by adding *one* to each of the specified multiple numbers in the problem, and then—

---

<insert>
233–235. In the problem given in 236–237, let *x*, *y*, and *z* represent the money held by three merchants, and *u* represent the money in the purse.
The conditions are:
*u* + *x* = *a* (*y* + *z*)
*u* + *y* = *b* (*z* + *x*)
*u* + *z* = *c* (*x* + *y*)
(Where *a*, *b*, and *c* are the multiples given in the problem).
This can be rewritten as:
*u + x + y + z* = (*a* + 1) (*y + z*)
*u + x + y + z* = (*b* + 1) (*z + x*)
*u + x + y + z* = (*c* + 1) (*x + y*).
</insert>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Then,** $\frac{(a + 1) (b + 1) (c + 1)}{T} \times (y + z) = (b + 1) (c + 1) \dots \dots \text{I.}$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**where T =** $u + x + y + z.$ <note>T represents the total sum of the wealth of all individuals involved.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Similarly,** $\frac{(a + 1) (b + 1) (c + 1)}{T} \times (z + x) = (c + 1) (a + 1) \dots \dots \text{II.}$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**and** $\frac{(a + 1) (b + 1) (c + 1)}{T} \times (x + y) = (a + 1) (b + 1) \dots \dots \text{III.}$
**Adding I, II and III,**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\frac{(a + 1) (b + 1) (c + 1)}{T} \times 2(x + y + z) = (b + 1) (c + 1)$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$+ (c + 1) (a + 1) + (a + 1) (b + 1)$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$= S \text{ (say)} \dots \dots \dots \text{IV}$
**Subtracting separately I, II, III, each multiplied by 2, from IV, we have—**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\frac{(a + 1) (b + 1) (c + 1)}{T} \times 2x = S - 2 (b + 1) (c + 1),$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\frac{(a + 1) (b + 1) (c + 1)}{T} \times 2y = S - 2 (c + 1) (a + 1),$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\frac{(a + 1) (b + 1) (c + 1)}{T} \times 2z = S - 2 (a + 1) (b + 1).$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\therefore x : y : z : : S - 2 (b + 1) (c + 1) : S - 2 (c + 1) (a + 1) : S - 2 (a + 1) (b + 1).$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;By removing the common factors, if any, in the right-hand side of the pro-
portion, we get at the smallest integral <note>Whole number values.</note> values of $x, y, z$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This proportion is given in the rule as the formula.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It may be noted that the square root mentioned in the rule has reference
only to the problem given in the verses 236-237. <note>Original: "stanzas".</note> Correcting speaking, instead
of "square root", we must have '3'. <note>The translator suggests that for the general rule, a constant like 3 is applicable rather than a square root operation.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It can be seen easily that this problem is possible only when the sum of
any two of $\frac{1}{a + 1}, \frac{1}{b + 1}, \frac{1}{c + 1}$ is greater than the third.

This process then yields the value of the **money in the purse** <note>The "money in the purse" represents a common fund or an unknown value that, when added to an individual's holdings, changes their wealth relative to the others.</note> for each respective case.

->An example to illustrate this.<-

**236-237.** Three merchants found a purse that had been dropped on the road. The first merchant said to the others, "If I take this purse, I will become twice as rich as both of you combined, counting the money you already have on hand." What is the value of the money in the purse, and how much money did each of the three merchants have on hand?

***

**The rule for calculating the money on hand and the money in the purse when specific fractions of the purse, added to each person's own money, make their total wealth a certain multiple of the sum of the others' money:**

**238.** Take the sum of all the specified fractions mentioned in the problem, ignoring the denominators <note>In ancient Indian mathematics, this usually means reducing the fractions to a common denominator and then performing operations using only the numerators.</note>. Multiply this sum by the specified common multiple. From this product, subtract the results of the following: multiply each individual fractional part <note>reduced to a common denominator</note> by the product of the "number of persons minus one" and the common multiple; then diminish this last product by one. 

---

<note>This footnote provides the algebraic equivalent of the rule stated in verse 238. If x, y, and z are the amounts of money held by three merchants, P is the value of the purse, m is the common multiple, and a, b, and c are the fractions of the purse taken by each merchant, the formulas are:
x = m(a + b + c) - a(2m - 1)
y = m(a + b + c) - b(2m - 1)
z = m(a + b + c) - c(2m - 1)
These are derived from the equations: (Pa + x) = m(y + z); (Pb + y) = m(z + x); and (Pc + z) = m(x + y).</note>

->The rule for arriving at the money on hand, which, with the moneys begged <gloss>requested or borrowed</gloss> from others, becomes a specified multiple of the money on hand with the others:<-

**251½-252½.** The sums of the moneys begged are multiplied each by its own corresponding multiple quantity as increased by one. With the aid of these products, the moneys on hand are arrived at according to the rule given in stanza 241. These quantities so obtained are reduced so as to have a common denominator. Then they are severally divided by the sum—as diminished by unity <gloss>minus one</gloss>—of the specified multiple quantities respectively divided by those same multiple quantities as increased by one. The resulting quotients themselves should be understood to be the moneys on hand with the various persons.

**264½.** There were six merchants. The elder ones among them gave in order, out of what they respectively had on hand, to those who were next younger to them exactly two-thirds <note>original: "dvyamśa"; literally two-parts or two-thirds</note> (of what they respectively had on hand). ### The rule for arriving at equal amounts of money on hand, after a number of persons give each to the others among them as much as they (respectively) have (then) on hand:

**265½.** One is divided by the optionally chosen multiple quantity (in the problem). To this, the number corresponding to the men taking part in the transaction is added. The first man's amount (on hand to start with) is thus arrived at. This (and the results thereafter arrived at) are written down (in order), and each of them is multiplied by the optional multiple number as increased by one; and the result is then diminished by one. (Thus the money on hand with each) of the others (to start with) is arrived at. <note>This rule provides a procedural algorithm for solving systems of linear equations common in medieval Indian algebra.</note>

->*Examples in illustration thereof.*<-

**266½.** Each of three merchants gave to the others what each of these had on hand (at the time). Then they all became possessed of equal amounts of money. What are the amounts of money which they (respectively) had on hand (to start with)?

**265½.** The rule will be clear from the following working of the problem given in *stanza* 266½:

1, divided by the optionally chosen multiple 1, and increased by the number of persons, 3, gives 4; this is the money in the hand of the first man.

This 4, multiplied by the optionally chosen multiple, 1, as increased by 1, becomes 8; when 1 is subtracted from this, we get 7, which is the money on hand with the second person.

This 7, again, treated as above, *meaning*, multiplied by 2 and then diminished by 1, gives 13, the money on hand with the third man.

This solution can be easily arrived at from the following equations:
4 (a - b - c) = 2 { 2b - (a - b - c) - 2c } = 4c - 2 (a - b - c) - { 2b - (a - b - c) - 2c }.

**267½.** There were four merchants. Each of them obtained from the others half <note>original: "ardha"; meaning half or one-half</note> of what he had on hand at the time of the respective transfers of money. Then they all became possessed of equal amounts of money. What is the measure of the money they respectively had on hand to start with?

### The rule for arriving at the gain derived equally from success and failure in a gambling operation:

**268½-269½.** The two sums of the numerators and denominators of the two fractional multiple quantities given in the problem have to be written down one below the other in the regular order, and then in the inverse order. The summed up quantities in the first of these sets of two sums are to be multiplied according to the <term>vajrāpavartana</term> <note>A method of cross-reduction or cross-multiplication used to simplify ratios or solve proportions.</note> process by the denominator, and those in the second set by the numerator, of the fractional quantity corresponding to the other summed up quantity. 

The results arrived at in relation to the first set are written down in the form of denominators, and those arrived at in relation to the second set are written down in the form of numerators; and the difference between the denominator and numerator in each set is noted down. Then by means of these differences, the products obtained by multiplying the sum of the numerator and the denominator of each of the given multiple fractions in the problem with the denominator of the other are respectively divided. These resulting quantities, multiplied by the value of the desired gain, give in the inverse order the measure of the moneys on hand with the gamblers to stake.

<insert>
268½-269½. Expressed in modern algebraic terms:
The initial stake of the first gambler (x) = [ (c + d) * b / ( (c + d) * b - (a + b) * c ) ] * p, and the stake of the second (y) = [ (a + b) * d / ( (a + b) * d - (c + d) * a ) ] * p. 
In these formulas, x and y are the moneys the gamblers start with, a/b and c/d are the fractional parts they take from each other, and p represents the final gain. This is derived from the linear equations: x - (c/d * y) = p and y - (a/b * x) = p.
</insert>

->An example in illustration thereof.<-

**270-272½.** A great man possessing powers of magical charm and medicine <note>This refers to a "Siddha," a person who has attained semi-divine status or magical abilities through asceticism or alchemy.</note> saw a cock-fight going on, and spoke separately in...

### The rule for separating the unknown dividend number, the quotient, and the divisor from their combined sum:

**273½.** Any suitable, optionally chosen number which is subtracted from the given combined sum shall be the divisor. By dividing the remainder—which is the total sum minus the chosen divisor—by that same divisor increased by *one*, the required quotient is found. That same remainder, when diminished by the quotient just found, becomes the required dividend number.
<note>This rule solves for three numbers (dividend $x$, divisor $y$, and quotient $q$) when their sum ($x + y + q$) is known. Mathematically: $q = (Sum - y) / (y + 1)$ and $x = (Sum - y) - q$.</note>

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

**274½.** A certain unknown quantity is divided by another unknown quantity. The quotient here, when combined with the divisor and the dividend number, equals 53. What is that divisor, and what is that quotient?

### The rule for arriving at a number which becomes a square either by adding a known number or by subtracting another given number:

**275½.** The sum of the quantity to be added and the quantity to be subtracted is multiplied by *one* as associated with whatever may happen to be the excess above the even number nearest to...

(that sum). The resulting product is then halved and squared. From this squared quantity, the possible "odd-making" excess quantity <note>This refers to an adjustment value used to ensure the numbers fit the properties of squares</note> is subtracted. The result is divided by **four**, and then combined with **one**. The final result arrived at in this manner is the required number, which surely yields an exact square root when the given quantities are applied.

### Examples in illustration thereof.

**276½.** A certain number, when increased by 10 or decreased by 17, yields an exact square root. If possible, O arithmetician, tell me that number quickly.

**277½.** A certain quantity, whether diminished by 7 or increased by 18, yields an exact square root. O arithmetician, give the answer after calculation.

**278½.** A certain quantity diminished by 2/3, or again that same quantity increased by 3/7, yields an exact square root. Tell me that quantity quickly, O arithmetician, after thinking out what it may be.

---

The rationale of this may be understood as follows:
$(n + 1)^2 - n^2 = 2n + 1$, which is an odd number; and $(n + 2)^2 - n^2 = 4n + 4$, which is an even number; where $n$ is any whole number. 
From these values ($2n + 1$ and $4n + 4$), the rule shows how we may find a number $n^2 + a$ when we know that the difference between the squares is equal to the sum of the two given values ($a + b$).

**278½.** <note>This note explains how to handle the fractions in the third example.</note> Since the quantities represented by $b$ and $a$ (as seen in the earlier rule at stanza 275½) are fractions in this problem—specifically 2/3 and 3/7—it is necessary to remove these fractions to simplify the calculation. To do this, they are first converted to a common denominator, becoming 14/21 and 9/21. These values are then multiplied by the square of the denominator ($21^2$ or 441), resulting in 294 and 189. These whole numbers are then used in the standard rule. Finally, the result found using these large numbers is divided by $21^2$ to provide the correct fractional answer for the original problem.

The rule for arriving at the square root of (an unknown) number as increased or diminished by a known number:

**279½.** The known quantity which is given is first halved and (then) squared, and then **one** is added (to it). The resulting quantity, either when increased by the desired given quantity or when diminished by the (same) quantity, yields the square root (exactly). <note>This formula states that if the given number is *a*, the required number is $(a/2)^2 + 1$. For example, if *a* is 10, $(10/2)^2 + 1 = 26$. Then $26 + 10 = 36$ (root 6) and $26 - 10 = 16$ (root 4).</note>

->An example in illustration thereof.<-

**280½.** Here is a number which, when increased by 10 or diminished by the same 10, yields an exact square root. Think out and tell me that number, O mathematician.

The rule for arriving at the two required square quantities, with the aid of those required quantities as multiplied by a known number, and also with the aid of (the same known number as forming the value of) the square root of the difference (between these products):

**281½.** The given number is increased by **one**; and the given number is also diminished by **one**. The resulting quantities when halved and then squared give rise to the two (required) quantities. Then if these be (separately) multiplied by the given quantity, the square root of the difference between these (products) becomes the given quantity. <note>If the given number is *d*, the squares are $(\frac{d+1}{2})^2$ and $(\frac{d-1}{2})^2$. Multiplying both by *d* and taking the root of the difference returns *d*.</note>

->An example in illustration thereof.<-

**282½—283.** Two unknown squared quantities are multiplied by 71. The square root of the difference between these (two resulting products) is also 71. O mathematician, if you know the process of calculation known as <term>citra-kuṭṭikāra</term> <note>Sanskrit: "Variegated Pulverizer," a complex method for solving indeterminate equations</note>, calculate and tell me what (those two unknown) quantities are.

---

**279½.** This is merely a particular case of the rule given in stanza 275½ wherein *a* is taken to be equal to *b*.

**281½.** Algebraically, when the given number is *d*, (half of *d* plus one) squared and (half of *d* minus one) squared are the required square quantities.

The rule for arriving at the required increase or decrease in relation to a given multiplicand <term>multiplicand: the number to be multiplied</term> and a given multiplier (so as to arrive at a given product):

**284.** The difference between the required product and the resulting product (of the given multiplicand and the multiplier) is written down in two places. To one of the factors of the resulting product, **one** is added, and to the other, the **required product** is added. That difference (written above in two positions as desired) is severally divided in the inverse order by the sums resulting thus. These give rise to the quantities that are to be added respectively to the given multiplicand and the multiplier, or to the quantities that are to be respectively subtracted from them. <note>This rule provides a way to adjust factors $a$ and $b$ so their product becomes $d$. The adjustments are $\frac{|d - ab|}{d + b}$ and $\frac{|d - ab|}{a + 1}$. For example, if you have $a \times b$ but want $d$, you change $a$ to $(a \pm \frac{|d - ab|}{d + b})$ and $b$ to $(b \pm \frac{|d - ab|}{a + 1})$.</note>

->Examples in illustration thereof.<-

**285.** The product of 3 and 5 is 15; and the required product is 18; and it is also 14. What are the quantities to be added respectively to the multiplicand and the multiplier here, or what is to be subtracted from them? <note>In the first case, where the target is 18, the difference is 3. Following the rule, the adjustments are $3/(18+5) = 3/23$ and $3/(3+1) = 3/4$. Thus, $(3 + 3/23) \times (5 + 3/4) = 18$.</note>

The rule for arriving at the required result by the process of **working backwards**:

**286.** To divide where there has been a multiplication, to multiply where there has been a division, to subtract where there has been an addition, to get at the square root where there has been a squaring, to get at the squaring where the root has been given—this is the process of **working backwards**. <note>original: *viparīta-karman*. This is a fundamental algebraic method in Indian mathematics where one starts with the final result of a series of operations and applies the inverse of each operation in reverse order to find the starting number.</note>

->An example in illustration thereof.<-

**287.** What is that quantity which when divided by 7, then multiplied by 3, then squared, then increased by 5, then... <note>The text of this example continues on the following page.</note>

***

<note>This footnote explains the algebraic logic of rule 284: The quantities to be added or subtracted are the difference between the desired product $d$ and the actual product $ab$, divided by $(d+b)$ for one factor and $(a+1)$ for the other. This ensures that $(a \pm \text{adjustment}_1) \times (b \pm \text{adjustment}_2) = d$.</note>

The rule for arriving at the number of arrows in a bundle with the aid of the even number of arrows constituting the common circumferential layer of the bundle:

**288.** Add *three* to the number of arrows forming the circumferential layer <note>the outermost ring of arrows</note>; then square this resulting sum and add again *three* to this square quantity. If this be further divided by 12, the quotient becomes the total number of arrows to be found in the bundle.

### *An example in illustration thereof.*

**289.** The circumferential arrows are 18 in number. How many in all are the arrows to be found in the bundle within the quiver? O mathematician, give this out if you have taken pains in relation to the process of calculation known as <term>manifold pulverization <note>original: *vicitra-kuṭṭīkāra*; a complex algebraic method used to solve indeterminate equations or "break down" complex problems.</note></term>.

Thus ends <term>manifold pulverization</term> in the chapter on mixed problems.

---

<note>
The formula provided here to find the total number of arrows is:
((n + 3)² + 3) / 12
where *n* is the number of arrows in the outermost layer. 

This formula is derived from the geometry of hexagonal packing. In a bundle of arrows (or circles of equal size), only 6 arrows can perfectly surround a central arrow. The next layer contains 12, the third contains 18, and so on. Each subsequent layer increases by 6. 

If there are *p* layers around a central arrow, the total number of arrows is 1 + 6(1 + 2 + 3 + ... + p). Using the standard formula for the sum of a series, this becomes 1 + 3p(p + 1). Since the number of arrows in the outermost layer (*n*) is equal to 6p, we can substitute *p = n/6* into the equation to reach the formula given by Mahāvīra. 
</note>

### Summation of Series.

Hereafter we shall expound in this chapter on mixed problems the summation of quantities in progressive series <note>These are arithmetical progressions, where a list of numbers follows a specific pattern of addition or subtraction.</note>.

The rule for arriving at the sum of a series in arithmetical progression, of which the common difference <note>the amount added to or subtracted from each successive number</note> is either positive or negative:

**290.** The first term is either decreased or increased by the product of the negative or the positive common difference and the quantity obtained by halving the number of terms in the series as diminished by *one*. Then, this is further multiplied by the number of terms in the series. Thus, the sum of a series of terms in arithmetical progression with positive or negative common difference is obtained. <note>In modern algebraic terms, this is expressed as: Sum = $n \times [a \pm (\frac{n-1}{2}) \times d]$, where *a* is the first term, *n* is the number of terms, and *d* is the common difference.</note>

->*Examples in illustration thereof.*<-

**291.** The first term is 14; the negative common difference is 3; the number of terms is 5. The first term is 2; the positive common difference is 6; and the number of terms is 8. What is the sum of the series in each of these cases? <note>For the first case, the series is 14, 11, 8, 5, 2. The sum is 40. For the second, the series is 2, 8, 14, 20, 26, 32, 38, 44. The sum is 184.</note>

The rule for arriving at the first term and the common difference in relation to the sum of a series in arithmetical progression, the common difference whereof is positive or negative:

**292.** Divide the given sum of the series by the number of terms therein, and subtract from the resulting quotient the product obtained by multiplying the common difference by the half of the number of terms in the series as diminished by *one*. Thus the first term in the series is arrived at. 

To find the difference: The sum of the series is divided by the number of terms therein. The first term is subtracted from the resulting quotient; the remainder when divided by half of the number of terms in the series as diminished by *one* becomes the common difference.

---

<note>
290. Using modern notation: $(\frac{n-1}{2} \cdot b \pm a) \cdot n = s$, where *n* is the number of terms, *a* the first term, *b* the common difference, and *s* the sum of the series.

292. To find the first term: $a = \frac{s}{n} - \frac{n-1}{2} \cdot b$; and to find the common difference: $b = (\frac{s}{n} - a) \div \frac{n-1}{2}$.
</note>

<term>arithmetical progression <note>original: *śreḍhī*; a sequence of numbers in which the difference between any two consecutive terms is constant.</note></term>, <term>common difference <note>original: *caya* or *uttara*; the constant value added to each term to get the next.</term></term>, <term>summation of series <note>original: *gaṇita* (in this context); the total value of all terms in the sequence.</note></term>, <term>Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha <note>The title of the work, meaning "Compendium of the Essence of Mathematics," written by the Jain mathematician Mahāvīra.</note></term>

### The rule for arriving at the sum of the cubes (of a given number of natural numbers) :—

**301.** The quantity represented by the square of half the (given) number of terms is multiplied by the square of the sum of *one* and the number of terms. In this (science of) arithmetic, this result is said to be the sum of the cubes (of the given number of <term>natural numbers</term> <note>the basic counting numbers starting from 1</note>) by those who know the secret of calculation. <note>original: "Algebraically, $(\frac{n}{2})^2 (n + 1)^2 = s_3$, which is the sum of the cubes of the natural numbers up to $n$."</note>

### The rule for arriving at the sum of the cubes (of the terms in a series in arithmetical progression), the first term, the common difference, and the number of terms whereof are optionally chosen :—

**303.** The sum (of the simple terms in the given series), as multiplied by the first term (therein), is (further) multiplied by the... <note>original: "Algebraically, $\pm sa (a \sim b) + s^2 b =$ the sum of the cubes of the terms in a series in arithmetical progression, where $s =$ the sum of the simple terms of the series. The sign of the first term in the formula is + or - according as $a >$ or $< b$." Here, $a$ refers to the first term and $b$ refers to the common difference.</note>

### The rule for arriving at the sum of (a number of terms in a series wherein the terms themselves are successively) the sums of the natural numbers:
<note>This refers to a "sum of sums" (Sankalita-sankalita). In this case, each term of the series is itself the sum of natural numbers from 1 up to a limit defined by an arithmetical progression.</note>

**305-305½.** Twice the **number of terms** (in the given series in arithmetical progression) is diminished by *one* and (then) multiplied by the square of the **common difference**. The quantity (so resulting) when multiplied by half the number of terms (in the given series) gives rise to the required sum of the series wherein the terms themselves are sums (of specified series).

### The rule for arriving at the sum of the four quantities (specified below and represented by a certain given number):

**307½.** The given number is increased by *one*, and (then) halved. This is multiplied by the given number and (then) by *seven*. From the (resulting) product, the given number is subtracted; and the (resulting) remainder is divided by *three*. The quotient (thus obtained), when multiplied by the given number as increased by *one*, gives rise to the (required) sum of (the four specified quantities, namely,) the **sum of the natural numbers** <note>the sum of 1, 2, 3... up to the given number</note> (up to the given number), the **sum of the sums** of the natural numbers (up to the given number), the **square** (of the given number), and the **cube** (of the given number).

<note>original footnote 307¾: This rule provides a single formula to find the combined total of four different values: $\frac{\frac{n \times (n + 1) \times 7}{2} - n}{3} \times (n + 1)$. The four values being added are (i) the sum of 1 to $n$; (ii) the sum of those sums; (iii) $n^2$; and (iv) $n^3$.</note>

**309½.** The number of terms is combined with *three*; it is (then) multiplied by the fourth part of the number of terms; (then) *one* is added...

### The rule for arriving at the sum of a series in geometrical progression wherein the terms are either increased or decreased (in a specified manner by a given known quantity):

**314.** The sum of the series in a pure geometrical progression <note>This refers to a standard series where each term is simply the previous term multiplied by the common ratio, before any additional quantities are added or subtracted.</note> (calculated using the given first term, common ratio, and number of terms) is written down in two separate positions. 

One of these sums is divided by the first term. From this resulting quotient, the number of terms is subtracted. This remainder is then multiplied by the specific quantity that is to be added to or subtracted from each term in the series. This resulting value is then divided by the common ratio after it has been diminished by one. 

The sum of the pure geometrical progression written in the second position is then modified: if the specified quantity was to be subtracted from the series, subtract this final calculated quotient from it. If the quantity was to be added, then increase the sum in the second position by this quotient. The result in either case provides the total sum of the modified series.

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

**315.** The common ratio is 5, the first term is 2, the quantity to be added to each term is 3, and the number of terms is 4. O you who know the secret of calculation, think this out and tell me quickly the sum of this series in geometrical progression, where the terms are increased in the manner described.

---

**314.** <note>original: "± (s/a - n) m ÷ (r - 1) + s"</note> <note>In modern algebraic notation, the sum of a series where each step involves both a multiplication (r) and an addition/subtraction (m) — such as $a, (ar + m), ((ar + m)r + m)$ — can be found using this formula. Here, $s$ is the sum of the simple progression, $a$ is the first term, $n$ is the number of terms, $r$ is the ratio, and $m$ is the constant addition.</note>

<term>first term</term>: The starting number of a mathematical sequence.
<term>quotient</term>: The result produced by the division of one number by another.
<term>remainder</term>: Here used to mean the result of a subtraction (the difference).
<term>algebraic sum</term>: The total value of a series of numbers, accounting for both positive and negative values.

### The rule for finding the first term, the common difference, and the number of terms, when given the "mixed sum" (the total of the first term, the common difference, the number of terms, and the sum of the series):

**317.** First, choose a number to represent the number of terms in the series; subtract this chosen number from the given <term>mixed sum</term> <note>The "mixed sum" is a combined total of $a$ (first term), $d$ (common difference), $n$ (number of terms), and $S$ (the sum of the series).</note>. **319.** The constant <term>velocity</term> <note>The steady speed of one traveler.</note> is reduced by the <term>first term</term> <note>The starting speed of a second traveler whose speed increases over time.</note> of the velocities in an <term>arithmetical progression</term> <note>A sequence where the speed increases by a fixed amount at each interval.</note>. ### The rule for arriving at the time and distance of meeting together, when two persons start from the same place at the same time and travel with varying velocities in arithmetical progression:

<margin>322½. Algebraically, $n = \frac{a \sim a_1}{b \sim b_1} \times 2 + 1$.</margin>

**322½.** The difference between the two starting velocities (the <term>first terms</term>) is divided by the difference between the two rates of increase (the <term>common differences</term>). This result, when multiplied by two and then increased by one, gives the time at which the two persons—both traveling with increasing speeds—will meet on their way.

The rule for arriving at the time of meeting of two persons starting at the same time and travelling in the same direction with varying velocities in <term>arithmetical progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.</note>, the common difference in the one case being positive, and in the other negative:

The rule for arriving at the time of meeting of two persons, starting at different times and travelling respectively with a quicker and a less quick velocity in the same direction:

**326½.** He who travels less quickly and he who travels more quickly—both move in the same direction. What happens to be the distance to be overtaken here is divided by the difference between those two velocities. In the course of the number of days represented by the <term>quotient</term> <note>The result of the division.</note> here, the more quickly moving person reaches the less quickly moving one.

**327½.** A certain person travels at the rate of 9 <term>yōjanas</term> <note>An ancient Indian measure of distance, roughly equal to 7 to 9 miles.</note> a day; and 100 <term>yōjanas</term> have already been gone over by him. The rule for working out the circumferential <note>Refers to the arrows forming the outermost ring or perimeter of the bundle inside the quiver.</note> number of arrows in the quiver with the aid of the given uneven number of arrows contained in the quiver; and *vice versâ*:

**328½.** The number of the circumferential arrows is increased by three and then halved. This is squared and then divided by three. On adding one to the resulting quantity, the total number of arrows in the quiver is obtained. When, however, the number of the circumferential arrows has to be arrived at, the reverse process is to be adopted in relation to these operations.

The rule for arriving at the number of bricks to be found in structures made up of layers of bricks one over another:

**330½.** The square of the number of layers is diminished by *one*, divided by *three*, and then multiplied by the number of layers. On adding to the quantity so obtained the product, obtained by multiplying the optionally chosen number representing the bricks in the topmost layer by the sum of the natural numbers beginning with *one* and going up to the given number of layers, the required answer is obtained.

**330¾.** Algebraically, the total number of bricks in the structure is determined by the formula: the square of the number of layers minus one, divided by three, then multiplied by the number of layers; to this is added the product of the number of bricks in the top layer and the sum of the series of layers. In modern notation: ((n² - 1) / 3) * n + a * (n(n + 1) / 2), where *n* is the number of layers, and *a* the optionally chosen number of bricks in the topmost layer. The number of bricks along the length or breadth of any layer is one less than the same in the immediately lower layer.

**333½—336½.** As each syllable found in a line forming a quarter of a stanza may be short or long, there arises a number of varieties corresponding to the different arrangements of long and short syllables. In arranging these varieties, a certain order is followed. The rules given here enable us to find out:
1. The number of varieties possible in a metre consisting of a specified number of syllables.

4. The ordinal position of a specified arrangement of syllables.
5. The number of varieties containing a specified number of long or short syllables.
6. The amount of vertical space required for exhibiting the varieties of a particular metre.

(2) The manner of arrangement of the syllables in each variety is arrived at thus:—

1st variety: 1, being odd, denotes a long syllable; so the first syllable is long. Add 1 to this 1, and divide the sum by 2; the quotient is odd and denotes another long syllable. Again, 1 is added to this quotient 1, and divided by 2; the result...

In ancient Indian mathematics, this was used to find the total number of possible rhythmic patterns.</note> The numbers in the chain of figures so obtained are all doubled, (and then in the process of continued multiplication from the bottom to the top of the chain, those figures which come to have a zero above them) are squared. The (resulting) product (of this continued multiplication) gives the number (of the varieties of stanzas possible in that <term>syllabic metre</term> <note>Original: *chandas*. A system of poetic rhythm.</note>).

The arrangement (of short and long syllables in all the varieties of stanzas so obtained) is shown to be arrived at thus:— (The natural numbers commencing with *one* and ending with the measure of the maximum number of possible stanzas in the given metre being noted down), every odd number (therein) has *one* added to it, and is (then) halved. (Whenever this process is gone through), a <term>long syllable</term> <note>Original: *guru*. Traditionally represented by a curved line or the letter 'S', but here indicated by the letter 'l' in the transcription.</note> is decidedly indicated. Where again odd, denotes a third long syllable. Thus the first variety consists of three long syllables, and is indicated thus *l l l*.

2nd variety: 2, being even, indicates a <term>short syllable</term> <note>Original: *laghu*. Represented by the symbol '|'.</note>; when this 2 is divided by 2, the quotient is 1, which being odd indicates a long syllable. Add 1 to this 1, and divide the sum by 2; the quotient being odd indicates a long syllable; thus we get *| l l*.

Similarly the other six varieties are to be found out.

(3) The fifth variety, for instance, may be found out as above.

(4) To find out, for instance, the ordinal position of the variety, *| l |* we proceed thus:—

Below these syllables, write down the terms of a series in <term>geometrical progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed, non-zero number called the common ratio (in this case, 2).</note>, having 1 as the first term and 2 as the common ratio. Add the

| l |
1 2 4
</margin>

figures 4 and 1 under the short syllables, and increase the sum by 1; we get 6: and we, therefore, say that this is the sixth variety in the tri-syllabic metre.

(5) Suppose the problem is: How many varieties contain 2 short syllables? Write down the natural numbers in the regular and in the inverse order, one below the other thus:

->1 2 3<-
->3 2 1<-

Taking two terms from right to left, both from above and from below, we divide the product of the former by the product of the latter. And the quotient 3 is the answer required. <note>This is an early method for calculating combinations ($nCr$), specifically $\frac{3 \times 2}{2 \times 1} = 3$.</note>

(6) It is prescribed that the symbols representing the long and short syllables of any variety of metre should occupy an <term>angula</term> <note>A traditional unit of measurement approximately equal to a finger-breadth.</note> of vertical space, and that the intervening space between any two varieties should also be an *angula*. The amount, therefore, of vertical space required for the 8 varieties of this metre is $2 \times 8 - 1$ or 15 *angulas*.

...if the number is even, it is immediately halved, and this indicates a <term>short syllable</term> <note>Original: *laghu*. In Sanskrit prosody, a short syllable has the time-value of one beat (*mātrā*).</note>. In this manner, the process—halving the value with or without the addition of *one* as the case may be, while noting down at the same time the corresponding long and short syllables as indicated—is to be regularly carried on until the actual number of syllables in the metre is arrived at in each case.

If the number representing the natural order of any given variety of a stanza—the arrangement of syllables of which must be found—happens to be even, it has to be halved, and this indicates a short syllable. If it happens to be odd, however, *one* has to be added to it, and then it is halved; this indicates a <term>long syllable</term> <note>Original: *guru*. A long syllable has the time-value of two beats.</note>. Thus, the long and short syllables have to be put down over and over again in their respective positions until the maximum number of syllables in the stanza is reached. This gives the arrangement of long and short syllables in the required variety of the stanza.

Where a stanza of a particular variety is given and its ordinal position—its rank among all possible varieties of stanzas in that metre—is to be found, the terms of a series in <term>geometrical progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where each term is multiplied by a constant to get the next. Here, the sequence is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...</note> commencing with *one* and having *two* as the common ratio are written down. The number of terms in the series must be equal to the number of syllables in the given metre. Above these terms, the corresponding long or short syllables are noted down. Then, the terms immediately below the position of the short syllables are all added together; the sum so obtained is increased by *one*. This gives the required ordinal number.

Natural numbers commencing with *one* and going up to the total number of syllables in the given metre are written down in the regular and in the inverse order, in two rows, one below the other. When the numbers in the row are multiplied (one, two, three, or more at a time) from the right to the left, and the products obtained from the upper row are divided by the corresponding products from the lower row, the quotient represents the result of the operation intended to arrive at the number of varieties of stanzas in the given metre containing one, two, three, or more short or long syllables in the verse. <note>This describes the formula for combinations, known in modern mathematics as binomial coefficients. It allows one to find how many ways one can arrange, for example, two short syllables in a six-syllable meter.</note>

# CHAPTER VI—MIXED PROBLEMS

The possible number (of the varieties of stanzas in the given metre) is multiplied by two and (then) diminished by one. This result gives (the measure of what is called) <term>adhvan</term> <note>original: *adhvan*. Literally "path" or "distance." In prosody, this represents the total linear space or number of units occupied if one were to write out every possible combination of long and short syllables for a given meter, leaving a space between each.</note>, (wherein an interval equivalent to a stanza is conceived to exist between every two successive varieties in the metre).

->*Examples in illustration thereof.*<-

337½. In relation to the <term>metre</term> <note>original: *chandas*. A rhythmic structure defined by a specific number of syllables.</note> made up of 3 syllables, tell me quickly the six things to be known—viz.,
(1) the (maximum) number (of possible stanzas in the metre),
(2) the manner of arrangement (of the syllables in those stanzas),
(3) the arrangement of the syllables (in a given variety of the stanza, the ordinal position whereof among the possible varieties in the metre is known),
(4) the ordinal position (of a given stanza),
(5) the number (of stanzas in the given metre containing any given number) of short or long syllables,
(6) and the (quantity known as) *adhvan*.

Thus ends the process of summation of series in the chapter on mixed problems.

# CHAPTER VII.

## CALCULATION RELATING TO THE MEASUREMENT OF AREAS.

1. To achieve the goal I have set before me, I bow again and again with sincere devotion to the most excellent <term>Siddhas</term> <note>original: *Siddhas*. In the Jain tradition, these are "perfected ones" or liberated souls who have attained infinite knowledge and are free from the cycle of rebirth.</note> who have realized the knowledge of all things.

From here on, we shall explain the sixth branch of calculation, which deals with the subject known as the *Measurement of Areas*. It is as follows:

2. The measurement of area has been classified into two types by <term>Jina</term> <note>original: *Jina*. Meaning "Conqueror" or "Victor," this is a title for the spiritual victors of Jainism. As Mahāvīra was a Jain, he credits the foundational principles to these spiritual teachers.</note> based on the nature of the result: that which is approximate for practical purposes and that which is minutely accurate. Taking this distinction into account, I shall explain this subject clearly.

3. Mathematical teachers, who have reached the far shore of the ocean of calculation, have described the various kinds of areas as being trilateral (three-sided), quadrilateral (four-sided), and curvi-linear (curved), each being further divided into their respective varieties.

4. A trilateral area is divided into three types; a quadrilateral one into five types; and a curvi-linear one into eight types. All other types of areas are, in fact, merely variations of these primary categories.

5. Learned men say that the trilateral area may be equilateral, isosceles, or scalene, and that the quadrilateral area also may be—

## Calculation relating to approximate measurement (of areas).

The rule for arriving at the (approximate) measure of the areas of trilateral <note>three-sided; a triangle</note> and quadrilateral <note>four-sided</note> fields:—

7. The product of the halves of the sums of the opposite sides becomes the (quantitative) measurement (of the area) of trilateral and quadrilateral figures. In the case of (a figure constituting a circular annulus <note>a ring-shape</note> like) the rim of a wheel, half of the sum of the (inner and outer) circumferences multiplied by (the measure of) the breadth (of the annulus gives the quantitative measure of the area thereof). Half of this result happens to be here the area of (a figure resembling) the crescent moon.

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

8. In the case of a trilateral figure, 8 <term>daṇḍas</term> <note>a unit of measurement approximately equal to 6 feet or 4 cubits</note> happen to be the measure of the side, the opposite side and the base; tell me quickly, after calculating, the practically approximate value (of the area) thereof.

9. In the case of a trilateral figure with two equal sides, the length (represented by the two sides) is 77 <term>daṇḍas</term>; and the breadth (measured by the base) is 22 <term>daṇḍas</term> associated with 2 <term>hastas</term> <note>a "hand" or cubit, usually 1/4 of a daṇḍa</note>. (Find out the area.)

---

7. A trilateral figure is here conceived to be formed by making the topside, *i.e.*, the side opposite to the base, of a quadrilateral so small as to be neglected. Then the two lateral sides of the trilateral figure become the opposite sides, the topside being taken to be nil in value. Hence it is that the rule speaks of opposite sides even in the case of a trilateral figure. <note>Essentially, the formula used here is: Area ≈ [(Side A + Side C) / 2] × [(Side B + Side D) / 2]. For a triangle, one side is treated as zero.</note>

As half the sum of the two sides of a triangle is, in all cases, bigger than the altitude, the value of the area arrived at according to this rule cannot be accurate in any instance. <note>This identifies that the author was aware this "Surveyor's Rule" provides a rough estimate rather than a precise geometric area.</note>

In regard to quadrilateral figures the value of the area arrived at according to this rule can be accurate in the case of a square and an oblong, but only approximate in other cases.

<term>Nēmi</term> <note>original: "Nēmi"; the rim of a wheel</note> is the area enclosed between the circumferences of two concentric circles; and the rule here stated for finding out the approximate measure of the area of a <term>Nemikṣētra</term> <note>original: "Nemikṣētra"; a field shaped like a ring or annulus</note> happens to give the accurate measure thereof.

In the case of a figure resembling the crescent moon, it is evident that the result arrived at according to the rule gives only an approximate measure of the area.

The rule for arriving at the (practically approximate value of the) area of the circle:

19. The (measure of the) diameter multiplied by *three* is the measure of the circumference; and the number representing the square of half the diameter, if multiplied by *three*, gives the (resulting) area in the case of a complete circle. Teachers say that, in the case of a semicircle, half (of these) give (respectively) the measure (of the circumference and of the area). <note>The author uses the ancient approximation of 3 for the value of <term>pi</term> (the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter). In modern mathematics, pi is approximately 3.14159.</note>

->*Examples in illustration thereof.*<-

The rule for arriving at (the value of) the area of an <term>elliptical figure</term> <note>an oval shape</note>:

21. The longer diameter, increased by half of the (shorter) diameter and multiplied by *two*, gives the measure of the circumference of the elliptical figure. One-fourth of the (shorter) diameter, multiplied by the circumference, gives rise to the (measure of the) area (thereof). <note>This ancient formula for the ellipse is a rough approximation. While modern math uses more complex calculations for the perimeter of an ellipse, the area formula given here simplifies to a practical rule for builders and surveyors of the time.</note>

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

22. In the case of an elliptical figure the shorter diameter is 12, and the longer diameter is 36. What is the circumference and what is the resulting area thereof? <note>This example applies the rule from the previous page: circumference = 2 × (longer diameter + half the shorter diameter). Using the values 36 and 12, the circumference would be 2 × (36 + 6) = 84.</note>

The rule for arriving at the resulting area of a <term>conchiform curvilinear figure</term> <note>original: "kamba-vṛtta"; a shell-like shape, often visualized as two unequal semicircles joined at their base</note>:

23. In the case of a conchiform curvilinear figure, the measure of the greatest breadth diminished by half the measure of the mouth and multiplied by *three* gives the measure of the perimeter. One-third of the square of half this perimeter, increased by three-fourths of the square of half the measure of the mouth, gives the area. <note>In modern notation, if *a* is the breadth and *m* is the mouth, the perimeter *P* = 3(a − ½m). The area is (P/2)² × ⅓ + ¾(m/2)².</note>

->*An example in illustration thereof.*<-

24. In the case of a conch-form figure the breadth is 18 <term>hastas</term> <note>a unit of length, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note>, and the measure of the mouth thereof is 4 *hastas*. You tell me what the perimeter is and what the calculated area is.

The rule for arriving at the resulting area of the concave and convex circular surfaces:

25. Understand that *one-fourth* of the circumference multiplied by the diameter gives rise to the calculated resulting area. Thence, in the case of concave and convex areas like that of a <note>This rule refers to the surface area of a <term>spherical segment</term>—the curved "cap" of a sphere, such as the inside of a bowl (concave) or the outside of a dome (convex). The text states Area = ¼ × Circumference × Diameter.</note>

***

<note>Footnote 23: If *a* is the diameter and *m* is the measure of the mouth, then 3 (a − ½ m) is the measure of the circumference; and { $\frac{3 (a - \frac{1}{2} m)}{2}$ }² × $\frac{1}{3}$ + $\frac{3}{4}$ × ($\frac{m}{2}$)² is the measure of the area. The exact shape of the figure is not clear from the description given; but from the values given for the circumference and the area, it may be conceived to consist of 2 unequal semicircles placed so that their diameters coincide in position.</note>

<note>Footnote 25: The area here specified seems to be that of the surface of the segment of a sphere; and the measure of the area is stated to be equal to (c / 4) × d, where *c* is the circumference of the sectional circle, and *d* is the diameter thereof. Modern mathematics defines the surface of a spherical segment as 2πrh, where *r* is the radius and *h* is the height.</note>

43. In the case of a bow-shaped field the calculated measure (of the area) is obtained by adding together (the measure of) the <term>arrow</term> <note>original: iṣu; the height or versine of the circular segment.</note> and (that of) the <term>string</term> <note>original: jyā; the chord of the circular segment.</note> and multiplying the sum by half (the measure) of the arrow. The square root of the square of the (measure of the) arrow as multiplied by 5 and (then) as combined with the square of the (measure of the) string gives the (measure of the) <term>bent stick</term> <note>original: dhanuṣ-pṛṣṭha; the arc of the segment.</note> (of the bow).

> 43. The field resembling a bow in outline is in fact the segment of a circle, the bow forming the arc, the bow-string forming the chord, and the arrow measuring the greatest perpendicular distance between the arc and the chord. If *a*, *c*, and *p* represent the lengths of these three lines, then, according to the rules given in stanzas 43 and 45 —
> 
> Area = (chord + arrow) × (arrow / 2)
> 
> Length of arc = Square root of (5 × arrow² + chord²)
> 
> Length of arrow = Square root of (arc² - chord²) / 5
> 
> Length of chord = Square root of (arc² - 5 × arrow²)

For accurate value see stanzas 73½ and 74½ in this chapter. <note>The author distinguishes between "practical" (approximate) formulas used by surveyors and "accurate" (exact) mathematical formulas presented later in the text.</note>

### *The rule for arriving at the arrow-measure as well as the string-measure in relation to a bow-shaped field:*

45. The difference between the squares of the string and of the bent bow is divided by 5. The square root of the resulting quotient gives the intended measure of the arrow. The square of the arrow is multiplied by 5; and this product is subtracted from the square of the arc of the bow. The square root of the resulting quantity gives the measure corresponding to the string. <note>These formulas are: Arrow = $\sqrt{(Arc^2 - String^2) / 5}$ and String = $\sqrt{Arc^2 - (5 \times Arrow^2)}$. These are practical approximations used in ancient Indian geometry.</note>

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

46. In the case of this already given bow-shaped field, the measure of the arrow is not known; and in the case of another similar field, the measure of the string is not known. O you who know calculation, give out both these measures.

### *The rule for arriving at the practically approximate value of the area of the circle which is circumscribed about or inscribed within a four-sided figure:*

47. Half of three times the measure of the area of the inscribed quadrilateral figure gives the measure of the area of the circle in the case in which it is circumscribed outside. In the case where it is inscribed within and the quadrilateral is the other way (i.e., <term>escribed</term> <note>Here referring to a circle inside a square/rectangle, where the square is "outside" or escribed.</note>), half of the above measure is the required quantity.

## The Minutely Accurate Calculation of the Measure of Areas.

Hereafter in the calculation regarding the measurement of areas we shall expound the subject of treatment known as <term>minutely accurate calculation</term> <note>The precise or "Sūkshma" mathematical method.</note>. And that is as follows:—

The rule for arriving at the measure of the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>The altitude or height; original: lamba.</note> (from the vertex to the base of a given triangle) and also of the <term>segments</term> <note>The two parts into which the base is divided by the perpendicular; original: ābādha.</note> into which the base is thereby divided:—

49. The process of <term>saṅkramaṇa</term> <note>A mathematical procedure for finding two unknown quantities when their sum and their difference are known. Original: saṅkramaṇa.</note> carried out between the base and the difference between the squares of the sides as divided by the base gives rise to the values of the two segments of the base of the triangle. Learned teachers say that the square root of the difference between the squares of either of these segments and of the corresponding adjacent side gives rise to the measure of the perpendicular.

---

49. Algebraically represented—
c₁ = ( c + (a² - b²) / c ) × ½ ;
c₂ = ( c - (a² - b²) / c ) × ½ ;

p = √ (a² - c₁²) or √ (b² - c₂²) . Here a, b, and c represent the measures of the sides of a triangle, c₁ and c₂ the measures of the segments of the base whose total length is c; and p represents the length of the perpendicular.

### The rule for arriving at the minutely accurate measurement of the area (of trilateral and quadrilateral figures):—

50. Four quantities represented (respectively) by half the sum of the sides as diminished by (each of) the sides (taken in order) are multiplied together; and the square root (of the product so obtained) gives the <term>minutely accurate measure</term> <note>Original Sanskrit: sūkshma. This refers to the exact mathematical result as opposed to a rough estimate used in trade or construction.</note> (of the area of the figure). 50. Algebraically represented:—
Area of a <term>trilateral figure</term> <note>A triangle.</note> = $\sqrt{s (s-a) (s-b) (s-c)}$ ; where *s* is half the sum of the sides, *a, b, c*, the respective measures of the sides of the trilateral figure ;
or = $\frac{c}{2} \times p$ , where *p* is the perpendicular distance of the vertex from the base.
Area of a <term>quadrilateral figure</term> <note>A four-sided figure.</note> = $\sqrt{(s-a) (s-b) (s-c) (s-d)}$ where *s* is half the sum of the sides, and *a, b, c, d* the measures of the respective sides of the quadrilateral figure ;
or = $\frac{b+d}{2} \times p$ (except in the case of an inequilateral quadrilateral) where *p* is the measure of either of the perpendiculars drawn to the base from the extremities of the top side.
The formulas here given for trilateral figures are correct; but those given for quadrilateral figures hold good only in the case of <term>cyclic quadrilaterals</term> <note>A four-sided figure whose four vertices all lie on a single circle. The author, Mahāvīrācārya, followed Brahmagupta in applying this formula, though it only produces the maximum possible area for a general quadrilateral.</note>, as in these formulas sight is lost of the fact that for the same measure of the sides the value of the area as well as of the perpendicular may vary.
</insert>

Hereafter (we give) the rule for arriving at the value of the diagonal of the five varieties of quadrilateral figures.

54. The two quantities obtained by multiplying the basal side by the (larger and the smaller of the right and the left) sides are (respectively) combined with the two (other) quantities obtained by multiplying the top side by the (smaller and the larger of the right and the left) sides. The (resulting) two sums constitute the multiplier and the divisor as also the divisor and the multiplier in relation to the sum of the products of the opposite sides. The square roots (of the quantities so obtained) give the required measures of the diagonals. <note>This describes the formula for the diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral, where the sides are $a, b, c, d$. The formula for diagonal 1 is $\sqrt{\frac{(ab+cd)(ac+bd)}{ad+bc}}$ and for diagonal 2 is $\sqrt{\frac{(ac+bd)(ad+bc)}{ab+cd}}$.</note>

### *Examples in illustration thereof.*

55. In the case of an equilateral quadrilateral which has all around a side measure of 5, tell me quickly, O friend who know the secret of calculation, the value of the diagonal and also the accurate value of the area.

---

54. Algebraically represented the measure of the diagonal of a quadrilateral figure as given here is—
$$\sqrt{\frac{(ac + bd) (ab + cd)}{ad + bc}}$$ or $$\sqrt{\frac{(ac + bd) (ad + bc)}{ab + cd}}.$$
These formulas also are correct only for **cyclic quadrilaterals** <note>A four-sided figure whose corners all touch the edge of a circle.</note>. **Bhāskarā-cārya** <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer.</note> is aware of the futility of attempting to give the measure of the area of a quadrilateral without previously knowing the values of the perpendicular or of the diagonals. *See* the following stanza from his ***Līlāvatī*** <note>A classic mathematical treatise named after the author's daughter.</note>:—

> <note>original: "लम्बयो: कर्णयोर्वैकमनिर्दिश्यापरान् कथम् । पृच्छत्यनियतत्वेऽपि नियतं चापि तत्फलम् !! स पृच्छकः पिशाचो वा वक्ता वा नितरां ततः । यो न वेत्ति चतुर्बाहुक्षेत्रस्यानियतां स्थितिम् ॥"</note>
> Without specifying either of the perpendiculars or the diagonals, how can one ask for a fixed area when the area is in fact indeterminate? Such a questioner is a demon (or a fool), and the one who answers him is even more of one, if he does not understand that the dimensions of a quadrilateral are not fixed by the sides alone.

60. The diameter of the circular figure multiplied by the square root of 10 becomes the circumference in measure. The circumference multiplied by one-fourth of the diameter gives the area. In the case of a **semicircle**, this happens to be half of what it is in the case of the full circle.

### The rule for arriving at the minutely accurate values relating to an elliptical figure:
<note>The term "minutely accurate" (Sanskrit: *sūkṣma*) distinguishes these formulas from "gross" or "approximate" (*sthūla*) calculations common in practical trade.</note>

The square root of this sum gives the measure of the circumference. This measure of the circumference multiplied by one-fourth of the shorter diameter gives the minutely accurate measure of the area of an elliptical figure.
